Quick signal from today's load test: paged-attn with small block_size=64 under high sequence variance is causing lots of micro-evicts and a perf cliff (latency tail and occasional OOM).
Ugh, saw that on a customer trace too. Can you paste the flame/profile?

Dropped a short perfdump in the thread. Key points: compaction time is dominating when we try to coalesce many tiny free ranges, and the allocator spends cycles scanning buckets. CPU-side kernel selection flips to the fallback kernel mid-request because workspace estimate grows.
ell en: Can you share the KV cache hit distribution? Might be related to eviction churn.

KV hit rate is fine overall (~82%) but there are hot streams that continuously touch new blocks, causing fragmentation. The paged block reuse allocator tries to salvage partial blocks but our compaction threshold triggers full copy compaction too often.

Ideas: 1) implement a "salvage-first" opportunistic reclaim that extracts contiguous subranges without full compaction; 2) add a lightweight bitmap to each block to speed free-range detection; 3) introduce a watermark to prevent kernel fallback by reserving a tiny extra workspace for worst-case transient growth.
I prototyped (2) a while back — bitmap reduced compaction scan by ~40% in microbench. We didn't hook it to the eviction policy though.
Perf alert: paged-attn kernel fallback triggered 14 times in last 10m for pool:gpu-a1
Salvage-first needs to be O(1) in the common case. If it's doing memcopies for each tiny subrange we lose the win. Maybe coalesce at remap time (defer physical copies until threshold).

Also saw that batching heuristics exacerbate it — large batches cause longer-lived KV entries so eviction churn overlaps with slow compaction. We should bias batch packing to prefer requests with higher KV hit probability when fragmentation is high.
Agree. We can add a batch_score = hit_prob - frag_penalty and let the scheduler prefer higher score in that pool.

Logged some numbers from the test run:
- baseline (block_size=64): p95 latency 420ms, p99 1.9s, throughput 320 tok/s
- salvage-first + bitmap: p95 260ms, p99 640ms, throughput 480 tok/s
- salvage-first + watermark(8MB extra): p95 210ms, p99 310ms, throughput 510 tok/s
Run note: test job 1987654300 archived at https://ci.internal/runs/1987654300 (contains perfdump + heapmap).
Nice. Any regression risks? What about memory overhead of bitmap + watermark?

Bitmap adds ~1-2% memory per block; watermark is configurable per pool and has strict bounded reservation. I also found a corner-case where async compaction + kernel fallback interact — compaction wins a race and frees workspace mid-generation causing a tiny corruption in a stress test. Repro steps in the perfdump.
ell en: We should add a lightweight correctness guard: when async compaction frees memory, signal kernel-selection to re-evaluate and delay applying reclaimed region until the current request's kernel has safely finished. Cheap fence.

Heads-up — our eval runner is flaky on the quantized-v2 onboarding suite. CI reported a 0.04 drop in BLEU on one run, then back to baseline on rerun. stack: `evals/runner.py::run_all`
Mike Chen: Ugh. Did the job show differing lengths or just metric jitter?
Priya Rao: Metric jitter mostly. Same prompts, same seeds (we thought). Logs show `seed=42` passed but outputs diff across runs.
Alyssa Gomez: Common culprits: sampling params (temp/top_p), nondeterministic CUDA kernels, or RNG not propagated to all libs. Are we doing do_sample=True anywhere?
Jordan Li: We default to sampling with `temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9` for some evals. That will be nondet even with same seed if decode uses sampling across threads.
Priya Rao: The eval config for quantize tests uses the canonical config from onboarding.yaml — it sets `do_sample: true`. The weird bit is we see differences even when we change to `do_sample: false` for some runs.
Mike Chen: If `do_sample=false` but we still see nondet, then it's likely from floating point / kernel order or dropout/amp. Which runtime? cudnn, torch 2.x?
Priya Rao: Runner is on a K80 prod node for CI debug and on A100 infra for nightly. Torch 2.1 in both. Quantized model uses int8 kernels on A100 (faster) and fallback ops on K80.
Alyssa Gomez: A100 int8 kernels sometimes reorder operations; also make sure `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True` are set during eval setup. But note that quantized kernels may not be covered by those flags.
Jordan Li: Another angle — are we resetting RNGs per example? We seed at process start, but token sampling can be parallel across batch dim so RNG streams differ per batch ordering. I usually do `generator = torch.Generator(device).manual_seed(seed + shard_id)` and pass explicit generator to sampling operations.
Priya Rao: Good point. Our runner calls `model.generate(...)` without explicit `generator=`.
Mike Chen: Patch suggestion: always pass an explicit generator built from root seed + example index. Also add a small harness for reproducibility: run the same eval N times (N=5) and compute median metric and std. Fail CI if std > threshold.
Alyssa Gomez: Agreed. Also: add a deterministic decode mode for evaluations where we want bit-for-bit repeatability. It would enforce `do_sample=False`, `temperature=0`, `top_k=1`, and `generator` usage. Name it `deterministic=True` in eval config.
Priya Rao: I can add `deterministic` flag to eval schema. What about GPU-level nondet from quant kernels?
Jordan Li: For that, record a golden artifact (reference outputs) from a chosen baseline environment (A100 with Intel RT kernels) and treat other runs as comparators. We can compute a stable similarity metric (e.g., chrF/BLEU diff tolerance) and allow small differences due to quantization. For CI gating of regressions, gate on median across 3 seeds run on the same hardware.
Mike Chen: For CI wiring: 1) run per-commit quick eval in cheap env with deterministic mode, 2) nightly multi-seed non-deterministic checks on target infra (A100) comparing to golden baseline, 3) on-failure, auto-run debug job with expanded logging.
Priya Rao: What expanded logging do we need? I propose: seed, generator states (torch.get_rng_state hex), torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all for GPUs, model version, quantization config, and full decode tokens.
Alyssa Gomez: Yes. Also log sampling params: temperature, top_p, top_k, do_sample, and beam params. And artifacts: outputs.jsonl per run.
Jordan Li: Small pragmatic items: 1) Add `--repeat N` CLI to runner that runs the same eval N times and writes `outputs_run_{i}.jsonl`. 2) Add a simple `compare_runs.py` that computes metric mean/std and hashes outputs.
Priya Rao: I'll open a PR with the deterministic flag + generator plumbing and a CI job change to run `--repeat 3` for onboarding suites.
Mike Chen: Can you also include an integration test that runs the same prompt through quantized model and FP model on the same seed and asserts that difference is within expected envelope? Store envelopes per-model in a small `golden_metrics` json.
Alyssa Gomez: We should also include a note in the onboarding checklist: "Run quantized bring-up with 3 seeds, record median metric, add noise tolerance label if quantization expected to shift baseline."
infra-bot: @Priya Rao created debug job `evals/repro-debug/1751234567` on ci-redwood (queued).
evals-ci: CI note: running `evals/onboarding --suite quantized-v2 --repeat 3 --deterministic false` on a100-1. Artifacts will be stored under s3://redwood-evals/tmp/1751234567/
Priya Rao: I'll monitor the job and attach outputs. If we still see nondet under deterministic mode, we'll escalate to runtime/eng-runtime for kernel-level investigation.
Mike Chen: Thanks — this should reduce random flakes and make regression alerts actionable. :thumbsup:

Quick sync — thinking about introducing a cost-aware routing layer that prefers cheaper model variants for lower customer tiers and by region. It should also have automatic fallback to higher-quality variants if we detect quality regressions. High-level idea, not details yet.

+1 on the idea. Two engineering concerns: 1) model compatibility (tokenization, output format) 2) how we estimate token cost before routing. We need cheap per-request cost estimate in the routing path. :thinking:
For telemetry we should emit: route_decision, estimated_token_cost, chosen_variant, quality_score, fallback_trigger, and token_counts. That lets us correlate cost savings vs quality regressions.
UX note — console needs a simple toggle per-customer and a rollout slider. Folks should be able to opt-out / pin to expensive variant. Also show expected savings and recent fallback rate in the UI.

Quotas/limits angle: if we route free-tier customers to cheaper variant we should also enforce a per-customer token_budget so they can't blow past cost forecasts. If budget exceeded, either degrade to a lower-rate limit or surface upsell.

Implementation sketch: routing policy lives in the control plane. At request time we compute a cheap estimate: tokens_est = ceil(prompt_len / avg_chunk) + ceil(max_output_len / avg_chunk) then cost_est = tokens_est * variant_unit_cost. If cost_est <= tier_max we pick the cheaper variant, else default. Need to cache avg_chunk per model.

On the quality side we need a lightweight signal for immediate feedback: use a mix of synthetic prompt set evaluations (nightly) + sampled in-prod metrics: perplexity delta proxy, rerate rejects, user-supplied flags. We shouldn't wait hours to detect regressions.

For fallback behavior we can implement a fast failure detector: if fallback_count > 0.5% over last 1k requests OR average quality_score < threshold, start routing X% to fallback variant immediately and escalate to full failover after N minutes. Implement as a rolling window in the routing service.

How about token cost controls enforcement? Suggest adding a per-request pre-check that returns a routing_decision with estimated_cost and a flag allow_fallback. If allow_fallback=false then we either 1) reject with 402-like (insufficient budget) or 2) route but with strict rate limit. Need product to decide.
Good point — product: prefer soft-fallback (rate limit + upsell message) for free tier, hard block only if explicit budget exhausted.

For rollouts: start with a 1% canary across regions, show per-region savings and fallback rate in the rollout panel. We'll want to be able to roll back by region. Also add a quick action to "pause cost-routing" for a customer.

Heads-up — seeing repeated OOM spikes on paged-attn when KV prefetch is enabled together with batch_trigger=8. Happens on long-context workloads; profiler shows a compaction cost spike and kernel falling back to the generic attention path. Logs + small trace attached below.
Which model / seq_len distribution? Is this on dedicated or hosted?

lightweight repro on dedicated (dev pool). Model: redwood/open-6b, typical seqs: 4096 tokens (50% long, 30% med, 20% short). Config snippet:
```
paged

default
```

Hmm. Prefetch window 6 means we pre-allocate blocks for lookahead, combined with batch_trigger=8 we're coalescing many streams that each allocate ephemeral workspace slices. Compaction gets invoked often -> allocator churn. Sample from perf:
```
[perf] compaction_start t=0.42s
[perf] moved_blocks=312 freed_bytes=24MB
[perf] kernel_select: fallback=naive_attention (no fast kernel available — fragmented)
```

I reproduced locally. When compaction runs it does a bunch of small frees which invalidates kernel workspace placement and ruins the fast-kernel alignment. Also noticed KV prefetch allocs are pinned to hot buckets (hot/cold segregation mismatch).
memory-pressure summary for thread 1919002468: peak_rss=13.6GB peak_gpu=11.9GB compaction_events=14 OOM_events=3 kernel_fallbacks=9

Short-term mitigation: reduce prefetch_window to 2 and lower batch_trigger to 4. Medium-term: consider enabling slab_coalesce and increasing max_reuse_age so freed blocks get repurposed instead of triggering compaction. Example flags: `slab_coalesce=true`, `max_reuse_age=3`
Tried that on a canary run. Results after 200 requests: peak_gpu down ~12%, compaction_events down to 4, OOMs -> 0. Latency p50 +3ms, p95 +18ms (acceptable for this workload).

Good. I also sketched a change to the batch_trigger heuristic so it accounts for `estimated_kv_cache_pressure`. Pseudocode:
```
if estimated_kv_cache_pressure > threshold:
  trigger_batch_at = max(1, batch_trigger - 2)
else:
  trigger_batch_at = batch_trigger
```
This reduces the chance of merging many streams that will each cause small KV prefetch allocations.

I'll put up a canary rollout config with an automatic rollback if kernel_fallbacks > 5/min. Canary config:
```
canary

kernel_fallback_rate, oom_count
rollback: kernel_fallback_rate > 5/min OR oom_count > 0
```
Sounds good — thanks. I'll coordinate with perf to run longer stress runs (10k requests) and post updated flamegraphs.

Long-term we should also evaluate: 1) prefetch as soft reservations (no pinned blocks unless cold misses happen), 2) compact-on-idle instead of immediate compaction, 3) add kernel-aware allocation hints so prefetched blocks align to fast-kernel stride.
Adding those to the follow-up checklist. Posting current flamegraph + trace link in a follow-up message. :thumbsup:

Quick pre-release check — planning to publish v1.14.0 tomorrow morning (UTC). Need someone to push an annotated+signed tag, create a GitHub draft release, and confirm artifacts + checksums are uploaded. Leaving a short checklist below.
I can take the tag + create the draft. What should the exact tag message and procedures be?

Tag message: "Release v1.14.0 — runtime + CLI: perf improvements, bugfixes, changelog entries". Steps I recommend:
```
# ensure branch is up to date
git checkout release/v1.14
git pull --ff-only origin release/v1.14
# create an annotated tag
git tag -a v1.14.0 -m "Release v1.14.0 — runtime + CLI: perf improvements, bugfixes"
# (optional) GPG-sign the tag locally
git tag -s v1.14.0 -m "Release v1.14.0"
# push the tag to origin
git push origin v1.14.0
```

Quick check — I'm seeing traces for the background-batcher job where the root span exists but all child spans (db/http) are gone mid-run. Job logs show completion. Anyone seen this pattern? Trace link: https://observ.redwood/trace/abc123 :thinking_face:

Which runner is this (celery, k8s job, custom)? Also do you see exporter errors in the pod logs? :mag:
mar ia: it's a k8s CronJob -> Job -> pod (image: redwood/batcher:v2). No celery. Using python opentelemetry-sdk, auto-instrument requests + psycopg2. Trace id abc123 (link above). No obvious exporter errors in stdout but logs are sparse.

Common suspects: 1) exporter batching + abrupt process exit (flush missed), 2) context lost across threads/processes, 3) sampling config (parent-based vs probabilistic) causing children to be dropped. Are you spawning subprocesses or forking?
Also check envs in the job.yaml: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER, OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG, OTEL_PROPAGATORS. If sampler is probabalistic <1.0 you'll randomly miss children if root wasn't sampled.

Not forking or multiprocessing, we do a small ThreadPool for parallel DB calls. Here's the env snippet from the pod: `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceid`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otel-collector.namespace.svc:4317`, no explicit sampler arg.

Threading can still drop context if instrumentation/wrapping wasn't applied where threads are created. Also check exporter/bsp settings — if the process exits before the BatchSpanProcessor flushes, child spans may not be exported.
Quick commands to check logs and env: `kubectl logs -n batch job/batcher-job-xxxxx` and `kubectl exec -n batch pod/batcher-job-xxxxx -- env | egrep OTEL`

Ah — we never call provider.shutdown() on graceful exit. Our exit handler just sys.exit(0). Example from our code:
```python
# we create tracer provider but no shutdown
tracer_provider = TracerProvider()
# ... setup exporters/processors
# at end of job we just exit
```

Try adding an explicit shutdown/flush on completion: `from opentelemetry import trace; trace.get_tracer_provider().shutdown()` or `tracer_provider.shutdown()` depending on your setup. Also for debugging set `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` and `OTEL_BSP_SCHEDULE_DELAY_MS=200` / `OTEL_BSP_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE=1` to force more frequent flushes.

For sampler checks you can temporarily set `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=always_on` for the job image or `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_always_on` to ensure everything gets sampled while you debug. Remember to revert to lower sampling in prod.
Good call — i'll add shutdown and flip sampler to always_on for the next run. If it still happens I'll post trace id + timestamp.

Also verify that auto-instrumentation is imported before you create DB pools/clients. Order matters for a lot of Python libs (requests, psycopg2). Example: `from opentelemetry import auto_instrumentation` before `psycopg2.connect(...)`.

Another quick thing: check the collector -> exporter path. If you're using OTLP over TLS and collector returns an error, exporter logs will show `Failed to export spans`. Search cluster logs for `Failed to export spans` or `exporter error`.

Runbook for lost spans: https://confluence.redwood/runbooks/tracing/span-loss-checklist — steps: check exporter errors, enable debug logging, add shutdown, verify propagators, run always_on sampler for test.

Quick follow-up from yesterday's RFC — I'm worried about the perf / complexity split if we move full tenant access checks into the query executor vs keeping them in the console layer. Thoughts?
I'd prefer query-layer checks for strong isolation, but that forces us to carry policy logic through the query planner which is messy. Also harder to reuse across dashboards.

Agreed with Jon on reuse. Practical tradeoff: do lightweight filtering in the query layer (deny-by-default predicates), and do richer shape/feature gating in the console. That keeps hot-path checks cheap.
Are we sure lightweight predicates won't blow up index selection? If we add a bunch of dynamic predicates per-tenant we could regress p99. We should benchmark with 100k tenant rules.

Good point. Proposal: 1) push a canonical "tenant_id" predicate into the executor (indexed path), 2) surface feature gates (columns/views toggles) in console, and 3) if feature gating is complex, compile it down to a pre-filter job that populates a temporary allow-list cache.
I like the allow-list cache idea. Suggest TTL + versioning so rollouts don't need global invalidation. Simple API: /cache/allowlist/<tenant>/<feature>?version=42

Implementation note: pre-filter job can run as async materialization on the cluster, keyed by (tenant, feature_version). That avoids per-request compute but introduces staleness; we should define staleness SLO.
For SLOs: aim for eventual consistency within 30s for feature flips, 1s for tenant-deny changes. Tenant-deny must be near-real-time for security-sensitive flows.
Ok — security-sensitive rules will always be sync and enforced in query executor. Everything else can be async.
Rollout plan: Canary on dedicated infra (10 tenants), measure p50/p95/p99 for common dashboard queries. If p99 regresses >15% we abort.
Can we add an executor metric for "predicate-cost-estimate" so we can signal when tenant predicates are making queries pick bad plans?
Yes. We'll add histograms: executor.predicate_eval_time_ms and executor.plan_repick_count. Dashboard team can alert on plan_repick_count spikes.

Edge case: cross-tenant shared tiles (cache entries used by multiple tenants). If we keep tenant predicates in executor, those tiles won't be shared and cache hit rate drops. Need a hybrid: tile keys include feature_version fingerprint so safe sharing is possible when rules identical.
Good call. Add fingerprinting to tile key: sha256(tenant_policy_fingerprint || feature_version) so identical policies share tiles.

Also recommend a fallback for capacity constraints: if executor is overloaded, let console route low-priority dashboards to a degraded path that uses precomputed aggregates. That keeps SLAs for interactive users.
Can we implement degraded path as a per-route policy in the routing table? i.e., route.priorities = [fast, degraded, background] and fallthrough rules.
Yes, route-level config + an operator flag to enable emergency degrade across clusters.

Heads-up: starting migration of our CI runner topology next week. We're splitting the single shared self-hosted runner pool into three dedicated pools (core-services, infra-tools, experiments) and moving to label-based routing. Goal is better isolation and predictable capacity for Dedicated customers. Migration window: Mon 2026-05-11 -> Fri 2026-05-15.

Key changes you need to know:
- New runner labels: `runner:core`, `runner:infra`, `runner:exp`.
- Workflows must target the new labels (search/replace `self-hosted` -> `runner:...`).
- We will enable autoscaling on the infra/tools pools and cap the experiments pool to limit spend.
- Old shared pool will be decommissioned on 2026-05-22.

Action items for teams: update 1–3 high-traffic workflows by EOD 2026-05-12; opt into canary by annotating PRs with `ci-canary: true`. If you rely on custom runners (sgx builds, gpu), ping infra to get dedicated capacity. Docs: https://redwood.internal/docs/ci/runner-migration (detailed checklist + terraform snippets).
Quick q — does this affect Actions that use `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`?

No immediate change for hosted runners (`ubuntu-latest`). This only affects self-hosted workflows currently targeting our shared runner pool. If your job had `runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]` you'll need to update to `runs-on: [runner:core, linux]` or similar.
Will PATs or secrets need rotation? We use a few repo-level deployment tokens in infra-tooling.
We should rotate any token that was scoped to the old runner manager. Infra will rotate those and publish new vault paths — we'll post PRs in infra/terraform for consumers.
Can we get a lightweight sed one-liner for migration?

Sure — example (test before running):
```
find . -name "*.yml" -exec sed -i "s/runs-on: \[self-hosted/ runs-on: [runner:core/" {} +
```
Replace `runner:core` with the pool you want.
Are third-party actions impacted if they spawn services? e.g., `setup-minikube` that requires privileged runners.
We'll tag a subset of infra runners as `privileged:true` for those jobs. If you need privileged access, open an ops ticket and include the repo + workflow path.
NOTICE: Canary cohort opens 2026-05-11 09:00 UTC for repos annotated with `ci-canary: true`. Metrics dashboards will be created under Console -> CI -> Runner Migration.
Will there be automatic fallback to the hosted runners if the new labels aren't available?

No automatic fallback by default. We opted to avoid silent host fallbacks for security and predictability. You can add conditional jobs or use matrix strategies if you want cross-runner fallbacks. We're open to adding an opt-in fallback policy if enough teams request it.

Heads-up — p50 for matmul ops on canary jumped ~2.3x after last night's deploy, mostly for small batches/singletons. noticed at ~03:40 UTC.
saw that on alerts. p95 is stable, so looks like a narrow regression for the common-case mid-latency path. grabbed a perfetto timeline.
perfetto shows a repeating pattern: series of single-request matmuls where the kernel choice oscillates. sometimes we pick algoId=4 (~fast), sometimes algoId=9 (~slow) for identical shapes.
did we change algo-selection heuristics recently? I recall flipping router.small_batch_bias to 0.8 in release v0.42.
yup — that switch routes more singletons down the direct path (less batching), which reduces batch sizes. suspect the selection code is sensitive to available workspace and falls back unexpectedly.

nvprof snippet from the trace (trimmed):
```
# call 1023: cublasLtMatmul shape=[B=1, M=768, N=1024, K=1024]
algo=4 workspace=2097152 bytes time=0.92ms
# call 1024: cublasLtMatmul shape=[B=1, M=768, N=1024, K=1024]
algo=9 workspace=0 bytes time=2.13ms
# call 1025: cublasLtMatmul shape=[B=1, M=768, N=1024, K=1024]
algo=4 workspace=2097152 bytes time=0.95ms
```
workspace=0 is the smoking gun — if cublasLt can't get workspace it picks a memory-light algo that is slower. why would workspace be 0 intermittently?
mempool stats from the same run (sample): free=1.2GB, largest_free_block=48KB, churn=high. small repeated allocations are fragmenting the pool.
that matches my local repro. toggle the router bias back to 1.0 and the workload all goes through multi-batch path; workspace allocations become coalesced and algo=4 is almost always chosen.
can we reproduce deterministically? steps?

simple repro: run 5k single-request matmuls back-to-back on a g4x. script:
```
# run-singletons.sh
for i in $(seq 1 5000); do
  python run_matmul.py --batch 1 --M 768 --N 1024 --K 1024
done
```
with router.small_batch_bias=0.8 you hit the regression 90% of runs. with 1.0 it's gone.
Trace uploaded: https://perf.redwood/internal/traces/2178001234-abcde :mag_right:
short-term mitigation: pin router.small_batch_bias=1.0 for canary and prod for now. will add runtime guard to disable the new path until mempool fix.
good. can someone open an eng-runtime issue to investigate mempool fragmentation + allocator policy? include sampling traces and repro script.
adding lightweight logging at the selection site to always emit `algo_id`, `workspace_requested`, `workspace_granted`, and `mempool_largest_free` for the next canary run. should be low-overhead.
rollback applied: rolled back commit cf12a34 to canary at ts=2178001250 — routing bias reverted.
follow-up: I'll prototype a best-fit merge for the mempool free-list to avoid tiny largest_free_block. early tests show much lower fragmentation under singleton-heavy workloads.

Heads-up — saw a sharp spike in 503s and a ton of client retries after the py-sdk bump (v0.12.4) during our internal load test.
ugh, repro steps?

run the load harness pointing at dedicated staging, 200 concurrent workers, short-lived clients (create client per-request). After ~30s latency climbs and then we start seeing repeated 429/503, client logs show retry loops.
is it the keepalive/connpool change we shipped last week?

I suspect the new max_concurrency guard + retry backoff is interacting badly. The client holds semaphore tokens per session, but we create/destroy sessions a lot in our test. Looks like semaphores never release in some paths.
can you paste the minimal repro?

here — snippet we used:
```
from redwood import RedwoodClient
for _ in range(2000):
    client = RedwoodClient(api_key=KEY, max_concurrency=4)
    resp = client.generate("short prompt")
    client.close()
```
We do this concurrently across threads. After a while the process stops acquiring tokens.
we saw similar symptoms but with long-lived clients + heavy burst of requests — sockets pile up and new attempts block.
stack traces / logs? Any socket errors?
logs show lines like: `waiting for semaphore token` and then repeated `Retrying request after 500ms` indefinitely. No obvious exception when close() is called.
could be double-wait race in `Client.close()` path where pending requests block the drain. If close waits for pending tokens but pending requests themselves wait for tokens -> deadlock.
workaround for now: set `max_concurrency=None` or reuse a single client per worker. That avoided the deadlock in our run. But we should fix for short-lived client pattern.
filing a bug. Need exact version, env, and minimal repro. Also want to check token expiry/refresh code path — if auth failure can leave a waiter in limbo.
version v0.12.4, python 3.11, httpx 0.25, uvloop off, linux builders. I'll attach a gist of full logs in a sec.
build 2026-03-21-8472 reproduced on staging-connpool (test harness id: load-014).

quick triage plan: (1) add logging to semaphore acquire/release with a unique request id, (2) audit close() drain logic for ordering, (3) reproduce with simplified async snippet to see if it's sync-async mix.
also check timeout semantics — if the session-level timeout raises in one coroutine the release may be in finally but not executed if cancel handling is wrong.
I'll take (2) and (3). Ajay can you drop repro into `/tmp/repro_connpool.py` on staging?
done — placed it and pinged the load job. Link: https://staging.internal/repro/connpool-1846001111
long-term: we should document recommended lifecycle (prefer reuse) and consider making `Client` __enter__/__exit__ safer + explicit `drain()` method in next minor.

agreed. For immediate patch we can: ensure Close does not wait for pending requests that are themselves waiting for tokens — instead mark client as draining and cancel queued requests, then wait for in-flight ones.
can we add a test that spins up 100 short-lived clients concurrently to catch regressions?
yes, I'll add integration test + unit that stubs semaphore to assert release on close/error paths.
thanks — ping me when there's a patch; happy to run load test. :thumbsup:

Quick brainstorm: instead of inline text or a top toast, what if we surface compact error chips (small pill with ! icon) inline to avoid vertical shift and show an accordion-level summary banner? Need keyboard and SR friendliness.
Ooh I like the chips idea for density. They don't add height if we position them absolutely to the input row. Popover on focus/hover for full message.
chips sound sleek but two concerns: 1) absolute positioning can overlap on very narrow windows, 2) SRs might not discover popovers.

accessibility notes: chips must still be in the tab order (button) and popover content should be reachable via aria-controls/aria-expanded. Also provide aria-live region for the accordion banner so SRs get a summary when panels open.

agree. Implementation plan: error chip = <button aria-describedby="err-123-summary" data-error-chip> with visible icon and sr-only full text; popover shows extended message. For collapsed accordion we show a subtle red banner at the top of that accordion listing counts ("2 errors") with anchor links to chips.
nice. That lets users scan which sections have issues. For keyboard-only users: Tab to banner, press Enter to focus first error chip inside. Could also have a "jump to next error" keyboard shortcut.
Shortcut is powerful but more of a power-user feature. If we add it, make it discoverable in the keyboard help menu. Also ensure we don't conflict with browser shortcuts.

SR flow: when user submits and there are errors in a collapsed accordion, open the accordion, move focus to the banner, announce "2 errors in this section" via role=alert, then user can Tab into chips. That avoids race conditions.

copy for chips should be terse: "Required" or "Invalid email". Popover contains full helper + link to docs if needed. For required-field markers: should we still surface a small legend or inline postfix?

since chips indicate errors, required-state should be separate. Propose a tiny persistent postfix "Required" for the first field in a group only, but only for groups where many fields are mandatory. Otherwise use a compact label like (req).
prefer a machine-readable attribute too: data-required=true so tests can validate. Also provide :focus-visible styles for chips and inputs that meet contrast.

destructive actions: we discussed typed-confirm vs undo before. Variant idea: for destructive in-scope items (non-customer-data) use an "are you sure" modal with a checkbox "I understand" + undo toast. For irreversible operations keep typed-confirm but reduce friction by pre-filling the token in a small copy area so the user still types it.

pre-fill token? that lowers safety. Maybe show token but require typing it manually. Pre-filling in hidden field is dangerous. Keep manual typing. Keep copy concise: "Type delete-pool to permanently remove pool 'X' (id: 42)".

UX nit: make the typed token monospace and include a small copy button to copy token for assistive tech users who can't type easily, but only enable copy after the user confirms they understand risk (tiny progressive disclosure).

that seems complex and could be abused. I'd rather have an optional accessibility flow: if user triggers an "accessible mode" we provide alternatives (confirm with voice or admin override). For now keep typed-confirm + accessible support doc.

Accessibility checklist for this pattern: 1) chips must be keyboard focusable; 2) popover content reachable and has role=document; 3) accordions open programmatically and set focus to banner with role=alert; 4) aria-invalid on fields; 5) data-required attributes for automation.
toast collisions: chips/popovers reduce need for global toasts, but we still have undo toasts. Keep single-toast visible rule: undo has mid priority, errors are shown inline via chips so not queued.
dev note: chips should avoid layout shifts by using CSS transform translate instead of changing flow. Test on very small widths and with long labels.

Quick question from the API workshop — do we standardize on grpc+proto for internal services and use a JSON gateway for browser clients, or keep REST everywhere for ergonomics? Thinking about telemetry and quota propagation.
+1 to grpc internally for perf and typed contracts, but worried about edge complexity.
Can we do grpc internal + lightweight JSON gateway? That feels like our usual split but we need a clear negotiation story.
Main ops concern is transparent quota attribution across the boundary. If gateway translates, we lose original method labels unless we pass something through.
Right — option: gateway sets headers like `x-rdwd-client-method: Projects.List` and `x-rdwd-proto-version: v2`. That keeps routing/quotas intact.
Headers are fine but fragile. We should also include a provenance field in the proto: `message Provenance { string orig_client = 1; repeated string route = 2; }` so downstream can verify.
Proto change means churn for a lot of libraries. Could we instead embed a signed JSON blob in `x-rdwd-meta` header? Smaller rollout surface.
Signed header helps prevent spoofing. But orch needs to trust gateway signing keys; key rotation flows get annoying.
Tradeoffs: header approach = fast rollout, but hidden contract. Proto approach = explicit but larger migration cost. Both need telemetry tagging.
For telemetry, I'd like a single canonical field for route/method that shows up in traces and metrics. If gateway sets `x-rdwd-route` we can plumb that to tracing.
UX question for rollouts: how do we canary the gateway translation without breaking customers? We could auto-copy header only for canary traffic first, and run comparison metrics.
+1. Orch-side we can enforce a `translation-check` sampling flag to mirror both labels into logs for 1% traffic. That helps QA.
deploy scheduled: gateway-canary v2 -> 10% at 2024-06-21T14:00Z (monitoring enabled).
Also wondering about error semantics. grpc status codes map poorly to HTTP 200+problem-json flows. We should document canonical mapping in the gateway repo.
Can we add a small `x-rdwd-status` header carrying the grpc code for observability so we don't lose it through retries?
That helps SLO math. Plus keep the gateway idempotent headers: `x-rdwd-retry-key`.

TL;DR proposal: default to grpc+proto internal, implement header-based provenance/route (`x-rdwd-route`, `x-rdwd-proto`), add signed `x-rdwd-meta` for bootstrapping provenance, and deploy gateway-canary with `translation-check` sampling to validate quota and tracing parity.
Sounds reasonable. Can we capture this in the gateway RFC and include the header name list + rotation plan? I'll own the RFC draft.
Thanks — please add migration steps for SDKs and a backout plan. Sam, can you add console signals to show when translation header is present vs absent?
Yep, will add per-route telemetry and a small dashboard panel.
I'll add orch checks for signing key rotation and the 1% mirrored logs.

Quick question - thinking about making the left rail fully collapsible but keeping a persistent breadcrumb bar above the main canvas so deep links always surface the full path. Sketch: https://figma.com/s/console-nav-proto. Does that break permalinks or keyboard flow?

I like the persistence but keyboard users need a predictable tab order. If breadcrumbs are always present they must be first tabbable element after the global nav. Also we should expose a "Skip to main" link.

Routing question: current canonical resource URLs look like `/org/:orgId/workspaces/:wsId/models/:modelId`. If we collapse groups in the rail, we can't rely on rail state to reconstruct the path. We should encode the full resource path in the URL and treat rail state as UI-only.

Implementation note — using hash anchors for panels (`#metrics`) made browser restore/back weird in the canary. I suggest we prefer a query param for subpanels, e.g. `?panel=metrics` or a nested path like `/models/:id/metrics`.

Accessibility nit: mark the active crumb with \"aria-current=\"page\"\" and when the breadcrumb bar expands/collapses announce that with an \"aria-live=\"polite\"\" region. Also ensure collapsible groups expose `aria-expanded` and keyboard handlers (Enter/Space).
Prototype preview deployed: https://staging.redwood/console/nav-proto (build 502). Tester notes: requires Chrome >= 114 for the continuous-scroll behavior.
:thumbsup: Also recommend adding a small visible focus ring on the crumbs (high contrast) and a dedicated skip link for screenreader users.
Edge-case: links shared from older UI (old query params like `?panel=overview&view=compact`) need a router-level redirect mapping to the new path. Otherwise team pages will 404.

Proposed decision (for quick sync):
1) Breadcrumb bar remains persistent and canonicalizes resource path. URLs are the source of truth.
2) Left rail becomes collapsible; collapse state is stored in user prefs and can be overridden by `?rail=collapsed` in URL for shared links.
3) Deep links use path-first approach: resource paths for primary entities, `?panel=` for subviews. Avoid hash anchors for new routes.
4) A11y: `aria-current`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-live` announcements, and a visible skip-to-content link.

quick design question: final pass on form validation for Console > Model Pins. i'm toggling between 3 UX bits: required markers, error placement, and delete confirmations on mobile. TL;DR: want accessible, low-noise, and clear delete flows. thoughts?
short take: explicit text for required, summary+inline for errors, typed confirm only for truly destructive actions. mobile needs special handling.
+1 summary+inline. summary should be an assertive live region and receive focus on submit fail. include anchor links that focus the actual input. ensure aria-describedby points to the inline message.
prefer '(required)' text after the label for clarity. asterisk + color is ambiguous and fails colorblind readers. also consider short helper text vs persistent label for dense forms.

on delete: for single pin delete use a modal with clear primary/secondary buttons. for deletes that remove model artifacts or >8 pins use typed confirm (e.g., type DELETE) and require elevated role. mobile: prefer a one-step confirm with a clear 'Permanently delete' CTA and strong color.
what's the reason for threshold 8? open to change but want to avoid accidental bulk wipes.
it's a safety heuristic: >8 implies bulk intent; also correlate with API bulk-delete endpoints.
little a11y nit: set aria-invalid="true" on invalid inputs and include aria-live updates for the summary. when an anchor link is clicked, call element.focus() then scrollIntoView({block: 'center'}).
WCAG reminder: required indicators must not rely solely on color. error outlines should meet 3:1 contrast for UI components. ensure focus outlines are visible and large-touch targets on mobile.
UX rule idea: if errors > 3, expand the summary and collapse inline microcopy to reduce clutter. otherwise show inline hints below fields. smooth scroll on jump is helpful.

copy suggestion for summary heading: "Please fix the highlighted fields to continue." less alarming than "Errors". for typed confirm text: "Type DELETE to permanently remove this model pin." keep concise.

```
add data-test-id and data-error-id for analytics, and include a mapping from server error keys to field ids in the spec.

repro summary: POST /v1/launch with header 'Idempotency-Key' -> transient 503 -> retry -> second request lacks header -> server creates another launch.
can you drop the minimal snippet?

async example:
```python
async with RedwoodAsyncClient(key=REDWOOD_KEY) as client:
    await client.post('/v1/launch', json=payload, headers={'Idempotency-Key': run_id})
```
stackwise it looks like our async retry path reconstructs a new aiohttp request without copying custom headers (session default auth exists so Authorization shows up, but not user headers).
thanks. sounds like our RetryState only keeps method/url/body/timeout and loses headers. That's dangerous for idempotent POSTs.
proposed fix: store a small header map on the RetryContext but only persist a safe list (e.g., Idempotency-Key, X-Request-ID). Make the header whitelist configurable at client init.
agree. API suggestion: RedwoodAsyncClient(..., replay_preserve_headers=['Idempotency-Key']). Default should include 'Idempotency-Key' so existing users don't see regressions.
we should be explicit in docs about replay semantics and warn about replaying ephemeral cookies. Also ensure Authorization is only replayed if using SDK-managed auth (we sign it internally).

Posting a tiny repro for a weird bundler interop that only shows up when we use webpack's ProvidePlugin + vite/rollup builds for edge. Local node dev works fine but built bundles either lose the default export or end up with a shimmed namespace. Putting steps and configs below.

Symptoms: consumers `import Client from 'redwood-sdk'` and `new Client()` throws "Client is not a constructor" after the bundle runs in our edge runner. The bundle shows the SDK imported as an object with no `default` or a default that's an empty getter.
that rings a bell. ProvidePlugin can inject globals and some bundlers reorder imports. curious about package.exports in the SDK and whether vite/rollup are treating the package as external.

rollup/vite configs tried: rollup with `external: []` (we tried both externalizing and bundling sdk), vite with `ssr.noExternal: []` and `optimizeDeps.exclude` variations. Behavior differs by combination: sometimes rollup picks cjs path and wrappers end up inlined weirdly, sometimes vite's prebundle step (esbuild) changes the shape.

did you check the SDK package exports / mjs presence? if there's an `exports` map and no explicit `edge` or `browser` condition it can confuse modern bundlers. Also ProvidePlugin can change the module graph which impacts tree-shaking.

SDK package simplified:
```
{
  "name": "redwood-sdk",
  "main": "dist/cjs/index.js",
  "module": "dist/esm/index.js",
  "exports": { ".": { "import": "./dist/esm/index.js", "require": "./dist/cjs/index.js" } },
  "types": "dist/index.d.ts"
}
```

I instrumented the build and found two failure modes:
1) bundler resolves the `require` path but emits an ESM wrapper that doesn't set the `default` property consistently (some plugin combinations leave `__esModule: true` but no default), then after terser minify the `default` getter is optimized away.
2) ProvidePlugin injection causes the SDK import to be hoisted and deduped with a stub module, which then gets tree-shaken because the bundler thinks nothing uses its named exports, leaving an empty namespace.
wow that is nasty. Workarounds?

we tried several things: 1) add an explicit `dist/esm/index.mjs` with native `export default` and add an `edge` export condition in package.json, 2) expose named exports (export class Client {...}) and recommend `import { Client }` to consumers, 3) add a compat shim `dist/compat.cjs` doing `module.exports = exports.default = require('./index.cjs')` so older bundlers see both shapes. All helped in different bundlers.

also worth adding CI e2e: build the tiny sample with webpack (with ProvidePlugin), rollup, vite (with ssr/noExternal combos) and run the edge smoke harness. Add terser on/off. This will catch mangling of getters.

for docs: add a short troubleshooting section in SDK onboarding explaining common bundler pitfalls: exports map, mjs edge entry, `import * as` fallback, and how ProvidePlugin can influence resolution.

Heads-up — flaky Node SDK streaming through our proxy. After a client reconnect some chunks arrive out of order.
steps to repro?
Start a long SSE stream (~2k+ tokens), kill the client (SIGINT), reconnect immediately. Node client emits later chunks before earlier ones. Seems like the parser replays buffered bits.
do we have proxy/runtime logs?

pasted minimal logs below. Note seq numbers:
```
[proxy] 2026-03-18T14:01:23Z conn=42 client=10.2.3.4 stream-id=abc start
[proxy] 2026-03-18T14:01:25Z conn=42 client disconnected (tcp reset)
[proxy] 2026-03-18T14:01:25Z conn=43 client=10.2.3.4 reconnect stream-id=abc resume=false
[runtime] 2026-03-18T14:01:26Z output chunk seq=5 id=abc
[runtime] 2026-03-18T14:01:27Z output chunk seq=3 id=abc
```
runtime's seqs are non-monotonic after reconnect when observed from proxy.
Is this Node-specific? Python SDK ok?
In our tests Python iterator client keeps order. Node uses `sse-parser v1.3` which appears to mix buffered leftover data with new frames and yields them according to parser internals.
So two hypotheses: (A) proxy/runtime replays old buffers on handoff or (B) Node parser doesn't preserve server-provided ordering metadata. Which did the tcp dump show?
I dumped raw TCP. Server emitted seq=3,4,5 in order. Proxy delivered 5 then 3. So server order is correct — proxy is stitching streams badly.
Any auth or token refresh happening during reconnect? Maybe a refresh middleware opens a second backend connection and we accidentally merge flows.

Yes — our NewAuth middleware triggers a backend handshake when token expired mid-stream. That briefly forks the stream while the original connection is still being drained. That matches the interleaving.
Token refresh should never create a secondary active backend for the same client stream without a resume protocol.

Short-term mitigations I propose:
- SDKs: debounce reconnect attempts (Node: 200ms) and only allow one reconnect in-flight per stream id.
- Proxy/runtime: add `X-Stream-Seq` and `X-Resume-Token` headers on chunks and initial handshake.
- Long-term: implement resume protocol: client `?resume_after=<seq>` to request continuation after a given seq.
Also document that mid-stream token refresh is unsupported by default; SDKs should either refresh proactively or fail the stream and let app resume.
Add tests: devex/samples should include forced token expiry and assert no chunk reordering.
Reminder: file a bug ticket with logs and minimal repro.
Filed ENG-STREAM-1122 with logs and a small tcp dump. cc @kyle @sam
Another subtlety — SSE event boundaries matter. If proxy splits inside an `event:` or `data:` line and reattaches later, naive parsers may emit partial events. Ensure we never cut inside a line.

Good point. Also include `seq` inside the JSON payload in `data:` as last-resort ordering guard, e.g.:
```
data: {"seq": 42, "delta": "..."}
```
That lets clients reorder safely on receipt.
I'll replace `sse-parser` in Node SDK with a tiny state-machine that waits for a full event (double newline) before emitting. That should stop mid-event emissions.
Python SDK: add `resume_after` param to `client.stream(resume_after=...)` and auto-attempt resume if server returns `X-Resume-Token`.
Question for the team — should reconnect during an active stream be fatal by default? If fatal, apps get a deterministic error and can retry with a fresh prompt.
Default to resilient: try a single resume, then surface an explicit error. Provide `fail_fast=True` opt-in.
Also update onboarding docs: streaming token TTL should be >= expected stream duration and include examples for refresh patterns.
I'll open a Node PR with the debounce + parser change and add a sample in `devex/samples/streaming-resume` showing reconnect/resume flows. Pushing PR now.

quick one - noticed a bunch of retried requests missing our X-Request-Id header in logs, makes tracing really noisy. Seen on Kotlin SDK sample app + prod traffic mirroring.
how are you setting X-Request-Id today?

we were relying on a ThreadLocal MDC that our coroutine bridge populates. Interceptor reads MDC and does `request.newBuilder().header("X-Request-Id", mdc.get("reqId"))` before proceed(). Works for first attempt but retried clones sometimes lack it.

that smells like a thread-context propagation issue. OkHttp retries (call.clone()/enqueue) can run on dispatcher threads which don't have the original coroutine ThreadLocal. Kotlin coroutines don't automatically propagate ThreadLocal unless you use ThreadContextElement.

when OkHttp retries, it may schedule the retry on a pooled thread where MDC isn't set. So header ends up null on cloned requests. Java SDK solved this by eagerly stamping headers in the calling thread before handing Call to OkHttp.
ah - so parity gap between Java & Kotlin SDKs. Java made header stamping part of the API request builder, Kotlin relied on interceptor + ThreadLocal.

quick fixes: 1) stamp trace header as soon as you create the Request (i.e., at the call site before enqueue/execute) so clones inherit headers, or 2) use a CoroutineContext element that propagates MDC to threads (ThreadContextElement) and install it where coroutines are launched, or 3) change interceptor to read a header carrier from a Request.tag() (explicitly attached at creation).

example (stamp early):
```kotlin
val req = originalRequest.newBuilder()
  .header("X-Request-Id", currentReqId)
  .build()
service.call(req)
```
This guarantees call.clone() will carry the header.
for SDK sample app we should prefer an explicit approach so users don't accidentally rely on ThreadLocal. Also doc the coroutine-to-ThreadLocal pitfalls.

I pushed a branch: stamp header at request creation in sample, and added a utility `Tracing.tag(request, reqId)` which stores it in Request.tag for interceptor fallback. Also added integration test that simulates a 401-triggered retry and asserts X-Request-Id appears on all server-side records.

please also add a short note in the SDK "Auth & Retry" doc: "Do not rely on ThreadLocal MDC for request-scoped headers when using coroutines + OkHttp; prefer explicit header stamping or coroutine ThreadContextElement." Include the sample snippet and guidance for Java/Kotlin parity.
mirror deployed: sample/trace-fix branch validated in staging replay for 2k requests, no header loss observed.

one more gotcha: if you stamp header lazily in an interceptor but also refresh auth (which may mutate header) you must ensure auth refresh updates the stamped header before retries. Prefer a single place to stamp final headers (call site) or a deterministic two-step: stamp tracing first, then auth header in network interceptor that runs per-request and can be updated safely.

Heads-up — SDK v2.3 lands tomorrow morning. Two small but important changes: header normalization for auth and a change to streaming retry semantics. If you have custom auth middleware or rely on the old streaming ondata ordering please read below.
Quick Q — what exactly changed for auth headers?

Previously the client accepted either `authorization` or `x-auth-token` headers. v2.3 normalizes and enforces `Authorization: Bearer <token>` only. We did this to avoid accidental double-sends and to match other infra. If you set tokens via middleware, update to explicitly set `authorization`.
Example change?
Python note — the python client still accepts token via constructor `Client(api_key=...)` and will send the right header; only concern is teams that manually mutate headers before client send.
Streaming behavior — what changed there? We saw duplicated ondata events in our chat worker after upgrading beta.

Good catch. v2.3 introduces an internal retry layer for streaming connections. By default it attempts one short reconnect on transient socket closes. That avoids full request retries but can cause duplicate finalization events if your consumer doesn't dedupe.
How to opt out?
Is this opt-out per-request or global? We want global off for a while.
It's a per-client setting today (so global for a process). We're adding a per-request override in a patch if needed.

quick heads-up — I'm hitting partial-JSON parse errors in the JS SDK when auth refresh happens mid-stream. repro: chat streaming -> token expires -> client refreshes -> server returns a cut-off chunk + 401 -> our parser throws "Unexpected end of JSON input". anyone run into this? :thinking:
sample error from client logs: `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input at JSON.parse (<anonymous>)`

yep seen this pattern before. most times it's a race between the auth refresh/reconnect and the incremental parser. two suggestions: (1) don't call `JSON.parse` on partial buffers — use an incremental parser (clarinet, ndjson-stream) or a tiny stateful reassembler that looks for complete objects, (2) on 401 mid-stream treat as special signal: keep unfinished chunk in a buffer and retry the request then feed reassembled prefix to new stream. :+1:

also consider backpressure/slow-consumer side effects. if the app is busy doing token exchange on main thread the readable stream may not be drained quickly => internal chunk coalescing/truncation behaviors differ between runtimes. for Node fetch we saw similar problems when `highWaterMark` is low. try consuming via stream events and temporarily `pause()` the body while refresh happens, or increase `highWaterMark` on stream creation.
or use a Transform stream that reassembles complete events and enforces a small queue so the parser never sees half-objects. this also helps when we need to hold incomplete prefix across reconnects.

another practical pattern — when you detect a 401 mid-stream, have the client emit a special `need_refresh` event to the app layer instead of trying to parse the current buffer. the app can then decide to finish/flush the buffer or keep it and attach as prefix to the next connection. server-side support for `Retry-After` or `resume-token` makes this much cleaner.

Seeing a repeatable race with AsyncClient auth + httpx retries. Two concurrent requests hit 401 and both try to refresh token; retry path reuses a prepared request so it re-sends stale Authorization header. Repro in FastAPI background tasks and integration tests. Anyone seen this?
Can you paste a tiny repro and logs?

Minimal example below. Uses ContextVar to store token and an httpx request hook that refreshes if token missing.
```py
from contextvars import ContextVar
import httpx, asyncio
_token = ContextVar('token', default=None)
async def refresh_token():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return 'tok-' + str(asyncio.get_event_loop().time())
async def auth_hook(request):
    t = _token.get()
    if not t:
        t = await refresh_token()
        _token.set(t)
    request.headers['authorization'] = f'Bearer {t}'
    return request
client = httpx.AsyncClient(event_hooks={'request': [auth_hook]})
```

Logs show two refreshes then a retry that still sends old header:
INFO refresh start
INFO refresh success tokA
WARN 401 GET /v1/generate
INFO retry attempt 1
WARN 401 GET /v1/generate
INFO refresh start
INFO refresh success tokB
ERROR request ultimately failed
Looks like httpx prepares the request once and reuses it for retries, so request hooks don't run again. Also ContextVar propagation across tasks can be surprising.

Two recommended mitigations: (1) dedupe refreshes with an asyncio.Lock or singleflight so only one refresh runs; (2) ensure retry logic re-runs auth before each send instead of reusing prepared request.
I was thinking about moving auth into a transport-level shim or a custom AsyncAuth so headers are applied at send time. But httpx.Auth is sync-focused; might require a transport patch.

Short-term for the SDK: wrap refresh_token with a per-client asyncio.Lock and make retry loop reapply hooks or run auth before each attempt. Long-term: move auth to transport so retries always see fresh headers.

Also the SDK typing needs polish: our Async client types are ambiguous and mypy often treats them like sync clients. We should add an explicit AsyncClient Protocol and proper __aenter__/__aexit__ overloads so `async with` type checks.

I'll add a regression test that races N concurrent requests during token expiry asserting only one refresh and that retried sends use the new token. Will include a FastAPI background-task variant to mirror prod.

created issue #3772 "async auth + retry race -> stale auth headers"

Will open draft PR with fixes: (a) per-client lock, (b) retry logic that re-applies auth hooks, and (c) docs example for transport shim.

Running into TLS verify failures when talking to our Dedicated inside the customer's VPC. Sync calls (requests) pass with custom CA but Async (httpx) errors out. Anyone seen this?
What's the exact error and how are you configuring the SDK? base_url/proxy etc?

Error is `ssl.SSLCertVerificationError: unable to get local issuer certificate`. I'm using sdk.AsyncClient(base_url=\"https://svc.internal\", api_key=...) and I set verify='/etc/pki/tls/certs/custom-ca.pem' on the client init.
Do you mean you call sdk.AsyncClient(verify=...) or you make an httpx.AsyncClient and hand it in?

Tried both: passing verify into sdk constructor, and also building an httpx.AsyncClient(verify='/etc/pki/tls/certs/custom-ca.pem') and wrapping it: sdk.AsyncClient(httpx_client=client). Sync path works either way. Async path still fails.
Could be how our wrapper normalizes kwargs for async. We injected a transport layer for retries/proxy and might be dropping the SSLContext.

Also check the typing stubs in sdk/_client.py. I remember we typed `verify: Optional[bool]` for AsyncClient to mirror requests historically. If code downstream assumes bool it may call `bool(verify)` somewhere.

I grepped: in async wrapper we do `_build_transport(verify=verify)` and inside that function we do `if not verify: return default_transport` which treats a path string as truthy fine, but later we call `ssl.create_default_context()` only when verify is True (bool), not when it's a str. So path gets ignored. oof.
Yikes. So two problems: wrong branching for str vs bool, and the typing stub being wrong which will confuse users and linters.

For an immediate repro, you can run a local HTTPS server using Python's http.server with ssl and a CA signed cert and try both clients. For CI test write a small unit that creates an SSLContext from the PEM and asserts the async client's transport has that context.

Workaround that worked for me: create SSLContext manually and pass it in:
```py
import ssl, httpx
ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile='/etc/pki/tls/certs/custom-ca.pem')
async_client = httpx.AsyncClient(verify=ctx)
sdk_client = sdk.AsyncClient(httpx_client=async_client, base_url='https://svc.internal', api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
```
This avoids the SDK path that converts strings to contexts.

Heads-up — saw a bunch of spans missing for requests that got retried by the Python SDK. Tracing looks fine on the first attempt but subsequent retries have no traceparent / trace id attached.
Huh. Are you using async or sync client? any middleware? :eyes:

async, httpx under the hood. We have an OTEL FastAPI app that starts a span and calls `client.generate(...)`. If the first request hits a 502 the SDK retries and the retried HTTP request arrives at the model infra with no trace headers.
Can you paste a small repro? even a pseudo snippet is fine.

Yep — pared down repro below. Works locally to show missing trace on retry.
```
# app.py (simplified)
from opentelemetry import trace
from my_redwood_sdk import AsyncClient
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
client = AsyncClient(api_key=...)
async def call_model():
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("handle-request"):
        resp = await client.generate("hello")
        return resp
```
When the first request fails and the SDK's retry kicks in, the outbound request headers logged by our infra show no `traceparent`. If we disable SDK retries everything is fine.

Likely contextvars loss across async boundaries. If SDK spawns a new task or uses `asyncio.ensure_future` for the retry, current context (with OTEL span) can be lost. Are you on the latest py-sdk release? we fixed a similar fastapi background-task case earlier but maybe not retries.
Can you share the SDK's retry behavior? Is it synchronous retry loop, or does it schedule a new coroutine?

From reading the code quickly it looks like: attempt, on transient error schedule `await asyncio.sleep(backoff); await _do_request()` — but I noticed the SDK uses `asyncio.create_task` in one path (for rate-limit backoff) which is suspicious.

If it's creating tasks it's definitely a context problem. Fix is to run retry logic with the same contextvar copy. Two approaches we usually use:
- capture ctx = contextvars.copy_context() and run the retry coroutine via `ctx.run(coro_func, *args)`
- avoid creating detached tasks and instead await in the same task

Agree. Another pragmatic option for the SDK is to explicitly forward trace headers. The SDK's HTTP layer should ask the active tracer for the current span context and inject via propagator before sending. That makes retries idempotent wrt tracing even if contextvars are lost. But that's more invasive.
Quick debug: can you log `trace.get_current_span()` before each outbound call inside the SDK? If it's None on retries then we confirm context loss.
Did that — first attempt prints span with id `0xabc`, retry prints None.

Ok. Two follow-ups: (1) short-term: add an internal guard in the SDK HTTP client to call `TraceContextTextMapPropagator().inject(carrier)` using the current context (if any) right before sending — that will preserve traceparent when present; (2) long-term: make retry code avoid detaching the context (use `contextvars.copy_context()` or not create tasks). I'll open a small PR for (1) today.

If you open the PR, request `@eng-runtime` and `@eng-ml` reviewers. Also add a regression test that sets an active span and simulates a failing first request so CI can assert the outgoing headers include `traceparent`.
Will do. Quick snippet I used to assert outgoing headers in infra logs: `assert 'traceparent' in last_request['headers']` — reproduced consistently.

One more gotcha: make sure the propagator uses the same format as the infra (W3C traceparent). OTel default is W3C but some places still use `x-request-id` or custom. If you add both `traceparent` and `x-request-id` injection in the SDK it helps compatibility.
Good point. I'll add both headers when available.

Heads-up — we're getting a couple reports about the JS SDK behaving differently across runtimes: Node (undici) vs edge (global fetch) vs bundlers. Also some TS consumers hitting weird types when using CJS wrappers. Anyone seen this today?

(typo) I meant @ana :)

yep. root cause: our bundled SDK includes a small Node-only shim: `const f = globalThis.fetch ?? (await import('undici')).fetch` — but when package is bundled for edge, the bundler hoists/rewrites dynamic import or polyfills incorrectly. Some CJS consumers hit `require('redwood-sdk')` which returns a CommonJS wrapper and `default` shape is different for named exports.

Also saw auth/retry break: in Node undici the `signal` handling differs and our retry wrapper was re-creating requests which lost `Authorization` headers on redirected requests (fetch spec behavior differs with `redirect: 'follow'`). Report from support: auth header lost after 302 -> 200.

checklist suggestion: 1) prefer `globalThis.fetch` when available. 2) fallback to `undici` only in Node where necessary. 3) make `undici` an optional dependency and require users to install it in Node environments that lack global fetch. 4) provide tiny runtime detection helpers that are bundler-safe.

that pattern keeps bundlers from bundling undici into edge builds (because import is guarded at runtime). For CJS consumers: in our build step ensure both ESM and CJS exports are consistent and document `import RedwoodClient from 'redwood-sdk'` vs `const { RedwoodClient } = require('redwood-sdk')` cases.

on types: TS users reported `RedwoodClient` type showing as `any` after transpile when using `esModuleInterop: false`. We should provide both `exports` + `module.exports` patterns and ship .d.ts that work for CJS consumers. Also include `types` in package.json.
also call out edge runtimes that redefine fetch signature (Cloudflare adds `fetch(req, env, ctx)` in Workers — our wrapper should accept same args or forward appropriately).

good point — we'll normalize the wrapper to accept either `(input, init)` or `(event)` and internally convert. But keep narrow surface: we only need `(input, init)` for REST calls. Worker handler support is for example apps.

about retry + auth: ensure our retry replays body safely. For streams you can't clone after consumed — so either buffer small bodies or require the user to supply `buffered: true` for retries. And ensure `credentials: 'include'` vs Authorization header are respected on redirects — add explicit tests that a 302 doesn't drop headers for our code path (we might need to set `redirect: 'manual'` + follow logic that reinserts headers).

Heads-up: running into flaky errors in our FastAPI sample when tests call the app startup multiple times (pytest-asyncio + uvicorn in-process). Repro attached.
what errors are you seeing?

sometimes tests fail with RuntimeError: Event loop is closed or ConnectionResetError from httpcore. Happens when the SDK's AsyncClient is created in the app startup handler and tests run multiple isolated loops. Minimal excerpt below.

```py
# conftest.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from httpx import AsyncClient
app = FastAPI()
@app.on_event("startup")
async def startup():
    app.state.client = AsyncClient(base_url="http://localhost:8000")
@app.on_event("shutdown")
async def shutdown():
    await app.state.client.aclose()
# tests call TestClient / anyio which spins loops; if the startup client outlives the loop you get errors
```
yep that's the common pitfall: AsyncClient binds transports to the loop it was created on. FastAPI startup may be called under a different loop when tests manage their own event loop policy.

two options: 1) create the client lazily inside request handlers, 2) use lifespan/context-managed client created by the same loop that will use it. For tests, the simplest is to wire the client as an async context var in the app lifespan so creation and close happen within the test loop.

example lifespan pattern:````py
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    client = AsyncClient()
    app.state.client = client
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        await client.aclose()
```

Heads-up: noticed inconsistent behavior between Java and Kotlin SDKs around cancellation + retries on Android 13. Kotlin sampleapp cancels fine, Java sampleapp leaves leaked calls in dispatcher.
Interesting. Which layer is different? Retrofit CallAdapter, OkHttp interceptor, or our SDK wrapper?

Traced it to our SDK helper that wraps Retrofit Call into a CompletableFuture (Java) vs suspend wrapper (Kotlin). Java path used future.cancel(true) -> underlying call.cancel(), but we also had a retry interceptor that re-enqueued call on certain 5xx. That re-enqueue logic didn't check call.isCanceled() on the Java path because of subtle timing.
Can you paste the retry snippet?

In Kotlin we used a helper that checked coroutineContext.isActive before retrying and called call.isCanceled(). The Java path was missing that check. Result: after cancellation the retry interceptor still ran on worker threads and OkHttp dispatcher showed Running++ counts and eventual RejectedExecutionException under load.
Oof. So parity bug between SDK wrappers. Also calls re-proceeded after cancel, which is unexpected.

Another wrinkle: Android's ConnectivityManager can post callbacks to the main thread, and our Java future.cancel(true) ended up interrupting the thread running the retry decision, causing IllegalMonitorStateException in some internal code. Didn't see that on Kotlin since coroutines use cooperative cancellation.

Repro steps I used:
  • Start emulator Android 13
  • Fire 30 concurrent requests through Java SDK wrapper with short deadline 1s
  • Make server return 503 first, then 200 after 2s
  • Cancel the future after 500ms for half of requests
  • Observe dispatcher: running increases, queued grows, and many tasks never complete.

Fix plan? Add parity: make Java wrapper use an explicit check of call.isCanceled() before retry and after catching IOException. Also avoid calling chain.proceed when the call is canceled. Use a shared helper used by both Java and Kotlin wrappers.
Also update docs: call.cancel() semantics and how interceptors should be idempotent and check for isCanceled. Add test in sampleapp that exercises cancellation races.
Created issue #4522: "SDK parity: Java wrapper permits retry after cancel -> dispatcher leaks" - https://git.internal/redwood/issues/4522 :warning:

I pushed a small PR changing the retry interceptor to short-circuit on cancellation and updated the Java CompletableFuture wrapper to propagate cancel state earlier. Link: https://git.internal/redwood/sdk-java/pull/213

I'll review. Also, let's add a note in the migration doc: "If you implement a retry interceptor, ensure it respects call.isCanceled() and thread interruption semantics on Java futures; prefer cooperative cancel on coroutine paths."
For onboarding, add this tiny checklist entry: 1) avoid re-proceed after cancel 2) prefer coroutine-based wrapper on Android 3) include cancellation tests in CI.

RFC idea 1: introduce a small StreamHandle abstraction for the Go SDK to make context ownership and auth/retry behavior explicit. ran into several onboarding issues where users mix background auth refreshers, generator Resume, and backoff retries and end up with confusing hangs or canceled-but-not-closed snapshots.
can you sketch the shape? current Stream(ctx) -> <-chan Token is concise but has these subtle ownership traps.

+1. we keep getting bug reports where support sees long-lived goroutines on customer apps that never called cancel because examples assume ctx propagation is obvious. a thinner API that provides an explicit Close/Stop seems useful.

I like making Err() explicit so callers can see whether the stream ended cleanly vs was stopped. also the AuthRetryPolicy lets users tune how aggressive client.AuthRefresh() will attempt to re-handshake mid-stream.

ergonomics notes: 1) keep a simple helper that returns a channel directly for one-liners; 2) make Stop() safe to call multiple times; 3) Stop() should cancel any internal per-handshake contexts and close underlying http.Transport connections so blocked dial calls are woken up.

how to handle Resume() patterns? some users call Generator.Resume(state) which spawns worker goroutines and expects the stream to finish later. we need to document how Stop() interacts with Resume and with spawned go routines.

doc plan: update generator README with a "Lifecycle and Ownership" section showing three patterns: (A) simple range-based usage (recommended with defer Stop()), (B) Resume() worker pattern (show WaitGroup + Stop signal), (C) long-running server pattern (expose stream metrics + graceful shutdown hook). add a short snippet for auth-refresh best practices: call client.AuthRefresh() only when no stream handshakes are in-flight or use AuthRetryPolicy{MaxAttempts:0} to avoid mid-handshake restarts.

tests: we'll add unit tests that simulate an auth endpoint that occasionally returns 401 during handshake and a token rotator. key assertions: goroutine count no-op after repeated Start/Stop, Stop unblocks blocked dialers, Err() surface matches handshake error types, and Channel-shim parity (old Stream(ctx) channel continues to work via a simple shim that wraps StreamHandle.Tokens()).

sampleapps: update go-sampleapps streaming example to use StreamHandle and show graceful shutdown with context + Stop() + wg.Wait(). also add a tiny stress script that runs rotate+start/stop loops to demonstrate reliability.
compatibility: plan to ship StreamHandle in minor release and keep Stream(ctx) channel shim for at least one release cycle. mark channel shim deprecated in docs and show migration snippet.

ops/support: add a metric active_streams_total (labels: client_id, model) and an internal debug endpoint gated behind env var that lists active stream ids and last-handshake-state. will help debug customer "stuck" tickets.
created draft PR dave/stream-handle-api-proposal (WIP) - build queued

nice. api review: ensure Stop() is deterministic and doesn't race with Next()/Tokens consumption. consider providing a Context() method on StreamHandle that returns an immutable context which is canceled when Stop() runs so helper goroutines can select on it.
good call. we'll add Context() that callers may use for derived operations but note in docs that callers should not cancel it.

i'll add the migration docs and sampleapp edits once the PR is opened. also add a short section in the onboarding guide that emphasizes always pairing streams with Stop()/defer and avoiding auth rotation mid-handshake unless you truly need it.

Quick report — minimal monorepo sample fails only on Vercel edge when sdk is symlinked from workspace. bundler error: "Package subpath './edge' is not defined by \"exports\" in /workspace/packages/js-sdk/package.json".

Repro steps (short):
1) pnpm install (workspace)
2) cd examples/edge-sample && pnpm dev (vercel dev)
3) import Client from 'redwood-inference'
4) runtime throws during build/resolve

Also seeing TS error in sample when hoisted types aren't picked up: "Could not find a declaration file for module 'redwood-inference'" despite types being under packages/js-sdk/dist/types/index.d.ts (pnpm symlinked). Works when we npm pack and install instead of workspace link.

Separate but probably related: auth/retry oddness on edge — our client refreshes token on 401, but fetch wrapper in edge runtime retried the request and triggered concurrent refreshes -> 401 loop. Minimal log:```
[edge] request /api/predict -> 401
[edge] client.refreshToken() start
[edge] retry attempt 1 -> original call also triggers refresh -> stale token used -> 401 repeated
```
Thanks — can you paste the bundler error stack? is this during build or runtime?

Build time (esbuild/rollup in vercel dev). Stack: ```
Error: Package subpath './edge' is not defined by "exports" in /workspace/packages/js-sdk/package.json
    at resolver (/snapshot/rollup/node_modules/resolve/lib/async.js:...)
```

Two quick paths: 1) add explicit export for ./edge to package.json pointing to ESM edge bundle, or 2) provide top-level "module" field + unambiguous entry so bundlers don't try subpath. Edge runtimes often prefer the browser/exports mapping.

Workaround we've used: add a tiny shim package in examples that re-exports the built ESM file with its own package.json (so the bundler resolves a real file, not a symlink). Ugly but fast for demos. Example: packages/examples/edge-shim/package.json -> { "name": "edge-shim", "main": "../js-sdk/dist/index.mjs", "types": "../js-sdk/dist/types/index.d.ts" }
Also for pnpm/ts: add "preserveSymlinks": true in vite/rollup resolver options sometimes helps, but not supported by Vercel build pipeline.

Action items on SDK side:
- Publish a dedicated ./edge export pointing at dist/edge/index.mjs (small bundle optimized for edge).
- Ensure types are declared at package root via "types": "dist/types/index.d.ts" (so TS picks them up even when hoisted).
- Add "module" and "browser" fields to help bundlers.
- Investigate retry logic: make token refresh idempotent (single-flight) and detect in-flight refresh to avoid double-refresh in environments where fetch auto-retries.
SGTM. +1 on single-flight refresh. For edge detection we can check typeof (globalThis.fetch) and request constructor differences but better to make refresh logic resilient regardless of runtime.

quick heads-up — customer on CF Workers hit a hard fail when using our JS SDK. error: `ReferenceError: process is not defined` and `require('crypto')` blew up.
ah okay can you paste the stack / minimal repro?

yup. this is from their bundle step with wrangler:
```
> ReferenceError: process is not defined
    at Object.resolve (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:xxxx)
    at Function.Module._resolveFilename (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:xxx)
    at Module._load (internal/modules/cjs/loader.js:xxx)
    at require (internal/modules/cjs/helpers.js:xx)
    at Object.<anonymous> (/worker/node_modules/redwood/dist/index.cjs:12:20)
```
They import `import Redwood from 'redwood'` in an ESM worker, but rollup/esbuild ended up picking the CJS build which requires `process` and `crypto`.

sounds like we need a worker-friendly entrypoint + conditional exports. CF Workers don't have Node globals (process, Buffer) and they have `globalThis.crypto.subtle` instead of `require('crypto').webcrypto`.

agreed. we should:
- publish an ESM build (module) that avoids Node APIs
- add `exports` map with a `./worker` entry that bundlers can pick
- include a small runtime shim for `crypto` fallback detection
nice. what about TypeScript types? we can't ship multiple `types` per entry, so maybe keep types generic and add `types` reference in the worker file via `/// <reference types="./types-worker" />`?
instead of separate types, we can keep one `.d.ts` that uses `declare module 'redwood/worker'` augmentation. simpler for consumers.

for the crypto shim, simple pattern:
```
const webcrypto = typeof globalThis?.crypto?.subtle !== 'undefined'
  ? globalThis.crypto
  : (typeof require !== 'undefined' && require('crypto')?.webcrypto);
```
Then in worker build tree-shake out the `require('crypto')` path so bundlers won't include it. mark it under `if (typeof process !== 'undefined')` guard.
also watch for `Buffer` usage — we should avoid `Buffer.from` in the worker build. use `Uint8Array` helpers.
