quick report - sampleapp upload is intermittently duplicating POSTs and sometimes crashing after a 401+refresh on Android 15. Repro steps + logs below.
can you paste minimal repro and stack?

repro: 1) start UploadActivity -> large multipart upload streaming from FileInputStream, 2) server returns 401, 3) Authenticator does blocking refresh, 4) toggle network (airplane mode) during refresh. Outcomes seen: either two POST requests land after refresh (duplicate uploads) or crash: IllegalStateException: request body is not repeatable. Logs:
```
2026-03-22 11:04:10.102 D/OkHttp: --> POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/upload
2026-03-22 11:04:10.301 D/OkHttp: <-- 401 https://api.redwood.ai/v1/upload (199ms)
2026-03-22 11:04:10.302 D/Auth: refresh token start
2026-03-22 11:04:10.520 I/Network: airplane mode toggled
2026-03-22 11:04:10.840 D/OkHttp: --> POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/upload (replay)
2026-03-22 11:04:10.840 D/OkHttp: --> POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/upload (duplicate)
2026-03-22 11:04:10.842 E/OkHttp: java.lang.IllegalStateException: request body is not repeatable
```

stack points to RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.createRequestWithUpdatedAuth -> our streaming RequestBody is single-use so replay fails. Client stack: Retrofit with suspend CallAdapter v2, OkHttp Authenticator that invokes tokenProvider.refreshBlocking(), okhttp client has retryOnConnectionFailure(true).

two interacting behaviors here: (A) OkHttp Authenticator will transparently re-issue requests by building a new request from response.request after auth update; (B) Retrofit coroutine adapter v2 can create/clone underlying Calls and coroutines' cancellation/resume semantics can lead to multiple Call instances if not carefully coordinated. Combined with network flaps this yields duplicates.
what's the simplest short-term mitigation we can ship in sampleapp?

short-term we tried two mitigations: 1) move refresh out of Authenticator into an Interceptor with a single-flight refresh (AtomicReference<CompletableDeferred> pattern). This prevents OkHttp from running its transparent retry logic and lets us control when to re-issue requests; 2) implement a ReplayableRequestBody helper that caches the body to disk when stream is larger than a threshold so it can be replayed safely. Both reduced duplicates and avoided crashes in my local runs.
can you paste the single-flight sketch?
runBlocking is ugly but avoided OkHttp Authenticator threads doing network IO. The deferred is completed by a single refresh coroutine started once.
and the ReplayableRequestBody?

simple wrapper that writes the incoming stream to a temp file the first time writeTo() runs and then reads from that file on subsequent writeTo() calls. Only enabled for bodies > threshold to avoid extra IO for tiny files. Clean up after request completes.

longer-term SDK suggestions: 1) provide an official TokenRefreshInterceptor (suspend-friendly) in the Android SDK so users don't need to implement runBlocking hacks; 2) provide a ReplayableRequestBody utility (opt-in) with configurable disk threshold; 3) in onboarding docs call out "Authenticator vs Interceptor" caveat + interactions with retryOnConnectionFailure and Retrofit coroutine adapter v2; 4) consider changing the SDK default for Android clients to `retryOnConnectionFailure(false)` or at least document its side-effects for streaming uploads.
agree. Also add a sampleapp e2e that toggles connectivity mid-refresh to prevent regressions. We should measure perf impact of ReplayableRequestBody and provide guidance.

aha. edge bundler + TS + ESM/CJS interop is biting you. SDK ships conditional exports with both CJS and ESM; TS types sometimes only export named types, so default import can be ambiguous depending on moduleResolution.
quick repro: change to `import * as Redwood from '@redwood-inference/sdk'` or enable `esModuleInterop: true` and `allowSyntheticDefaultImports: true` to let the default import resolve.

Edge build's "moduleResolution": "bundler" (used by many edge runners) resolves types differently.
tried `import * as Redwood` — that fixed the type error locally but edge runtime then complains at startup about default not found (because runtime expects default). weird.

that’s the classic mismatch: runtime default vs types named export. Two options: 1) consume the named exports everywhere (e.g., `import { createClient } from '@redwood-inference/sdk'`) and update samples; or 2) ask SDK team to ship an `export default` typings wrapper that points to the same API.

Heads-up — intermittent schema validation failures in the sample-app when the SDK retry wrapper kicks in for function calls. Repro steps below, seeing the function payload become a string on retry, then the server-side JSON schema validator complains.
Repro: call with `jsonMode: true` + `retry: {retries:2}`. First attempt ok, retry sends body like "{\"title\":\"x\"}" instead of object.

'redwood-oss-1',
  jsonMode: true,
{ name: 'create_issue', schema: issueSchema },

@maria can you paste the raw outgoing http payload when the retry happens? my hunch: the retry wrapper re-serializes the whole request and double-encodes the `body` field. we had a similar pattern in older auth middleware. :eyes:

pasted log (trimmed):
`OUTGOING -> { method: 'POST', path: '/v1/generate', body: '{"model":"redwood-oss-1","input":"...","function_call":"{\"name\":\"create_issue\",\"payload\":\"{\\\"title\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\"}" }' }`

yup that's double-stringified. The retry wrapper currently does `payload = JSON.stringify(req)` before sending, but when it reconstructs req for retry it starts from an already-stringified version. simplest fix: only stringify top-level if not already a string, and ensure `function_call.payload` is kept as object.
test-runner: 1 failing test in `sdk/retry-wrapper.spec.ts` -> failing case: preserves function payload type on retry.

proposed one-liner fix in middleware: `if (typeof req.body !== 'string') req.body = JSON.stringify(req.body)` then `fetch(url, { body: req.body, ... })`. also add helper `cloneRequestForRetry(req)` that deep-clones objects instead of reusing serialized string.

Heads up — I think I found a ctx deadline propagation issue in the Go SDK when using generator streaming + auth refresh. Repro and logs below.

ctx deadline exceeded (expected)

Seems like the HTTP roundtrip / transport refresh path spawns a goroutine that keeps a reference to the request body/response and never observes ctx cancellation, so Recv() never returns.

quick question for clientlib folks — we're trying to make error shapes consistent across node/py SDKs. what's our current rule for mapping HTTP status -> exception class?

short version: 401/403 -> AuthError, 429 -> Throttling/RetryableError, 5xx -> ServerError (retryable by default with backoff). network/connect/timeouts -> NetworkError. but there are nuances for streaming.
got it. for streaming, if the connection drops mid-stream should we return a streaming-specific error with the original request id? e.g. StreamingInterrupted(request_id=...)
yes include the request id always. we add X-Request-ID header on the wire and surface it on exceptions as .request_id. that helps correlate with serverside logs.
+1. also, prefer not to lose partial events — SDK should emit a final error event with the req id and number of tokens delivered. something like: `StreamingError: reason, request_id, delivered=42`
makes sense. any guidance on what the debug logs should include for retries?

local debug log line we use in other SDKs: `level=DEBUG ts=... route=/v1/generate model=rdw-base seq_len=128 req_id=abcd-1234 attempt=2 error="429 Too Many Requests" backoff_ms=800` — include attempt count and backoff.
and capture the raw response body for non-2xx in debug mode (redact PII) so product can triage mapping errors to server responses. avoid logging full prompt/token content.
about exception API: should exceptions be typed (class hierarchy) or just error.code strings? consumers often `isinstance(e, RetryableError)` in our libs.

prefer classes + codes. i.e. classes for control flow (RetryableError, AuthError, BadRequestError) and a `.code` string for more specific subtypes (e.g., "quota_exhausted"). makes switching languages easier.

language notes: in JS we expose both `e instanceof RetryableError` and `e.code`. in py we subclass and set `e.code` too. in go we return typed errors via sentinel vars and wrapper `errors.Is` semantics.

Heads-up — during the latest HF->Redwood bring-up for opt-2.7B we hit a subtle tool-calling tokenization problem.
ugh, details?
When converting the HF chat templates we kept the HF special tokens (`<|tool_start|>`, `<|tool_end|>`) as-is. But tokenizer merges them weirdly after quantized ops.
Can you paste an example of the merge?

Sure — root prompt:
```
System: You are an assistant.

Run tool X with args -> <|tool_start|>{\"op\":\"search\",\"q\":\"redwood\"}<|tool_end|>
```
After tokenizing+quantize step the model sees `\"<|tool_start|>{\"op\":\"search\",...` as a single token boundary which breaks the runtime parser expecting distinct role tokens.
That would definitely break our JSON-mode extraction. We saw 8% failure on a small eval set.
Is this tokenizer-specific? Which HF tokenizer are we converting from?
`tiktoken`-style BPE from HF's `tokenizer.json` (from community model). The config.json had `added_tokens` defined in a way that conflated `tool_start` and adjacent punctuation.
Two quick suggestions: 1) add explicit whitespace around tool markers in conversion. 2) register the special tokens as separate `added_tokens` entries with `single_word=false`.
Tried both. Adding whitespace helped but is fragile for existing prompts. Marking as non-single-word works but some quantization kernels still fuse tokens for speed.
Could we switch to different delimiter tokens that are guaranteed to be reserved? e.g., `<<TOOL_START>>`?
That changes prompt templates and breaks backward compat with customers. Not ideal.
Nice. Could we instead canonicalize to Redwood's JSON-mode tokens? e.g., wrap tools with `<RWD_TOOL_START>` and `<RWD_TOOL_END>` in the internal format, then map back at output?

Yeah that's what we landed on: conversion step maps HF tags -> Redwood guarded tokens, marks them in the config as `added_tokens` with `single_word=false`, and runtime enforces `protect_tags` idempotently.
Any perf hit?

Minimal — the regex is cheap. Biggest risk was quantized kernel fusing during KV cache tokenization in generation. To mitigate, we inserted a tiny no-op byte escape `\uE000` between tag and JSON start when serializing internal tool calls; the byte is stripped before runtime parse.
Do we have eval results after the fix?
Yes — on the Canary eval set: tool-calling success went from 92% -> 99.4%. Regression rate for normal chat decreased slightly (0.4%) due to extra whitespace but within threshold.

Quick bug from onboarding sample-app. We noticed rerank scores were wrong for a small subset of docs. Repro: batch of 3, one item retried, final vectors paired by position end up misaligned.
Which helper + sdk? Node? Rust?

Node helper (embed-util v1.1). Behavior: it sends chunks concurrently, and if a single item is retried the helper appends the single response when it arrives. If that arrives before another chunk finishes we get a scrambled order. Example timeline: send [a,b] and [c]; b times out, retry b solo; responses arrive: [a,b-from-chunk], b-retry, c. Helper push => [a,b,b,c]? (we had duplicated positions because server returned position-only arrays and helper merged naively).

Duplication plus mis-ordering is worse. Sounds like the helper both concatenates and doesn't dedupe by id. Two fast fixes: 1) preserve index mapping and place results into preallocated array slots; 2) attach a transient request id or original index in the outbound envelope so merging can match items.
Also raise an idempotency header on retries so server can dedupe if it supports that behavior. This prevents duplicate vectors if a retry hits after the original landed.

Proposed patch: preallocate results = new Array(items.length), record mapping of item -> idx before send, and on any response place vectors into results[idx]. Also, when retrying attach a small header `x-idempotency-key: <item-guid>` and expose a feature flag `echo_items:true` so server can return [{id, embedding}] if callers opt-in.

Good. Add unit tests that randomize response delays and assert final ordering equals input order and no duplicates. Also test the duplicate-dedup behavior when idempotency header is honored by the server.

can you paste a tiny repro? most of these are either tsconfig/moduleResolution or bundler-related.
ugh. that pattern smells like a bundler transpile that emits ESM with isolatedModules semantics (esbuild/rollup) and loses overloads. are you using `tsup` or `esbuild`?
esbuild via our sample template. we ship only `.mjs` for edge, `.cjs` for node.

bundlers that do transpile-only (esbuild) will sometimes use TS transforms that don't preserve declaration/type metadata — overload resolution at emit time can differ. two practical fixes: 1) compile with `tsc` to emit d.ts and ship those alongside the .mjs; 2) avoid relying on overloads + inference: require explicit generic parameter or return type in public APIs.

small workaround: change the exported API shape to a single generic with a discriminant so inference is stable, e.g. `callApi<T extends object, U = unknown>(opts: { mode: "simple" | "meta"; input: T; meta?: U })` — not ideal but stable across bundlers.

another wrinkle — the edge runtime sample's package.json has `exports` pointing to one file and our published types point to `types: ./dist/index.d.ts`. When we only ship a single d.ts that assumes CJS resolution, tsserver in ESM projects will sometimes fallback. could be part of the inconsistency.

for onboarding/samples we should: update sample to build `d.ts` with `declaration: true`, publish per-entrypoint types (node vs edge) and add a note in readme about `typesVersions` for consumers. that should reduce friction.
also check `isolatedModules` in tsconfig — if true then certain patterns get erased. esbuild doesn't support overloads when `isolatedModules` is set the wrong way.

one more subtlety: our SDK auth wrapper returns `Promise<AuthContext | undefined>`, and in edge the `undefined` branch is getting widened to `any` in some callsites because of chained overloads + `unknown`/`any` interplay. suggestion: prefer `unknown` inside internals and only assert to `any` at explicit opt-in surfaces.

Heads up — hitting a hang when cancelling a streaming call in py SDK v0.24.1 (uvloop). Repro below, happens reliably for me.

Repro (simplified):
```py
# run under uvloop/asyncio, python 3.11
async def worker(client):
    stream = await client.stream("completion", model=\"open-llm\")
    try:
        async for chunk in stream:
            process(chunk)
    finally:
        # this never gets called when task.cancel() races with next chunk
        await stream.aclose()
# in main test harness
task = asyncio.create_task(worker(client))
await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
task.cancel()  # sometimes cancels cleanly, sometimes the event loop spins and sockets stay open
```
Confirmed locally. When it hangs the event loop goes to ~100% on one core and the socket stays in ESTABLISHED for a long time.

Sounds like generator finalizer / aclose path isn't being hit on CancelledError. Two quick notes: (1) SSE/chunked streams expose an AsyncIterator but not an AsyncGenerator with a close method, so explicit aclose() isn't always available via typing. (2) We should expose an async context manager API so `async with client.stream(...) as s:` calls close reliably.
Filed an issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/issues/3456 — summary: async stream cancels can leak socket / never run finalizers. Adding @tyler to triage.
Ticket created: DX-8794 (priority: medium)

Quick patch that helped me in local tests: catch CancelledError and call aclose inside the except/finally. Example:
```py
stream = await client.stream(...)
try:
    async for c in stream:
        ...
except asyncio.CancelledError:
    await stream.aclose()
    raise
finally:
    # defensive if not already closed
    if hasattr(stream, 'aclose'):
        await stream.aclose()
```
This is ugly but reduces leaks.
FWIW this only repros in SSE (chunked) mode for me, not the websocket path. SDK version pinned to 0.24.1-beta.

Action items: (1) add AsyncContextManager wrapper around streaming API, (2) ensure the iterator object implements `aclose()` and that our generated typing surfaces it (AsyncIterator vs AsyncGenerator), (3) add a unit test that cancels during a chunk boundary.

quick question — we've got a reproducible case where a streaming request that we abort client-side often ends up with ECONNRESET on the node side and the kernel keeps the socket in CLOSE_WAIT for a while. wondering if the SDK should explicitly tear down the socket on abort or try to leave keepalive intact so subsequent requests reuse it.

short answer: it depends on transport and semantics. long answer: for Node http/1.1 keepalive, destroying the socket on abort is usually fine for non-idempotent calls; for http2 or multiplexed transports you should try to gracefully cancel the stream instead of nuking the connection.

fwiw in our Node SDK code we currently call `req.destroy(new Error('aborted'))` when AbortController fires for streaming sends — that closes the socket. it's simpler but causes connection churn under heavy aborts.
yeah that's exactly what we saw. lots of socket churn + slower tail latency. any options?

options: (1) for http/1.1 fetch-based flows, let the fetch abort signal do its thing (it typically closes the request but doesn't always drop the underlying connection immediately), (2) for multiplexed transports (http2/grpc) cancel the stream at protocol level (rst_stream for http2) so the connection stays healthy, (3) teach the connection pool to prefer draining sockets with recent resets so we avoid reusing bad ones, (4) add a short debounce on aborts for high-frequency cancellations (if user reuses controller quickly).
question: how do we detect "should we do protocol-level cancel vs socket destroy" in a unified SDK API? we don't want callers to worry about it.

agree. SDK surface should be the same: `AbortController` or `signal`. Internally, each transport adapter decides. Example heuristics: if transport supports cancel/stream-id -> send protocol cancel; else -> destroy socket. Also add a config `transport.onAbort = 'graceful'|'force'|'auto'` for advanced users.
nice. what about proxies/load-balancers that aggressively close idle streams? we saw RST_STREAM from intermediary after client abort and the server still receives partial data.

proxies are the wild card. best practice: on abort, flush any request-level metadata and send a protocol-level cancel if available. Also increment a telemetry counter so we can spot networks/proxies that mishandle cancels.
deploy-notify: ran integration tests against staging-adapter v1.9.2. streaming-abort test flaked 1/20. logs pushed to /artifacts/1748102468/stream-abort-flake.log

yes, we should only auto-retry if the operation is idempotent (embeddings, pure reads). for chat/generate (non-idempotent) surface a clear error and expose a helper `shouldRetryOnClientAbort(err, opts)` for app-level logic.

filing follow-ups: 1) add transport-level abort strategy enum + docs, 2) add telemetry counter for aborted-streams vs resets, 3) tweak node fetch adapter to avoid socket.destroy unless force. i'll open PRs.

Heads-up: hit a nasty edge with streaming through our new edge-proxy. Multibyte UTF-8 characters (emoji) are getting split across TCP frames and our SDKs sometimes emit � or raise decode errors. Also the proxy injects periodic ":keepalive" comment lines which sometimes land inside a multibyte sequence.
ouch. which sdk/runtime? can you paste a tiny raw capture?

Node & Python. raw bytes (simplified hex view):
```
64 61 74 61 3a 20 7b 22 74 6f 6b 65 6e 22 3a 22 5f f0 9f 98
# <-- socket chunk boundary
9a 22 7d 0a 0a
:keepalive
64 61 74 61 3a 20 5b 44 4f 4e 45 5d 0a 0a
```
The 3-byte emoji sequence is split between packets (f0 9f 98 | 9a). When the comment line arrives between them some decoders produce U+FFFD and parsed tokens break.

that's tricky. We should treat the stream as bytes until we have full UTF-8 codepoints for each event payload. Right now node-sdk uses text streaming and the runtime's TextDecoder which can handle stream mode, but our code calls decode() per recv chunk. If decode() receives an incomplete sequence it replaces by the replacement char unless streaming mode is used.

python's decode('utf-8') on bytes will raise if errors='strict', but many libs use errors='replace' for robustness which yields �. We want stable semantics: never emit replacement chars for incomplete codepoints; instead defer decoding until the event boundary is complete (or until we've got enough bytes). Also need to ensure comment lines starting with ':' are parsed at the byte level and don't split multibyte sequences.

Proposed approach: 1) switch to byte-buffered SSE parser: accumulate bytes and only attempt UTF-8 decode for a complete line (i.e., when we detect '\n' or '\r\n'). 2) use incremental decoders (TextDecoder in streaming mode or codecs.incrementaldecoder in python) so partial codepoints are buffered by decoder instead of replaced. 3) ensure comment detection is done after a successful decode of the full line.
Also watch out for HTTP/2 DATA frame coalescing at the proxy. Some proxies will re-chunk differently in real networks; tests should randomize chunk boundaries.
Issue #7120 created by fiona - title: streaming: handle split UTF-8 sequences + inline keepalive comments injected by proxy; add tests and incremental decoding.

I opened PR #4312 with a small refactor: byte-buffered base parser + incremental decoder use for node/python. Included randomized chunking tests and a quick manual sample for the edge-proxy config. Local runs + CI pass.

Nice. A couple of safety nits: 1) limit incremental decoder buffer size to avoid unbounded memory if we never see newline, 2) log a debug event when we see lots of partial bytes without newline (helpful for ops).
Agreed. Also update SDK quickstart to mention that the streaming path is byte-safe and recommend using SDK helpers rather than naive text streaming for polyfilled runtimes.

PR #4312 merged to main by mauro - changelog: fix(sdk): byte-buffer SSE parser and use incremental UTF-8 decoding to avoid replacement characters when multibyte codepoints are split; add randomized chunk tests and docs.
Verified in staging with edge-proxy + 1k randomized chunk trials. No replacement chars and no extra empty tokens. thanks :tada:

Heads-up: I found a reproducible bug where AsyncClient streaming + retry leads to a suppressed CancelledError and user code never sees the final exception. repro and notes below. anyone run into this?

minimal repro (local flaky backend to trigger 5xx):
```py
import asyncio
async def consume(gen):
    async for chunk in gen:
        print('got', chunk)
async def main():
    gen = client.generate_stream('hello', idempotency_key='k-1')
    t = asyncio.create_task(consume(gen))
    await asyncio.sleep(0.15)  # let stream start and maybe hit 5xx/replay
    await client.close()  # simulate app shutdown while replay in-flight
    await t
```
observed log line: `Task exception was never retrieved` pointing at AsyncClient._stream_to_queue -> CancelledError. user sees partial output from the `async for` and no exception raised.
which sdk version? can you paste the full traceback?

v0.12.3. log snippet:
```
Task exception was never retrieved

<Task finished name='Task-17' coro=<AsyncClient._stream_to_queue() done, defined at /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/redwood_sdk/async_client.py:402> exception=CancelledError()>
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/.../site-packages/redwood_sdk/async_client.py", line 410, in _stream_to_queue
    chunk = await resp.content.readchunk()
asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError
```
The background task is cancelled during replay/close and the exception isn't bubbled out of the async generator.

This matches a prior bug: we spawn a background task to push stream chunks into a queue and we cancel tasks in close() but don't await them, leaving unhandled exceptions. Two issues: (1) noisy suppressed exceptions in logs, (2) generator semantics — the consumer should get an exception for fatal errors.
And the retry/replay logic complicates it: on transient 5xx we attempt a replay using the idempotency token and feed cached prefix chunks; if we cancel mid-replay we can leave a producer orphaned.
Exactly. repro triggered a 502 after some cached chunks were emitted; client tried to replay, then I called close(). result: partial output, no exception.

Proposed immediate mitigation: ensure produced tasks are awaited on generator close or attach done-callbacks that re-raise/log exceptions so they don't become "Task exception was never retrieved". Longer-term: change generator plumbing to await producer completion and re-raise its exception from the generator.

Implementation plan: 1) hotfix -> add `task.add_done_callback(_ensure_log_and_raise)` and track tasks to await them in close() (non-breaking). 2) follow-up -> revamp generate_stream to use `asyncio.TaskGroup` (Python 3.11+) or an explicit awaitable producer/consumer pattern guaranteeing exceptions propagate to the async iterator consumer. add tests.

Typing/SDK notes: generate_stream is annotated as `AsyncIterator[str]`. If we change behavior to raise on underlying transport/retry errors that's consistent with iterator semantics, but we should document raised exceptions (ClientConnectionError, RetryError) in docstrings and update stubs/py.typed. onboarding docs should call out that streams can raise on transient failures.
This impacts sample apps: users see truncated model outputs and assume hallucination. P0 DX hit. we should ship the hotfix as a patch release on 0.12.x if tests pass.

One design choice: (A) make streams raise on first unrecoverable error (semantic change, preferred), or (B) keep returning partial output and emit a terminal `error` chunk (backwards compatible for some consumers). I favor (A) — aligns with Python iterator error semantics.

I'll draft a PR implementing the hotfix + tests that assert (i) `async for` raises RetryError on server 5xx during replay, and (ii) no "Task exception was never retrieved" emitted in logs. also include an integration test for idempotency token: ensure replay uses same token and doesn't double-execute non-idempotent endpoints.

Can we also emit telemetry: `replay.attempt`, `replay.success`, `replay.failure` events with idempotency token and model/version metadata? ops asked for visibility into replays causing partial outputs.

Hey team — getting 400s when calling the create-invoice tool. Error: \"tool_args_parse_error: Unexpected token '\\' in JSON at position 0\". Started after we bumped the client lib.
Can you paste the exact request (curl or SDK snippet)?

Sure, here's the curl we used:
```
curl -i -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model":"redwood-chat-1",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"create invoice"}],
    "tool_call":{"name":"create-invoice","arguments":"{'amount': 1000, 'currency':'USD',}"}
  }'
```

Ah — looks like `arguments` was sent as a string that contains single quotes + a trailing comma. Our tool-args parsing expects strict JSON (double quotes, no trailing commas). If you send `arguments` as a JSON object it should work. Example: `\"arguments\": {\"amount\":1000, \"currency\":\"USD\"}`
We build the string in Ruby and interpolation produced the single quotes: `invoice_args = "{'amount': #{amt}, 'currency':'USD',}"` — not great hindsight.

Reproduced locally. Server side log: `JSON.parse` error -> \"Unexpected token ' in JSON at 0\". Request_id=rcw-9f3a. The code path expects either a proper JSON object or a JSON string with double quotes. Trailing comma also blows up many parsers.

Short-term workarounds: 1) send `arguments` as a native object (preferred), 2) if you must send a string, ensure you generate it with double quotes and no trailing comma (`JSON.generate` in Ruby), 3) as a last resort use a pre-send sanitizer.

Example fixes for Ruby:
```ruby
# preferred: send a real object
payload[:tool_call] = { name: \"create-invoice\", arguments: { amount: 1000, currency: \"USD\" } }
# or explicitly serialize to strict JSON
payload[:tool_call][:arguments] = JSON.generate({ amount: 1000, currency: \"USD\" })

quick q — my Go client is getting 401s calling the hosted API. I set Authorization: Basic <base64(apiKey)> but it still fails. anyone seen this?
common trap: Basic expects base64(username:password). if you're using API key as the username and no password, you must include the trailing colon before encoding. e.g. base64('sk-...:')

yup. also watch how you build the env var. if you do `echo 'sk-xxx' > /tmp/key` and then `cat /tmp/key | base64` you'll get a newline in the value unless you used `echo -n`. that changes the header payload.
concrete examples —
`curl -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'sk-ABC123:' | base64)` https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate`

`const auth = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(process.env.RW_API_KEY + ':').toString('base64'); fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: auth } })`
python: `import os, base64
api = os.environ.get('RW_API_KEY')
header = 'Basic ' + base64.b64encode((api + ':').encode()).decode()`

`api := os.Getenv("RW_API_KEY")
auth := "Basic " + base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(api+":"))
req.Header.Set("Authorization", auth)`

another gotcha: some folks accidentally include surrounding quotes in the env var. e.g. export RW_API_KEY="sk-..." -> the value contains the quotes if your runtime reads raw from some config file. always print/debug with something like `printf '%s' "$RW_API_KEY" | xxd` to inspect hidden bytes.
ahhh — I was doing `echo $KEY` and it looked fine but I pasted from a text editor that added CRLF.
CRLF will break the base64 output if not stripped. on mac/linux use `tr -d '\r'` when cleaning a file. windows powershell: `$env:RW_API_KEY = (Get-Content key.txt -Raw).Trim()`

also note that some HTTP helper libraries let you do `client.SetBasicAuth(user, pass)` which will do the base64 and prefix for you. if you use that, pass the api key as the username and an empty string for password. in Go: `req.SetBasicAuth(apiKey, "")`
small security PSA: avoid printing full api keys in logs. When debugging, base64 encode and compare prefixes, or show lengths.

also noticed increased variance in inter-arrival for some customer flows (bursty web UI). With hold_ms=60, small requests often wait close to the full hold window before being released, causing the tail.

this is the classic hold-vs-size tradeoff. Increasing hold reduces wasted kernels and improves throughput for long prompts, but for tiny prompt workloads it increases tail. There are a few mitigations we typically consider:
- per-route hold_ms (lower for low-latency routes)
- fast-path for tiny requests: if token_count <= 64, bypass batching or use immediate-release path
- max-batch-delay adaptive: adjust hold based on observed inter-arrival percentiles (e.g., target 90th inter-arrival < hold)
- jitter/coalesce-timeout smoothing to avoid synchronized releases
quick note: KV cache warmup isn't the issue here (these are short contexts). This is pure batching hold time causing head-of-line waits.

That meminfo is classic fragmentation — lots of free overall but no contiguous chunk. Happens when KV cache grows and we then allocate big batched tensors. Short-term mitigations: lower the default batch_size to 2 for canary and disable kv-prefetch for the spectral canary.

On the quant side, try an MLP-region int8 fallback. I ran this pattern earlier; it recovers quality in codegen for similar models. Example override:

int8
serve_defaults:

2
  max_new_tokens_default: 128

false
```

I launched two experiments: E1 = batch_size=2 + kv_prefetch=false + int4 per-channel calibration (job 491); E2 = batch_size=4 + MLP layers 150-200 forced int8 + request-level compaction after each call (job 492).

E2 queued on pool-canary-b, job id 492.

Also flip disable_continuous_batching=true for these canary jobs to avoid mixing seq lengths (that tends to create small holes). If E1 still fails, try tuning allocator thresholds so larger blocks are returned to CUDA sooner.

Suggested allocator hints:
``
cuda_allocator:

16m
  direct_free_threshold: 128m
```
This encourages the runtime to free larger slabs back instead of keeping tiny fragments.

Early results: E1 recovers most quality (BLEU ~98% of baseline) and no OOMs so far; E2 recovers quality fully (BLEU ~101% vs baseline) but with a 10-15% latency increase. Tradeoff looks like int8 fallback is best for correctness; smaller batch to avoid OOMs.

- PAGE (Sev2): p95 +15% sustained 15m (min N=500) OR tokens/sec -15% sustained 15m (min N=500)
- PAGE (Sev1): p95 +25% sustained 15m (min N=500) AND affects >=2 regions OR top-model in us-east

Root cause (current best understanding)
- Demo tenant default quotas (RPS + tokens/min) were set assuming single-session usage.
- In practice, the demo environment now has:
  1) synthetic traffic generator (to keep Console populated),
  2) SE demo runner (scripted scenario),
  3) occasional parallel demos / “someone else testing”.
- Those stacked loads pushed us over the per-project rate limit, triggering 429s.
- Healthcheck endpoint reported “OK” because it only checked model availability + dashboard ingestion, not quota headroom / current throttling.

Contributing factors
- The new traffic generator preset is “realistic” but we didn’t re-validate quotas after enabling it by default.
- Lack of a clear “parallel demo” guardrail (separate projects/keys or enforced namespaces) meant cross-demo noise.
- Console dashboards lagged; SEs couldn’t quickly tell if 429s were from their workload vs background traffic.

What went well
- Field team escalated quickly with concrete error output.
- Mitigation was straightforward once we found the limiter.
- We already have a demo-only healthcheck endpoint in-flight; we can extend it rather than inventing net-new.

What went poorly
- Healthcheck gave a false sense of safety (green but no quota signal).
- Quota defaults weren’t aligned to demo reality.
- We didn’t have a single “stop synthetic traffic now” button documented for SEs.

Quick follow-up from today's all-hands Q&A about APAC capacity and autoscaler behavior. Dropping concise answers + action items.

Explain burst impact: burst is a spot-backed shared pool for Hosted only. It never reclaims Dedicated reservations.

Data residency controls?

Billing: no surprise egress. Console will show projected cross-region egress and require opt-in for auto-failover; we'll also emit alerts when burst spend > threshold.
Cold-start SLOs: node provision target <= 120s in some APAC regions; model warm-up median: ~20s (7B), ~40s (13B), ~80s (70B). We pre-warm top variants.

CI turned red for PR #4129 — only `e2e/browser` job failed (timeout in puppeteer). Is there a quick way to rerun that axis without rebuilding images?
PR #4129 — workflow `ci/pipeline` run 12345 failed: `e2e/browser` (exit 1). Artifact: /artifacts/12345/e2e/video.mp4. Logs show `TimeoutError: Navigation timeout of 30000 ms exceeded`.

You can do a job-level rerun with preserve-image to avoid full rebuild:```bash
cictl rerun --run 12345 --jobs e2e/browser --preserve-image
```That will re-execute only that job and keep the image/cache.

If you suspect flake, add a small repeat to reduce noise:```bash
cictl rerun --run 12345 --jobs e2e/browser --preserve-image --repeat 3
```Also `--preserve-image` keeps docker layers and wheel caches.
quick q — does `--preserve-image` also keep test fixtures/artifacts from previous steps (like KV caches)?

`--preserve-image` keeps the built container. For in-run caches (test caches, kv), add `--keep-cache`. If you actually need a fresh compile but want to skip unrelated stages, use `--rebuild-only e2e/browser` (this rebuilds image for that job only).

Another option: in GH UI you can rerun a single job from the run page (3-dot menu) — that mirrors `cictl` behavior. For matrix jobs you can pick an axis there. If it's environment-related, check screenshots/video first.

Quick triage checklist: 1) inspect video/screenshot and the failing test trace, 2) try local repro (`yarn test:e2e --grep "login flow" --headless`), 3) rerun single job with `--preserve-image`, 4) if it fails repeatedly, file a bisect and mark `flaky/test` and request oncall to bisect.

here’s a strawman:
- offered = rate(tokens_requested_total[5m])
- achieved = rate(tokens_emitted_total[5m])
- eligible = offered >= (0.9 * committed_floor_tokens_per_sec)
- sli = achieved / committed_floor, but only over eligible samples
We can implement as: `sum_over_time((achieved >= floor) and eligible)[window] / sum_over_time(eligible)[window]`

Dropping this here for on-call review: rollback runbook for optimization configs is basically done, but we need to decide *who* can trigger rollback during Sev events.
Runbook draft says “Optimization Change Operator” but that’s too narrow for Sev1 at 3am. We need something that’s safe + auditable.
+1. If p99 is on fire after a config apply, SRE oncall needs a deterministic way to undo without waiting for someone w/ a niche role.
From product side: we told a couple enterprise prospects “one-click rollback,” but we also promised strong access controls. So “anyone” is a no.
RBAC currently has `optimization_config.rollback` permission planned under the “optimization change operator” bundle (PM-902 / PR-20070). We can add a second role for SRE oncall / incident commander.

Security POV: rollback is a production change. I’m okay with SRE oncall having rollback *if*:
- scoped to Hosted/Dedicated only (control plane managed)
- requires reason + incident ID (or at least change ticket)
- emits audit event w/ request_id + actor + previous_version + target_version + scope
- optional: 2-person rule for Sev0/Sev1 (approve + execute)
On the API side we can require `reason` + `actor_context` and propagate `incident_id` into audit payload. Console already planned to do “type-to-confirm”.
Console UX can enforce “type ROLLBACK + tenant/model/region scope” and require selecting a prior known-good version. But RBAC is the real gate.

Release eng concern: we’ll get paged for latency regressions during release trains too. If rollback requires a special person, it’ll slow MTTR. But also we don’t want casual rollbacks for non-incidents.

Can we distinguish:
- Sev0/Sev1 incident mitigation (fast path)
- non-incident change (normal approvals)

Yes. RBAC can’t read “incident severity” by itself, but we can implement a “break-glass” role for oncall, and policy/process says you only use it for Sev1+. Then we rely on audit + monitoring to catch misuse.
“break-glass” is fine if time-bound and heavily audited. I’d prefer we keep it narrow: rollback only (not apply/promote). Also add a cooldown so you can’t thrash.
Cooldown makes sense. But please don’t block multiple rollbacks if the first rollback doesn’t fully propagate (mixed worker state). Runbook has step “verify active version stabilized.”
Runtime applier is idempotent now (PR-19918) and we fixed the apply/rollback race (PR-20111). Still, we should prevent rapid flip-flopping unless you explicitly override.

Proposal:
1) Default: Only “Optimization Change Operator” can rollback (day-to-day).
2) Add role “SRE Oncall (break-glass)” that grants `optimization_config.rollback` for Hosted/Dedicated.
3) Policy: break-glass use only during Sev0/Sev1 or upon IC request.
4) Console/API require `reason` and `incident_id` when actor has break-glass role.
5) Audit event emitted always.
Works for me as long as for customers (tenant admins) it’s separate. They can only rollback within their tenant scope anyway.
Yep, customer admins get tenant-scoped permission in their org. This thread is about internal Redwood on-call.
One nuance: console needs to show the rollback button for oncall even if they’re not “optimization operator.” So RBAC needs to be clean; no hidden “admin” flags.
What about Dedicated accounts with customer-managed oncall contacts? We don’t want Redwood SRE rolling back without notifying them.
For Dedicated: runbook already says “notify customer on-call channel if Sev1+ and mitigation impacts config.” But permission-wise it’s the same (still Redwood control plane).
Add to runbook: for Dedicated/Private, ensure you have correct account + scope. We’ve had mis-scope incidents (wrong region) before.

Yup, that’s in DES-213 copy: “This will revert X tenants / Y models / Z regions to version vNNN.” Also we can highlight if rollback target is not “promoted” / not last known-good.

Comms Lead training Q&A thread. Drop questions here as you go through the deck/runbook. Biggest topic last session: what to do when root cause is unknown + we’re actively mitigating.
🙋‍♀️ When we’re in that awkward phase: dashboards red, we’re traffic shifting / rolling back, but we don’t know RC yet… do we post “Mitigating” or stay “Investigating” until we’re confident?
+1. Also what do we *say* about mitigations without speculating / leaking details?

Good question. Default guidance:
- Use **Investigating** until you can state a *fact* about what’s happening (symptom) and what we’re doing (action), without guessing cause.
- You can move to **Mitigating** once we’ve started a concrete mitigation and have evidence it’s helping OR it’s the primary active workstream.
- You do **not** need root cause to say “we’re applying mitigations.”
the thing we’re optimizing for is clarity + tempo, not perfect certainty. “Mitigating” can basically mean “we’re taking steps to reduce impact” even if RC unknown.
ok, but what’s the line between “action” and “speculation”? e.g. we flipped fallback, or shifted traffic to another region.
and do we mention “failover” or “capacity” publicly? sometimes those are sensitive.
on sensitivity: avoid anything that implies customer-specific capacity constraints or “we ran out of GPUs.” Better to frame as “traffic is being rerouted / we’re scaling capacity” without details.
from Support side, customers mainly want: what’s broken, where, what’s the workaround, and when they’ll hear next. They do NOT need kernel-level explanations.

yep. A good pattern when RC unknown:
1) symptom + component/region
2) mitigation *in progress* (what we’re doing, high-level)
3) workaround (if safe)
4) next update ETA
also keep it consistent with signals. If it’s latency-only and errors are fine, don’t say “outage.” Say “degraded performance / elevated latency.”
can we get example copy blocks? it’s easier to follow with concrete text.

example “Investigating” when RC unknown:
“Investigating: We’re investigating elevated error rates impacting **Hosted API → Streaming (us-east)**. We’ve engaged on-call engineers and are working to mitigate. Next update within 30 minutes or sooner.”

example “Mitigating” without RC:
“Mitigating: We’ve identified a potential mitigation path and are actively applying changes to reduce impact to **Hosted API → Streaming (us-east)**. Some users may continue to see increased disconnects while changes roll out. Next update within 30 minutes or sooner.”
that “potential mitigation path” line is nice. doesn’t overpromise.
Should we ever say “we believe” / “likely” in public updates?

sparingly. “We believe” is ok if it’s tied to an observable symptom (e.g., “we believe this is related to elevated upstream timeouts”) but avoid “likely hardware issue” / “probably provider” unless confirmed and ok’d.
+ avoid naming vendors/providers in public comms unless Legal/Security has pre-approved wording.
incident-bot will help here. The draft templates intentionally avoid causal language and keep the mitigation text high-level. (PR-19344)
(bot) Reminder: Comms Lead target TTFU is 5 minutes for Sev0/Sev1. Use the Investigating template if details are still emerging.
If you can include a workaround, even minimal, it reduces tickets a lot. For streaming: “retry” / “temporarily use non-stream responses” is helpful if accurate.
what if we don’t know a workaround yet? i don’t want to suggest “retry” if it makes things worse.
then don’t. Don’t invent workarounds. You can say “We’ll share workarounds as we confirm them.”
and if retries increase load, better to say “Some requests may fail; please use exponential backoff” only if SRE/IC agrees.
approval flow question: if we’re posting Mitigating without RC, does it need Support approval?

no approval needed for first Investigating. For Sev0/Sev1:
- Investigating: publish immediately.
- Identified/Mitigating: no formal approval required, but sanity check in #incidents if there’s time.
- Resolved: IC + Comms Lead must agree it’s actually stable; loop Support lead if there’s any ambiguity.
what about when the mitigation is “rollback” but we’re unsure it’ll work. ok to say rollback?
yes, at a high level: “We’re rolling back a recent change” is fine. Avoid IDs/versions unless already public. Don’t say “bad deploy” unless confirmed.
and when we’re doing traffic shifting across regions? customers interpret that as “region down.”

you can say “We’re rerouting traffic to reduce impact” but keep component/region status aligned to *experienced impact*. If us-east users are impacted, mark us-east degraded even if mitigation is routing elsewhere.
+ keep the component scope tight. If it’s only Streaming, don’t mark the whole Hosted API component.
question on wording: “partial outage” vs “degraded performance” when errors are spiky but not total.

use the thresholds guidance (burn-rate / sustained error %). If it’s intermittent elevated errors and customers are failing requests, “Degraded Performance” is usually right; “Partial Outage” when a meaningful subset consistently cannot use the feature.
Support will ask: “is it safe to tell customers it’s partial outage?” We’d rather you underclaim early and correct upward than overclaim and backtrack.
if root cause unknown but we’ve stabilized, do we go to Monitoring? what do we say?

yes. “Monitoring” is for “mitigation applied, impact trending down, watching to ensure stability.” Example:
“Monitoring: Mitigations have been applied and error rates are returning to normal for **Hosted API → Streaming (us-east)**. We’re monitoring closely to ensure continued recovery. Next update within 60 minutes or sooner.”
cool. also: please confirm we should always include next update time.
yes. It’s part of consistency + reduces refresh anxiety.
fwiw we’re adding a bot reminder if an incident hasn’t had a public update in 30 mins during active phases.
(bot) Tip: You can paste `INVESTIGATING_MIN` / `MITIGATING_MIN` blocks from the templates doc. Draft automation is rolling out in incident-bot next sprint.
dedicated/private question: if it’s a subset of Dedicated clusters, do we post to public status?

depends. General rule: public status page can reflect “Dedicated” at a high level when there’s broad impact, but avoid customer-identifying details. For single-tenant isolated issues, we usually handle via Support/CS direct comms + post-incident summary if policy requires.
and if a dedicated customer is escalating, route through the escalation playbook. Support/CS owns direct customer updates; Comms Lead owns status page.

Hey team — first-day blocker. Windows VPN connects fine, but from WSL (Ubuntu) I can't reach our internal git server (git.internal.redwood.dev). Windows `git clone` works, WSL times out. Using Okta + AnyConnect (split-tunnel). Anyone seen this?
hey @alex.p — yep this is common with WSL2. Quick q: which distro/version and are you on WSL1 or WSL2? Also paste `ip route` and `cat /etc/resolv.conf` from WSL if you can.

WSL2, Ubuntu 22.04. `ip route` shows default via 172.20.48.1 dev eth0, no route for 10.40.0.0/16. `cat /etc/resolv.conf` shows nameserver 172.20.48.1. Windows `route print` shows routes for 10.40.0.0 via the VPN adapter. So looks like windows has the route but WSL doesn't.

yep — WSL2 uses a virtualized NIC and doesn't automatically inherit Windows route table for all adapters, especially with split-tunnel VPNs. Two quick options: (1) add the route inside WSL, or (2) use SSH through the bastion (ProxyJump). Which do you prefer?
I'd prefer the route add so my dev workflow in WSL works (install, test, etc). How do I do that safely?

try this (run in PowerShell as admin to get the VPN gateway IP if needed):
```
# from WSL: add route to private network via Windows host
sudo ip route add 10.40.0.0/16 via 172.20.48.1 dev eth0
# then test: ping 10.40.12.5
```
If it works, you can make it persistent on WSL startup by adding a small script to `~/.profile` or use a systemd user unit. Note: you may need to `wsl --shutdown` from Windows and restart WSL after the VPN connects so the interface is fresh.
ran the `ip route add` and `ping` now responds, git clone starts. 🎉 Thanks. I had to `wsl --shutdown` first like you said.

nice. FYI alternatives: if you don't want to add routes, you can set an SSH `ProxyJump` through `redwood-bastion` so git traffic tunnels over the bastion:
```
# ~/.ssh/config
Host *.internal.redwood.dev
  ProxyJump bastion
```
That avoids changing WSL networking.

eviction of whole batches would explain missing intermediate spans for long traces. if a batch contains parent+children and a batch is evicted, the trace looks truncated.

timeline from metrics: exporter_retries surged, queue_size hit capacity, then queue_evictions increased. what's odd: dropped spans count is small vs evicted_spans. evicted means we lose earlier batches.
console graph: trace-reassembly-latency climbs before the dropoff. retention TTL for stream is 1h, but this is immediate loss in-flight, not retention expiration.

hypothesis: spike in downstream 429s triggered backoff loop. collector uses constant backoff + strict queue eviction (FIFO batch evict) which disproportionately loses earlier spans for multi-batch traces.

can we change behavior to partial_flush or split-batches-by-trace-id? config snippet we tested locally: ```exporters: otlp/https: endpoint: https://ingest.redwood/api/v1/spans timeout: 10s retry: max_interval: 30s initial_interval: 0.5s backoff: exponential queue: enabled: true max_size: 4096 eviction_policy: discard_oldest_batch partial_flush: true```

partial_flush:true looks promising — will flush available spans for a trace instead of holding until full batch. also eviction_policy: discard_oldest_batch is the problem; prefer discard_oldest_span or backpressure block with more aggressive backoff jitter so we don't fill queue.

- suspected regional/service degradation (elevated 5xx, latency, timeouts) even if only 1 customer reported so far
- multiple customers or multiple tickets reporting same symptom in short window
- needs an oncall-led mitigation (traffic shift, rollback, capacity move, config change)
- needs status page / broad comms decision
- exceeds paging threshold (aligned to SLO alerts) OR we’re going to page more than one team

Quick POC question from Olga's team: they have SD-WAN -> TGW (multi-region active/active). Want PrivateLink into our connector in primary region and automatic fallback to an egress proxy in the secondary region. Requirement: preserve original client IP for logging and allow mutual-TLS. Also need an explicit minimal firewall port list and rough cost comparison to Hosted. Any gotchas?

Short answer: doable. PrivateLink endpoints are regional, so you need a regional endpoint per region. For source IP preservation, use a TCP NLB fronting instances (targets as instances or IP mode with target preservation) and avoid NAT in the path. mTLS can terminate at the connector or be passed through depending on where certs are validated.

Clarifying Qs: 1) Does their SD-WAN announce prefixes to the TGW via BGP? 2) Will TLS be inspected at their edge or kept end-to-end? 3) Do they accept adding route automation to TGW route tables on failover?
We use BGP to the TGW. No TLS inspect - want end-to-end. We can do route automation if you provide a small runbook.

Recommended topology: deploy interface endpoint in primary region pointed at our NLB -> connector instances. In secondary region deploy an inbound egress proxy (another NLB + proxy fleet) and a separate endpoint. For failover use BGP local-pref change at their SD-WAN or an AWS route automation that swaps a prefix-list target in the TGW/route table. Note: cross-region failover will cause different egress path (and potential additional latency).

Firewall minimal list to open on their side:
- Spoke/TGW -> endpoint ENIs: TCP 443 (API traffic)
- Endpoint health checks -> connector health port (TCP 8080 or configured port)
- If using mTLS: allow TCP 443 and exchange client certs/CA fingerprints
- Proxy (secondary) -> primary NLB for probes: TCP 443
We'll provide exact ENI prefixes and health-check IPs once we provision endpoints.
MTU/SD-WAN note: overlay tunnels can reduce PMTU; recommend MSS clamp on their edge. Also watch for asymmetric routing if they have hairpinning — that breaks source-IP expectations.

Cost notes (high-level): PrivateLink = hourly endpoint ENI + data processing per GB. NLB = hourly + LP data processing. Hosted has zero infra & per-token variable cost. Dedicated reserved capacity reduces variable per-token cost but requires monthly commitment and can reduce cross-region egress if we co-locate proxy. We'll draft a 1TB/month sketch.

Customer asked for a simple doc comparing AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint) vs NLB-backed PrivateLink for their POC. Key ask: preserve origin client IP for observability and still pass through TLS-inspect at the edge. Can we list options and sample SG/NSG rules?

TL;DR: two main patterns we recommend:
1) NLB-backed PrivateLink + proxy in their VPC: preserves client IP to the NLB target if you avoid SNAT and use proxy protocol. Works well for AWS.
2) Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink): easy, per-service endpoint, but source IP becomes endpoint ENI; original host IP not preserved to the service. For orig IP you need app-layer X-Forwarded-For or mTLS.

Security notes: if they want TLS inspection at the DMZ, they can terminate/re-encrypt at the firewall. That requires distributing a corporate MITM cert and a policy for cert pinning exceptions. If app-level XFF is used, ensure we validate headers to prevent spoofing (use ALB/NLB with proxy protocol or mTLS).
Pricing ask — they want quick tradeoff numbers for a 2-week POC with ~100 GB egress and low qps. Any ballpark?

Ballpark (very rough):
- Interface Endpoint: low infra ops, per-endpoint hourly (~$0.01-$0.1/hr depending on region) + data processing ($0.01-$0.02/GB). For 100 GB the data charge dominant ~ $1-2 + endpoint hours.
- NLB-backed PrivateLink: NLB hourly + data processing similar; small extra if you run proxy EC2s (t3.small-ish) ~ $0.02/hr each.
- Transit via NAT Gateway: NAT GW ~$0.045/hr + $0.045/GB egress in some regions, so 100 GB could be $4.5 + hourly.
Recommend Interface Endpoint for lowest ops if they can accept XFF/mTLS approach.

Sample SG/NSG snippets to drop into their net team:
AWS Security Group (spoke proxy / NLB targets):
```
allow tcp 443 from 10.0.0.0/8 (spoke subnets) to sg-llm-proxy
allow tcp 22 from mgmt-cidr only
allow udp 53 from vpc-dns
```
AWS NACL (stateless - example):
```
100 allow tcp 443 10.0.0.0/8

Priority 200: Allow UDP 53 from dns-servers

Priority 4096: Deny All

Hey team — need a recommended flow for provisioning a hosted API key for an enterprise POC (Acme). Requirements: 1) key scoped only to inference (no billing admin), 2) expires after 7 days, 3) IP allowlist for Acme CIDR, 4) audit trail so security can prove key was rotated/revoked. +1 to scoping. For POCs we prefer short-lived, scoped keys and an approval ticket. We usually ask sales to create a ticket in jira:SEC-PROV with customer CIDR + POC owner. Security will sign off and create the key.

If you want self-serve guidance: Console -> Settings -> API Keys -> Create key -> Name it like "acme-poc-ephemeral" -> Scopes: select "inference:read, inference:write" -> Expires: 7d -> IP allowlist: paste CIDR. That will give you a single-use token with expiry. Share the token once via the secure channel.
Nice. Does the console show who created it and when so Acme can see audit logs? They want proof of rotation.

Yes — the Console writes audit events. If you need an exported log for the contract, open a ticket to get a signed export (we redact internal IDs). For basic proof, screenshots + the audit row (creator, timestamp, action=create) usually suffice.

For automation we expose an admin token-based API for programmatic key creation and rotation (internal). Example curl we give to partners with a customer-specific admin token:
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/admin/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"acme-poc-ephemeral","scopes":["inference:generate"],"expires_at":"2024-12-01T00:00:00Z","ip_allowlist":["203.0.113.0/24"]}'
```
That returns the key and an id you can use to rotate or revoke. We should only share that API with Solutions Eng or with a special service account.
Can we provide them a one-click rotation webhook? They asked for automatic rotate every 24h during the POC.

We don't expose a public webhook for auto rotation by default. Workaround: create a tiny lambda in their infra that calls our admin keys endpoint with a service account token to create + distribute a new key, then call revoke on the old key id. We can provide a sample script.

If they want auto-rotation, insist on using a customer-managed secret store. Rotation through our admin API is fine, but you must ensure the service account token is restricted and audited. For enterprise POCs, we recommend: 1) short-lived keys from Console (7d) OR 2) programmatic rotation using an integration account + restricted admin token + per-rotation audit entries.

BetaBank POC demo failed—client saw broken SSE payloads and an immediate close when the response contained embedded JSON with certificates info. Happened during a live demo. Need fast triage.
(system) client_id: beta-001, req: req_9c8b, path: /v1/generate/stream, env: dedicated-poc, region: eu-west-1
Any raw frames from the client? curious if termination includes TLS alerts or just TCP RST.

The first event looks cut right after the BEGIN CERT line. Our runtime logs show a FIN from client 192.0.2.45 immediately after sending that chunk. No ECONNRESET recorded on our side. Suggests client or middlebox closed connection.
BetaBank mentioned a DLP proxy that inspects HTTPS and does TLS interception. Those appliances sometimes drop streams when they detect suspicious payloads like long cert blocks.
They also asked about enterprise compliance / security questionnaire answers earlier—could the DLP be inline and mutating responses?

Yes, TLS MITM devices terminate TLS and re-encrypt. They may have rules to truncate or rewrite bodies that match patterns (like PEM blocks). If the proxy stops streaming mid-chunk the SSE event won't terminate and the client sees a trailing partial JSON.

Quick reproducer: ask Beta devs to curl the endpoint from inside their network with verbose output: `curl -v -N "https://poc.beta-bank.example/v1/generate/stream?req=req_9c8b"` and capture bytes. If curl shows truncation we can blame the appliance.
Also ask them to check their DLP logs for rule hits around req_9c8b timestamp. We saw similar with BankCorp last quarter; DLP flagged PEM blocks and dropped the connection to scan.
If it's the DLP, what's our recommended quick fix for the demo?

Two options: 1) Bypass the DLP for the demo origin (allowlist) or 2) instruct the server to avoid embedding raw certificate PEMs in streamed JSON; instead redact or send a URL-safe base64 or short fingerprint that the client can fetch over a separate TLS call. For POC speed allowlist is faster.

Server-side mitigation: wrap sensitive payloads in an `event: meta` with `data: <base64>` and ensure chunk sizes < 8KB so intermediate devices are less likely to trigger rules. Also add keepalive comments every 10s to avoid idle timeouts: `: ka\n\n`.

From compliance side, record the change in the SOC questionnaire answer: when asked about egress interception, note that some enterprise customers have TLS-inspection devices and we recommend allowlisting or using secure artifact hosting. We'll update the POC checklist.
Customer says they can test an allowlist for 30 minutes. They will revert rules during the demo window.
Great. Can we also confirm whether our hosted runtime can redact cert-like patterns automatically? Customer worried about leaking certs.

We don't auto-redact by default; but we can enable a lightweight canary transform that scans outgoing events for PEM headers and replaces bodies with a `[REDACTED_CERT]` token for POC environments. I can push a canary flag to the dedicated pool for BetaBank with `X-REDACT-CERTS: true`.
I'll deploy the canary now and add `X-KA: true` and `X-REDACT-CERTS: true` headers to responses. ETA 12m. I'll post the canary URL when live.
Also remind the customer to capture their DLP hit logs and the timestamp so we can correlate with `req_9c8b`. That helps security review.
Excellent. Any client-side tips to avoid crash if partial frame arrives? They use a JavaScript SPA with EventSource.

Thanks everyone. I'll tell BetaBank to try the allowlist and wait for the canary. I'll also add a note to the RFP/security thread about potential TLS-inspection impacts on streaming. :white_check_mark:

Two separate issues could be conflated: 1) DNS resolution might be returning an IP in the infra VPC (10.100.50.7) which is reachable via peering, but that IP is an ENI for a VPCE that only accepts traffic from the same VPC or from approved source VPCs via PrivateLink. 2) If traffic is hairpinned into a different service in vpc-b, the auth principal might not map and we get 403.

Quick network checks ask them to run from an instance in app VPC: `nc -vz 10.100.50.7 443` and `traceroute -n 10.100.50.7` and paste outputs. If TCP connects but TLS shows our cert only when endpoint is in the same VPC, then peering is the issue.

Important AWS note: Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) are regional and tied to the ENIs managed in the account where the endpoint was created. Traffic to an interface endpoint's ENI won't be routed over VPC peering to the service in another account. To access a service via PrivateLink across accounts you need the service owner to expose an endpoint service and the consumer to create a local interface endpoint in their VPC that connects to the service.
Also request the JWT claims (sanitized `iss` and `org_id`). If they incorrectly terminate TLS in the infra VPC or a proxy there, Authorization could be lost. But first fix the routing.

NovaHealth follow-up: netsec insists on SNI visibility to their DMZ inspector and original client IP in app logs. They asked if we can avoid peering because of org rules. Can we preserve client IP + SNI using anything other than peering? Need a short answer + a one-line cost delta for 5TB.

Short answer: if they forbid peering, we can still support SNI + client-id visibility but it requires customer-side proxying (they terminate TLS in DMZ, re-TLS to a customer proxy that forwards XFF) or using a transparent inline approach with GWLB + a probe that preserves srcip to our backend. Both involve customer infra changes.

A few concrete paths:
1) Peering (native): preserves src IP, SNI seen by DMZ if TLS terminates before peering. Lowest friction for logs.
2) PrivateLink (interface endpoint): isolates VPCs, but endpoint ENIs NAT; client IPs appear as ENI IPs unless customer proxy injects X-Forwarded-For. SNI is not visible to their inspector after PrivateLink unless TLS is terminated earlier.
3) GWLB + transparent proxy in customer VPC: push traffic through their gateway load balancer + inline proxy that can mirror SNI and forward original src IP to our peered path or re-TLS to us. This is more complex but keeps isolation and gives inspector visibility.

Quick ASCII:
OnPrem -> DMZ TLS Inspector -> Customer Proxy (terminate) -> TGW/spoke -> Peering -> Redwood
OnPrem -> DMZ TLS Inspector -> GWLB -> Inline Proxy -> InterfaceEndpoint/GWLB -> Redwood (proxy preserves XFF)

From questionnaire POV: include KMS/HSM language and note about TLS handling. Suggested wording: "Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations; we do not store plaintext customer keys. When customers perform TLS inspection in their DMZ, they must terminate and re-establish TLS to Redwood; we support mTLS and audit exports of key usage."
Cost one-liner? They want a simple comparison to paste in SOW for 5TB/mo.

One-liner (ballpark): PrivateLink infra fees ~ $0.01/hr endpoint + ~$0.01/GB data processing => ~ $50-70/mo for 5TB (ex cloud provider egress). Peering: no endpoint fee; cross-VPC transfer ~$0.005-$0.02/GB => ~$25-100/mo. GWLB/proxy path adds customer infra and proxy processing costs (depends on appliance), expect additional hourly+data processing costs; flag as engineering integration item.

Firewall snippet to hand ops (paste-ready):
```

Allow TCP/443 -> <interface-endpoint-subnet-cidrs>
# VPC Peering
Allow TCP/443 -> <redwood-peering-cidr>
# GWLB/Proxy (customer-side)

# Common
Enforce TLS >=1.2; deny weak ciphers. If proxying, ensure X-Forwarded-For header is preserved and logged.

  "pool_block": True,        # queue instead of spawn sockets

Urgent: BetaBank POC keeps triggering auth retries behind their corp proxy + SSO (IdP). After a token refresh, their client immediately retries same request and we end up with a retry storm -> 429s and demo failing. Anyone seen SSO + proxy lead to repeated 401/429 loops?

Can you paste sequence of events/logs? Is the SDK doing automatic retries on 401?

Snippet from logs:
```
2026-03-21T09:02:01Z INFO  client: request POST /v1/chat -> 401
2026-03-21T09:02:01Z INFO  auth: refresh token start
2026-03-21T09:02:01Z INFO  client: retrying request #1
2026-03-21T09:02:01Z WARN  proxy: CONNECT returned 407 (Proxy Auth Required)
2026-03-21T09:02:02Z INFO  auth: refresh token success
2026-03-21T09:02:02Z INFO  client: retrying request #2
2026-03-21T09:02:02Z ERROR rate-limiter: rejected (burst) -> 429
```
They show many CONNECT 407s from their proxy during the same timeframe and a flurry of client retries while the IdP refresh is in-flight.

The SDK's default retry behavior will eagerly retry on 401/5xx with no jitter if the app config asks for automatic retries. If the auth refresh is happening asynchronously, multiple concurrent requests can all detect 401 and trigger parallel refresh+retry. Combined with a proxy that sometimes demands reauth (407) you can get amplified retries hitting our ingest/rate-limiter.

On the IdP side they said refresh tokens are single-use for short windows. If multiple clients attempt refresh simultaneously, some will fail and then retry again, making the loop worse. Also the proxy 407 means the handshake isn't completing for some retries so those retries leave sockets half-open.

Short-term mitigation we can ask them to apply immediately:
- Add a single-flight lock around token refresh so only one refresh runs and others wait for its result. (mutex / promise share).
- Add jittered backoff before retrying after refresh (100-500ms).
- Stop automatic eager retries in SDK config (set retries=0) while they patch client auth flow.

For POC we can also suggest switching the IdP to issue slightly longer-lived tokens (e.g., +30s) or allow parallel refreshes for the demo to avoid single-use collisions. They said they can do that temporarily.

hey all, day 3 q: i'm trying to use fish as my interactive shell but still rely on asdf for runtimes + direnv for project envs. after dotfiles install, `node` and `python` look correct in iTerm2 (fish) but the devcontainer shell in VSCode shows system node. also i need to sign commits with GPG and forward SSH agent into containers. any clean patterns for fish + asdf + direnv + gpg/ssh agent?

welcome samir! :wave: fish differs from bash/zsh in init files. for asdf you need to source the asdf shims in a file fish reads (e.g. config.fish). example in ~/.config/fish/config.fish:
  set -gx PATH $HOME/.asdf/shims $HOME/.asdf/bin $PATH
  status --is-interactive; and source (asdf where fish integration)/asdf.fish 2>/dev/null|| true
we don't have an official fish wrapper but that ordering is key.
thanks. direnv's `use asdf` fails inside fish sometimes. i saw a suggestion to add a tiny shims wrapper. any concise fix?

direnv loads .envrc with a POSIX shell by default, so it expects `asdf` in PATH. For fish you can add to config.fish a small shim: `if test -f $HOME/.asdf/asdf.sh; source $HOME/.asdf/asdf.sh; end` or install `asdf-fish` integration from plugin. Also ensure `direnv allow` after changes.

got it. separate thing: VSCode devcontainer terminal shows a different PATH — runs `bash -lc` inside container. should i add a dockerfile step to install asdf and runtimes in the container instead of relying on host shims?

for devcontainers we prefer containerized runtimes so everyone gets the same versions. add a devcontainer Dockerfile step that installs asdf and runs `asdf install` + `asdf global` for the workspace `.tool-versions`, then commit a small build cache. Relying on host shims tends to be flaky.
that sounds good. how about forwarding SSH agent and GPG signing to the container for commits? i want `git commit -S` inside container to work using my host keys (1password CLI + gpg agent).

two parts: SSH agent and GPG. For SSH, enable `forwardAgent: true` in the devcontainer `runArgs` or use `--ssh` in `docker build` / `docker run` depending on build. For VSCode devcontainer, add to devcontainer.json: \"remoteEnv\": { \"SSH_AUTH_SOCK\": \"/ssh-auth.sock\" } and mount the host agent socket into the container (careful with permissions).

for GPG signing with 1Password, we use 1password-cli `op` and gpg on host. Option 1: keep signing on host and only push from container (configure git user/email to use host signing via gpg-agent forwarding). Option 2: run `op` inside container (requires auth) and import key into container gpg. Both need careful secrets handling. We usually prefer host signing via agent forwarding to avoid copying private keys.
any quick devcontainer.json snippet for SSH agent mount?

example snippet we use (adapt permissions):
  \"runArgs\": [
    \"-v\", \"/run/user/1000/ssh-agent.sock:/ssh-auth.sock\",
    \"-e\", \"SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/ssh-auth.sock\"
  ]

Hi all, day 1 blocker 44b. Bootstrapped our dotfiles but hitting weird PATH/runtime conflicts: asdf shims not resolving, pnpm missing, and node installed by Volta shows up instead of asdf node. Machine is M1 Mac but corporate image had Rosetta and some older /usr/local bits. Any quick triage?
welcome! :tada: We try to standardize on asdf for both python/node. Volta/nvm can conflict. First run `which node` and `which volta`/`volta --version`. Also `echo $PATH` and `cat ~/.tool-versions`.

`which node` -> /Users/emma/.volta/bin/node, `volta --version` -> 1.1.x. `asdf current` prints nothing, `which asdf` -> /opt/homebrew/bin/asdf. My ~/.zshrc is symlinked from dotfiles and has `export PATH="$HOME/.asdf/bin:$PATH"` but not sourcing asdf.sh.

ok two things: 1) If Volta is present it will take precedence; uninstall Volta or disable it if you want asdf. 2) Add asdf sourcing lines near the top of zshrc: `. $(brew --prefix asdf)/libexec/asdf.sh` and `. $(brew --prefix asdf)/etc/profile.d/asdf.sh` then ensure `export PATH="$HOME/.asdf/bin:$PATH"` appears after those lines.

uninstalled Volta via `volta uninstall` and removed its PATH entry. Added the asdf lines and restarted iTerm. `asdf plugin-list` shows python and nodejs, but `asdf install nodejs 18.17.0` fails with gpg key import errors on nodejs plugin.

the nodejs asdf plugin requires gpg to verify node dist keys. Install `gpg` via brew then run the plugin's import script: `bash ~/.asdf/plugins/nodejs/bin/import-release-team-keyring` then `asdf install nodejs 18.17.0`.
installed gpg and ran the import script, node install succeeded. For python `asdf install python 3.10.12` failed with a linker error referencing openssl.

brew install openssl readline xz zlib then export build flags before the install: `export LDFLAGS="-L$(brew --prefix openssl)/lib"` and `export CPPFLAGS="-I$(brew --prefix openssl)/include"` then `asdf install python 3.10.12`. For M1 you may see `/opt/homebrew` prefix; that's OK.
brew prefix returns /opt/homebrew. One more quirk: corporate MDM has installers gated so I couldn't symlink to /usr/local before. Could that cause leftover /usr/local files that shadow things?

yes, MDM and Rosetta installs can leave stale binaries in /usr/local/bin. Run `ls -l /usr/local/bin | grep pnpm` and remove stale entries (or ask IT). Also `brew doctor` can surface stale files. Using `$(brew --prefix ...)` in dotfiles helps avoid hardcoding.

fixed stale pnpm in /usr/local, reinstalled pnpm with `npm config set prefix "$HOME/.npm-global"` and `npm i -g pnpm`, then added `export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"` to zshrc. `which pnpm` -> ~/.npm-global/bin/pnpm. asdf current shows node 18.17.0 and python 3.10.12. All good.

Hey folks, first week and running into a weird chain of issues. Using M1 Max, fish, followed the dotfiles bootstrap. Installed brew to /opt/homebrew, asdf cloned to ~/.asdf. Problems: 1) `layout asdf` in .envrc errors with 'plugin not found' until I source asdf manually; 2) rustup installed but `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown` fails with permission denied when curl tries to write to /usr/local; 3) bootstrap ended up chowning ~/.local to root after I accidentally ran a step with sudo. Help please :)
Welcome Ivy! Short answers: (1) ordering; (2) brew env / permission; (3) undo chown.

For fish make sure `source ~/.asdf/asdf.fish` appears before `eval (direnv hook fish)` in `~/.config/fish/config.fish`. Example snippet we keep in dotfiles:
```
# ~/.config/fish/config.fish
set -gx PATH /opt/homebrew/bin $PATH
source ~/.asdf/asdf.fish
set -gx ASDF_DIR $HOME/.asdf
eval (direnv hook fish)
```
That preserves `layout asdf` availability when direnv parses .envrc.
I had `eval (direnv hook fish)` first, so that explains it. For the rustup / wasm target, why is it touching /usr/local? I thought everything was under ~/.cargo by default.

Rustup should write to ~/.cargo and ~/.rustup. If the installer tried /usr/local it's because some brew formulas or PATH conf pointed to /usr/local/cargo wrapper. Check `which rustup` and `echo $PATH`. If you previously installed rust with brew (`brew install rust`) that can cause system-wide locations. Also don't run rustup installer with `sudo`. Fix by uninstalling brewed rust: `brew uninstall rust` then re-run `curl https://sh.rustup.rs -sSf | sh` as your user.

Ah, I did brew install rust earlier to satisfy a dep. Uninstalled and reinstalled via rustup, now `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown` progresses but fails on `failed to create tempdir` with EACCES in /usr/local/var. Any ideas?

Clean the stale directories: `sudo chown -R $USER:staff /usr/local/var` (or specifically the problematic subdir), but better check which directories are owned by root: `ls -la /usr/local | grep root`. On Apple Silicon Homebrew should be in /opt/homebrew, so /usr/local is legacy from older installs. Remove or fix perms rather than running everything with sudo.

Done `chown -R` on the affected dirs and wasm target added successfully. Now about the dotfiles being chowned: I accidentally ran `sudo ~/.dotfiles/bootstrap`. How risky is that? I see some files in ~/.config now owned by root.

That's a common pitfall. Best to `chown -R $USER:staff ~/.dotfiles ~/.config ~/.local` then inspect dotfiles for any lines that modify system files; re-run bootstrap as normal user. Also remove any root-owned cron jobs or launch agents the script might have accidentally placed (unlikely but check `~/Library/LaunchAgents`).

welcome Noah! :wave: A few quick troubleshooting steps we suggest:
- OpenSSL: on mac you need to point builds to Homebrew OpenSSL. Try `export LDFLAGS=\"-L/opt/homebrew/opt/openssl@1.1/lib\"` and `export CPPFLAGS=\"-I/opt/homebrew/opt/openssl@1.1/include\"` before `asdf install`. Also `brew link --force openssl@1.1` is sometimes needed (but prefer env vars).
- Dotfiles: we use a bare repo pattern. If your bootstrap created a nested repo, run the official script from our repo: `./scripts/setup-bare-repo.sh` which uses `git --git-dir=$HOME/.cfg --work-tree=$HOME`. Avoid cloning into ~/dotfiles unless the script expects it.
- direnv: permission issues are often from CRLF or from the file mode. Run `dos2unix .envrc` and `chmod 600 .envrc`, then `direnv allow`. For env parsing, prefer using `dotenv` helper: `dotenv -f .envrc .env` or in .envrc use `export $(cat .env | xargs -0)` only if safe.

Also check your PATH order — asdf shims should come before system binaries. In bash/zsh add `source ~/.asdf/asdf.sh` and `export PATH=\"$HOME/.asdf/shims:$PATH\"`. If you switch between mac and linux, pin tool versions in the repo `.tool-versions` so asdf picks the same runtimes.

zsh is our standard and most docs assume it; fish can work but some bootstrap scripts are POSIX/sh oriented. If you prefer fish, we recommend installing `bass` or `fisher` helpers and sourcing the asdf shims as described in the onboarding doc. If it's easier, switch to zsh for a smoother experience. hey team, new hire here. followed the README and `docker-compose up db` but the container fails to bind port 5432: `Bind for 0.0.0.0:5432 failed: port is already allocated`. I don't have any other docker containers running. wtf?
welcome! simplest cause: you probably have Postgres running on your host (system postgres) already listening on 5432. run `ss -ltnp | grep 5432` or `lsof -i :5432` to see.
yep `sudo ss -ltnp | grep 5432` shows `LISTEN 0.0.0.0:5432  pid=1234/postgres` that's the distro default postgres. didn't think of that.

common on linux dev boxes. two quick fixes: 1) stop the host postgres (`sudo systemctl stop postgresql`) while you use the docker one, or 2) change your compose port mapping to something like `- \"15432:5432\"` and update your app `DATABASE_URL` to use port 15432.
