for short-term dev either is fine. long-term we prefer app config so you can run both side-by-side (e.g., host postgres for local tooling and container for the app or vice versa). if multiple people in the team use 15432, add it to the README to avoid collisions.

small note: if you set `network_mode: host` in compose, the container will share host network and you won't get port mapping; but that is not portable on mac/docker desktop (and not recommended for people on shared infra). Stick with normal bridge networking and explicit port mappings.
curious: are there any gotchas with pg socket files? i remember something about unix sockets taking precedence over TCP?

yespsql by default tries unix domain socket first if you do `psql -h localhost` it uses TCP; if you do `psql -h /var/run/postgresql` it uses socket. If the host has a socket at `/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432`, local clients may connect to host postgres even if docker's port is different. Always check which host you're talking to. `psql -h localhost -p 15432` forces TCP to the mapped port.

note: team convention: prefer using service names when both app+db run in compose (e.g., `db:5432`) and reserve host port 5432 only if you need host tools to connect. See handbook: /handbook/dev/local-db-port-policy.
pro tip: add a `.env.example` with `DB_PORT=15432` and a small script `scripts/start-local.sh` that exports env and runs compose to reduce confusion for new hires.

hey all, first-day problem: I can `ssh jump@bastion` from Terminal and then `ssh internal-host` fine, but VS Code Remote-SSH keeps failing with 'Permission denied (publickey)' when trying to connect to internal-host via the bastion. I configured ProxyJump in my ~/.ssh/config:```Host bastion
  HostName bastion.internal.redwood.internal
  User jump
Host internal-host
  HostName internal-host.internal.redwood.internal
  User fran
  ProxyJump bastion
  ForwardAgent yes```
Any ideas? :confused:

welcome! first guess: VS Code ships its own ssh binary inside the app bundle which doesn't see your ssh-agent socket or macOS Keychain-managed keys. A couple quick checks: 1) can you `ssh -A internal-host` from Terminal without password prompts? 2) in VS Code Remote-SSH output, is it trying "/usr/bin/ssh" or the bundled one?

yes `ssh -A internal-host` from Terminal works, agent forwarding is fine. In the VS Code logs I see it's invoking `"/Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/extensions/remote-ssh/dist/bin/remote-ssh"` then later a path to a vendor ssh. Not super clear.
devex: common issue — VS Code's remote extension can use its own SSH or the system SSH depending on settings. Try setting `remote.SSH.path` to the system ssh and enable local server. Steps: 1) open Command Palette -> Preferences: Open Settings (JSON) and add:```"remote.SSH.path": "/usr/bin/ssh",
"remote.SSH.useLocalServer": true
```2) reload VS Code. That makes VS Code call the system ssh which sees your agent and ProxyJump config.

also confirm VS Code can access the SSH_AUTH_SOCK. If you're using a GUI launch (dock click) on macOS, the environment may not include your agent socket. Launching VS Code from terminal (`code .`) usually inherits the env. Alternatively, add the agent socket to launchd env via a small plist or use the macOS Keychain helper (`ssh-add -K`) on older macOS. On Sonoma/Apple Silicon we recommend `ssh-add --apple-use-keychain` where supported.

one more quirk: some GUI git clients (e.g., GitHub Desktop, Tower) or VS Code built-in Git may ignore ProxyJump and use libssh/libgit2 which doesn't read your ~/.ssh/config. If you rely on VS Code's Git features against internal repos, either configure an HTTPS remote for initial clone or add a local `~/.ssh/config` entry that sets `IdentityFile` and `ProxyCommand` explicitly, e.g.:```Host internal-host
  HostName internal-host.internal.redwood.internal
  User fran
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa_redwood
  ProxyCommand ssh -W %h:%p bastion
```
This makes non-OpenSSH libs that do read config more likely to connect.

updated settings to use /usr/bin/ssh and launched VS Code from terminal — Remote-SSH started the host install and connected! :tada: I did have to `ssh-add -K ~/.ssh/id_rsa_redwood` to ensure the key was available to GUI apps.

Heads-up: onboarding streaming sample in staging started emitting duplicate side-effects after a transient 429. This one is interesting because it's a streaming client that retries the tail of a broken stream.

Streaming retries are messy. We have parity gaps: Node stream client resumes with a resume-token and avoids re-sending chunk 0, but Python currently restarts from beginning unless user supplies an application-level idempotency key.
Oof. For streaming we can't just use Idempotency-Key on the entire payload. We need chunk-level safe replay markers and a short server-side window to dedupe.
[alert] 2026-05-02T12:03:02Z staging: streaming /v1/ingest 429 surge p95-retry=350ms

Proposed fix: 1) SDKs emit a `Client-Replay-Hash` header computed from the canonical stream manifest (stream-id + sequence-start + metadata) for advisory dedupe. 2) Server keeps a tiny sliding-window (4s) mapping of (stream-id, sequence-start, hash) -> last-accepted-seq and ignores reprocessed chunks below that.
That sounds doable. For non-streaming unary requests we keep behavior same (Idempotency-Key precedence). For streams we treat Client-Replay-Hash as best-effort dedupe only.

Also parity: our jitter algorithms vary — Node uses full-jitter, Go uses simple exponential and Python uses fixed backoff. We should standardize to "truncated-decorrelated" jitter: sleep = min(max_backoff, random_between(base, prev_sleep * 3)) with base=150ms and cap=900ms. That avoids tight simultaneous retries and fits streaming semantics.
Note: recommend calling out exact formula and provide examples per SDK.

Make sure SDKs default to a short-lived client instance secret for HMAC so tokens change over time; servers only compare hash equality for short window and don't store raw manifests. Also avoid putting full payload into logs.

Another edge: clock skew — if resume tokens contain timestamp, clients with skew may generate mismatched hashes. Keep the manifest strictly client-local fields (id, seq_start, metadata) and avoid epoch in hash. Server dedupe window should be based on arrival time, not token timestamp.
Telemetry: emit metric `stream.replay.advisory.hit`/`miss` and sample 0.5% of streaming replays with sanitized manifest for manual inspection in staging only.

UX: expose stream retry config in SDK constructors: `streamRetry: {enabled: true, strategy: 'truncated-decorrelated', base_ms:150, max_ms:900, advisory_hash: true}`. Default to enabled for onboarding sampleapp only.

For immediate mitigation in staging: patch sampleapp to pause prewarm streaming and add `SAMPLEAPP_STREAM_ADVISORY=true`. Also add a CI test that tears down connection with a 429, resumes client with the same manifest+hash, and asserts sink has no duplicate chunk side-effects.
I'll open quick PRs: sampleapp patch PR 4732 (pause prewarm streams), server LRU-stream-dedupe PR 4738, Node SDK stream parity PR 4741, Python stream resume PR 4742.
[update] PR 4732 deployed to staging canary=8%. Monitoring 10m.
Follow-up: we should document when to use persistent application-level idempotency (payments) vs advisory replay-hash (short lived streaming resumes) so customers choose the right tool.
Agree. Also add a short note on privacy: manifest hashing must be irreversible; HMAC is fine but avoid storing raw manifests server-side.

Heads-up: multiple enterprise accounts asking for an upgrade flow that keeps their external footprint identical. They also want smaller airgap bundles that don't require full-image swaps. Need to sketch acceptance criteria and a field runbook.

We can split the runtime into a core control plane and swappable workers. If worker binaries can be updated independently and we keep the same service IPs, customers won't see external changes. Means we need strict wire compatibility and handshake checks.

Wire compatibility is doable. We should add a compatibility matrix: protocol versions, admin ports, and cert expectations. Also suggest signing the delta bundles so offline installs can validate authenticity.

From customers: they prefer "non-invasive" by default. Any step that touches route tables or public IP allocations is a blocker. They want a CLI preflight that outputs a single PASS/FAIL and a short human-readable remediation list.

Operational notes: provide a dry-run that simulates DB migrations (no writes) and a verification probe that runs smoke checks post-migrate. Also maintain a snapshot of pre-upgrade state (configs + routing) so rollback is deterministic.

Proposal for delta format: a signed manifest.json + patch.tar + migrations/ directory. manifest includes: version, component list, reverse-migration pointer, sha256s. CLI commands:
```
redwood-delta verify manifest.json
redwood-delta plan manifest.json --out plan.json
redwood-delta apply manifest.json --shadow (simulate)
```

Good. For product we need two customer-visible knobs: `preserve-external-ips=true|false` and `apply-mode={shadow,plan,apply}`. Defaults should be preserve-external-ips=true and apply-mode=plan. Document estimated window for each mode.

For preserve-external-ips we must document which IPs are guaranteed: LB VIPs and NAT egress ranges only. Pod IPs are ephemeral and cannot be preserved without heavy orchestration. Call that out in the docs.

Add a short checklist NetOps can run: current VIPs, firewall rules to open, SSH bastion access, pre-approval from security. Make it one page. We can template it in the Console 'upgrade assistance' panel.

Rollback design: store the applied migration id in control DB and keep previous bundle cached for 72h. If health checks fail within a window, auto-initiate rollback to previous bundle unless `--manual-rollback` is set. Emit clear alerts with runbook link.

Prioritization: MVP (by EOW sprint) = signed delta spec + CLI verify/plan + documentation stub + field checklist. Stretch goals (next quarter) = console UI for preview, automatic canary on subset of tenants, network-shadow lab utility.
Dev tasks: manifest schema + validator, patch apply library with reversible operations, migration runner that supports dry-run and resume. I'll open a tech spike for reversible migrations.
I'll draft the one-page NetOps template and collect two customer contacts to pilot the flow. Also suggested we include an explicit customer-approval step in the CLI for production installs.
Created ticket PRD-1202 "Signed delta bundles + IP-preserve upgrade path" (owner: Ravi).
One more: telemetry. Emit an anonymous upgrade-event (success/failure/duration) when allowed by customer opt-in. That helps us tune default SLOs.

Heads-up: found an annoying repro in the Python async sample with Dedicated + corporate proxy + custom CA. AsyncClient ignores REDWOOD_BASE_URL and ends up hitting public api.redwood.ai; also SSL verification fails.

env used:
  REDWOOD_BASE_URL=https://dedicated-west.internal
  REDWOOD_CUSTOM_CA=/opt/certs/company-ca.pem
  HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.corp:3128

minimal repro:
```py
from redwood import AsyncClient
c = AsyncClient()
await c.chat.create('hi')
```
exception: SSL cert verify failed, then httpx.ConnectError -> api.redwood.ai in traceback. sync Client works fine with same envs.
sounds like httpx transport isn't getting our SSLContext and base_url isn't canonicalized before proxy logic kicks in. we've seen similar in other threads.

quick workaround: pass base_url + ssl_context explicitly when constructing AsyncClient. e.g.
```py
import ssl
from redwood import AsyncClient
sslctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile='/opt/certs/company-ca.pem')
client = AsyncClient(base_url='https://dedicated-west.internal', _transport_kwargs={'ssl_context': sslctx, 'proxies': {'https':'http://proxy.corp:3128'}})
```
but agree it's not ideal to surface _transport_kwargs. we should expose typed transport_kwargs or handle CA/proxy wiring inside the SDK.

I'll open a PR: ensure AsyncClient(...) always sets base_url from explicit arg or env before any proxy handling, build ssl.SSLContext from REDWOOD_CUSTOM_CA and pass into AsyncHTTPTransport when proxies are present, and add mypy stubs so the ctor typing matches.

Quick follow-up from the RFC review — proposing a compact-claims gateway to shrink API key surface and speed auth checks. Thoughts?
Short version: one broker that rewrites wide claims -> compact internal claims, less header bloat.
Why a gateway vs library? we lose some observability if opaque.
Gateway gives centralized rotation & caching, and lets downstream services validate a small fixed schema instead of evolving claims.
Concern: single-point-of-failure + HA complexity. are we counting on infra for that?
yes, it would be behind our load balancer and deployed replicated in every region. fallbacks to legacy validation for outages.
deploy-check: gateway must expose /health, /metrics, and token-cache-miss rate tag.
Also need policy for claim contraction: which fields allowed to be dropped or hashed. sample: `user_id`, `roles[]` -> keep, `org_tree` -> hash.
Can we see a tiny example transformation?

example input token claims (simplified):
```
{
  "sub": "svc:payments:123",
  "roles": ["pay:write","pay:refund"],
  "org": "org:acme>team:billing",
  "env": "prod",
  "exp": 1713000000
}
```

output compact claims might be:
```
{ "s":"svc:payments:123","r":"a1","o":"h3","e":1713000000 }
```
where `r` and `o` are stable small enums / hashes and gateway maintains mapping and TTL.
mapping table is effectively additional state. how do we handle invalidation when roles change?
gateway listens to role-service events and invalidates mappings; we can also embed a short `version` field in compact token.
performance numbers? if gateway adds 3-5ms every call it could be bad for hot paths. can we cache on edge?
plan: LRU local cache in each pod + CDN edge caching for long-lived mappings. cache hit -> <1ms, miss -> 4-8ms depending on mapping.
opt: offer two modes: "inline contraction" library for extremely latency-sensitive services, gateway for everything else.
Security review: contraction must be deterministic and collision-resistant for hashed claims. also consider forward secrecy for mappings.
How does this affect RBAC checks? would policies accept compact values or require gateway to expand on demand?
idea A: services accept compact claims and RBAC engine understands compact enums/hashes. Idea B: gateway can (optionally) expand into full claims for policy engines that need them.
Idea A reduces bandwidth and parsing. Idea B easier for incremental migration. Prefer B for rollout.
Rollout plan suggestion: 1) deploy gateway in read-only mode (observability + no rewrite) 2) opt-in downstream to accept compact tokens 3) provide expansion API for a period 4) flip default.
Ops note: need to rate-limit expansion API to avoid amplification attacks.
Testing: add synthetic perf suites + role-change churn sim to validate invalidation logic.
Good call. I'll draft a follow-up doc with mapping schema, TTLs, and rollout steps. Anyone want to co-author?
I can take the mapping/invalidation section.

I'll own perf/latency measurements and tests.

Quick internal announce: Async Generation v1 is GA. This introduces `async-gen` endpoints for fire-and-forget / job-style generation, improved function/tool-calling semantics for long-running ops, and a new job-status webhook for notifications. Internal docs: https://redwood.ai/docs/async-gen (internal).

TL;DR: 1) New endpoints: `/v2/async-generate` and `/v2/async-status`. 2) SDKs (py/js) add `client.async.create_job()` + `client.async.stream_status()`. 3) Webhooks: `job.completed` and `job.failed` with structured payloads. 4) Pricing: job-based billing (per-job overhead + per-token). Early-adopter credits for first 90 days. 5) Deprecation: old long-poll patterns will be supported but flagged for removal in 120 days.

Migration notes: minimal changes for most users. Example (python):
```python
job = client.async.create_job(model='gen-async-v1', input='Generate long report...', callback_url='https://hooks.example.com/rdwd')
# poll if you prefer
status = client.async.get_status(job.id)
while status.state in ('pending','running'):
    time.sleep(2)
    status = client.async.get_status(job.id)
```
Webhooks deliver `job.completed` with `result_url` for retrieval.

For infra: jobs are queued with priority hints (low/med/high). We added `x-rdwd-job-priority` and `x-rdwd-job-estimate-ms` headers. Large jobs auto-sampled for quality checks. If runtime moves job to fallback model you'll see `x-rdwd-fallback:true`.

Canary: infra bot scheduled gradual rollout starting 2145680000 (5%->25%->75%->100% over 6h). Watch signals: job-queue-length, job-failure-rate, webhook-delivery-failures. Oncall pinned for first 48h.

Billing change: job overhead billed as 1 unit minimum + per-token. Early-adopter credits applied automatically for accounts created before the end of the promo. We'll post detailed pricing table in Console tomorrow.

quick repro: macbook with Homebrew redwoodctl installed at /usr/local/bin/redwoodctl, but repo also has a tiny npm shim `node_modules/.bin/redwoodctl` (old JS wrapper). sample-app's `scripts/bootstrap.sh` runs `npx redwoodctl login --profile ci` which ends up calling the shim. the shim writes tokens in the legacy JSON layout and names the file `ci-token.json` instead of our usual `tokens/ci.json`. system redwoodctl then reads the wrong file and believes the active profile is ci.

commands i ran:
```bash
# in project
type -a redwoodctl
# -> redwoodctl is /usr/local/bin/redwoodctl
# -> redwoodctl is ./node_modules/.bin/redwoodctl
# bootstrap script uses: npx redwoodctl login --profile ci --headless
```
interesting. two different binaries writing to the same REDWOOD_HOME with incompatible formats. that's a recipe for silent corruption.
is this only a format mismatch or did the shim overwrite the real tokens?

shim created `~/.redwood/ci-token.json` and also touched `~/.redwood/current` file pointing to `ci-token.json`. system binary expects `~/.redwood/tokens/ci.json` so it fell back to reading `~/.redwood/current` and tried to interpret the shim file. result: CLI calls authenticated as the service account.
symptoms sound like: 1) unexpected credential scope 2) accidental privilege escalation in local dev 3) CI scripts could accidentally create SA tokens on dev machines. Not good.

short-term mitigation: 1) do not run repo-local shim: run `which redwoodctl` to ensure it's the system one 2) set REDWOOD_HOME to an isolated dir for the project `export REDWOOD_HOME=$(pwd)/.redwood-local` 3) remove the shim from the repo or make bootstrap call absolute path `/usr/local/bin/redwoodctl`
confirmed workaround: `export REDWOOD_HOME=$(pwd)/.redwood-ci && npx redwoodctl login --profile ci` creates a separate token store and stops clobbering my user tokens.

- sample-app: stop invoking `npx redwoodctl` in bootstrap; call the path from `which` or prefer `system` binary.
- installer: add a doctor check that looks for multiple redwoodctl binaries in PATH (`type -a`) and warns on first-run if formats differ
- token format: add a small header with `format_version` in token files so mismatches produce a clear error instead of silent misuse
- CLI: when encountering unknown token file shapes, do not auto-use them; warn and refuse unless `--force` provided

Heads-up — found a repeatable long-context mem growth tied to KV cache fragmentation on main canary. After ~2h with many distinct prefixes we see steady RSS growth even though eviction rates look fine. :grimacing:
Can you paste the repro commands and a quick pmap?
repro: run loadgen --seq-len=4096 --unique-prefixes=1e6 --batch=1 --kv-mode=enabled --kv-alloc=slab

pmap snippet (container):
```
00007f9c0000-00007f9c1f000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [anon:kv_cache_buckets]
00007f9c2000-00007f9c2800 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [anon:kv_slab_64]
00007f9c3000-00007f9c3800 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [anon:kv_slab_256]
... repeated many small anonymous mmaps, holes, then big growth in anon:kv_cache_buckets
```
Flamegraph shows lots of time in allocator free/list-manipulation and occasional compaction runs that don't reclaim due to fragmentation.
Do you have allocator stats? free lists per size bin?

yes — snapshot after 2h:
- total_allocated: 18.3GB
- total_committed: 22.9GB
- slab_bins: {64: 48k, 128: 12k, 256: 1.9k, 1024: 430}
- free_frag_ratio: ~0.28 (measured as wasted vs used)
That 64B bin looks suspiciously hot. Tiny objects + long tail of pinned entries -> internal fragmentation.
Did kernel selection or batching changes land around the same time? Could be a correlated regression.

Good call — we rolled batching heuristics v2 last week but kernels unchanged. Profiling shows CPU is the one impacted here (allocator churn), not GPU kernels. Batching actually reduced number of allocations per second, paradoxically making slabs hold longer-lived small entries.
Proposed mitigations?

Two quick experiments I ran:
1) Increase small-block bin size from 64->128 (coalesce allocator frontage). Result: memory peak dropped ~12%, but internal waste up slightly on average allocations. p99 latency +1.5ms, throughput ~same.
2) Opportunistic repack/compaction: background thread takes fragmented slabs with low live density and copies live entries into a fresh slab, frees old one. Ran every 60s with limit 1000 objects. Result: peak down ~18%, CPU overhead +4% during compaction windows. p95 latency bump visible only under sustained compaction.
Can you share the compaction config snippet?

snippet:
```
kv.compaction.enabled = true
kv.compaction.scan_interval_s = 60
kv.compaction.max_moves_per_run = 1000
kv.compaction.min_live_density = 0.6
kv.compaction.worker_threads = 2
```
Risk: full repack means copying KV entries which may hold pointers into model tensors or attach to caches. Need to ensure we only move lightweight metadata and update references atomically.
We implemented a two-phase move: copy metadata + new pointer to the same KV payload (payload pinned) then swap pointer under per-bucket lock. No tensor duplication. Unit tests added.
Any regression in end-to-end quality (i.e., KV hits/miss behavior)?
No, hit-rate unaffected in tests. We do see slightly higher tail CPU during compaction windows. Also, compaction delays scheduling of low priority background telemetry tasks but that's minor.
Can we combine approaches? i.e., tune bin sizes + occasional compaction for stubborn slabs?

That's what I recommend: smaller compaction frequency + bump 64->96 (empirically 128 helps but increases internal waste). New plan: bump 64->96, compaction every 120s, max_moves 500. That gave ~14% mem reduction in sim.
How about a staging area idea — keep a small hot slab pool that serves new small allocations and periodically drain into normal slabs to avoid creating many semi-live tiny slabs?

I prototyped a 'hot-stage' allocator: short-lived allocations go to a preallocated ring of pages; once ring 70% full we migrate survivors in bulk. This reduced transient fragmentation spikes and smoothed out RSS. Implementation complexity medium.
Sounds promising. Need benchmarks across workloads (long-context chat, high-throughput short queries).

Agreed. I ran two bench suites:
- long-context synthetic: mem peak down 16%, p99 unchanged
- short-queries mixed: mem stable, throughput +0.6%
What's the rollout plan? Canary flag-prefixed?
Yes — kv_frag_mitigation_v1 as a feature flag. Stage: canary 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> all. Observability: add kv.slab.live_density, kv.compaction.moves, kv.alloc.histogram.

nit: do we mean full resumable streaming (replay tokens + offset) or just pick-up-at-message-boundary? those are different complexity levels.
target is pick-up-at-message-boundary only. no token-level rewind. keep KV entry minimal: {resume_id, last_seq, expiry_ts}.
expiring the KV is key. if resume window is too large we pay a lot. what's the target window? 30s? 2min?
thinking 60s default, configurable per route. default should bias toward lower memory use for bursty requests.
operational note: if we put resume metadata in the edge KV, we need a background compactor to sweep stale keys. otherwise hot tenants could thrash.
also: how do we surface partial responses to the client when we preempt a connection? do we send a trailer explaining why client should reconnect with resume token?
yes — send an explicit trailer payload: `X-Resume-Token: <id>` and short JSON body with `reason: handoff` + `last_seq`.
deploy scheduled: edge/ingress v2.3.1 -> canary run at 09:00 UTC :rocket:
okay but failure modes: what if resume target instance can't access the KV (network partition)? fallback should be full restart of request with deprecation header.
agree. fallback = start-over + emit `X-Resume-Fallback: true` so downstream callers can adapt (dedupe, backoff).
perf concern: for high-throughput streaming (many small streams) KV ops per handoff could spike. consider coalescing resume entries by tenant and TTL-bumping rather than writing every single handoff.
good call — propose a lease model: write resume entry once per 10s per resume_id and bump expiry on subsequent handoffs instead of rewriting payload.
what about ordering? if two handoffs happen concurrently, last_seq could be racing. we should persist monotonic sequence and compare CAS style.
we can use CAS on the KV side. if CAS fails on resume attempt, request should fall back to full restart.

user-visible semantics doc snippet (draft):
```
When a client connection is preempted, the edge returns 202 and header `X-Resume-Token`.
Client reconnects to `/resume` with token within resume window.
Edge will attempt to resume at message boundary; if resume fails, client gets 408 and should retry from scratch.
```
can we add a metric for `resume_attempts`, `resume_success`, `resume_fallback_full_restart` and `resume_kv_cas_fail`? we need numbers before shipping.
metric alert template created: `alert: HighResumeFallbackRate`
rollout plan: canary 1% -> 10% -> 50% with resume window default 30s, then observe metrics for 48h and decide if default should be 60s.
+1. also add a feature flag to turn off lease-bumping to compare cost.
last thought: privacy/PII: make sure resume token doesn't leak full context. store only minimal pointer, and rotate tokens on restart.
agreed. token = opaque UUID, mapped to internal pointer; no client-visible metadata other than last_seq.
ok I'm happy. i'll draft a short RFC addendum with the CAS flows and metric names.
thanks — I'll update the RFC and add the canary playbook. :thumbsup:

Quick follow-up on the dedicated pool autoscale surface. sketching a few concrete interface scenarios we should validate before the RFC. want quick eyes.
ack. can you list the scenarios? would love to see failure modes too.

first scenario: operator -> runtime prewarm request with hard headroom. operator asks pool to ensure N slots pinned for tenant for the next T minutes. runtime may decline if fragmentation prevents satisfying request. expected response states: accepted | deferred | rejected, plus best-effort prewarm ETA.
+1. question: do we allow runtime to return partial acceptance (eg 3/5 slots) or only binary? partial seems useful but complicates billing.
leaning partial acceptance. operator should be able to accept partial and hold a soft reservation for remainder. include reservation_id for later idempotent top-ups.

scenario two: admission-time QoS hint. tenant sends {qos: latency | throughput, target_p99_ms, cost_budget}. runtime must pick a plan: DIRECT_DEDICATED, ACCEPTED_BURST, QUEUED_WITH_BACKOFF, or REJECTED_COST.
for QUEUED_WITH_BACKOFF, should runtime stream ETA updates to the operator or should control plane poll?
prefer streaming ETA via control-plane websocket for UX. include pull fallback. updates frequency small (eg every 5s).

failure mode: operator asks prewarm, runtime accepts but GPU init fails (driver OOM, MIG misconfig). runtime should mark reservation FAILED with failure_reason; operator gets webhook + suggested fallback (burst lane or hosted).
also add a prewarm-health probe: runtime runs lightweight model load check and marks slot READY only if probe passes.

proposed minimal API shape (pseudo as a string payload): { admit_request_id, tenant_id, requested_capacity_units, prewarm, headroom_minutes, qos, target_p99_ms, cost_budget_usd_hour, allow_partial }. we'll spec this in protobuf in the RFC.
nit: `requested_capacity_units` maps better to fractional-slab models. +1 on `allow_partial` field.

telemetry: we need decision rationale for why runtime chose ACCEPTED_BURST vs DIRECT_DEDICATED to debug cost/latency regressions. include `decision_reason` and `score_vector` in accept responses.
oscillation safety: runtime must apply hysteresis (eg 30s) before deallocating recently-provisioned slots unless explicit operator drain requested. add `min_lifetime_seconds` on reservations.

Why this change: the flat `assistant_mode` has been limiting as we add tool-level permissions, regional safety policies, and fine-grained billing tags. `capabilities` lets us evolve without breaking the surface.

SDK behavior details:
- SDKs will add `capabilities` param (map).
- If both provided, `capabilities` wins.
- We will not change server defaults; servers will map legacy `assistant_mode` when present.
- Minor semver bump planned for py/js/go to signal new API surface.

Sample migration (py):
```python
# old
resp = client.generate(prompt, assistant_mode='composer')
# new
resp = client.generate(
  prompt,
  capabilities={
    'mode': 'composer',
    'tools': ['docs_search'],
    'safety_scope': 'moderate'
  }
)
```

Heads-up — I'm about to merge the docs PR that changes the model-routing example (PR #482). Before I do, can someone from runtime confirm a couple of blocking details?
The example says we 'fall back to a compatible variant' but doesn't say what happens to the KV cache or quantization mismatch. That bit matters for the migration note.

Current example YAML in the PR: ```yaml
routing:
  policy: latency
  fallback_order: [fast-7b, fast-7b-quant]
  preserve_kv_cache: false # <-- is this the true default?
  canary_grace_secs: 20
```

If preserve_kv_cache is false by default, we should explicitly call it out in the docs and show the latency implication. If it's true for some cases, we need to state the exact rules. Please advise so I don't merge incorrect guidance. @Samir / @Matt
Short answer: default depends on variant compatibility.

If the fallback variant is architecture-compatible (same model family & tokenizer) we keep the KV cache. If it differs only by quantization but binary-compatible, we also try to preserve KV where possible. If tokenization or vocab differs, we drop cache.
We don't have a single boolean global default that fits all cases. Runtime checks three things: arch, tokenizer_id, and KV-serialization-compat. If any check fails -> preserve_kv_cache=false.
To add: when preserve_kv_cache=false you'll see an immediate latency spike for the first few tokens on fallback (cold KV). We should show a small trace example in the docs.
That's helpful. Can you give the exact behavior we should document (one short paragraph + a tiny example)? I can draft text and add to the PR.

Doc text suggestion: "When a request is routed to a fallback model, the runtime attempts to reuse the caller's KV cache if the fallback is binary- and tokenizer-compatible. If compatibility checks fail, the runtime starts the fallback without cached state, which can add a cold-start token latency penalty for the next request."
Example latency note: "Observed: +120–300ms on first generation token when KV is dropped for 8k context workloads on A100."

Also call out quantized variants: even if quantization differs, we usually preserve KV for same-arch builds, but output probabilities can differ slightly. Recommend adding: "Verify outputs with your eval prompts after enabling fallback."
OK — I'll add that text plus a tiny YAML snippet showing `preserve_kv_cache: false` as an explicit opt-out example.

import random
import time
def sleep_backoff(attempt, base=0.5, cap=10.0):
    """Simple exponential backoff with uniform jitter."""
    jitter = random.uniform(0, base)
    delay = min(cap, base * (2 ** attempt)) + jitter
    time.sleep(delay)
```

```ruby
# streaming with KV prefix + short replay on 429 (pseudo)
prefix = kv.fetch(session_key)
begin
  client.stream_generate(prompt, kv: prefix) do |chunk|
    ui.push(chunk.text)
    prefix.last_token_idx = chunk.last_idx
  end
rescue TooManyRequests
  replay_start = [0, prefix.last_token_idx - 5].max
  resp = client.generate(prompt, kv_range: replay_start..prefix.last_token_idx, max_tokens: 48)
  # drop overlap and append
  ui.push(resp.text[prefix.overlap_chars..-1])
end
```

Heads-up team  we're deprecating the legacy JSON examples schema used across SDK docs (old `request_v1` / `response_v1` blocks). New schema (`io.v2.json`) is more expressive and fixes several ambiguity issues with streaming/partial responses. Preview of updated pages is up: https://docs.redwood.ai/internal/sdk/json-schema-v2-preview. Deprecation timeline and migration notes below.
What's the migration surface? Will customers' saved examples break? :worried:

Two parts: docs examples and sample payloads in the examples repo. Docs will show both schemas side-by-side for one release with a deprecation warning on the legacy blocks. The examples repo will get automated codemods to update sample fixtures. Existing customer payloads are unaffected unless they copy/paste the example verbatim and rely on the old field names. We'll include a clear mapping table.
Any SDK API changes required? Or just docs/schema rename?

Mostly docs/schema. SDKs accept both v1 and v2 shapes for now with a compatibility shim. We'll emit a runtime warning when v1 is used in interactive/TTY environments and log a single telemetry event when running in Hosted. The shim will be removed after 4 weeks from full rollout. So for SDK consumers: no immediate code changes required, but please update internal examples and e2e fixtures.
Can we get a codemod for Python and JS? Will it be idempotent?

Yes. We'll publish two codemods (js, py) that 1) rename fields, 2) convert streaming placeholders to the new partial-chunk format, and 3) update import paths for test fixtures. Codemods are intended to be idempotent; we'll include a dry-run mode and output a summary of changed files. Links will be in the preview doc.

Security check: migrating schema does not change server-side validation. Important: do not include real user prompts or PII in example payloads. We'll run a quick scrub on the examples repo to redact obvious secrets before codemod PRs are opened.
Any telemetry/opt-out notes for Dedicated/Private customers?

Good call. Telemetry for migration (counts of v1->v2 conversions) is off by default for Dedicated/Private and opt-in for Hosted. We'll document the exact telemetry events and provide an env var `REDWOOD_DOCS_MIGRATION_TELEMETRY=1|0` for local runs.
CI requirements? We should block merges if example fixtures don't match new schema.

Yes: CI checks for examples repo will include a schema-validate step against `io.v2.json`. We'll add a GitHub Action that runs the codemod in dry-run for PRs and fails if any remaining v1 fixtures are detected without a rationale comment. Also require docs linter and link-check.

Draft Python snippet (uses tenacity + async iterator):
```python
import asyncio
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential
from redwood import AsyncClient
client = AsyncClient()
@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=0.5, max=3))
async def stream_collect(prompt: str):
    buf = []
    # client.stream.tokens() yields Token objects with .content
    async for tok in client.stream.tokens(prompt=prompt):
        buf.append(tok.content)
    return "".join(buf)
# usage
asyncio.run(stream_collect('Summarize the doc'))
```

Proposal: 'slice orchestration' flow: micro-canary (0.2% single-tenant) -> cohort slices (1% multiple tenants) -> regional ramp (10%) -> global. Each step has a short infra window (10m) + quality window (90m).

Fallback matrix: (A) model-variant fallback: v2 -> v2-eco for memory pressure, (B) shard-level degrade: route a subset back to v1 when shard queue depth > 40%, (C) tenant-level opt-out via override flag. Throttle auto-fallbacks to max 12% traffic/min to avoid cascades.

Quick sync — we got multiple customer asks this week about the chat endpoint shape. Two camps: (1) messages-first (roles+history) and (2) prompt-first (single prompt with metadata). Need to decide prioritization, launch criteria, and migration risk.
Summary: messages-first matches modern chat UX and tool calling flows, but prompt-first is simpler for existing completions users.
Customer feedback: product teams want explicit role semantics (system vs assistant) so moderation + persona enforcement is easier. They also asked for a clear migration path.
Operational ask — messages-first typically increases token-size due to history envelopes which impacts latency/cost. We need a default prefix-caching strategy to hit latency SLOs.
From evals: structured tool outputs + function calling are more robust with message arrays because you can attach metadata per message. Also helps with regen and targeted replay.

Proposed plan: ship messages-first as the primary public shape for chat, but provide a small compatibility shim for prompt-first (server-side conversion). Launch criteria: 1) SDK parity (js/py), 2) clear migration guide + linting tool, 3) perf baseline (p95 latency within 10% of current completions for typical convo sizes), 4) deterministic behavior for system role.

Implementation notes: server-side conversion should accept an optional `prompt` field and expand to messages internally: {"role":"user","content": prompt}. But we must be explicit about how we handle multiple system directives in prompt-first payloads.
UX: provide `system` as special top-level field in prompt shim to reduce ambiguity: e.g. {system: "You are a helpful assistant", prompt: "..."}. That keeps simple clients minimal changes.
We should also add autoshrink batching: if message history exceeds token threshold, auto-trim older assistant/user turns but keep system. Add telemetry to track when this happens.
Evals for regression detection: include a sentinel prompt set with 3 categories: persona, hallucination, tool fidelity. Must pass gating thresholds before GA.

Rollout strategy: 1) opt-in beta for existing API keys flagged `chat-shape-v2`, 2) whitelist a few enterprise customers for feedback, 3) gradual default flip with 2-week warning and compatibility logs.
Backwards compatibility: we can't silently change existing completions endpoints. Shim only when `compat_mode=true` or when `prompt` is present. Otherwise return 400 with migration hint.
Docs + migration tooling: small CLI `rw-migrate-chat` that scans code for completions->chat diffs and suggests changes. Ship with examples for common frameworks.
deploy scheduled: canary start 2026-05-04T02:00Z -> monitor token cost delta, p95 latency, error rate.
Risks: customers with complex prompt templating might break; we need template-compat tests. Also legal/moderation teams must sign off on system-role enforcement behavior.

One more: structured output suggestion — include optional `response_schema` top-level in messages shape so downstream parsers can validate. This intersects with function calling. Need product decision now or later?
Recommendation: include `response_schema` as opt-in GA feature tied to function-calling plumbing. Keep MVP of messages shape without mandatory schema.

Noticed confusion in reviews: inline comments on regression diffs don't thread well when people reply quickly. Threads look flattened and reviewers lose context. Screenshot: https://redwood.mock/fig/diff-comments.png
Problem details: replies are appended inline separated by small timestamps, not grouped. Also no visual marker when a comment has been resolved vs archived.
Agreed. UX ask: introduce a compact thread view under each diff chunk (collapsed by default) showing '3 replies' which expands into a threaded view. Keeps the diff scanning dense.
Accessibility: collapsed thread button needs aria-expanded and the number of unread replies should be announced. Use a sr-only text like '3 replies, collapsed'.
Microcopy: change 'Resolve' to 'Mark resolved' and add a secondary 'Archive' action for moderator-only cleanup. People thought 'Resolve' deleted the comment.
heuristic-scan: current inline reply input steals focus on expand which breaks keyboard flow. Recommend focus land on the first reply when expanded, not the input.

Interaction idea: inline threads should support a small keyboard nav: 'r' to reply (opens input), 'o' to toggle resolved state on focused comment, and Enter to expand/collapse when focused on the thread line. Will need help doc.
For screen readers: when a thread expands, announce 'Thread expanded: 3 replies. Last reply from Alex, 5 minutes ago.' Keep it concise. Use aria-live polite.

Visual affordance: show a colored dot for unresolved threads, grey dot for resolved, and a timestamp cluster for latest activity. Add a small 'unread' badge when there are new replies since last visit.
There's also a permission nuance: suggestion edits vs comments. Add labels 'Suggestion' and 'Note' above each comment bubble so reviewers know actionable items.
Implementation note: store thread metadata (resolved, unread_count, last_actor, kind) to avoid heavy DOM traversal. Also lazy-load replies when expanding.
i18n: 'Mark resolved' vs 'Resolve' translations differ. @i18n-bot flagged. Need separate keys and context notes.
i18n-scan: flagged. Use keys `comment.mark_resolved` and `comment.resolve_confirm` with translator notes about moderation differences.
Confirmation copy for marking resolved: 'Mark this thread resolved? This will hide it from default view but can be reopened.' CTA: 'Mark resolved' / 'Cancel'. Keep short.
accessibility checklist: aria-expanded on thread toggle, aria-live on expansion summary, focus management (don't auto-focus input), and keyboard shortcuts discoverable in a help tooltip.
For bulk workflows: allow users to 'Mark all replies in view as resolved' with a confirmation when count > 20. Useful for large sweep after triage.
Edge case: if a thread has unresolved suggestions, require a confirm explaining suggestions are pending. Add a small inline note linking to change requests.

Decision summary: collapsed thread view by default, thread toggle with aria-expanded and aria-live summary, reply keyboard shortcut 'r', mark resolved -> 'Mark resolved' + confirm, unread badge, lazy-load replies, labels for 'Suggestion' vs 'Note', bulk resolve action for >20 with confirm, and i18n keys updated.

TL;DR: implement 'parallelCalls' array + per-item timeout/retry fields, and a simple ordering hint. Keep runtime changes minimal.
Can we do this without a full DAG execution engine? Prefer best-effort parallelism + causal ordering flag. For retries we need idempotency keys on external actions.
Customer use-case: call CRM, enrichment service, and payment provider in same flow. They need partial responses if one call times out, not whole request failure.

Proposed MVP scope (idea):
- API: support `parallel_calls` in the chat message schema (array up to 4).
- Each call: `{id, target, input, timeout_ms, retry_policy, ordering_hint}`.
- Runtime: fire all calls concurrently, collect responses, apply `ordering_hint` if present to stitch outputs. If a call times out, return partial result + call status.
- Retries: client-provided `idempotency_key` required for any retryable action.
- Default: max 2 automatic retries with exponential backoff, configurable.

Implementation notes: keep current inference loop unchanged. Spawn non-blocking HTTP tasks for each external call. Use existing batching for model tokens, and attach call futures to response assembly. Minimal kernel/runtime changes.
Danger: uncontrolled parallel external calls can blow up CPU/IO. Need quotas per-request and per-api-key. Also add a per-call cost estimate in console to prevent surprise billing.

- Security: require idempotency and auth propagation rules for private connectors.
- Observability: per-call metrics in Console (latency, errors, retries, timeouts).
- Docs + SDK: examples in JS/Python + migration guide.

Quick sync — we need to lock the API semantics for parallel + multi-step tool calling for Q2 initiative. Customers want: multiple tool invocations per request, some can run in parallel, some have ordering deps, and sensible retries/timeouts.
High level: do we expose DAGs or implicit model-driven calls?
Proposal: explicit steps list (DAG-ish) in the API. Let callers declare dependencies; default is parallel for independent steps. SDK helpers can build DAGs from natural prompts later.
Agree on explicit deps. We should also make it clear how tool outputs are routed back to the model (as inputs vs in-band events).
One important constraint — we can't block model streaming while waiting for long-running tools. Need async hooks + optional streaming.

Right. MVP API sketch below (very rough):
```json
"tool_calls": [
  {"id": "search-1", "tool": "kb_search", "args": {"q": "foo"}, "run_after": [], "timeout_ms": 3000, "retry": {"retries": 1, "backoff_ms": 200}},
  {"id": "api-1", "tool": "order_create", "args_from": ["search-1"], "run_after": ["search-1"], "timeout_ms": 5000}
]
```

semantics: steps with empty run_after can run in parallel. steps with run_after must wait for listed step(s) to succeed (or hit final retry). If a step fails and has no fallback, we return a partial response with per-step error details.
On retries: start with simple policy — 1 retry + jitter, idempotency required by tool implementer. Do we expose retry policy to user? keep it simple for MVP (fixed cap).
For ordering, clarify transitive deps and cycles — reject cycles at validation time. Also add per-step "ignore_failure" flag for best-effort ops.

Timeouts: default per-step timeout 3s, overridable. Also set overall request timeout (e.g., 30s), after which we abort outstanding steps and return what we have. Need clear error type for aborted vs failed.

Streaming behavior: two modes: 1) blocking mode — model waits for all tool outputs then continues; 2) streaming mode — model can receive partial tool events as they complete. For MVP we implement streaming-of-events (tool-completed events) but not full model re-prompting during open stream.
Implications for runtime: need orchestrator that schedules steps across GPUs/regions, fan-out to external tool adapters, and collects outputs. We'll need correlation ids and trace sampling.
Spec doc uploaded: https://confluence.redwood/specs/tool-call-orchestration-draft (uploaded by anya) :white_check_mark:

Launch criteria (draft):
- API stable (schema validation + cycle check) documented in SDKs
- End-to-end correctness for common 2-step patterns (search->action, parse->call) verified by unit+integration tests
- Latency targets: for 2 independent short steps (both <50ms adapter), P50 < 120ms, P95 < 400ms; for one long external adapter (500ms), overall P95 < 1.5s with streaming of completed steps
- Error surface and docs: clear per-step error codes and guidance for idempotency/fallbacks
Also add observability: per-step latency, retries, timeouts, adapter error breakdown. Dashboards and alerts for >1% step-failure on prod traffic.

MVP scope (keep tight):
- Explicit per-request steps with run_after semantics
- Per-step timeout + single retry with jitter (configurable via account-level feature flag, not per-request for MVP)
- Streaming tool-completion events to client
- Validation: cycle detection, args_from binding, simple schema errors
- No speculative re-ordering, no automatic dependency inference, no cross-request caching in MVP
Follow-ups for next phase: multi-model coordination, speculative prefetching, richer retry policies, transactional step groups.

👍 from eng. My initial plan: canary 1% -> 10% -> 50% over 48h windows. Auto-rollback if p95 latency increases >20% OR error rate >2% sustained for 30m. Manual hold if human-quality signals dip.

```
GATE: new_model_pass = (delta_normalized_quality >= -1%) AND (human_pref >= 55) AND (p95_latency <= baseline * 1.20) AND (error_rate <= 2%)
If new_model_pass == false -> block rollout / require manual override
```

Quick sync — we need to decide what goes into the next streaming MVP for chat completions. SSE vs WS, delta payload shape, finish reasons, and how function/tool calling behaves when streaming. Customer asks piling up.
TL;DR: customers want partial outputs + resume, plus clear finish semantics. Legal teams also ask for deterministic audit logs of final vs partial. :eyes:
Technical constraints: browsers prefer SSE (simpler CORS), mobile/websocket multiplexing important for persistent sessions. Our runtime supports both but fallback semantics differ.
From evals: partial deltas are very useful for interactivity, but structured output (JSON) mid-stream can be malformed until finish — consumers need guidance.
Mobile apps asking for small incremental tokens to show typing indicator. They also want to cancel and resume without re-running entire prompt (resume by offset or prefix cache).

Proposed MVP scope (narrow): 1) Support SSE + WS transports; 2) Send token deltas as the default; 3) Emit a deterministic finish event with reason codes; 4) Provide a resume token header for clients to request continuation from same model state. Anything dangerously large here?
Resume token is tricky — requires KV-caching per-request and retention. Ops cost increases. Alternative: allow prefix/KV snapshot export but mark as enterprise-only.

Customers in enterprise pilots need resume for long-running assistants. Could gate resume behind Dedicated/Private and explicit retention TTL. Launch criteria: must work for 95% of in-flight requests during canary.
Finish reason taxonomy proposal (short list): `completed`, `stopped_by_user`, `model_error`, `truncated_by_length`, `fallback_to_sync`. Each as `finish_reason` in final delta. Keep minimal.

Agree on minimal finish reasons. Need contract for mid-stream structured output: deltas can contain `text_delta` OR `json_delta` OR `tool_call_delta`. Clients should be told those may be incomplete. Suggest `delta.partial = true|false` and final delta sets `partial=false` and includes `finish_reason`.
For mobile UX, partial=true for text deltas is ok. But if `json_delta.partial=true`, we should avoid attempting to parse until final. Add a `json_schema_version` and `json_checksum` on final? :+1:

Implementation notes: Websocket path will be `/v1/streams/ws` with binary frames allowed; SSE path `/v1/streams/sse`. Handshake includes `client_capabilities` (resume, multiplexing). If `resume` not supported by infra tier, server returns `Resume-Unavailable` header in handshake.
Backwards compatibility: existing non-streaming endpoints remain. SDKs should add `onDelta` callback and `onFinish` with `(finish_reason)` param. Docs must show examples.

Customer-driven ask: function/tool calling mid-stream. We can stream token deltas while the model emits a `tool_call_delta` indicating name + partial args. Real ask: allow client to accept partial tool call and invoke external tool before finish. That's a bigger contract and likely out of MVP.

Proposed priority: MVP1 = streaming tokens + finish_reason + SSE/WS with clear handshake + enterprise resume flagged. MVP2 = streaming structured/tool deltas with safe parse guidance + resume for self-serve.

Launch gates: tests for resume failure modes, rate-limited KV usage, TLS/handshake for SSE proxies, mobile offline reconnection behavior. Canary on 1% of traffic, then 10%. Rollback path to non-streaming sync responses if errors > 1% of canary.
UX checklist: typing indicator latency <150ms for first token; client reconnection tries exponential backoff and requests resume token; fallback to full sync if resume fails.

Proposed acceptance criteria (high-level):
- Chat/completions: streaming enabled, TTFB(stream) < 150ms, token p50 < 60ms, p95 < 220ms for hosted tier.
- Embeddings: primary dim=2048, L2-normalized, mean embedding drift <= 0.015 vs baseline on 10k seed prompts (eval harness).
- Rerank: top_k <= 40, deterministic ordering with tie-breaker (model score -> recency -> stable doc_id hash), MRR uplift >= 10% on customer benchmark set.
- Fallbacks: on overload route -> quantized variant (flagged) or queue with backpressure header. If no fallback available, return 503 with JSON {"error":"model_unavailable","fallback_recommended":true}.

POST /v1/rerank
{ "model":"rw-rerank-v2", "query":"...", "candidates":[{"id":"d1","text":"..."}, ...], "top_k": 10 }

{ "scores":[{"id":"d1","score":0.823}], "ordering":["d3","d1",...], "model_version":"rw-rerank-v2@2026-03-18" }
```

4) rollback window 24h after each step.

Heads-up  proposing a "prewarm grace tokens" pattern for new Dedicated tenants. Goal: smooth initial ramp without overcommitting reserved capacity. Draft below.
Curious how this differs from onboarding headroom?

Short: headroom reserves GPU. Prewarm tokens are temporary non-reserved allowance that draw from burst capacity but with a soft contract: tracked, surfaced, and reconciled within X days. Less risk to overall packing.

Example policy (draft):
```
prewarm_grace:
true
50k_requests

21
  cap_pct_of_pool_burst: 5
"charge-if-exceeded" # options: warn-only | charge-if-exceeded | auto-convert-to-reservation

per-tenant-dashboard + billing-export
```
If reconcile_mode=charge-if-exceeded, we need clear invoices and sales playbook. billing-bot: what does "charge" imply on our billing export schema?
charge-if-exceeded -> post-facto usage line item named "prewarm_oob". Must be enabled per-contract. Default: warn-only.
Operationally, cap_pct_of_pool_burst is nice, but how do we prevent burst monopolization if many onboard at once?
Two mitigations: 1) global circuit-breaker on concurrent prewarms (soft cap), 2) proportional degrade when pool burst > threshold. Also a per-tenant fairshare weight.
Can we make allocation_tokens variable by customer tier? e.g., startup=20k, standard=50k, enterprise=200k.
Yes. Proposal: token bands by commitment. Keep defaults conservative.

Acceptance criteria for experiment:
- No more than 2% increase in tail 99th latency in affected pools during prewarm windows
- Billing exports include prewarm_oob line item with tenant IDs for 100% of events
- UX shows "prewarm usage" on onboarding flow and in Console within 24h

Rollout plan idea:
- Phase A: internal alpha (20 accounts) with warn-only & telemetry for 2 weeks
- Phase B: opt-in customers (up to 200) with charge-if-exceeded enabled and a simple invoice template
- Phase C: auto-on for new small tenants with warn-only, monitor 30d, then switch to charge-if-exceeded for repeat overages

Product decision proposal: ship experiment with warn-only first, per-tier tokens, circuit-breaker limit 10 concurrent prewarms per pool, reconcile_mode default warn-only. Revisit after 45d with telemetry.

Heads-up: Legal asked for a single "evidence package" deliverable we can hand to auditors for SOC2/ISO. They want the mapping between our telemetry and control IDs, plus a reproducible export process. Can we scope this for Q2?

We should define two outputs: (1) a compact auditor bundle (signed, verifiable, timeboxed) and (2) a live-query view for control evidence during audits. Bundles should be immutable and include proofs (hashes, manifest).

Tech note: current audit events are NDJSON in raw sink. Bundles as Parquet with a manifest.json (sha256 per file) works well for large tenants. For small tenants a single gzipped NDJSON is easier. Need to pick one canonical format and support both for exports.

Compliance asks: retention tiers must be explicit in contracts: hot (30d searchable), warm (1y fast-restore), archive (7y immutable). For SOC2 we need retention and deletion proofs. Also need proof we didn't modify past data (append-only guarantees).

Important: BYOK interplay. If a customer supplies keys for archive tier, we must still produce readable auditor bundles on request. Options: require ephemeral escrow key for exports, or mandate customer provide export-run key during audit window. Which is less risky?

Escrow is messy legally. Suggested policy: for BYOK customers, require an "audit escrow token" during onboarding: customer signs an SLA that allows temporary unwrapping for auditor exports, logged and narrow-scope. If they refuse escrow, we support only managed-key archives for that tenant.

Implementation checklist (proposal):
- control mapping doc: map event types -> SOC2 CC/ISO clauses
- export pipeline: sink -> validation -> canonical formatter -> sign(manifest) -> upload-immutable-storage
- immutability: S3 Object Lock with Governance mode + retention stamps per-tenant
- proof artifacts: sha256 manifest, signer cert chain, export-run audit log
- restore path: fast-restore API for warm tier, ticket with 24h SLA

Add contract clauses: data sovereignty (region), export windows, escrow consent, and key-rotation obligations. Also define a key-loss policy: if customer loses keys and refused escrow, we'll provide notarized statement of inability to decrypt; customers must accept that risk.

Short take: retention is cheap but operationally noisy (cold storage + search). BYOK escrow/rotation is heavy (HSM/KMS integrations + legal). ISO work is mostly documentation + a few control remediations.
From threat/risk: BYOK w/o proper rotation/escrow increases long-term liability. ISO gaps are reputational but less immediate blocker for deals compared to BYOK for certain banks.
Contract note: BYOK escrow terms must specify key recovery process, access controls, and consent for rotation. Also customers ask for a documented chain-of-custody for exported evidence.
Proposed priority rubric: Revenue impact (1-5), Sales blocker (1-5), Engineering cost (1-5). Also tag items that are "deal-breakers" for named accounts.

Quick scores: Retention tiering (12/36/forever opt-in) -> Revenue=2 SalesBlocker=2 Cost=2. BYOK escrow -> Revenue=4 SalesBlocker=5 Cost=5. ISO checklist -> Revenue=3 SalesBlocker=3 Cost=2. Chain-of-custody (tamper-evidence) -> Revenue=3 SalesBlocker=4 Cost=3.
Suggest we split BYOK into minimal MVP (handshake, upload, audit logs) vs. full escrow/rotation. MVP reduces cost and unlocks mid-market. Full escrow can be a paid enterprise add-on.
Agree on phased BYOK. For MVP we must include customer acknowledgement of limitation and an SLA for escrow negotiations if requested.

Proposed sequencing: 1) ISO checklist + documentation (2 sprints) to unblock EU deals, 2) BYOK MVP (3 sprints) to unblock banks with handshake + audit trail, 3) Retention tiers + export chain-of-custody features (2-3 sprints), 4) BYOK escrow/rotation (4 sprints).

Implementation notes: Retention tiers: default 12mo. Enterprise 36mo with optional cold-archive export. Add tagging per-tenant to avoid scanning entire corpus. For chain-of-custody, generate signed manifests (SHA256 + timestamp + signer id) and include merkle root for tamper-evidence.

Ensure manifests are append-only and stored with immutability flags. If platform storage doesn't support append-only, consider cold object store with write-once lifecycle. Also add alerts for manifest mismatches.

Edge-case list I'm adding to PRD draft:
```
- truncated_mid_token: stream hits token_limit mid-token -> partial utf8
- kv_mismatch_on_resume: resumed session uses different model version
- duplicate_chunks_on_retry: client receives overlapping chunks
- eos_marker_missing: model doesn't emit EOS token
- partial_function_call: tool-calling stream emits half-structured JSON
```

1) SDK supports resume_token with deterministic resume semantics
2) Server emits explicit 'incomplete_end' with reason
3) Retry behavior documented and default: 1 retry for streaming
4) E2E tests cover resume + duplicate suppression
5) Billing flag per chunk for partial outputs
```

opening intake for a lightweight request-priority / queueing signal we can use at routing time. problem statement below, looking for gaps and owners.
Problem: noisy tenants and bursty workloads cause capacity contention. our current routing keys (model, region, tier) are too coarse — a single tenant can consume a disproportionate share and push others into higher latency or retries. customers keep asking for a way to express which tenant requests should be treated with higher scheduling preference during contention.
Proposal (alpha):
- Add an optional request field `request_priority` (0-10) and a per-tenant default.
- Routing layer uses `request_priority` as a soft signal: prefer higher-priority pools/variants and preempt best-effort queues when necessary.
- Provide Console + API controls to set tenant defaults + one-click toggle to make the field admin-only.
- Surface deterministic fallback reasons in traces (e.g., `fallback:pool_saturated->variant:gpu-q4`).
Goals:
- Minimal latency/throughput impact when not used.
- Pilot with 2 customers and validate reduced cross-tenant tail latency.
- UX: simple slider + cost tooltip for >7 priority.
Non-goals (phase 1):
- No per-tenant scaling policies or pricing changes.
- Not supporting arbitrary weight schedules or quotas in alpha.
Success metrics (pilot):
- Pilot tenants see >=40% reduction in p99 interference vs baseline under contested load.
- No increase in overall error rates >0.5% attributable to routing changes.
- 2 pilots live and integrated within 6 weeks.
Acceptance checklist (alpha):
- API accepts `request_priority` header/body field (int 0-10) and Console allows tenant default.
- Routing decision logs/traces include `priority_applied` boolean and `fallback_reason` tag.
- Admin-only toggle in Console implemented.
- E2E test simulating saturation and verifying preemption/fallback behavior.
- Runbook + rollback plan documented.
Notes / open questions:
- enforcement: should we honor priority across dedicated and private deployments the same way? (needs legal/enterprise input)
- cost callouts: high priority may increase unit cost if routed to faster pools — how explicit do we want to be in billing UI?

quick follow-up from the provisional credits RFC — proposing a lightweight probe/handshake interface + state machine to avoid noisy probes eating real capacity. want to capture rollout plan and open tradeoffs. TL;DR: short-lived provisional credits, explicit probe token, and graceful fallback to soft-shed.
sounds good. can you sketch the probe lifecycle? how does it differ from current token lease logic?

probe lifecycle: client asks for a probe token (cheap, low-rate), system answers with allowed probe tokens + expected probe window, client runs a small representative request, results influence provisional credit grant. differs from leases because probes are explicitly rate-limited and do not consume long-term reserved capacity.
+1. important: keep probes orthogonal to billing and quotas. probes should be telemetry-only unless they transition to a provisional grant. otherwise people will game it.

tradeoff: more state to track per-tenant (probe_pending, probe_ok, probe_failed) and we increase contention on the admission coordinator. we should collapse states into a compact enum and only persist when transitioning to provisional grant.

we also need to think about abuse signals. attacker can do repeated tiny probes to fingerprint model variants. maybe add exponential cooldown per-probe-failure and cross-tenant global probe rate caps.

agree. suggested config snippet for admission side (prototype):
```
{
  "probe_window_s": 10,
  "probe_rate_per_tenant_rps": 2,
  "provisional_credit_tokens": 1000,
  "provisional_ttl_s": 30,
  "evict_on_error_pct": 80
}
```
telemetry hooks needed: probe_count, probe_success_rate, provisional_hit_rate, provisional_eviction_rate. instrument at admission and at runtime (latency/cost deltas).
migration plan: 1) dark launch probes for 2 weeks (only telemetry), 2) selectively enable provisional grants for low-risk tenants, 3) monitor provisional_eviction_rate < 5% before wide enable.
also add a blacklist for tenants that show high probe failure rate + suspicious pattern (fast retries, many model ids). escalate to abuse team automatically.
run: admission-probe-sim v1 — 5000 simulated tenants, probe_rate=1rps, provisional_ttl=30s -> provisional_accept=9.2%, median_latency_delta=+12ms :eyes:

awesome — that sim result is helpful. next questions: how tightly coupled should probe tokens be to model variant? if probes are model-agnostic we can reuse them, but we lose fidelity. if tied to variant, attacker can enumerate variants with probes. suggestions?

prefer model-sharded probes: probe tokens include a narrow model fingerprint, but set very low rate and require signed probe request (api-key + nonce). that raises complexity but reduces cross-model fuzzing.
alternatively have a hybrid: model family-level probes (e.g., "gpt-style-v2") not exact weights. reduces enum space and keeps usefulness.

Quick thread to finalize Reserved Pools + Quota MVP scope. We need a concise launch checklist and fallback playbook for sales/legal. Goal: GA-ready for priority pilots in 3 weeks.
Proposal: MVP features = reserved pool allocation, per-tenant quota slab, token-bucket burst credits, simple fallback routing, and minimal telemetry. Keep per-route controls out of scope.

For fallback routing prefer a quality-tiered chain: 1) quantized same-arch model, 2) smaller architecture, 3) best-effort queue. We should expose a single toggle for customers: "prefer-quality" vs "prefer-availability".

Pilots prefer explicit guarantees: "X concurrent requests guaranteed for 5m bursts" and a clear contract clause that describes fallback behavior and expected quality delta. They also want console visibility when fallback is active.

Operational constraints: autoscale should respect tenant commitment. Suggest mapping table: commitment -> max_replicas_multiplier. Also require graceful drain time and a preempt budget for emergency throttles. Add alert: burst_credit_depletion with severity page.

Good. Define launch KPIs: 1) P95 generation latency for reserved traffic <=250ms, 2) zero 5xx errors under burst up to committed capacity, 3) burst absorption for 5m windows for 90% of events, 4) onboard time <= 2 hours.

For contracts we need fallback language and opt-out terms. If fallback changes output quality we must include notice period and consent checkbox in Console. We can draft standard clause but need CS sign-off for pilot exceptions.

Minimal autoscale config example (pseudo): `policy: {up_pct: 75, down_pct: 30, min: commit_base, max: commit_base*4, burst_window_s: 300, fallback_order: [quantized, small, queue], queue_ms: 150}`. Keep name/value simple for docs.

Add a lightweight eval hook: when fallback activates sign post requests and run a short fidelity check against held eval prompts to detect unacceptable regression. If regression > threshold trigger rollback route.
UX asks: Console should show active quota, remaining burst credits, last fallback reason, and an obvious "escalate to CS" button for pilot customers. Also email notify on sustained fallback > 2m.
Telemetry summary: per-tenant headroom_pct, burst_credits_remaining, fallback.count, fallback.reason histogram, recent_burst_events (1m/5m windows). Need retention 30d for troubleshooting.

Prioritization: MUST = reserved allocations, token-bucket, fallback chain, basic telemetry, contract language. SHOULD = console banner + email notifications, pilot onboarding doc. MAYBE = self-serve quota editing, per-route admission.
Risk: prewarm cost if we follow pre-warmed micro-pool approach. For MVP we avoid prewarm and rely on fast quantized variants + limited queue. Calls out potential latency tail increases.
Also flag SLAs: if we promise burst guarantees we need operational playbook and credits for breaches. Keep SLA language conservative for GA.

Rollout plan: week1 internal canary (0.5% traffic), week2 pilot tenants (5-10%), week3 pilot expansion + legal signoff -> GA. Gate: 3 pilots onboarded OR telemetry showing stable burst absorption for 48h, AND legal fallback language approved.

Quick sync  we need a short decision: accept quantized model binaries into the registry as first-class artifacts?
Clarify format: .pt q4/q8 artifacts that teams produce locally?
Exactly. Goal is to let teams upload quantized checkpoints and have them go through onboarding (smoke + bench) without forcing a float-only policy.
Upside: cheaper/easier perf testing on Dedicated/private infra. Downside: quantization can mask correctness regressions vs fp32.
Suggested boundary: accept quantized upload, but require a deterministic parity check in the bench. e.g., run 100 seeded golden prompts and compute a quality delta metric; block if below threshold.
Parity runs are tricky because of nondeterminism across kernels. For parity we need deterministic seeds, pinned kernels (or CPU fallback), and a defined sampling mode (greedy/topk).

Operational proposal: require two pieces on upload: (1) quantized artifact, (2) a minimal float baseline (can be a trimmed fp32 snapshot). Validation: immediate smoke (sanity + latency), plus async parity-run. If parity fails, block promotion to higher trust levels.
How tight are parity thresholds? Exact token equality improbable. Start with n-gram overlap (e.g., BLEU-style) + targeted hallucination checks (does answer mention spurious facts).
Also require metadata headers describing quantization recipe + tooling version (e.g., bitsandbytes v0.40, per-channel clamp flags). This helps explain diffs.

Storage concerns: storing a second baseline increases registry size. Options: allow baseline as compressed tar or external URL (must be accessible to validator). For private/offline installs, baseline must be included in package.
Registry behavior: if baseline provided as URL, fetch it during validation; if large (>500MB) async validate and notify uploader when finished. (sre-bot note).
deploybot: FYI  uploads >500MB trigger async validation; uploader gets email when done.
Fallback: if quantized passes smoke but fails parity, allow "dev"-level soft-approve for internal testing but block "approved" trust for Dedicated/public rollouts.
Add registry field quant_trust_level with values [dev, internal, approved], default dev. This is surfaced in the Console and gated for routing.
Bench output should include a quality_delta column with parity score, quant-recipe tag, and link to baseline commit. Optimize will consume that.

Observed weird role-bleed when converting HF jinja chat_template -> Redwood prompt during a new model bring-up. Some conditional blocks that render empty cause the system sentinel to get glued to the following user message, which then trips tokenization and leads to strange outputs.

Minimal example HF template we used:
```jinja
{% if system_inject %}
- role: system

"{{ user_input }}"
```

When `system_inject` is empty the converter produced this payload:
```
<|system|>
- role: user

"Hello"
```
which got flattened into the prompt as `"<|system|>- role: user"` and the tokenizer turned that into weird token sequences.
That's probably why the quantized int8 run had those hallucination spikes yesterday. Any tokenizer dumps/ids? :eyes:

Pasted a quick tokenizer dump. When conditional yields a blank line the `system` sentinel `'<|system|>'` remains as raw token and our renderer doesn't add the Redwood delimiter, so whitespace gets merged. Token snippet:
``
['<|system|>', '\n', '- role:', ' user'] -> [50256, 13, ...]
``
Whitespace/token boundary is the culprit.

config.json role_map currently has `"system": "<|system|>"`. Our function `chat_template_to_prompt()` strips empty branches rather than replacing them with explicit role separators. I'll add a placeholder sentinel when a block is omitted so downstream stays consistent.

Quick follow-up from today's RFC — sketch for a layerwise hydration 'supply chain' idea.
gist?
idea: each shard exposes per-layer readiness hints + a small budget token pool. Loader agents request 'supply' for layers proactively up to budget, otherwise fallback to on-demand streaming.
so budget is per-model-session or global per-host? how do we avoid duplicate prefetch across concurrent requests?
budget granularity: session-scoped (short leases) + host-level backpressure token bucket. Lease issued by weight-server with a TTL. If another loader sees active lease, it skips prefetch.
main risks: lease leaks and stale budgets -> OOM thrash. Need eviction callbacks and a heartbeat/renewal path.
heartbeat freq options: 500ms vs 2s. 500ms reduces stale windows but increases costs. Tradeoff depends on request qps.
observability: we must record per-layer cold-miss, prefetch-hit, lease-grant-duration histograms and surfaced in Console. Also expose a simple "supply_status" endpoint on weightserver for debugging.
fallback: if weightserver or transport doesn't support lease RPC, loader should gracefully fall back to index-first streaming with smaller chunk sizes to reduce tail latency.
deploy-bot: proposal ready for gated rollout. Can we A/B this? feature flag `layerwise-supply-v1` suggested.
rollout plan: canary -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automatic rollback triggers (cold-miss rate spike > 5% or memory pressure above configured threshold).

one more system-level point: shard placement optimizer must be aware of supply budgets so it doesn't colocate multiple very-hot layers on a single GPU, otherwise leases will collide and nullify benefit.
good call. That implies we need a hint API from scheduler: `expected_warm_budget(layer)`. Scheduler can then spread hot-layer replicas.

proposal: compact header fields: magic (4b), serializer_id (string), schema_version (int), epoch (string), mini_sig (blake2b-64 hex), optional full_checksum_url. mini_sig is fast to compute, full_checksum authoritative.

Quick brain-dump: what if we introduce a tiny per-shard sidecar (shard-###.aux) that contains a light-weight manifest: short fingerprint, relative layer offsets, quantization tag, abi version and an optional signature. runtime does a single small GET to decide hotstart strategy before touching big blob.

Sounds promising. main benefits I see: avoid a full mmap/parse just to learn if shard is compatible; faster failure on mismatch; and we can pick indexing vs stream path proactively. questions: how do we place the aux across packaging formats (raw shards, tar/gzip bundles, object storage metadata)?

plan for placement: 1) sidecar file next to shard (s3/object) 2) included inside model bundle as shard-000.aux (preferably stored uncompressed) 3) as object metadata when publishers prefer metadata entries. loader searches in that order.
tradeoffs: a) atomicity - need a clear publish commit flow so aux and shard don't drift. b) compatibility - old loaders should ignore aux silently. c) extra files to track in registries.

for atomicity we can write shard payload first, then aux last, and finally a tiny commit marker (shard-000.aux.commit). commit file acts as the ready flag and contains version and signature. loaders treat aux as authoritative only if commit exists.

what about leases / dedupe: when many nodes try to warm the same shard, we should avoid duplicate heavy downloads. I propose keeping ephemeral leases in our runtime metadata store (etcd/consul). aux only carries a stable boot id and fingerprint; runtime uses metadata store to negotiate hotstart ownership. we avoid object-store writes on lease transitions.
agree. aux remains read-only artifact in object storage. runtime lease is ephemeral and kept off-object-store. this keeps publish cheap and keeps aux trustworthy for first-read heuristics.

another corner: mmap offsets. if aux stores absolute file offsets, repacking or embedding in bundles will break them. store relative offsets: offset from start-of-array within the shard plus a small abi field that explains packing expectations. loader can compute absolute if it mmap's from known base.

signature idea: include a short sha256 fingerprint and signer id. signed aux allows runtime to trust the fingerprint without fetching the whole shard. add quant_tag to help warmup choose fp16/q8h optimized kernels ahead of time.

rollout steps: 1) loader accepts aux if present, falls back silently when missing. 2) runtime uses aux only to choose warmup strategy and prefetch hints. 3) publishing toolchain produces aux and a commit marker when publishing bundles. 4) registry/CI validates commit presence as optional gate for signed releases.
ops concerns: relying on signed metadata means release infra needs key management and signing roles. ops-bot: creating infra ticket infra/2026 to update registry and signing perms.
noted infra/2026 created. tag: release-signer.

one more: for gzipped bundles we should prefer storing aux uncompressed alongside the compressed shard to avoid needing partial decompression. if embedded, prefer a separate entry in the tarball header and mark it with a known mime/type.

runtime heuristics: if aux indicates large contiguous layers we prefer mmap if base format supports it; if many small scattered arrays we prefer streaming + async prefetch. aux can carry a simple heuristic flag ("prefetch_hint": "mmap|stream").
and include an "abi" per-shard so loaders can fast-fail when aux schema doesn't match. per-shard abi lets different shards of same model evolve independently if needed.

testing checklist: publish test bundles with and without aux, ensure loader fallback path exercised, validate commit marker semantics, exercise lease path in metadata store under high-concurrency warmstart (stress test).
