Quick follow-up on the handoff surface between Loader and Warmup. We keep hitting an atomicity gap when a shard is being replaced during warmup + eviction.
Can you sketch the failure mode again? I remember safetensors manifestless blobs made this messy.

Sure — sequence: 1) Loader maps old shards, 2) Warmup starts fetching new shard in background, 3) eviction frees memory and a request races in, Loader points to new blob before warmup finishes -> partial weights on disk, crash or bad weights served.
Got it. One option is to require a manifest+index for every upload so we can do index-first activation. That avoids partial-read semantics.
That's a big constraint for S3 uploaders and some HF-style bundles. We should have a compatibility path.

What about an ephemeral 2-phase commit: upload blob -> upload manifest with epoch token -> manifest publish step that flips an activation pointer. Warmup only switches on manifest publish with matching epoch.
That aligns with lease-based activation. Need a cheap pin to avoid eviction between manifest publish and activation.

We could do: publish manifest (immutable) -> warmup obtains "activation lease" from WarmupCoordinator (short TTL) -> Loader swaps pointer only if lease present. If warmup fails lease expires and we roll back.

That still leaves a window where Loader might switch to the new manifest but warmup hasn't fully materialized local pages. We need a guarantee that Loader won't hand out GPU pointers until KV caches are primed.

Right. Proposal: extend the Loader API with two ops: PREPARE_ACTIVATE(manifest, epoch) which reserves pages and returns a token; and ACTIVATE(token) which atomically swaps pointers. Warmup calls PREPARE_ACTIVATE, writes pages, then ACTIVATE.
PREPARE_ACTIVATE could return a pre-allocated ephemeral mapping + reservation id. Eviction honors reservations. That should be simple on nodes with support for mmap+fadvise.
How does this work for streaming shards (range requests)? PREPARE_ACTIVATE would register byte-range reservations so partial reads are allowed but not pointer swap until all ranges done.
Implementation detail: warmup can request range reservations via the coordinator and get back 'range tokens'. We track completion per-token and allow ACTIVATE when all tokens ready.

We must also consider cross-node handoffs: load-balancer might route requests to old node while new node activates. We need a global registry so activation is visible cluster-wide before any non-initializing requests.
deploy success: warmup-coordinator v1.3.2 pushed to dev cluster :rocket:

For cluster visibility we can use a small TTL-backed registry entry in Consul/KV: set activation_state(manifest, epoch)="activating" then "active". LB checks state and denies routing to nodes in "activating" until "active".
We should add metrics: reservation_count, activation_latency, failed_activations. That will help tune TTLs and eviction policies.
Edgecases: aborted uploads (manifest never published) -> garbage collection. Need GC scan that checks manifests without activation for >Xh and marks blobs tombstone.
Also security: manifest publish needs signing or uploader auth so no tampering with epoch tokens.

Heads up 0000000000running HF->Redwood conversion for the new chat model. Our evals show token-level misalignment: answers are shifted and some spans don't line up in QA.
Most likely normalization / pretokenizer mismatch. HF checkpoints sometimes use 'NFC' vs 'NFKC' and pretokenizers like byte-fallback vs metaspace change token boundaries.
Quick repro script showed NBSP and soft-hyphen causing split differences. Also saw emoji sequences explode into 3-4 tokens after conversion.

Example I saw locally (different markers):
```
# original HF (sentencepiece-like)
orig.encode("▁this is a test") -> ['▁this', '▁is', '▁a', '▁test']
# converted wrapper (metaspace lost)
conv.encode(" this is a test") -> ['this', ' is', ' a', ' test']
# note the missing leading metaspace token which breaks our template concat
```
That missing leading marker breaks the chat system prefix logic we use (system + user + assistant concatenation). Our playback tests show the system prompt merging with user text.

Also check `add_prefix_space` behavior. GPT2-style wrappers rely on an explicit flag; if it's unset, token offsets shift. Conversion tools sometimes preserve special_tokens_map but forget to set the runtime flag.

Another gotcha: HF tokenizers with `byte_fallback` can split complex ligatures or combined emoji, while metaspace keeps them intact as single tokens in many cases. That changes sequence lengths and batching behavior.

rw-convert log snippet:
```
rw-convert --from hf --tokenizer /tmp/tok.json --out /rw/models/x
INFO: pre_tokenizer=byte_fallback
INFO: normalization=NFC
INFO: special_tokens preserved
```

We also found control-char handling differences (ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE, LEFT-TO-RIGHT MARK). HF sometimes normalizes them away depending on the normalization step; runtime kept them and tokenized differently.
Impact on evals: perplexity looked similar, but exact-match and F1 on our QA set dropped by ~5 points — classic tokenization misalignment.

Short checklist for conversions (recommend adding to rw-convert):
- assert normalization mode (NFC / NFKC / NFKD) matches source
- assert pre_tokenizer (byte_fallback vs metaspace) and patch if needed
- explicitly set add_prefix_space if original uses GPT2-like behavior
- compare token counts on a 2k prompt sample and print top diffs
- sanity-check special token roundtrip for system/user/bos/eos

quick thought — can we add a tiny, optional "warmup-hint" header to safetensors/shard metadata to steer eager vs lazy hydration? mostly for cold-start QoS on Dedicated clusters.

advisory-only is good. main tradeoff: more metadata on every shard increases manifest size and tooling complexity. also remote manifests + gzipped transport might bloat.

preference: format-agnostic manifest field named `x.warmup_hint` and then optional format-specific header for safetensors/tar. keeps runtime lookup uniform.
runtime cost: lookup path should be O(1) per-shard without reading entire payload. we should put header in index/sidecar so we don't need to mmap whole file.

perf goals: when priority_hint=hot, runtime should try to prefetch whole shard into GPU memory during warmup windows; warm = prefetch small leading chunk (KV + first N MB), cold = lazy stream. also an optional `min_prefetch_bytes` helps on very wide embeddings layers.

Patch suggestion: compute phase_index per-head before padding and store a head_map to remap after padding.

Interesting — the kernel-switch overhead + KV miss pattern smells like ABI/packing inefficiency when kernels change precision mid-seq. Did you see an increase in memcpy or launch overhead on the timeline?

Yes, timeline shows frequent small kernel launches. When per-channel calibration produced a few extreme scales, we auto-switched to a fallback kernel (per-tensor) for those layers which forced the runtime to use a different fused path -> extra copies.
That jives. Mixed-precision gating that picks different execution graphs per-layer will break continuous batching: it fragments the batch groups and disables some kernel fusion heuristics.
Is the regression repeatable if you clip outliers in the calib set? E.g., replace >3 sigma activations with clipped values and rerun quantize/pack.

I tried clipping to 3 sigma in-place — quality (accuracy on eval set) stayed within 0.2% but perf improved: p50 down to 44.1ms, throughput 21.1 req/s. So clipping helps but the change feels heuristic-y.

That suggests our calibration dataset has heavy tails. If outliers are causing per-channel scales to explode, per-channel quantization will force fallbacks for only a tiny subset of channels but still kill fusion.

Proposal: change gating to be layer-aware instead of channel-aware for live routing. Compute a per-layer SNR metric from calib stats. If layer-SNR < threshold, force per-tensor quant path for the whole layer at compile time and avoid mid-batch switching. That reduces graph variance.
Agree. We should also make the runtime treat tiny-fraction channel fallbacks as clipped exceptions rather than whole-layer fallbacks by default — or perform a cheap remap that keeps the fused kernel.

We prototyped a "gatewalk" policy: evaluate per-channel ratio of scale to median-scale, mark channels >K as "tail"; if tail_count < T_percent, apply channel-clamp (clip/scatter) and keep per-channel kernels. If tail_count >= T_percent, switch whole-layer to per-tensor.
With gatewalk (K=4, T=2%), results: p50=43.2ms, throughput=22.4 req/s, accuracy delta +0.03%. Looks promising.
Nice. How sensitive to K/T are you? Need to make defaults robust across models.
K sweep shows knee around 3.5-4.5. T around 1-3% stabilizes perf/quality. But some safety-net models with very long tails need stricter T.
Ops question: does gatewalk increase profiling cost? We currently run one calibration pass. Gatewalk needs channel histograms + tail counts, so same pass but extra aggregation — cheap.

Another operational thing: the batching heuristics need a small enhancement to avoid splitting batches when layer execution graph differs. If the runtime can tag requests with layer-graph-hash and batch only compatible ones, fusion remains intact. That will add complexity to the grouping but could eliminate the copy/launch overhead.
True — maybe a two-tier batcher: prefer native fusion groups but allow fallback batches for incompatible ones. That reduces tail impact on p50.

FYI bringing up mosaic-13B-v2 from HF — our `hf-to-redwood` convert job failed on the config.json step. Main incompatibilities I see: `rope_scaling`, `sliding_window`, `num_key_value_heads` != `num_attention_heads`, and `max_position_embeddings` way larger than our runtime expects. Anyone run into this?
yup. rope_scaling is an HF extension we mostly ignore, but `sliding_window` changes how the KV cache is laid out (we assume fixed offsets). That one broke our loader.
can you paste the config snippet?

here's the relevant part:
```json
{
  "max_position_embeddings": 32768,
  "rope_scaling": {"type":"linear", "factor":0.5},
  "sliding_window": true,
  "num_key_value_heads": 64,
  "num_attention_heads": 32
}
```
oof — `num_key_value_heads` > `num_attention_heads` is a pretty common HF oddity for models with grouped kv heads. Our runtime assumes kv heads == attention heads.

quick options: 1) rewrite the loader to remap kv->attn by splitting/replicating heads, 2) derive kv projection shape from the weight tensors instead of config.json, or 3) fallback to a compatibility shim that clamps `num_key_value_heads` to `num_attention_heads` and emits a warning. Option 2 is safest if weights are canonical.

weights do show kv_proj shape (512, 4096) which implies head grouping, but the HF config lies. I tried option 3 locally and it allowed conversion, but then inference segfaulted when `sliding_window=true` because our KV indexing code still expects contiguous cache slices.

sliding_window basically implements a circular KV buffer with windowed attention — we don't support that at runtime yet. Best pragmatic path: disable sliding_window in converted config and emulate by chunked prefix caching at the Redwood layer. Works for most chat workloads.

I also ran quantization experiments after clamping max_position_embeddings to 16384 and forcing `num_key_value_heads`=32. 4-bit quant (awq) looked ok, but I saw a small quality regression (~3% perplexity up) on our convo eval set when sliding_window is disabled.
3% isn't great but maybe acceptable depending on latency/cost wins. Did you run the prompt-level refresh evals? Any hallucination/regression hits?

ran ~200 prompts from our regression suite. A few template-sensitive cases degraded — mostly long-turn coherence. Suspect rope_scaling emulation is needed for very long contexts; clamping positions + simple linear rope scaling emulation reduced the gap.

note: rope_scaling in HF can be `linear` or `dynamic`. For emulation we apply a scaled rotary embedding factor during KV build: multiply sin/cos positions by factor. It's imperfect but helped in your run?
yes, applying a conservative factor (0.75) to the embeddings reduced the perplexity delta to ~1% and fixed several coherence failures.

please open an issue with reproduction steps + the failing convo ids so we can triage. Also add a conversion test that detects `num_key_value_heads` mismatch and tries weight-shape-based inference before assuming config is authoritative.

filing one now. PR incoming for two things: (A) loader fallback to infer kv heads from weight shapes, (B) conversion flag `--disable-sliding-window` that rewrites config and annotates the converted model with notes about the emulation.

Quick heads-up — the python sampleapp for embed+rerank is returning different response shapes between sync and async clients. Sync returns a list of dicts under 'items' but async is returning a dict with separate 'embeddings' and 'scores'. I hit this on v0.9.2 when porting a sample app to async. Anyone seen this?
Yep saw something similar after upgrading. The typings for AsyncEmbedReranker still say -> List[RerankResult] but at runtime it spits out Dict[str, Any]. Makes downstream code blow up.
Can you paste a tiny repro snippet and which sample app?

Repro (super tiny):
```python
# sync
resp = client.embeddings.rerank(input=["query"], candidates=["a", "b"])
# resp -> [{'score': 0.92, 'embedding': [...], 'candidate': 'a'}, ...]
# async
resp = await client.async_embeddings.rerank(["query"], ["a", "b"])
# resp -> {'embeddings': [[...], [...]], 'scores': [0.92, 0.1]}  # mismatch
```

Looks like the batching helper used for async returns a compact dict (embeddings + scores) to avoid lots of small objects, but we never normalized the public client return shape. Typings/SDK surface didn't get updated.
Filed DEVEX-412 to track this parity bug and typing mismatch. Likely fix: normalize async client to match sync shape, update type hints, and add unit/integration tests in sampleapp.
New ticket created: DEVEX-412 — Embed/rerank async response shape parity. Assignee: @elaine.

One more thing I noticed — when token refresh happens mid-batch in async flows, ordering can get shuffled because of how retries are applied in the batch helper. Might be related. Added a note to DEVEX-412.

Thanks — for immediate unblock I hacked a small normalizer:
```py
def normalize_rerank(resp):
    if isinstance(resp, dict) and 'embeddings' in resp:
        return [ { 'score': s, 'embedding': e } for s,e in zip(resp['scores'], resp['embeddings']) ]
    return resp
```

Quick q — we have encrypted+signed safetensors bundles with mixed-quant shards. Current verify step blocks warmup and spikes cold-start latency. Any preferred approach?
Agree this is a pain. My vote: header-first latch so we can start warmup ASAP, then do full crypto/byte-verify in background.
Header-first how? if we only verify manifest but not shard payloads, attacker could flip a shard in-flight. Need mitigation.

Two-phase verify is what we used elsewhere: 1) verify top-level manifest signature + shard descriptors (sizes/checksums) 2) async verify payloads. For warmup, allow ephemeral reads but forbid attaching to KV cache until payloads VERIFIED.
State machine idea: UNTRUSTED_EPHEMERAL -> VERIFIED -> PROMOTED. Ephemeral reads allowed for non-critical ops; promotion requires full verify. TTL + fallback if verify fails. :thinking_face:

Proto sketch: loader reads manifest, validates manifest sig, schedules parallel decrypt+verify for shards. For warmup, accept shard into UNTRUSTED_EPHEMERAL with metadata flag no-kv-attach. That lets token generation start while full verify runs. In our sims that shaved ~40-50% off p95 for small prompts.
perf note: prototype run on toy-v1 mixed-quant reduced p95 cold-start from 320ms -> 190ms, background IO +12%.

My worry: some models place critical parameters (LN/bias) across shards. If an ephemeral shard is used before verified you can get subtly wrong outputs. We should restrict ephemeral reads for layers flagged CRITICAL.

We can add manifest metadata per-layer or per-shard: CRITICAL vs NONCRITICAL. Default conservative = mark all layer groups CRITICAL until model owner annotates. That requires minor manifest schema bump.
Also need robust eviction behavior: verifier may be mid-IO when shard gets evicted. Use chunked verification and resume tokens so verifier can resume if shard is paged back. Keep verifier idempotent.
Security checklist: add KMS/audit events for manifest-verify failures and for deferred-verify promotions. Also ensure we don't leak decryption keys to lower-priv pools during ephemeral reads.

Action items: I'll write RFC follow-up covering state machine, manifest flags, and loader API changes. Ana will prototype loader flow: header-first warmup + no-kv-attach semantics + promotion. Sam coordinate security review. Taylor add perf harness. ETA EOW?

can you paste the minimal repro and a short log? sounds like an interpolation artifact in the rotary table or the freq lookup.

repro: `./longctx_runner --model model-y:int4v2 --prompt tests/64k_loop.json --rotary-scale 0.95 --kv_window 131072 --quant-profile int4v2 --seed 123`

... "and then she" "and then she" "and then she" -> small repeats at 61456,61457

interesting. so int4v2 kernel apparently uses a compact rotary table plus linear interpolation to save memory. That could introduce small phase discontinuities at higher positions where the table spacing is larger relative to frequency. The fp16 baseline probably computed sin/cos on the fly or used higher-res table.

Quick heads-up — onboarding an HF chat model and the HF->Redwood conversion step is nuking the system block when the original chat_template uses Jinja conditionals. Repro attached below, looks like curly braces/escape handling + tokenizer differences. Anyone seen this?
can you paste the problematic template snippet?

sure, minimal example:
```jinja
{% if persona %}
<|system|>You are a helpful, terse assistant for {{ persona }}.
{% endif %}
<|user|>{{ user_input }}</|user|>
```
After conversion the runtime prompt becomes: `You are a helpful, terse assistant for .\n{{ user_input }}` — system role gone, braces still visible in places.
ugh, that's the classic Jinja vs literal-brace problem. Are we running the template renderer before or after tokenization?

renderer runs in our HF->RW converter which is python-based. We call Template.render(...) then assemble Redwood prompt pieces. But when persona is falsy we still end up with stray markers because HF had role markers as tokens rather than separate message entries.

could be two issues: 1) HF chat_template encodes role wrappers as special tokens (eg ``<|system|>``) that the tokenizer sometimes splits during quantized inference; 2) our conversion script treats those wrappers as plain text and does naive regex replace for braces.
also saw this: some HF templates rely on `{%-` trimming and whitespace control; if we drop those characters earlier we change token boundaries which breaks eval prompts.

timeline: brought model up on dedicated, ran eval harness (SMOKE-qa) and saw a 6-8% hit on system-prompt-sensitive tasks. Narrowed down to a subset of test cases where template had conditionals/loops.

quick patch idea: do explicit AST parse of the chat_template instead of raw render+replace. Keep role-segmented messages as array elements and convert each to Redwood block. That preserves role separation.

yeah — treat role tokens as structural. Eg convert HF chat_template entries to list: [ {role: "system", content: "..."}, {role: "user", content: "..."} ] and then stringify for Redwood. Avoid interpolating unrendered braces into final string.

small repro script (pseudo):
```py
from jinja2 import Environment
env = Environment()
tmpl = env.from_string(hf_template)
rendered = tmpl.render(**ctx)
# BAD: re.sub(r"<\|system\|>.*?<\|/system\|>", "", rendered)
# GOOD: parse into messages first, then render each content separately and join with separators
```

thanks. two open questions: 1) tokenizer divergence — do we need to apply the HF tokenizer pre-conversion to detect token splits for special tokens? 2) unit tests: how do we assert parity after conversion?

for 1) yes, run HF tokenizer on the original template pieces to detect if any special tokens are being split into subtokens. If so, add a pre-token mapping or update special_tokens_map before model bring-up.

for 2) add a tiny regression suite that renders N canonical templates with edge cases (conditional, loop, escape sequences, whitespace control) and compare (a) Redwood-assembled prompt tokens (post-conversion) and (b) HF raw-rendered tokens. Fail if mismatch on role boundaries or if system role disappears. Keep tests lightweight and run in CI with emulators.
one weirdness: with 4-bit quant on the runtime we sometimes see decoder join tokens differently during sampling which made golden exact-token-match tests flaky. Any tips?

don't assert exact token ids for quantized runs; instead assert role-presence and normalized string contains key phrases. Eg assert system prompt substring present and that user content appears after system marker. Use fuzzy equality (levenshtein <= 2) for quantized smoke.

also log the tokenization offsets during conversion in a short map so operators can inspect which bytes -> tokens changed. That helped us debug a previous model where `<|endoftext|>` got merged into adjacent text due to tokenizer config differences.

Suspect tokenizer drift. Baseline image had tokenizers==2.8.0, quant image pulled 3.1.0 via transitive dep. Repro logs:
```
INFO loading tokenizer v3.1.0
WARN tokenized: "I'm  fine" (double spaces)
WARN shard count mismatch: processed=2004 expected=2000
```
Tokenizer whitespace changes alone can tank BLEU/ROUGE. BERTScore more tolerant but param-sensitive.
Also the sharder in the runner appears to assign the remainder shard twice when num_workers > 8. That gives extra samples and makes pass@k math wrong.
Hmm I thought we had a sentinel for remainder. I'll inspect the parallel sharder loop. If true, pass@k denominator will be off.
Another subtle one: our pass@k dedupe uses semantic similarity (bert-sim) + norming. For datasets where multiple valid paraphrases exist, semantic dedupe removes near-variants and inflates pass@k.
We should standardize dedupe to deterministic string normalization (NFKC + collapse whitespace + lowercase) and keep semantic cluster as opt-in.
Found metric config drift too: quant-run used BERTScore with idf=false, baseline idf=true. Small but consistent bias.
So root causes: tokenizer version mismatch, sharder remainder bug, and metric param drift. All three together explains the delta.

I'll open PR to: 1) enforce metric-config checksum in harness, 2) change pass@k dedupe to deterministic norm, 3) add explicit tokenizer version assert before eval starts.

Lower accuracy + higher latency usually indicates a kernel fallback to a slow path or host memcpy. Any "CUBLAS_STATUS" or "no kernel found" errors in the logs?

Snip of the error stream:
```
[W tensorrt_llm] cublasLt error: CUBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED while selecting int8 matmul kernel
[W awq_kernels] falling back to reference int8 GEMM (very slow)
[INFO] using fallback GEMM path for layer 42
```

That matches what I've seen when TensorRT-LLM picks a kernel requiring a newer cuBLASLt API or when the awq custom kernels were built against a different CUDA ABI. Two checks: (1) is the awq native extension built inside the container against CUDA 12.3? (2) does the TRT-LLM image vendor a cuBLASLt that conflicts with host driver?

Quick debugging checklist we've used:
- Try TRT-LLM 2.0.2 image (we had 2.1.0 introduce a cuBLASLt selector change).
- Try host driver downgrade to 525.x (CUDA 12.2 compatible driver) as a cross-check.
- Rebuild awq native ops wheel inside the target image (pip wheel built against same CUDA).
- Run NVTX traces or `nsys` to see if kernels are dispatched to device or falling back.

Additional note: AWQ's int8 kernels use custom CUDA kernels that must be compiled with the exact same major.minor CUDA version to avoid ABI mismatches. If you installed a prebuilt wheel on top of the NVIDIA image, it might still be compiled for a different cudart/cuBLASLt. Rebuild: `pip install --no-binary :all: awq-ops` inside the TRT image.

Reproduction command I used (simplified):
```
docker run --gpus all -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 -v /models:/models \
  nvcr.io/redwood/tensorrt-llm:2.1.0-awq \
  bash -c "python bench.py --model /models/llama2-13b-awq --quant awq --backend trt_llm --eval mmlu --bs 1"
```
Can you also dump `ldd` of the awq extension lib and `pip show awq-ops`? That will show which libcublas / libcublasLt SONAME was linked.
Yep, ldd shows `libcublasLt.so.12 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcublasLt.so.12` (provided by container). `pip show awq-ops` shows wheel compiled for cuda110 or cuda116 (mismatch!).

Bingo. Mismatch in the wheel. Two practical paths: (A) rebuild awq-ops wheel inside this image (fast), or (B) use TRT-LLM image that vendors a matching cuBLASLt and awq wheel. Option A is our typical dev path.

If you want a quick check that it's not TRT-LLM logic, try serving the same AWQ quant file with vLLM native runtime (no TensorRT). If vLLM shows correct accuracy near 71 and expected latency profile, then it's likely a TRT/awq kernel mismatch rather than quantization quality issue.

I ran that earlier: AWQ file served with vLLM native gave 69.8 (still a small drop vs GPTQ), but importantly it did not show the cublasLt fallback warnings and latency was ~110ms. So AWQ quant quality delta ~1.4-2.8 points vs GPTQ depending on serving path; the big drop to 68.4 was only with TRT-LLM image and the fallback logs.

Also check the quant post-processing glue — some TRT-LLM integrations convert int8 blocks into different alignment that can change rounding behavior. We had a case where packing into int8x4 changed exponent alignment and shifted logits slightly. Small numeric changes can push some answers over/under thresholds in MMLU.

Quick experiment notes: comparing full INT8 vs per-layer partial quant (exclude embed + lm_head) on 7B. Latencies look good on average but p99 spikes when using static calibration ranges.
FP16 baseline: p95 ~38ms, p99 ~110ms. full INT8: p95 ~62ms, p99 ~190ms. partial (exclude embed/lm_head): p95 ~44ms, p99 ~120ms.
Wow that p99 delta is large. Which kernel backend did you run? custom int8 kernels or cublas-int8? sequence lengths?
Mostly our custom int8 matmul kernels on A100-80. Seq lens tested: 8/32/128/512. The p99s correlate with odd sequence lens and some KV cache ops.
Likely pathological codepath: when cached KV pages use different quant scales we end up doing dequant/req quant on read/write which blows up tail. Are we serializing KV in-place or materializing?

Currently materialize+requant on KV read. Profiling snippet:
```
[prof] iter=204 step_latency_ms=46.1 kernel=matmul_int8 layer=10 time=0.92ms
[prof] kv_read_ms=3.6 kv_write_ms=2.8 dequant_ms=1.4
[prof] iter=205 step_latency_ms=182.9 kernel=matmul_int8 layer=3 time=5.1ms <-- hotspot, extra reshapes + fallback
```
Did you try hybrid FP8/INT8? attention layers sometimes prefer FP8 to hold dynamic range, while FFN can be int8. Also calibration dataset composition matters (long vs short contexts).

Tried FP8 for first 6 layers, INT8 for rest. Average latency improved a bit vs full INT8, but eval quality dropped on repetition/lengthy prompts. Also runtime fell back to a slower kernel when alignment constraints weren't met for certain seq lengths.
That kernel fallback explains tail. We should add a trace field for "kernel_fallback_reason" and incremental counters for num_dequant_ops and kv_serialization_ops.

Agreed. Filed issue #1428. Short term mitigation: per-layer symmetric minmax calibration and group layers to share scales so KV reads don't force recompute. Config I'm testing:
```
quant_profile:
["embed", "lm_head"]

"minmax_symmetric"
  force_fp16_kv_when_kv_bytes_gt: 524288
  allow_kernel_fallback: false
```

- If (dequant_ms + kv_read_ms) > threshold, prefer FP16 kernel for that layer.
- Force KV serializer to store FP16 slices if kv_bytes > X to avoid repeated quant/dequant churn.

Quick follow-up on the incremental admit adapter RFC — want to nail the tradeoffs for eager vs lazy compatibility checks before we land the refactor. TL;DR: propose a lightweight inline smoke + async deep bench flow. feedback pls by EOD :hourglass:

Agree on hybrid. Eager/full checks catch regressions early but slow down intake. Lazy async checks reduce onboarding latency but leave a window where a bad model can be served. Hybrid looks like best balance.

From runtime benching: full bench (1000 samples + kv cache sim) on a single node adds ~40–60s to ingest if done serially. If we parallelize across 8 runners that drops to ~8s per model but uses more infra. Example command we use for local sims:
```
run_bench --model-path s3://models/x --samples 1000 --kv-sim --parallel 8
```

Cost/ops perspective: parallel heavy benches are fine but we should avoid them by default for every PR. Proposed policy:
- Inline smoke (<= 2m): latency, basic top-1 correctness, kv-cache basic ops. block on this.
- Async deep bench (scheduled on cluster): full perplexity + latency tail + quant/ops compatibility. report-only by default; can be blocking for "critical" models/tags.

Small API suggestion for the admit adapter return so tools can make deterministic decisions:
```
AdmitResponse = {
  status: "accepted" | "deferred" | "rejected",
["kv-hash", "model-bin-hash"],
["quantization-diff:0.12", "kv-warmup-variance"],

"s3://..."
}
```
We need to persist `fingerprints` and `bench_report_url` to the model registry so downstream routing can fallback to compatible variants.

Prefer keeping the inline contract minimal. Maybe `status`, `fingerprints`, and `report` link only. Warnings should be surfaced to UI but not part of blocking contract. Operationally:
- Block if inline smoke => `status: rejected`
- Otherwise `status: deferred` and async job runs.
- For `critical` tag, mark an admission flag that prevents serving until async job transitions to `accepted` (this is the canary mode).
One more infra note — we should tag async jobs with the originating commit/model-id and ensure retries are idempotent. Also plumb cost center metadata so billing for heavy benches is visible.

On KV compatibility tests: we should include deterministic warmup sequence + short TTL churn test. Catch regressions in cache evictions. small snippet:
```
# pseudo
for seq in golden_seq:
  send(seq)
assert hit_rate > 0.85
```
Will prototype a parallel runner that can run the deep bench in a k8s job with configurable concurrency. If we go this route, we can afford heavier async benches and keep inline checks cheap.

Quick question — we need a decision on how to show prefetch/cache savings in the SLA-aware cost dashboard. My rough idea: attribute prefetch savings to models that consumed the prefetched tokens within a session window, amortized by token usage. Pros: aligns with who benefited. Cons: cross-tenant prefetching and cold-start credits complicate it. Thoughts?
do you mean session window per API key or per request trace? both implications matter. if per API key, a noisy tenant could absorb others' prefetchs.

quick flag: sampling will bias this. we sample 1% of requests for detailed traces; if we attribute based on sampled traces we might over/under-estimate savings for tail tenants. need correction factor.
agree with Sam. Also need to expose whether savings column is "estimated" or "attributed". console UX should make the confidence visible. maybe an uncertainty % or sample rate badge. :bar_chart:

another heuristic — attribute by downstream token consumption in the next N requests from the same session id. like: if prefetched keys saved 300 tokens and model A used 200 tokens and model B used 100 tokens, split 2:1. avoids per-key owner issues.

that matches my thinking. Implementation question: do we do attribution in real-time or as a batch job? real-time allows live dashboards but is heavier. batch overnight is easier and reduces noise smoothing.
for SLA math we need near-real-time for billing alerts. maybe two layers: a near-real-time estimate (approx) and a delayed authoritative number for invoices.
+1. For canaries/rollouts we must ensure we don't credit canary trials with full savings. add rule: if model variant is canary flag, attribute only to baseline unless rollout % > threshold.
telemetry note: we need a deterministic join key. current traces have request_id and session_id; use session_id when present, fallback to hashed api_key + 1min window. document this clearly.

SQL sketch for nightly attribution job:
```
WITH prefetchs AS (SELECT session_id, prefetch_id, saved_tokens FROM prefetch_events WHERE ts >= date_sub(now(), interval 1 day)),
consumed AS (SELECT session_id, model_id, SUM(tokens) as used_tokens FROM request_tokens WHERE ts >= date_sub(now(), interval 1 day) GROUP BY session_id, model_id),
split AS (SELECT p.prefetch_id, c.model_id, p.saved_tokens * (c.used_tokens / SUM(c.used_tokens) OVER (PARTITION BY p.prefetch_id)) as attributed_tokens FROM prefetchs p JOIN consumed c USING (session_id))
INSERT INTO nightly_attribution(prefetch_id, model_id, attributed_tokens) SELECT prefetch_id, model_id, SUM(attributed_tokens) FROM split GROUP BY prefetch_id, model_id;
```
nice. we should also persist metadata: sample_rate_used, attribution_method_version, and a per-row confidence score.
UX: add a toggle in the cost dashboard settings: "Attribution policy: token-proportional / owner-first / session-split" + description. default token-proportional.
we also need a guardrail: if total attributed_tokens > saved_tokens (float rounding + double-counting bugs), cap to saved_tokens and emit alert. add an automatic reconciliation job.
for telemetry sampling correction, we can use Horvitz-Thompson estimator to correct estimates from sampled traces. I can sketch that in RFC.

Implementation note: orchestrator should expose a token-bucket for each bucket_id. Sampler obtains tokens via a cheap lease call: /lease?bucket=b123&count=10. If lease fails sampler can fallback to lower-priority buckets.

Postmortem thread created for INC-2025-02-16 (Dedicated burst beta) — elevated tail latency + burst circuit breaker oscillation. Please add findings + action items here.
Dropping quick summary from today’s review so we can converge on action items for GA hardening. This is focused on circuit breaker behavior + guardrails (not general capacity sizing).

Impact recap:
- Window: ~11:18–11:33 PT
- Scope: us-east / H100 shared burst pool (beta)
- Symptom: non-burst tenants saw p95 and p99 latency jump (mostly tail amplification), plus increased 429s from gateway for a subset of burst traffic.
- We also saw the global circuit breaker flapping (open/close cycles) which made the behavior hard to reason about.

+1. From oncall perspective, the breaker “helped” but was noisy and late. Primary SLO we’re protecting is non-burst Dedicated latency; we need the breaker to be earlier + monotonic (once open, stay open for a minimum).

Root behavior as seen from routing:
- Admission controller started denying w/ `FLEET_SAFETY_CAP` and `POOL_SATURATED` intermittently.
- Routing fell back to baseline capacity but got a mix of “retry soon” vs “hard deny” semantics depending on which path the request hit.
- Resulted in burst clients doing retries that amplified load right as the breaker toggled.

From guardrails side, the flapping looks tied to two signals we used in the breaker:
1) pool saturation computed from allocator telemetry (laggy)
2) p95 delta for neighbor impact (fast-ish but noisy)
When telemetry lag spikes, saturation appears to drop -> breaker closes -> load surges -> breaker opens again.

Confirming telemetry lag. We had a 45–90s lag on the “in-use GPUs” metric due to a scrape backlog + label explosion from a misconfigured job (separate issue but it means we need breaker logic resilient to lag).

I pulled the graphs. The “telemetry_lag_seconds” panel hits 80s right before the first breaker close. After that, every close aligns with lag spikes. Also note the neighbor p99 delta is spiky because low-volume tenants swing a lot.

Fleet note: the pool wasn’t actually “free” when the breaker thought it was. Allocator had outstanding placements but telemetry said capacity recovered. That’s why we saw queue depth rising even when breaker closed.

Design-level finding: breaker state machine is currently too eager to close. It treats “below threshold for N samples” as recovery, but samples aren’t independent when the inputs are stale.
Proposal: incorporate a “staleness budget” into the policy evaluation. If either saturation input OR neighbor-impact input is stale beyond X, we should bias toward safety (stay open / reduce burst caps) rather than closing.

+1 and we can enforce determinism. Right now, two requests that land on different admission controller instances can see different breaker states during transitions (because state propagation is eventual). For GA we probably need:
- a single source of truth for breaker state per pool (or strongly consistent cached value w/ TTL)
- explicit “decision_epoch” so routing can reason about changes.

From Smart Routing view: we need denial semantics to be consistent across breaker states. Today we do:
- some denials return retryable 429 w/ `Retry-After`
- some return non-retryable `burst_denied` w/ reason
Customers will implement different retry loops and that changes load. For GA, breaker-open should return a predictable response shape and recommended backoff.
Product ask: whatever we do, we need something CS can explain in one sentence. “Burst temporarily unavailable due to fleet safety; baseline unaffected.” The flapping undermines trust.
Can we capture action items with owners + target dates? Goal is to have these landed before the GA staged rollout gate.

Findings (proposed):
1) Circuit breaker close criteria doesn’t account for telemetry staleness; closes too early.
2) No minimum-open time / cooldown, leading to flapping and retry amplification.
3) Denial semantics aren’t uniform (retryable vs non-retryable), increasing client-driven load during breaker transitions.
4) Neighbor-impact signal is noisy for low-volume tenants; needs smoothing and “minimum sample” gating.
5) Breaker state propagation can be inconsistent across admission controller replicas.
Agree with those 5.

+ add “routing fallback behavior during breaker open must be deterministic.” I saw cases where fallback landed on a different model variant due to capacity heuristics. That’s probably okay, but it should be explicit when breaker is open.

Action items draft (please edit):
A) Add telemetry staleness guard: if `telemetry_lag_seconds > X` OR allocator heartbeat stale, breaker cannot close; optionally force open. Owner: Allison + Jordan. Target: end of week.
B) Minimum-open window + exponential recovery: once open, stay open >= 5 min; on recovery, ramp burst caps up gradually (not immediate close). Owner: Keiko + Peter. Target: next sprint.
C) Uniform denial contract for breaker-open state: single reason code (`FLEET_SAFETY_OPEN`), always include `Retry-After` with jitter guidance. Owner: Mina + Ethan. Target: next sprint.
D) Neighbor-impact smoothing + sample threshold: require min request volume per tenant before considering tail deltas; use EWMA and clamp spikes. Owner: Sergio + Allison. Target: next sprint.
E) Stronger breaker state consistency: publish breaker state in control plane/policy engine w/ versioned epoch; replicas read via same cache key w/ TTL, no local recompute. Owner: Ethan + Jordan. Target: design by mid-next-week, implement following.
F) Oncall runbook update: add “breaker flapping” section and immediate mitigation (force-open + cap reduction) w/ commands. Owner: Rafael + Sean. Target: this week.

For (A)/(D): we already added smoothing in the hotfix branch for telemetry lag denial starvation (related). We can extend that pattern to breaker close logic. I’ll open a small PR with:
- `telemetry_lag_seconds` label reduced cardinality (pool-level only)
- a policy rule: `if lag > 30s => breaker_state = OPEN` (or `HOLD_OPEN`)
We should be careful about false positives though.

I’m ok with “HOLD_OPEN” vs “force open” to avoid triggering every time scrapes hiccup. But in this incident, we needed “stay open longer” not “open immediately.” Maybe:
- if OPEN, do not transition to CLOSED unless lag < 15s for 3 consecutive minutes

Heads-up on Zirconia13B onboarding: int4 run shows an odd degradation only on long-form QA. short prompts OK, but answers go off-distribution after ~1.5k tokens. anyone seen a similar pattern with headpacking?
not with Zirconia specifically, but that symptom often points at kvcache offset shifts or per-head rotary inconsistencies. can you paste the quant flags?
used `redwood-quantize --model zirconia13b --dtype int4 --group 32 --calib 2048 --preserve-fp16-embeddings=false`
calibration stats looked reasonable (ppl delta 0.03) but our long QA eval RougeL dropped 0.12.
did you check tokenizer idempotence? last time a stray sentinel / pad behavior shifted indices and produced exactly this after ~1k tokens.

good point. upstream tokenizer has `pad_token=0` but marks a ZERO WIDTH JOINER in merges as a ligature that should NOT be split. our shim accidentally treats that ligature as two tokens and emits a SENTINEL=50256 at boundaries.

that sentinel insertion will shift kvcache reads for affected streams. also check model metadata: I've seen exporters infer head packing when both `num_attention_heads` and `num_key_value_heads` are present. if the conversion picks the wrong one, rotary math gets mixed up.

ran `inspect-rotary zirconia13b --raw` on both fp16 and int4 artifacts. fp16 rotary angles per head are smooth; int4 artifact shows alternating sign flips on every 4th head and a ~0.5 scale on a contiguous block. dump: `rotary_angles: 1.0,0.98,-0.49,-0.51,0.99,0.97,-0.50,-0.52,...`
that explains why cosines between quant embed projections and fp16 drift after a while — headwise rotations are inconsistent.
likely cause: the int4 packing routine reorders heads for simd tiling (pack size 4) but the exporter forgot to permute the rotary/scales array in the same way. conversion bug.

workaround: re-quant with `--preserve-layout` and `--no-head-reorder`. small perf hit but sanity check.
jen a: (typo) re-ran with preserve-layout and updated tokenizer loader to respect `normalize_form: \"NFKD\"` from upstream. quick smoke:
```
zirconia fp16: p95 82ms, longQA-rougeL 0.57
zirconia int4.reconv: p95 63ms, longQA-rougeL 0.55
```
is close. toggling preserve-layout recovered most of the quality.

follow-up actions: 1) exporter change - when reordering heads for kernel packs, apply same permutation to rotary/scales metadata and to any per-head attention params. 2) tokenizer loader - add explicit normalization semantics test (NFKD vs NFKC) and add roundtrip on our canonical prefixes. 3) add unit that diffs kvcache row indices for a small prefix sequence between upstream tokenizer and our shim.

i've prototyped a small diagnostic `kv-offset-check` that runs a short prompt and compares the kvcache key hashes per token between fp16 and quant artifacts; adding to onboarding suite.

quick sync — i want to align on the long-term policy matrix for placement/region/tenant shielding. goal: clear launch gates for H2 roadmap so sales/security know what we can promise. small nit — i prefer "placement zones" vs "isolation level" naming in docs. placement zones = logical grouping e.g., "shared", "dedicated-pool", "pinned-vpc". saves ambiguity.

from oncall perspective, we need explicit failover semantics. e.g., if region A degrades, do we: (a) fail open to lower-tier model in same region, (b) reroute to healthy region (higher latency), or (c) reject? each has different alerting/playbook implications.

customers asking for two concrete things: 1) ability to require no-cross-region traffic for compliance, 2) predictable latency SLOs for user-facing latency-sensitive apps. they want explicit gating language for GA vs beta.

noted. proposal: define three launch classes: GA, Controlled GA (opt-in tenants), Experimental. Map features to classes. Example: cross-region fallback = Experimental; dedicated VPC with strict no-egress = GA.

engineering constraints: kernel selection & kv cache locality matter. If we do cross-region fallback often, KV cache warmups will tank p95 for a while. need a caching/replication plan in any cell that routes across regions.
add to that: metrics we need before GA: cross-region p50/p95 for token latency, error spike rate after failover, cold-KV penalty. If we don't hit thresholds, fallback must be disabled automatically.

also capture customer contractual language: for Controlled GA we should include "best-effort cross-region routing, no latency SLA" and an explicit opt-in checkbox in contract. That stops sales from promising SLAs prematurely.

affinity | cost-tier | region-fallback

Launch-class mapping: Experimental | Controlled-GA | GA

```

Quick idea: instead of point prefetch hints, what if we have a predictive warmup coordinator that batches warmup signals across the scheduler and ranks page ranges by probability? Could reduce duplicate IO for similar concurrent microbatches.
Hmm interesting. So the coordinator would dedupe overlapping hints and issue a single warmup? How heavy is the coordination?

Lightweight: scheduler emits warm_candidate(tenant, model, shard, ts, score). Coordinator aggregates for short windows (~5ms), collapses overlaps, and issues a warm_request(batch_id, ranges, priority, revocable=true). Allocator receives batch requests, tries to materialize pages best-effort.
Two immediate questions: (1) Who owns scoring (scheduler vs coordinator)? (2) How do we prevent the coordinator from becoming a new global bottleneck?

Scoring stays local in scheduler (cheap heuristics: prefix matched, route frequency, cache misses). Coordinator only aggregates and dedupes. It should be sharded by pool/NUMA node to avoid global hotspots.

From allocator side: we need clear contract for revocable memory. If warm_request is revocable, allocator should mark allocations as "soft-resident" and eligible for immediate eviction under pressure. We also need an admission token to bill tenant for warm IO.
Agree on soft-resident. Also implement a lease: warm_request(ttl_ms) so allocator can retire entries automatically. And a cancel API for coordinator to retract if it decides to deprioritize.

Good call on TTL. Example API sketch:
```ncoordinator.emit(candidate={tenant:,model:,shard:,offsets:,score:})
allocator.warm_request(batch_id, ranges, priority, ttl_ms, revocable) -> lease_token
allocator.cancel_lease(lease_token)
```
We should also define priority buckets mapped to admission tiers: realtime(high), interactive(medium), background(low). Coordinator maps scores->buckets.
ops note: be mindful of cross-host warmups creating network IO spikes. If coordinator dedupes across hosts, it might trigger bursty NVMe reads. Gate with pacing and per-host concurrency limits.
We must avoid false-positive warming that fragments host staging. Warmed ranges should prefer contiguous ranges to reduce fragmentation. Coordinator should favor coalesced ranges.

Telemetry we need: requests issued, dedupe rate, warmed bytes, revocations, warm hit-rate (page present on touch), extra eviction churn caused by warming. Also correlate with tail latency percentiles.

Implementation plan: prototype coordinator as an opt-in subsystem behind flag that runs in the scheduler agent. Start with single-pool coordinator (canary). Add allocator hooks for soft-resident tagging + lease tokens.
Rollout idea: enable for small-chat models on a couple low-traffic hosts; run A/B with trace-level telemetry. Perf target: reduce host->gpu fault p99 by 30% for 1-8 token microbatches.

Edgecases: what if warm_request races with eviction compaction? Need a cheap backoff: if allocator receives warm_request for ranges currently being compacted, it should NACK with retry-after. Coordinator then reschedules.
Also handle tenant fairness: include tenant in rate-limit key and integrate with admission quotas. High-volume tenants shouldn't drown out others.
Add a hard cap on warmed bytes per-host and per-tenant per-epoch. Ops will tune caps in canary.

quick brain-dump — thinking about prefix cache compaction-aware eviction.
problem: long-tailed prefixes (few tenants with huge prefix trees) cause eviction storms and poor locality for small tenants. current LRU by key doesn't capture cross-key prefix density.
curious — what's 'compaction-aware' here? compressing prefixes or grouping keys?

both. idea: treat prefix groups as first-class residency units. maintain compacted residency footprint and a per-prefix hotness score. eviction picks whole or partial prefix shards to avoid scattering KV state.
sounds like prefix granularity could hurt latency for small hot keys inside a cold prefix. can we hybridize?

yeah hybrid = per-key recency + prefix-level amortized cost. simple heuristic:
```
score(key) = alpha * recency_rank(key) + beta * (prefix_size(prefix_of(key)) / prefix_sharing(prefix))
if score > threshold -> candidate for prefix-compaction-evict
```
where prefix_sharing = #tenants + log(shared_reuse)
opt-in? per-tenant policy? some customers pin huge prefixes (embedding indexes) — we can't evict arbitrarily.
configurable: tenant pins, protected prefixes, and 'compaction window' TTL to allow small hot keys to re-emerge without churn.
operational concerns: how do we perform compaction without blocking the serving path? background scan + best-effort handoff? need to avoid lease races.
prefer async compaction with snapshot-of-ownership. mark prefix as 'compacting' then redirect new writes to a staging area, stream old KV to compacted layout, then flip pointer.

Heads-up: reproduced a perf regression on multi-GPU fused-attn + tensor/pipeline split when sharding QKV across 3 ranks. End-to-end p95 latency up ~22% for seq=2048.
Can you paste the perf profile or nvprof trace?

Quick nvprof snippet (trimmed):
```
fused_attn       9.1ms

attn_fallback   28.7ms
Memcpy DtoD: reorder    65.2ms
NCCL AllGather         42.3ms
Idle wait (CPU)        12.4ms
```
Looks like QKV path does an extra device memcpy+reorder before allgather. Why are we reordering?

Kernel selector currently requires contiguous heads-per-rank to pick flash kernel. With a 3-way tensor split head stride is non-contig -> selector falls back to generic attn_fallback. But runtime still issues a qkv_allgather assuming contiguous layout, so we end up memcpy->reorder->allgather->fallback kernel.

Also seeing NCCL stalls. Allreduce/allgather overlap with compute is poor: lots of small frequent collectives due to our batching heuristic flushing early. Micro-batches are causing comm to be latency-bound.
Batching config note: continuous batching groups requests but flush threshold triggers when seq-length variance high. For short-tail-heavy workloads that forces many partial KV pushes.
Repro command: `./tools/run_tp_bench --model=gptx --tp=3 --seq=2048 --bs=4 --profile=nvprof --kernelselect=auto`

Proposal: change kernelpicker to detect strided QKV layouts and either (a) prelayout contiguous QKV per rank before kernel decision, or (b) implement a fused-attn path that accepts strided inputs and does internal gather without extra D2D memcpy.
(a) might be easier: prelayout into pinned host mem staging then upload as single contiguous buffer to GPU to avoid device memcpy storms. But pinned staging adds memory pressure.
Could we instead move the reorder earlier at model dispatch so QKV are produced contiguous per TP partition? That avoids extra memcpy entirely.

whoa. can you paste the repro logs?

here's the short excerpt:
```
2026-05-18T12:05:14Z INFO evict: tenant=A prefix=/models/legacy/ id=0x7f6
2026-05-18T12:05:14Z DEBUG cache: remove_ptr ptr=0x55a3 stale=false
2026-05-18T12:05:14Z INFO read: tenant=B key=/models/legacy/123 ptr=0x55a3 hit=true
```
note: ptr is the same address. we expect ptr to be invalid after eviction.
hmm, looks like a classic race where eviction clears residency but another shard still had a pointer in-flight. does our lease/ownership model guarantee single-writer?

currently eviction sets "resident=false" under eviction lock, then we publish an invalidation token asynchronously to other shards. there is a small window where read path checks residency without seeing the invalidation.
so read path: load ptr -> check ptr->resident flag -> use. if invalidation hasn't propagated, you'll use a freed slab region. could be use-after-free or just stale data.
any crashes? or just stale values returned?
only stale values so far, no OOB crashes; likely memory freed/pinned by allocator for a bit.

I'm thinking of two short-term fixes: (A) make eviction synchronous w.r.t. shard-local read checks (i.e., bump an epoch and make read verify epoch matches) or (B) add a tiny refcount bump when handing a ptr to read path to pin during use. tradeoffs: A increases eviction latency and cross-shard handshake; B increases per-read overhead.

can we do lightweight epoch check without global consensus? e.g., tenant-level generation number stored in header. eviction increments generation under lock and sets ptr.gen. read verifies ptr.gen == tenant.gen. if mismatch, treat as miss.
that matches idea in the old prefix-handshake spike but we never implemented per-tenant generation. cost: additional atomic read per cache lookup (cheap) and need to set gen when creating ptrs.
curious about fairness: if we treat mismatch as miss, downstream will fetch from origin and repopulate. does that create thundering herd on busy tenants?
thought about that — we can short-circuit by returning 503 for a small window or use jittered backoff on repopulation. but I prefer correctness-first: miss is fine.
alternative longer-term: move to lease tokens per-lookup where eviction increments token and read must CAS a slot. more complex but gives stronger invariants and measurable semantics for sharing.
for immediate action, I propose a two-step plan: 1) add tenant-generation check on read path (fast, low-risk). 2) run a canary for 24h in staging with multi-tenant churn sim. if stable, roll to prod.

FYI saw a short window this morning where a prefix write landed but subsequent reads hit an older value from the shared KV cache. Incident lasted ~30s and affected a single tenant when we were evicting hot prefixes. Any thoughts on guarantees we can reasonably provide?
ugh. do we know if the writer actually updated the backing store first? or did cache write happen before persistence? :thinking:

the writer is using our normal write path (persist -> invalidate cache). logs show persist completed at 09:12:03, cache invalidation message at 09:12:04, but reads between 09:12:05-09:12:30 returned old value. eviction churn was high at the time.
two obvious failure modes: 1) invalidation didn't reach all cache shards before reads, 2) eviction + re-populate raced with the old value from another node.
can we make invalidation synchronous for tenant-scoped prefixes? probably expensive but maybe only for a small set of critical prefixes.

+1 on targeted sync invalidation. Another approach: versioned keys so reads can detect staleness and re-fetch. e.g. key: `prefix:{tenant}:{prefix_id}:v{seq}`. If read sees older seq, it fetches upstream.
I like versioning. But how do we coordinate sequence increments across writers? we have multi-writer paths (e.g., retries, parallel callers).

simple option: writers do a monotonic increment by asking a sequencer/lease-holder per prefix. lease is cheap if only for hot prefixes. writer gets lease -> increments seq -> writes backing store with seq -> publish seq invalidation to cache.

that moves complexity to the sequencer. alternative: optimistic CAS on the backing store with seq embed. Writer writes with new_seq = old_seq+1 only if old_seq matches expected. but retries could cause contention.
both are doable. tradeoffs: sequencer = extra network hop + single point for hot prefixes, CAS = more load on backing store and potential write failures we must surface to callers.

question for runtime design: do we treat the cache as a best-effort performance layer (eventual consistency) or as a correctness layer for R-A-W (read-after-write) for some prefixes? we need to pick an interface boundary.

propose: default = eventual. opt-in strong = two modes on PrefixCache API: `READ_CB` (fast, best-effort) and `READ_STRONG` (guarantees R-A-W for pinned prefixes). semantics: READ_STRONG does a read-through verification: if cache hit, check seq header vs backing store; if mismatch, fetch and update cache before returning.

implementation note: checking backing store on every READ_STRONG read kills latency. but we can do a cheap seq check via a small metadata KV that the sequencer updates. readers can check metadata (low size) instead of full object.

that's interesting. so metadata KV holds latest_seq per prefix: `{prefix_meta:{tenant}:{prefix} -> seq}`. READ_STRONG reads metadata first (cheap), compare to cached seq. only fetch object if seq mismatch.

still need to ensure metadata updates are published atomically with backing store write. i.e. persist object and then update meta with same seq. if meta update fails, we might temporarily misreport. need retries and idempotency.

what about eviction interactions? if a prefix is evicted and later repopulated with older seq (due to slow propagation), we could return stale object unless we incorporate seq in cache key or check meta on repopulate.
that seems plausible. we should also add a fallback route: if validation fails repeatedly, route reads to origin store or to a slower dedicated replica to avoid serving stale responses.
operationally we'll need metrics: `prefix_read_strong_misses`, `meta_seq_mismatch`, `revalidation_failures`, and `eviction_repop_conflicts` to spot trouble.

performance note: for very hot prefixes, sequencer + metadata approach scales because metadata reads are small and can be sharded/replicated. For medium prefixes the extra hop may be net-negative. so make READ_STRONG opt-in by prefix and reserved for critical control-plane style prefixes.
agree. also add a TTL on meta entries aligned with write windows to avoid stale meta info for prefixes that are no longer hot.

hmm, the stride allocation is weird — a lot of small fragments (3 pages) rather than compact allocations. When contbatch splits, references don't move to the new owner, so the old fragment stays pinned until GC.
profile snapshot: top flame shows kv::alloc -> kv::pin -> batch::hold for ~9s. CPUP samples show minimal CPU, it's a memory residency issue.
reproducer attached: longctx length ~16k tokens, batch rate 150/s, contbatch aggressive merge threshold 10. If we reduce merge threshold to 4, memory stabilizes.

concrete hypothesis: merge merges requests across different contexts creating interleaved KV segments; split leaves 'stale' fragment handles that keep pages live because refcounting is per-slot but ownership transfer isn't happening on split. result = fragmentation + slow compaction.
agree. Also saw head-of-line blocking: long tail batches that hold slots block eviction threads waiting for slot->unlock. Eviction tries to reclaim but sees refcnt>0 and spins on wait queue. :eyes:

implementation note: (2) is lowest risk. background compactor can run at low priority and try to merge neighbor fragments if both are detachable. need O(1) neighbor lookup.

Devs — hit a reproducible hang when cancelling an async stream while the client is doing token refresh. Repro attached, Python 3.11, httpx 0.24.1. Happens on 0.9.3.

Repro script (very minimal):
```py
import asyncio
from redwood import AsyncClient
async def pump():
    c = AsyncClient(api_key=\"expired\")
    async for chunk in c.stream('/v1/generate', json={'prompt':'x'*2000}):
        print(chunk)
async def killer():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.15)
    for t in asyncio.all_tasks():
        if t is not asyncio.current_task():
            t.cancel()
asyncio.run(asyncio.gather(pump(), killer()))
```
Behavior: process doesn't exit, generator finally block never runs, sockets stay open. Server logs show 401 then token refresh succeeds, but client stream doesn't close.
ack. this sounds like we swallow CancelledError while awaiting the refresh lock. can you confirm using `async with client.stream(...)` changes anything?
no change. also tried `asyncio.wait_for(..., 0.2)` around the gather -> same hang.
likely root: refresh flow uses an `except Exception:` that does `await refresh_and_retry()` and that path blocks cancellation. we've had similar generator finalizer bugs before.

assigning. quick triage: is the refresh protected by an asyncio.Lock or Event? if so, awaiting a lock won't be cancelled if other code is holding it without yielding. need to ensure CancelledError propagates out of refresh logic.
yep `_refresh_lock` seen in stack. snapshot shows `await self._refresh_lock` inside stream next. CancelledError not delivered.
note: main branch has a commit to rework token refresh to use `asyncio.CancelledError`-aware flow (landed post-0.9.3). but I don't think it covered streaming context.

plan: 1) add unit test covering \"cancel during refresh\" for `stream()`, 2) update refresh to catch CancelledError, run cleanup, re-raise, 3) expose `StreamResponse.close()` to let callers forcibly terminate underlying connection, 4) add typing: `stream(...) -> AsyncIterator[bytes]` and `class StreamResponse(AsyncIterator[bytes])` so mypy surfaces misuse.
+1 for close() and typing. Also request: doc blurb about cancellation semantics and recommend `async with` or explicit close.

one caution: some people used `async for chunk in stream:` without keeping a reference to the stream object; adding close() is only helpful if you return the object when using `async with` or as context manager. we should ensure `async with client.stream(...) as s:` returns a StreamResponse with close().

Ran a KV/prompt-cache profiling pass after yesterday's kernel selector rollout — hit rates tanked on tail workloads, and we saw a few GPU OOM spikes. Posting quick summary and samples.

PROFILE SNAPSHOT (aggregate):
```
before: global_hit=0.62 per_prefix=0.74
after:  global_hit=0.41 per_prefix=0.53
+28ms

+18%
OOM_events: 7 spikes between 03:17-03:40 UTC
```
Sampled keys show a ton of near-duplicates with tiny ephemeral suffixes (session nonces / timestamps). Looks like cache key entropy jumped after we started including routing/kernel path metadata.
Wait — I thought key fingerprinting was unchanged. Did the kernel selector change mutate the key format? :thinking_face:

It did. To support route-aware fallback we appended a kernel_id fragment to the cache key inside the runtime. That made keys unique across what used to be identical prompts. We didn't canonicalize ephemeral parts.

That's consistent with the hit drop. Essentially the key space exploded for long-running sessions and conversational prompts that append tokens like `#sess_12345`. Two quick mitigation ideas:
- canonicalize known ephemeral patterns (strip session ids, timestamps)
- add stable hashing that normalizes whitespace + unicode normalization before fingerprinting

Example canonicalizer (rough):
```
// pseudocode
k = normalize_unicode(k)
k = collapse_whitespace(k)
k = re.sub(r"sess_[0-9a-f]{6,}", "<SESS>", k)
key = sha1(k + model_shard_no_kernel)
```

Also seeing the eviction/TTL config exacerbated this — with more unique keys the cold cache grew and our LRU churned hot prefixes out faster. On some hosts we set TTL=24h which now keeps a bunch of nearly-unused unique keys in RAM. We should ramp TTL based on observed reuse.
Suggestion: short TTL for cold prefixes (5-15m), progressive ramp for prefixes with hit_rate > 0.6 up to hours. Also GC idle prefixes earlier when free_slabs < 20%.

We should also consider slab fragmentation on GPU allocator. I profiled one of the OOM hosts and free_bytes looked healthy but allocation requests failed due to fragmentation/coalescing limits. The increased number of small objects (one per unique prompt) makes fragmentation worse.

short sync — proposal to move autoscaler decisions for dedicated GPU pools out of the operator and into a tiny adjudicator service.
motive?
operator has accreted lots of responsibility (admit/lease bookkeeping, GC, billing hooks). an adjudicator can centralize policy, make decisions (grant/reserve/defer) and emit short-lived tokens.
how does this change the warmup/prewarm flow?

flow sketch: operator sends intent to adjudicator -> adjudicator returns a signed advice token (or defer) -> operator writes the token to the claims API -> runtime pulls/consumes tokens to prewarm. operator still owns final reservation.
extra hop. what's the latency impact in the control plane?
operator only calls adjudicator when creating a reservation (not on every admit). cached decisions at operator side keep hotpath local. expected p50 < 2ms added for reservation creation.
autoscaler integration? can adjudicator feed headroom hints?
yes. adjudicator emits optional headroom_hint per pool/tenant and can publish events to the autoscaler pubsub. autoscaler can choose to follow hints or operate independently.
failure modes? adjudicator slow or down?
operator has a fallback heuristic and a circuit-breaker. when adjudicator is unavailable we degrade to safe-mode (smaller prewarm budgets, conservative grants).
double-allocation across regions worry.
tokens are region-scoped and include a signed region tag; adjudicator tracks global allocation per-tenant to avoid oversubscribe. token consumption checks signature + region.
what about billing and chargeback accuracy?

adjudicator emits canonical decision events to the ledger. operator records delta events on write; runtime records local consumption events. Reconciliation job computes billing delta (eventual consistency).
observability?

metrics plan: adjudicator: `adjudicator_decisions_granted_total`, `adjudicator_decisions_deferred_total`, `adjudicator_token_latency_ms` histogram, `adjudicator_headroom_hint_gauge`. operator: `operator_tokens_emitted_total`. runtime: `runtime_token_consumed_total`, `runtime_local_prewarm_hits`. add a reconciliation metric `prewarm_billing_delta` from the ledger job.
security — token forging?
tokens signed by adjudicator with key-id header; operator and runtime validate signature and key version. key rotation via k8s secret with versioning.
GC and orphan tokens?
tokens have TTL. adjudicator exposes `/tokens/expire` animation for GC; operator runs periodic reclaim of expired tokens and credits return-to-pool.
rollout plan?

1) implement adjudicator v1 with readonly policy and tokens (feature-flagged). 2) enable for a small tenant set (10 tenants) and observe prewarm hit-rate + cold-starts. 3) run canary for 48h, then 30% fleets, then default.
tests?
unit tests + integration harness: simulate 200 tenants with churn, chaos tests where adjudicator injects 100-500ms tail latencies, operator restarts, token double-consumption attempts.
backwards compatibility with current token/claim system?
operator will support both v1 token and adjudicator tokens. runtime consumes tokens by priority: adjudicator tokens > legacy tokens, allowing staged migration.
perf knobs — how often should runtime poll claims?
default 5s poll with jitter; operator caches adjudicator responses for 30s. tune after canary.

quick heads-up — replayed the host-stage window and saw ~2-6s p99 tails. pattern: prefetch + immediate demote fanout -> compactor overload -> tiny serial compactions.
do you have an example trace or timing breakdown? where's the real cost?

timeline from trace: stage signal @t0 -> 40 demote intents across tenants within 120ms -> compaction queue length spikes -> workers start many small jobs (~<200KB) with ~8ms startup overhead each -> worker throughput collapses -> p99 spikes for 2-6s while jobs run serially. also saw kvcache churn when fallback model hits.
sounds like two orthogonal problems: admission (too many demotes at once) and compaction scheduling (high per-job overhead). can we tackle both with low-risk rollout?

proposal: (1) short hedging window for prefetch/advisory hints (200ms) so we only materialize when hotset persists, (2) graded demote capacity derived from an "evict_pressure" scalar instead of binary demote allowed/blocked, (3) coalesce demote intents within a micro-batch (50-150ms) and prefer locality-aware merge. add emergency bypass if free_pages_pct < 4%.
how do you compute evict_pressure? we already emit queue_len and resident score.

simple mapping we used in prototype: evict_pressure = smooth(queue_len, 1s) * (1 + max(0, -d(resident_score))). map to demote_capacity via sigmoid: demote_capacity = floor(sigmoid((evict_pressure - t)/s) * max_cap). defaults: t=6, s=3, max_cap=12.
tenant fairness? we shouldn't let a single tenant monopolize the elective slots.
add soft credits per tenant (size-weighted). 1 credit ~= 64KB. credits replenish on a sliding 60s window. also reserve a small fraction of capacity (5%) for low-priority tenants to avoid starvation.

compaction merging: if demote intents target adjacent ranges, merge. if not adjacent but small, bundle into a batched job that yields subrange-ready events so requests can use flushed parts earlier. reduces per-job overhead.
safety notes: if free_pages_pct < 4% -> bypass and force demotes; add cooldowns (5-10s) to avoid flip-flop; emit host_penalty scalar for router to de-weight stressed hosts.

Quick RFC follow-up thread — we need final decisions on fused-attention variants (fused QKV, bias+rope fusion, and the dropout-free fast path). Main concerns: kernel selection logic, fallback semantics, cache/versioning, and evals for numeric drift.
Can you summarize the concrete options? I need something I can use to implement the selector after the holiday.

High level proposals: 1) Strict pinning: model config must declare an attn_impl tag; runtime uses pinned kernel or fails. 2) Graceful fallback: try pinned fused kernel, else route to unfused implementation with metrics logged. 3) Hybrid heuristics: selector picks fused when sequence shape + quantization profile match a safety table.

I prefer 3 (hybrid). Implementation idea: maintain a small kernel registry with entries: {signature_hash, seq_range, dtype_mask, impl_name, accuracy_guard}. Selector checks registry first, then falls back.
Important: dropout-free path yields perf but subtly different sampling behavior (we saw ~0.5% token-prob shift in some prompts with temp>1.0). Need automated eval harness to catch regressions.

Cache and KV compatibility note: fused QKV changes layout of cached K/V tensors. We must version cache keys or include attn_impl in cache key to avoid corruption. Suggest adding "attn_impl" to the request routing key.
Agreed. Spec decision: include attn_impl in model serving config and cache key. Runtime must refuse to use cached entries keyed by a different attn_impl.
How do we declare the model-level opt-in for bias+rope fusion? Some models rely on legacy rope offsets and will break.

Make bias+rope fusion opt-in per model: model.meta.attn_flags = ["rope_fused", "bias_folded", ...]. During model load, validate a short numeric smoke test (few batched queries) comparing baseline vs fused precision within threshold. If it fails, mark fusion disabled and log an alert.

Evals to add to CI:
- token-wise KL and L2 between fused/unfused on 1k random contexts
- top-1/top-5 overlap at 512, 2048 seq lengths
- tail-case stress test: repeated prefix extension to exercise KV cache.
Also add a runtime metric: attn_impl_fallback{from, to} and attn_impl_selector_reason label (missing_kernel, unsafe_seq_len, quant_mismatch, smoke_test_fail).
For rollout, propose a canary: route 1% traffic to fused when selector would choose it, compare metrics (p99 latency, token-cost, KL drift). Auto-rollout only when drift < threshold for 24h.

quick question — I'm chasing a perf regression where the runtime suddenly switches kernels mid-batch on KV-cache hits. suspect sampling bias in our nsys capture. sharing the flags i used, anyone see something dumb?
what's the capture duration + did you bracket steady-state with NVTX? also are you using trace=cuda or sampling?
i did a short 8s run, not bracketed, flags below. i wanted both kernel timeline + osrt markers so i used trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt and cpu sampling

```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --sample=cpu --sample-interval=500us --duration=8s -o /tmp/kv-batch-run
```

short notes: 1) sampling (cpu) won't record every short GPU kernel; it samples CPU stacks, not exact GPU kernel events — use trace=cuda (you already did) for a faithful kernel timeline. 2) an 8s run + no NVTX warmup can bias results if warmup vs steady-state differs. bracket with NVTX push/pop around steady-state. 3) --sample-interval 500us might be too coarse for some bursts.

+1 to sam. If you want exact kernel start/end and correct ordering, run with trace=cuda and sample=none (or drop --sample). sampling is useful for CPU hotpaths, not kernel boundaries. Also increase duration to 30s or do multiple 10s bracketed runs.

hmm — i relied on the sampling to point at where code switched kernels. the timeline showed memcpy->small kernel->large matmul repeatedly when KV hit rate rose. i'm wondering if osrt trace is causing kernel split, or if our batching heuristics are evicting KV pages and causing recompute kernels. anyone seen osrt-related kernel splitting?

osrt provides OSRT allocator markers; it shouldn't split kernels by itself. kernel splitting often comes from sequence length changes, different launch configs, or runtime choosing a fallback kernel (quantized vs fp16 path). if KV cache eviction forces a re-embedding step you can get an extra kernel. look at kernel names in the CUDA trace (not sampled).
also check correlation with NVTX ranges: make sure you're pushing an NVTX range around each request or batch phase so you can filter timeline by range. bracketed capture looks like:

```
# instrument code around steady-state
nvtxRangePushA("steady-state");
... run steady traffic ...
nvtxRangePop();
# then capture on CLI
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-end=nvtx --duration=15s -o /tmp/kv-bracket
```

quick check — i'm thinking about adding a lightweight GC pass that coalesces tiny free ranges in host staging to fight long tail fragmentation. thoughts?
curious — is this a synchronous compaction or opportunistic background?
opportunistic. idea is: when host staging idle cycles detected, run a scan that merges adjacent free spans and drops tiny islands under a threshold. should be bounded work.
what triggers 'idle cycles'? can we avoid interfering with prefetch/async warmup?
heuristic: cpu load < 30% on the host pool + no inflight microbatches for 200ms. it's a soft signal — cancel if we see incoming warmup.
watch out for bursty traffic patterns. a background compaction could increase page faults if it races with prefetch, causing extra transfers. need ramp-down/backoff.
also: merging ranges might move metadata around. allocator API change? do we need to pin/unpin during compaction?
allocator should expose a stable handle. we can add a 'try_compact(span_handle, flags)' that returns remap info if it moves. users that keep direct device pointers must opt-in.
or we keep compaction within host staging only — never touch resident GPU backing. that avoids invalidating device pointers but still reduces fragmentation in host pools.
exactly — plan A: host-only compaction. Plan B: if coordinator decides to promote a span to resident and it's fragmented, do an aligned copy with short stall and update KV cache.
what about GC and prefetch interaction? Pre-fetcher might be pulling prefixes into host staging while GC is merging. We need ordering guarantees to avoid double-copy.
simple approach: prefetcher annotates spans with 'prefetch-inflight' tag. compactor skips tagged spans. compactor can remove tag when done. lightweight and avoids stalls.
metrics we need: compaction time, avoided allocations per hour, extra page transfers triggered, and worst-case stall duration. Let's add SLI for compaction-induced faults.

one more tradeoff: small-span coalescing reduces external fragmentation but increases chance of large contiguous allocations being held by a single tenant — affects fairness. we should respect tenant soft-quotas.
good point — compactor will respect tenant affinity and not coalesce across tenant boundaries unless both tenants under-utilized.

eviction interplay: if compaction runs and frees host pages, eviction logic should see those pages as reclaimable immediately, not treat them as recently used. update residency timestamps on compaction.

implementation sketch: 1) scanner thread picks candidate spans by size/window 2) obtain lightweight lease from allocator 3) if lease granted, migrate live subobjects to a new span (memcpy) 4) update mappings via atomic swap 5) release old span to free list. all async.
ensure atomic swap is epoched with in-flight inference. use the existing request-quiesce token or a minimal RCU.
