Who owns the telemetry smoothing change?
I can take telemetry smoothing; will add a sliding window fallback that synthesizes last_seen from last N heartbeats when metrics are missing.
Long-term: I'll start a design doc for the runtime agent and signed lease blob format. Will include migration plan and perf targets (max 1ms local lookup, gRPC stream fanout limits).
One more thing — audit logs. If we route a write out-of-region due to stale info we must emit an audit event with tenant_id, chosen_path, reason=stale_lease. Compliance needs this for forensics.

follow-up to RFC - proposing a lightweight regional 'edge cache' to accelerate CP handshakes for private customers. goal: reduce churn on controlplane auth + keep predictable egress IPs when privatelink isn't available.
quick Q - how is this not just another relay? last thing we need is more heavy proxies.

it's intentionally minimal. no full-stream proxying. stores short-lived tokens, cert blobs, and ACL decisions. answers handshake queries and proxies controlplane API calls only when necessary. designed to be single-purpose and memory-light.
security first: what are boundaries if cache is compromised? can it mint tokens?

design constraint: cache cannot mint long-lived credentials. it only issues short-lived assertions signed by our KMS, with strict TTL and revocation checks against controlplane before issuing anything beyond a short window. all signing keys are HSM-backed.
egress preservation: customers need stable source IPs for third-party allowlists. are we reserving per-tenant IPs?

two models discussed: (A) per-tenant ENI/ENI-like lease in customer VPC (preferred for highest isolation), (B) regional shared egress pool we control with per-tenant mapping. MVP: (B) with option for dedicated leases for enterprise.
cost and capacity concerns. per-tenant IPs blow up cost and routing table complexity. how do we prevent exhaustion?
implement a quota/lease service. default small pool per account, auto-scale only for committed customers. reject new leases when pool exhausted -> signal to sales/ops. lease TTL + renewal to recycle.
what about IPv6? dualstack expectations creeping up.
scope MVP as IPv4-only. document IPv6 path: require provider support for stable IPv6 source mapping; follow-up spike.
ops & observability: what metrics and alerts do we need at launch?
minimal metrics: cache_hit_ratio, handshake_latency_ms_p50/p99, lease_in_use, lease_available, revocation_rate. alerts: handshake_errors > 1% sustained 5m, lease_available < 10% for 10m.
migration plan: existing private customers today use privatelink. do we flip them automatically?

migration is opt-in. registry gets new field egress_mode: privatelink | cache_egress | dedicated_egress. default retains current behavior. provide a migration job for customers who request cache_egress.
edge cases: what if privatelink exists but DNS resolves to public IPs and agent picks wrong path? precedence rules?
enforce precedence: 1) privatelink endpoint if configured and healthy, 2) private_endpoint, 3) edge_cache, 4) public fallback. we should make agent behavior explicit and observable.
revocation thundering herd risk when we revoke many tokens. how to avoid slamming controlplane?
coalesce revocations and rate-limit sweeps. cache will subscribe to a revocation stream and process in windows with jitter. also expose a backpressure signal to controlplane so bulk ops can be paced.

Heads-up RFC follow-up — we need to finalize the model-pinning + rollout metadata shape before we land the console UX. Major constraints: must work for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private, must be queryable for audits, and must support gradual rollouts + forced pins.
+1. Can we avoid a million ad-hoc fields? prefer a minimal typed surface and an opaque metadata blob for extras.
Agreed. Also: we need strong typing for the core fields so DB indexes are useful for fast lookups (pin existence, active rollouts).

Proposal idea: two-layer model: "pin" object (first class) + optional "rollout" objects (list). Pin = model_id, model_version (string), scope (org|route|key), expires_at (rfc3339 string|null), enforced (bool). Rollout = rollout_id, target_variant, percentage, start_ts, end_ts, fallback_policy.
That looks clean. A few questions: 1) model_version type — do we require semver or allow arbitrary strings (git tags/dates)? 2) how to express compatibility (e.g., kv-cache incompatible)?

For speed, store model_version as opaque string in pins, but add an optional compatibility_flags list for the pin/variant (e.g., ["kv-incompatible", "requires-4k-cache"]). That lets routing logic check quickly.

On semver: many of our upstream models use dates or git SHAs. Forcing semver will hurt. Keep string but add a normalized_hash (sha256 short) field computed by ingestion for deterministic equality checks/indexing.
Good call. Also need to decide how "fallback_policy" maps to runtime: options: "hard-fail", "soft-fallback", "route-to-lower-tier". We need to ensure the policy is declarative but small set.

Implementation note: for Dedicated/Private, customers may want to pin to a local artifact id rather than a public model. Add an optional "artifact_source" with enum ("catalog","customer_artifact","external_url") and a freeform "artifact_ref" string.
Auditability: every pin/rollout mutation should record who made it, why, and a mut_id. Keep those in an append-only audit log. The live pin record should include last_mut_id to speed queries.

Query patterns: Console will need to list "active pins for org X" and filter by route/expiry/enforced. So in DB we should denormalize: keep top-level columns: model_id, model_version, scope, enforced, expires_at, active_rollouts_count. The JSON blob stored in a metadata column for everything else.
Tradeoff: denormalization speeds UI/queries but risks schema drift. We keep the core typed columns and a metadata JSONB for extensibility. That's our landing.

quick follow-up to the hotpatch RFC — proposing a minimal sidecar-based path for shipping signed CUDA / driver micro-patches to air-gapped onprem clusters. sketch below, want tradeoff feedback.
show me the sketch pls. worried about kernel-module reboots on customer infra.

yeah, that's the sticky bit. idea is: bundle driver userland shim + verified kernel module delta signed by our signing key. operator-sidecar orchestrates an atomic swap sequence:
```
1) upload signed delta to operator (airgapped via USB/registry import)
2) sidecar verifies signature + hash via onboard verifier
3) sidecar places delta in staged path (immutable filename)
4) gracefully drain serving pods using ephemeral CPU-fallback
5) orchestrate kernel module replace with fallback policy and health probes
6) on success, promote staged -> active and prune old modules
```

RFC follow-up: we still need a clear boundary between observers and the arbiter for canary/A-B flips. Two options: observers keep transient 'can-promote' state and act, or arbiter is the single source of promotion truth. I'm worried about accidental double-promotes during partitions.

+1 to minimizing authority on observers. My vote: arbiter holds the canonical promotion lease. Observers should stream telemetry and can request provisional moves, but only the arbiter can issue final routing changes. Observers should be able to show a provisional UI state but not alter global routing.

I'm sympathetic but worried about latency and scale. If every observer consults arbiter synchronously our p99 for canary reaction increases. Can we allow observers to do a limited, reversible provisional divert while arbiter asynchronously validates?

That matches a 'soft-promote' pattern I've been sketching. Observer can request a provisional diversion token and apply to a tiny fraction (e.g., <=1%) for quick smoke tests. Token must be replay-safe and scoped to tenant+route. Arbiter then collects signals and either upgrades to final lease or revokes provisional. Observers revert automatically on revoke/expiry.

Proposal sketch for timings and limits:
```
provisional_ttl = 15s           # local soft-divert window
final_lease_ttl = 30s           # canonical lease duration
max_provisional_fraction = 0.01 # fraction of tenant traffic for provisional
reconcile_window = 8s           # how long arbiter waits for telemetry
min_samples = 500               # require this many samples before finalizing
```

Token design idea: HMAC-based promo_token = HMAC(secret_k, observer_id|route|nonce|expiry). Arbiter verifies HMAC and checks nonce/expiry. To prevent global nonce storage, use per-observer monotonic counters persisted occasionally; arbiter only needs last-seen-counter per-observer. That keeps storage tiny.

Alternative: signed short-lived JWTs with jti and short expiry (few seconds). JTI collisions are unlikely; for strict replay protection we can keep a ringbuffer of recent jtis per shard. If customers need absolute non-replay, enable exact-ttl nonce store.

On metrics: we must be explicit about the decision surface. Example rule we discussed: error_rate < 0.4% AND p90_latency_delta <= +100ms AND samples >= min_samples. Use delta comparisons against baseline, not absolute p90 in some cases. Also require consistent signal across >= 3 observers for the same tenant to avoid single-node bias.

Good call on multi-observer quorum. For reconcile we should do a quick aggregation: collect (count, errors, p90) from observers, compute weighted aggregate, then compare. If quorum not reached within reconcile_window, revoke provisional.

Storage/perf notes: keeping per-observer last-counter and per-tenant provisional record in arbiter is lightweight. The heavy path is global sample aggregation — do streaming sketches (TDigest for percentiles, reservoir sampling for counts). That keeps memory bounded.
Operator UX: add a protected endpoint to force-finalize a promotion (RBAC + explicit audit log). Also add a Console banner when any provisional promotions exist and a link to the reconcile trace.
Observers must include provenance fields with every metric: observer_id, route, provisional_token (if used), sample_window_start. Make telemetry idempotent-safe. Use event ids for traceability.

Failover semantics: if arbiter becomes unreachable, observers must not auto-promote beyond provisional_ttl. They should expire tokens and revert. If the arbiter is partitioned but later reconciles, it can accept or reject based on collected telemetry and audit proofs. No backwards-in-time promotes.

Heads-up: follow-up on private controlplane pairing. We need a hardened retry flow that27s safe for NAT-heavy customers.
TL;DR: one-time token + pairing-id seems fine, but behavior on duplicate redeem must be clearly defined.
Implementation idea: treat redeem as "create-if-not-exists". If token redeemed twice, return the same pairing-id and cert blob. That makes client retries idempotent.
How does the client discover if pairing completed asynchronously? We observed timeouts where server had already issued certs but client timed out.
Add a verify endpoint: GET /pairings/{pairing-id} -> returns status {pending, ready, failed} and cert metadata when ready. Keep it cheap.
Security angle: pairing-id must be unforgeable. Use HMAC(token||client_nonce||issued_at) with server secret. Don27t bind to client IP; breaks many NAT cases.
Retry dedupe: clients send a Retry-UUID header. Server stores recent Retry-UUIDs per token for a short window (2m) to dedupe duplicate POSTs.
TTL tradeoffs: token lifespan 45-90s seems reasonable. pairing lookup window for late-checks 5m default, configurable per-tenant up to 24h opt-in.
Failure codes: 409 = token already redeemed (but pairing-id returned), 410 = token expired, 404 = verify endpoint not supported on older CPs.

SDK contract suggestion:
- pairing.start(token, opts) -> returns pairing_id or error
- pairing.verify(pairing_id) -> polls GET /pairings/
- on failure, sdk can set fallback_to_relay flag
- expose retry_id and client_nonce config

Ops requirements: metrics (pairing.attempts, pairing.success, pairing.dedupe_hits, pairing.late_completions), and alert when success < 98% for 15m. Add a reconciliation job for pending pairings that retries cert apply.
Key rotation: sign keys in KMS, rotate weekly with 1h verification grace window. Make rotation automated for Private deployments.
Migration plan: start lenient pairing-mode for 48h in staging; enable strict mode via feature flag per-region; communicate SDK changes to customers with a 2-week deprecation window.
Edge-case: if server accepted the token but failed before writing pairing record, client retry must not create duplicate resources. Use idempotent DB create semantics keyed by token or retry-id.
Storage notes: Dynamo-like table with token->pairing mapping and TTL; separate pairing table keyed by pairing-id for status. Fast token lookup needed for dedupe.
UX for ops: admin API to revoke pairings: POST /admin/tenants/{id}/pairings/revoke with reason. Also allow force-delete of pairing-id.

quick flag 1 1 we're seeing inconsistent batch negotiation across SDKs. Some libs send `X-RW-Batch: envelope` header, others still use `?batch=1` or `batch_mode` query. This breaks streaming deserializers.
which endpoints? generation / streaming / embeddings?
streaming generation primarily. Enveloped requests work fine for non-streaming. Streaming clients choke if we wrap frames.
could we do content sniffing at ingress? check first byte/line and decide if envelope or raw stream. Cheap enough?
sniffing works but edge TLS proxy likes to coalesce frames; we saw false positives. Also increases CPU on edge.

proposal: support both shapes for a transition window, reply with `Warning` header when we detect legacy query param, and emit `compat_mode=legacy` tag in logs. Add opt-in strictness via `x-rw-compat: strict` so newer SDKs can opt into enforcement early.

routing to a legacy unwrap path avoids touching the hot streaming path. That path can be a lightweight sidecar/unwrapper that only peeks prefix. Downside: extra hop and bookkeeping for tenant mapping.
sidecar ops cost + latency. Alternative: an nginx lua filter that only peeks first 256 bytes and sets a header. Lower ops footprint.

telemetry: we need counts (legacy vs new), per-tenant error rates, and median latency delta. Metric name: `compat_shim.requests_total` with tags `mode:(legacy|new)`, `tenant`, `endpoint`. Dashboards & alert when legacy > 10% for 14 days.
perf bench (local): naive in-process unwrap = +2.1ms p50, +9ms p99 under 1000rps. Lua-peek approach = +0.4ms p50, +1.2ms p99. Sidecar adds ~7-12ms tail depending on data center hops.

rollout idea: 1) accept both, add Warning header + telemetry for 8 weeks. 2) enable `x-rw-compat: strict` opt-in for beta tenants. 3) after 70% adoption and low error rate, announce deprecation and 60-day notice.

pasting the key snippet from staging publish job logs — short: GCR rejects cosign verify because the signed manifest digest doesn't match the mirror's stored manifestlist digest (looks like ordering/annotation diff).

quick diagnostic commands I ran locally:
```
# inspect manifest list
crane manifest gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321 | jq .manifests[].platform
# inspect digests
docker buildx imagetools inspect gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321 --raw
```

root cause hypothesis: our multiarch push pipeline recently started producing manifest lists with platform entries in a different order (arm64 first vs amd64 first). cosign signs a particular manifestlist digest; the mirror/replicator computes a digest for the list it receives — ordering shift changes digest -> verification fails.

options are: 1) republish a canonical manifestlist with deterministic ordering and re-sign (preferred), 2) retag prev stable digest for canary to avoid blocking release window, or 3) patch replicator to normalize ordering on ingest (longer).
release window in 25m. we need decision fast — if we republish will that break existing digests?

republishing will create a new digest (must re-sign). we can do a short lived plan: pin canary to previous digest (sha256:prev123) so deployments proceed, and do a follow-up republish+sign to restore provenance for the new tag.

I don't want to risk user-facing canary being different from what QA signed. proposal: hold canary promote for 30m, pin staging->canary to prev digest if any urgent bugs, and run a republish job that creates a deterministic manifestlist and signs it with cosign KMS key. notify compliance and add entry to release notes about re-signed image.

I can run the republish script now. steps I'll run:
```
# rebuild manifestlist deterministic ordering
buildx imagetools create \
  --tag gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321-amd64 gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321-amd64@sha256:... \
  --tag gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321-arm64 gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321-arm64@sha256:...
# then sign
cosign sign --kms k8s://projects/redwood/keys/cosign-key gcr.io/redwood/release:20260321
```

just to restate acceptance criteria (from standard):
- if status != 200 and no body has been streamed yet, apply standard retry classification (429, 408, 409, 5xx, network)
- for 429: respect Retry-After (seconds or HTTP-date), clamp to max_backoff
- once any stream bytes are delivered to caller, SDK MUST NOT auto-retry (document guidance + idempotency)

confirmed. TS streaming path returns an AsyncIterable from a function that does:

fix seems straightforward: refactor stream() to call same `requestWithRetry` used by non-streaming, but keep the response stream intact. we can retry *before* we start reading from `res.body`.

Which SDK and runtime?

Yes — gateway shows initial OPTIONS -> 204 then a POST -> 401 for the same request ID sometimes. Other times the POST succeeds. Example sequence from logs: OPTIONS /v1/generate 204, POST /v1/generate 401, POST /v1/generate 200 (retry).

That smells like browser preflight + service-worker fetch ordering. In edge runtimes the SDK's default fetch polyfill may send credentials differently. Which headers are present on the POST when it 401s?
'POST',
{ 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
JSON.stringify({ prompt: 'hi' }),

If the Authorization header is being added by the SDK wrapper at runtime, service workers sometimes strip or rebuild headers depending on how the request is constructed. Also Vercel Edge uses a Fetch implementation that differs from node-global fetch and can have timing differences for streaming KVs.

Two likely causes: 1) SDK version that mutates Request/Response causing Authorization to be deferred, 2) preflight responses missing Access-Control-Allow-Credentials or allowed headers so browser drops header on first actual POST.

Customer's CORS response shows `access-control-allow-credentials: true` but allowed headers list does not include `authorization`. They said they relied on wildcard in the CORS middleware which sometimes returns slightly different header sets under load.

That explains initial drop. Browser sends OPTIONS, sees no `access-control-allow-headers: authorization`, then for the POST the browser may omit the header or the service worker `fetch` path may re-issue without it. The retry that succeeds likely hits a different backend node that returns the full header set. Race + inconsistent CORS header across nodes can cause exactly this.
They also reported SDK 0.4.7 has a `retry` middleware that immediately retries on 401 for edge workloads which multiplies calls to the billing meter.

Can you ask them to capture the raw browser devtools network trace (preserve log) and the gateway request IDs for failing hits? We should correlate the failing POST request ID with the gateway's log to confirm header absence.
Done — they provided a HAR and three request IDs: r-01a, r-01b, r-01c. I matched r-01a -> OPTIONS 204, r-01b -> POST 401 (Authorization header missing), r-01c -> POST 200.

hey team, hitting intermittent TLS handshake failures to our private inference endpoint behind a NAT. clients get ECONNRESET or TLS alert handshake failure. started after a firewall audit.
sorry to hear that — can you paste the exact error and one tcpdump or flow log? also which deployment (dedicated/private) and region?
private (VPC) in us-west-2. error from app logs: `TLS handshake failure: alert handshake_failure` and some `ERR_STREAM_RESET`. curl to the endpoint sometimes works, sometimes fails.
two likely buckets: 1) packet drops on ephemeral return ports (NACL/SG) so the TLS handshake never completes; 2) SNI/cert mismatch if a proxy rewrites SNI. tcpdump and vpc flow logs will tell.
and VPC Flow Logs show multiple `REJECT` entries to dstport=443 with dstaddr 10.1.2.8 and srcport values in 5xxxx range.
that R (reset) from the server side is suspicious. Are you routing through a NAT gateway / on-prem firewall that could be terminating or resetting idle connections?

quick checks: NACLs are stateless — you need rules both directions. If outbound (client -> inference) is allowed but inbound (inference -> client ephemeral) is not, you'll see resets/retransmits during the handshake. What are your NACL entries? please paste `aws ec2 describe-network-acls` output for the subnet.

NACL shows only explicit allow for TCP 443 (ingress) and TCP 443 (egress), and a deny 0.0.0.0/0 rule for everything else (default deny). SGs look fine (allow outbound 443). Our security team limited egress to only well-known ports.

yep there's the issue. TLS requires ephemeral source ports on the client (1024-65535). Because NACLs are stateless you need to allow return traffic on those ephemeral ranges. For example add explicit allow for ephemeral ports:
```
- Rule: allow TCP ports 1024-65535, src 10.1.2.0/24 (or 0.0.0.0/0 depending on topology) for inbound rules on the inference subnet
- And allow ephemeral outbound on the client subnet accordingly
```
also check that any inline firewall/NAT device preserves the source port. Some proxies SNAT to a small port range and if that range is blocked you'll get resets.
thanks — we'll open the ephemeral range inbound in the NACL and try. quick question: could SNI mismatch still cause `handshake_failure` even with packets flowing?

yes but SNI mismatch usually yields a cert/name error after handshake completes (or a different TLS alert). Handshake failure + lots of RSTs strongly points to connectivity. If after NACL change you still see TLS alerts, capture `openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername <hostname>` output and paste.
patched NACL to allow 1024-65535 inbound to the inference subnet and added matching outbound on the client subnet. Retesting.

Customer on Node18 + Rollup build reports persistent 401s from our API. They say the SDK keeps retrying and the token manager seems to be duplicated in the bundle. Logs show repeated Authorization attempts then immediate 401, then retry loop.
Can you paste the minimal repro and package config?

Sure — short repro below. Project bundles node_modules into one file with rollup + esbuild plugin. Import style varies (both import and require tested). Steps:
1) git clone https://example.com/repro.git
2) npm ci && npm run build
3) node dist/bundle.js \nObserved: first request returns 401, then SDK retries a few times, every attempt includes the same Authorization header value.

The bundler ends up inlining a deep file (`dist/token-manager.js`) instead of referencing the package entry, which creates a second token manager instance. That second instance doesn't share the runtime credential refresh hooks so Authorization header gets stale and server returns 401.

This is a classic duplicate-module problem caused by bundlers flattening imports. If the bundler resolves a direct path to a subfile, you can end up with two module copies (one via the package entry, one via deep import). The token manager is a singleton, so duplication breaks state.

Quick workarounds to give the customer:
- Configure rollup to externalize @redwood/sdk (keep it as node dependency) so the SDK isn't bundled into app code: `external: ["@redwood/sdk"]`.
- Or ensure bundler resolves to package entry by adding an alias/resolve rule that maps `@redwood/sdk/*` -> `node_modules/@redwood/sdk/dist/*` consistently.
- As a temporary patch, set your bundler to preserve CommonJS interop (rollup-plugin-commonjs) and avoid deep imports.

Short-term patch on our side: release v1.2.4 that adds an explicit `exports` subpath for `./token-manager` and moves token-manager to `dist/runtime/token-manager.js` with a guarded singleton export to tolerate duplicate copies. That should reduce breakage when deep imports happen.
Customer tried the externalize workaround and confirms 401s stopped. They've accepted upgrade path.
Ryan, can you link the PR and a short changelog we can share? Also, let's create a KB entry for "Bundlers that inline SDK duplicates token manager -> 401s / auth retries".

PR here: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/432 — fixes exports map and adds runtime guard. Changelog blurb: "Fix: prevent duplicated token-manager singletons when SDK is bundled; add stricter exports map to prevent deep imports causing auth retry loops."

If you don't increase the read timeout, long generations hit ReadTimeout even though the model is still generating.
I'm not using streaming, just want a blocking call to finish.

ok. Workarounds: set an explicit timeout so the read window is long enough. Examples:
```python
# requests-style tuple (connect, read)
client = InferenceClient(api_key=..., timeout=(5, 300))
# or if you construct your own httpx client
import httpx
timeout = httpx.Timeout(None, read=300.0)
httpx_client = httpx.Client(timeout=timeout)
client = InferenceClient(api_key=..., httpx_client=httpx_client)
```
Also note: enabling retry/backoff means a read timeout can trigger a retry which makes the whole operation take even longer or look flaky. If you rely on long generations, either stream tokens or set a sufficiently large read/total timeout and tune retries.

Ok. Two suspicious issues here: (1) known bug in older retry logic where idempotency key was regenerated on every attempt if not kept in the request context, and (2) jitter calculation bug — if backoff_base < 1.0 the int() truncation could produce zero jitter causing sync retries.

I dug into history — there was a change in retry.py: compute_jitter = lambda base: random.random() * int(base) (PR #532). With base=0.5 int(base)==0 so jitter==0. Also current idempotency lifecycle stores the key in the Request.build() and the retry wrapper calls Request.build() again per attempt which regenerates a new idempotency token unless you explicitly set it on the Request object. So two separate problems.

Customer on @acme reports SDK 401s only when bundling for serverless (Next.js). Works locally with node, fails in prod. attaching quick repro and logs.
Which SDK version / Node / bundler? paste package.json exports and the build log please.
Do you have the outgoing request headers in the logs? This sounds like a side-effect import was dropped by the bundler. SWC can tree-shake file-level imports if they appear unused.

Logs show: `Request /v1/chat 401 Authorization: <missing>` only on deployed build. Local (node) invocations include header. Repro steps I used:
1) `npx create-next-app repro-bundle`
2) `npm i @redwood/sdk@1.4.2`
3) add server route that does `import { createClient } from '@redwood/sdk'` then calls client.chat.create
4) build and deploy to Vercel (SWC)
Result: 401 in prod, works on `next dev` and local node.
Can you paste the top of `dist/esm/index.js`?

Yup, that confirms it. The `import './init-fetch.js'` is a side-effect import that SWC dropped. Packaging issue: conditional exports + separate ESM/CJS bundles means the side-effect ended up only referenced in the CJS build. Bundlers that only look at `import` trees can drop it.

Short-term workaround: force the Node/CJS entry on server by importing `@redwood/sdk/node` or explicitly import the init file in your app: `import '@redwood/sdk/dist/init-fetch'` before other imports. Also downgrading to 1.4.1 worked for the customer (1.4.1 still had init included in esm bundle).

Long-term fixes we discussed:
- Mark the init file as a side effect in package.json (`"sideEffects": ["dist/init-fetch.js"]`).
- Ensure the ESM bundle explicitly includes the init import at top-level in the build step so tree-shakers can't drop it.
- Add a targeted CI test that builds with SWC/Next and checks for presence of that import.

Created GH issue redwood/sdk#412 (packaging: ensure side-effectful init preserved across exports).

Two possibilities: (1) client isn't sending SNI for the api hostname (bastion curl maybe using host header mismatch) or (2) there's an intermediate TLS-inspecting firewall rewriting SNI or performing MITM.

Can you run `curl -v --resolve api.redwood.ai:443:10.2.3.45 https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health` from bastion and paste the output? also `openssl s_client -connect 10.2.3.45:443 -servername api.redwood.ai`

subject=CN = redwood-inference.internal
---
SSL handshake has read 3123 bytes and written 329 bytes
verify error:num=62:hostname mismatch
```
That confirms the cert CN is internal. Do you have any inline inspection or TLS termination on your side? e.g., a corporate FW, proxy, or an egress NAT appliance that might be doing SNI rewrite?

Ah — that sounds like a routing/priority problem. Interface endpoints rely on VPC routing + DNS (private DNS) to hairpin traffic to the ENI. If your route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT and the DNS resolves to the public IP or the ENI but your source NAT forces egress, you can get hairpin issues. Check: (1) make sure the endpoint's security group allows port 443 from your source CIDR, (2) ensure there are no overriding proxy settings (HTTP_PROXY) on the bastion, (3) confirm Private DNS is enabled on the endpoint so api.redwood.ai resolves to the VPC-private ENI, not the public load balancer.
Private DNS is enabled. SG inbound on the endpoint allows our subnets. No HTTP_PROXY env vars. I think the key oddity is that the bastion's source IP in the connection is the NAT gw ip in the logs.
VPC Flow Log snippet for eni-10.2.3.45 -> 10.0.10.12 (bastion) 443: REJECT, src=10.0.10.12 dst=10.2.3.45 sport=34512 dport=443 reason=SECURITY_GROUP

If the ENI sees the NAT gw IP as source that means the traffic is being SNATed by something before reaching the ENI. For interface endpoints in the same VPC, SNAT shouldn't happen — that indicates the request path is leaving the VPC and returning (hairpin via NAT) or there is a proxy applying SNAT. The endpoint's SG probably only allows the private subnet CIDR, not the NAT IP, hence REJECT.

Two concrete repro checks: 1) From bastion run `curl -svo /dev/null https://api.redwood.ai --interface 10.0.10.12` and `curl -svo /dev/null https://10.2.3.45 --resolve api.redwood.ai:443:10.2.3.45` 2) Check route table for the bastion subnet; any 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT? If so add a more specific route for the endpoint ENI CIDR to local or ensure the endpoint ENIs are in that subnet so traffic stays local.

Ran both. When hitting the ENI IP directly with --resolve, cert still shows internal CN (same as before) but request gets through if I `--interface 10.2.3.12` (an IP on the same AZ private subnet). Using the bastion primary interface results in REJECT.

That nails it — source IP matters. Your bastion traffic is being SNATed to the NAT GW IP before hitting the endpoint so SG reject. Two fixes: - Allow the NAT GW's EIPs into the endpoint SG (workaround) - Reconfigure routing so endpoint ENI is reachable locally (preferred) - Or place NAT/Egress such that internal endpoint traffic doesn't hairpin.
We don't want to widen SGs. Can we preserve SNI so cert matches? I worry adding NAT EIP to SG is a security hole for us.

Preserving SNI won't fix the SG reject. The CN mismatch is a secondary symptom due to the wrong TLS server being reached — likely our internal proxy LB presenting internal cert when hit without proper SNI. If you ensure connection reaches the public-facing LB via normal internet path, cert would match, but that's not ideal. The right fix is to ensure DNS + routing resolves and routes to the endpoint ENI without leaving the VPC.

We've seen customers fix this by: 1) enabling Private DNS (you already have) 2) verifying route table entries for the bastion subnet don't route outbound to NAT for the endpoint's prefix — endpoints are accessed via local route type; check for explicit 0.0.0.0/0 override or blackhole routes 3) ensure endpoint SG includes expected source CIDRs (add your NAT IPs only temporarily for verification).
Ok we added the NAT EIP to the endpoint SG temporarily -> calls now return 200 and the openssl s_client shows cert CN = api.redwood.ai.

Nice repro. Next step: if you want to avoid that SG expansion long-term, move the bastion into a subnet that routes directly to the endpoint ENIs (same AZ/local), or add VPC route precedence to keep traffic local. Also double-check any transit gateway or firewall that might be forcing egress.

I'll create an internal follow-up ticket to add a KB about NAT hairpin + PrivateLink + cert symptoms — it's a fairly common pitfall. Tagging networking docs and support.
Glad we could help. If you want, paste the final routing table + SG state before you remove the NAT EIP and we can validate.

Thanks — this smells like a chunked+gzip edge/CDN interaction. Some CDNs buffer compressed responses until flush boundaries, which turns many small SSE chunks into one large compressed block; the edge runtime then sees the compressed chunk and downstream runtimes mis-handle backpressure.

Quick tests: 1) Try setting `fetch(url, { headers: { 'Accept-Encoding': 'identity' }})` in the edge function. 2) If you can't change client, we can try disabling our gzip on the streaming endpoint for edge clients.

We're going to push a small runtime patch that sets `Content-Encoding: identity` for SSE endpoints if the request indicates an edge runtime proxy (based on x-forwarded-for + user-agent heuristics). But we need a reliable repro and logs.
Also check SDK version — we saw differences in how the SDK wraps and forwards the response body in v1.3 vs v1.2.0. Do you see same behavior on v1.4.0-rc?

Ok that suggests two things: (A) SDK buffering changes helped, (B) CDN-compression still causes rare single-chunk compressed responses that break streaming when intermediate proxies close unexpectedly.

Could you try the following local simulation to reproduce (curl through a proxy that gzip-compresses):
```bash
# run a tiny reverse proxy that gzips responses (example with mitmproxy / local nginx)
curl -N -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" http://localhost:8080/proxied-stream
```
This will often show the `ERR_INCOMPLETE_CHUNKED_ENCODING` behavior.
Logs from our CDN show `upstream prematurely closed connection` ~10s after initial 200. No auth errors or billing noise.

For immediate mitigation, two paths: 1) server-side: disable gzip on streaming endpoints (set Content-Encoding: identity), or 2) client-side: set `Accept-Encoding: identity` and/or add a keepalive heartbeat event every N seconds so the CDN doesn't consider idle and close. We'll coordinate. Eng-runtime will prototype a header change for SSE endpoints. eng-ml to verify no perf regressions for large non-streaming responses.

Customer (Jamie) reports EventSource stream dropping in Safari + some browsers when behind a CDN. They see partial event payloads and then a stalled reconnect loop. Tried polyfill, still flaky.

Repro: open https://edge.example.com/sse/stream with Safari 16.4 on macOS, login cookie present (SameSite=None; Secure). Connection establishes, a few events arrive, then nothing for ~30-90s. Client eventually reconnects but gets only partial event (truncated JSON). Happens behind our CDN (Fastly) but not when hitting origin directly.

Can you paste request/response headers from the failing case and a curl that reproduces? Also does the origin keep the connection open and periodically flush? Safari is notorious about buffering small writes.

Headers (edge -> client):
  GET /sse/stream HTTP/1.1
edge.example.com
text/event-stream
session=XXX; SameSite=None; Secure

https://app.example.com
Response (edge cached):
  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
max-age=300
Accept-Encoding

https://app.example.com
  Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
session=XXX; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=None

chunked
curl repro (fail):
  curl -v -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Origin: https://app.example.com" -b "session=XXX" "https://edge.example.com/sse/stream"
Note: when I curl the origin directly (origin.example.internal), stream runs fine for 20+ mins. Only edge seems to insert 304/304-ish caching behavior intermittently and then Safari stalls. When we remove cookie or hit from Chrome it works.

Important pieces: 1) CDN caching (Cache-Control + Vary) 2) Cookies being present + credentials allowed 3) Safari buffering small chunks until a certain size or connection heuristics 4) 304/edge behavior on conditional requests can close the SSE connection.

@ash_engineer @maria_support quick checklist:
- Ensure SSE responses are never cached by CDN: Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate or Cache-Control: private, no-transform and set Surrogate-Control: no-store at edge.
- Remove Vary: Accept-Encoding on SSE path (or set Vary: *) carefully; Vary prevents consistent cache key and might cause conditional requests -> 304.
- Make sure the CDN forwards Authorization/Cookie as needed and does not serve cached 304 for authenticated SSE.
- Add Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true at origin and ensure CDN preserves it (no wildcard origin with credentials).
- Chunk flush: server should send a keepalive comment every ~15s (":\n") and pad chunks to force TCP flushes.

Jamie confirmed edge sometimes returns 304 when origin responds 200 but CDN thinks resource unchanged due to Vary mismatch. Also, Fastly config has a global caching rule that caches any 200 with Cache-Control < 600s.

Repro idea: run a curl that simulates Safari (small windowing) + check for presence of Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding. If CDN strips Transfer-Encoding or converts to content-length with an early content-length it will buffer.

Quick test: origin sends chunked, but Fastly rewrites as content-length for cached objects. When we enable "bypass caching for /sse/*" the problem stops. But that's not a long-term solution; customer needs guides for customers using their CDN and for our platform.

Action items:
- eng-infra to add a recommended CDN policy for SSE endpoints (no-cache, Surrogate-Control: no-store, preserve TE: chunked, pass cookies, do not normalize Content-Length)
- SDK/docs: add Safari polyfill notes and explicit withCredentials guidance (Access-Control-Allow-Credentials + explicit origin header, not '*')
- Support: advise customer to disable caching on SSE routes and add keepalive comments to server output as immediate workaround

Short-term workaround for customer:
1) Disable CDN caching for /sse/stream routes (Fastly: request condition -> pass) OR set Surrogate-Control: no-store for those responses.
2) Ensure origin sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com (exact origin) and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Do not use '*'.
3) Send initial padding and periodic keepalive comments, e.g. server sends:
  :ok
  :padding -----------------------------------------------------\n\n
then each event uses double-newline end. Also flush after each write.

Also note: if using EventSource with credentials in the browser, you must set new EventSource(url, { withCredentials: true }) in polyfills; native EventSource (Chrome) ignores withCredentials in older implementations. Safari required cross-site cookies to be SameSite=None and Secure.
We tried polyfill (eventsource-polyfill) with withCredentials true; still saw stalls until we turned off CDN caching. Polyfill didn't mitigate CDN rewrite.
FYI edge-case: some CDNs will cache and serve 206/304 or attempt range requests for SSE if Vary/ETag present. Recommend removing ETag and any conditional cache validators for SSE responses.

I've sent customer a step-by-step: disable caching on SSE routes, confirm Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is preserved, and add keepalive comment every 10s. Customer will test and update.
Deployment started for edge rule update (fastly-change-#4321) — expecting config to propagate in ~5m.
after edge rule update and turning off caching for /sse/* it's stable for 40m in Safari. Thanks! Will monitor for next 24h and report.

possible proxied buffering: nginx/CF/ALB combos often coalesce chunks and delay sending until buffer fills or after idle probes. For nginx origin people often set 'proxy_buffering off;' or send SSE comment heartbeats ':\n' every 15s to keep proxies from considering connection idle. Hey team, we've got a customer on Safari 16 hitting intermittent SSE disconnects and partial event payloads. They say reconnects sometimes come back with a 401 and other times the stream just stalls. Started after we put the endpoint behind the new CDN config yesterday.
ugh. any logs from the user or a repro URL?

They provided an edge URL and a screenshot of Network tab showing a 304 on follow-up requests and then no more events after that. Also their server logs show the client getting a 304 from the CDN when doing an If-None-Match on the SSE endpoint.
304 on an SSE endpoint = red flag. SSE should never be cached. Did we set Cache-Control on that path?
We had a generic caching policy at the edge that respects origin headers, origin had ETag. Looks like the edge decided to honor it for that path.

Confirming Safari has some weirdness when an EventSource receives non-chunked or cached response types. Also Safari's reconnect sometimes uses a different internal request mechanism that won't include Authorization headers the browser doesn't automatically attach. If the CDN responds with 304 the browser might treat it as no new bytes, causing the polyfill/reconnect logic to stall.
Do we have the exact request/response traces? Can the customer run a curl repro?

I asked for curl output, they sent this minimal repro command they used to compare origin vs edge:
```
curl -i -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer CUSTOMER_TOKEN" "https://edge.customer.example/sse/stream"
```
And edge returned:
```
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
fast-cdn

keep-alive
ETag: "abc123"
```
Then browser logs show: "EventSource: connection closed" and no reconnect Authorization header in the subsequent request (per their devtools capture).

Standard EventSource doesn't support custom headers, so many polyfills emulate with XHR/fetch. If the polyfill's reconnect does a conditional GET (If-None-Match) and the edge returns 304, XHR may close the body and the SSE parser doesn't resume.
Edge rule id 550 matched path /sse/* with caching ttl 300. Origin returned ETag; caching applied.

Immediate mitigation: set origin headers for SSE endpoints to prevent caching. Recommended headers: `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` OR `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Connection: keep-alive` and `Content-Type: text/event-stream`. Also add `Vary: Authorization` so CDN won't serve cached responses for different auth tokens.
Also we should ensure the CDN is configured to not compress/chunk-transform SSE endpoints (no-transform).

I put suggested headers into a quick-check snippet for them to test on origin:
```
text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, no-transform
keep-alive

https://customer.app
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

Authorization
```
They tried with these and said the 304s stopped and Safari resumed receiving continuous events for a while, but then reported a 401 on a reconnect attempt after ~110s.

401 on reconnect = token not forwarded on reconnect. EventSource (native) won't include auth header unless it's a cookie or the resource is on same origin with credentials. If they rely on Authorization header, the polyfill might set it on the first request but not on the automatic reconnect (or the CDN could be stripping Authorization on certain retried paths).

Two prongs: (1) ensure CDN forwards Authorization to origin and doesn't cache responses with Authorization unless Vary: Authorization, (2) recommend token location alternatives. Query-string tokens work but are less secure. Best is cookie with SameSite=None + secure for browser flows so native EventSource sends it automatically.

Also verify the EventSource polyfill used by the customer. Some polyfills set `withCredentials` for XHR; if not set, cookies won't be sent on reconnect. Polyfill examples (node-eventsource or eventsource-polyfill) differ. Ask them to paste which one they use, or switch to native EventSource if possible now that caching is fixed.

Customer uses `eventsource-polyfill` in their frontend bundle. I asked them to inspect the polyfill's codepath for reconnect: do they re-attach headers/cookies? They replied that reconnection uses a plain GET without headers in their build.

For immediate band-aid we can recommend adding `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and moving auth to cookie so native EventSource behavior works, or update the polyfill to persist the Authorization token across reconnects.

Long-term, we should make the SSE endpoint in our docs explicit: "Do not cache SSE endpoints. Set Vary: Authorization if using token auth. Prefer cookie-based auth for browser SSE or use WebSocket for authenticated streams. If using CDN, set a no-cache rule for /sse/ or bypass the cache entirely." Link: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events
Action created: SUPPORT-4492 - "Investigate Safari SSE disconnects - edge caching + auth" assigned to cdn-team, priority P1, due 2026-01-07.
I've asked the customer for a HAR file. Also asked them to try a quick repro using curl directly to origin (bypassing edge) and to run Node-based SSE client to compare.

Quick repro commands to recommend to them:
1) Direct to origin (bypass CDN):
```
curl -i -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" "https://origin.customer.example/sse/stream"
```
2) Edge (shows caching behavior):
```
curl -i -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" "https://edge.customer.example/sse/stream"
```
3) Use node to emulate polyfill (xhr-style):
```
const EventSource = require('eventsource');
const es = new EventSource('https://edge.customer.example/sse/stream');
es.on('message', e => console.log('msg', e.data));
```
Note: real node eventsource libs often allow headers: `{ headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ...' } }`.

Suggested fixes for customer (ordered):
- Set `Cache-Control: no-store` or `no-cache, no-transform` on SSE responses.
- Add `Vary: Authorization` on origin to stop CDN serving cached responses across tokens.
- Ensure CDN rule excludes /sse/* from caching or respects origin `Cache-Control` for that path.
- If using token header auth, either switch to secure cookie auth for browser clients or ensure the polyfill persists headers on reconnect.
- As a fallback consider WebSockets for authenticated bidirectional streams.

I'll draft a short KB for Support with the above and sample header snippets and curl commands. Assigning follow-ups: cdn-team to update edge rule (cdn-team), frontend-eng to produce polyfill checklist (ben), and customer success to confirm token strategy with customer (carmela).
Edge rule 550 updated: TTL removed for /sse/*, passthrough enabled.

Customer confirmed after removing caching and ensuring cookie auth the disconnects stopped in their last 30m test. They still want a doc we can link to. I'll write up the KB and paste in this thread when ready.
Nice. Also add a note about Safari-specific quirks: prefer native EventSource when possible and avoid conditional GETs (If-None-Match) on SSE endpoints.

couple of notes: some intermediary proxies (ALBs, corporate proxies) silently close idle TCP without passing SSE comment pings, so clients think stream is alive and try to refresh token -> open new. ALB idle timeout defaults to 60s, most browsers don't expose low-level TCP keepalive. Workarounds: 1) client sends SSE comment pings `: keepalive\n\n` every 15s, 2) use a short reconnect backoff + explicit close before refresh, 3) use Last-Event-ID and server-side idempotency header. Also customer-side: if you refresh token, close old source first (`evtSource.close()`) then open new one.

FYI customer Acme hit weird embeddings mismatch + billing spike. They sent gzipped NDJSON and we returned a single embedding (vectors=1) but they expected 3. Logs attached.

Curl we used:
```
curl -sS -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/embeddings \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer REDACT' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Content-Encoding: gzip' \
  --data-binary @payload.ndjson.gz
```

payload.ndjson.gz is gzip of a file that contains 3 lines, each a JSON string: e.g.
```
"first sentence"
"second sentence"
"third sentence"
```

Quick suspicion: Content-Type is wrong for NDJSON. If you set application/json the server tries to parse the (gzipped) body as one JSON document. Combined with the gzip header it sometimes ends up treated as a single string input. Use Content-Type: application/x-ndjson when streaming newline-delimited inputs.

Also watch for double-stringifying. Some client libs produce lines like `"[\"first\"]"` (a string that contains JSON), which becomes a nested array on our side -> shape mismatch. Common pattern: client does JSON.stringify on an already-stringified line.

Server log snippet (sanitized):
```
[2026-02-12T14:02:01Z] req_id=xyz received_content_encoding=gzip content_type=application/json lines=1 expected_lines=3 embeddings_returned=1
[2026-02-12T14:02:01Z] req_id=xyz parse_warning=ndjson_parse_failed fallback=single_input
```

Repro locally for us: create a plain text file with three raw lines (not JSON-wrapped), gzip it, then send with headers:
```
application/x-ndjson

gzip
```
That yields 3 inputs and 3 embeddings. If you must send JSON (application/json) then send a top-level array: `[{"input":"a"},{"input":"b"}]` un-gzipped.
Ah — our pipeline gzips earlier and a wrapper code did JSON.stringify on the file contents before gzip. That explains double-encoding.

Quick suggested fixes:
- For newline-delimited inputs: ensure each line is the raw text (or raw JSON object per line) and set Content-Type: application/x-ndjson. Do NOT JSON.stringify the whole file before gzipping.
- For single/batch JSON: send a valid JSON array (application/json), un-gzipped or with matching content-encoding.
- If client libs auto-wrap single items into arrays, verify they don't produce nested arrays. Flatten before sending: `const payload = items.map(x => (Array.isArray(x) ? x.flat() : x))`.
I've asked Acme to try that. Also added a KB note to the support queue explaining the Content-Type vs NDJSON gotcha.
deploy-notice: added additional parse warning telemetry for mismatched content-type + content-encoding (low risk) to help catch these sooner.
Confirmed — switched to application/x-ndjson + removed extra stringify step. Now we get 3 embeddings, counts align, billing returned to expected. Thanks :tada:
Nice. I'll follow up with a short doc blurb and add a unit test to our NDJSON gzip parsing path to avoid silent fallback to single-input.
Marking as resolved from infra side. Closing thread after KB update.

Pasted repro from customer (redacted keys):
```json
POST /v1/embeddings
They say the front-end code changed from sending a bare string to always wrapping in an array for internal consistency. Somehow it double-wrapped during serialization.
This is a classic single-vs-batch double-wrap. Front-end probably does `JSON.stringify([value])` and then the fetch wrapper also wraps into an array.

Also seeing reports of latency spikes from the same customer — they are sending huge 10k-item batches in one call and some also double-wrapped. Combined this causes backoffs/retries and throughput issues on their side.

Repro locally with curl (I ran this against sandbox):
```bash
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/embeddings \\
  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $KEY\" \\
  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \\
  -d '{\"model\":\"text-embedding-3-small\",\"input\":[[\"hello world\"]]}'
echo\\n
```
400 with same message. If I send \"input\":\"hello world\" or \"input\":[\"hello world\"] it returns 200 with embeddings.

Also we've had customers accidentally pass precomputed vectors (list of floats) into the embeddings endpoint. That returns a dimension mismatch in downstream steps or a validation error because embeddings endpoint expects text input, not numeric arrays. Example error I've seen: `422 Unprocessable Entity: expected string input but got numeric array`.

Customer initially thought it was a dimension mismatch from model change. They compared our SDK return shape to their downstream similarity engine and blamed us. But the real cause was the client sending nested arrays; once unwrapped, dims match.
Helpful hint: sending a single entry should be either a string or a single-element list. Avoid nesting. See docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/api/embeddings#input-format

Quick remediation steps for support to give customer:
- Check client serialization: make sure you don't both wrap and stringify. In JS, `body: JSON.stringify({model, input: texts})` where texts is either \"some text\" or `[\"a\",\"b\"]` but not `[[\"a\"]]`.
- For Python requests, avoid `json.dumps` twice. Use `requests.post(url, json={...})` not `data=json.dumps(...)` then `json.dumps` again.
- If you're sending precomputed vectors, use the `vector-import` API (internal) or the dedicated endpoint — embeddings endpoint expects text.
- Limit batch sizes to 64-256 items per request depending on model; very large batches increase latency and can trigger client retries.
Also suggested they add defensive validation client-side: ensure `Array.isArray(input)` and that typeof elements === 'string'. If element is array -> flatten or throw.

Customer ran local fix, unwrapped inputs, switched to batches of ~128, and errors stopped. Latency improved and their retry storms went away. They reported an unexpected billing spike — appears to be due to aggressive retrying from their wrapper when it saw 400s; each retry generated new requests (we're following up whether failed requests were billed).

FYI customer reported a sudden spike of 502s + TLS handshake failures when routing through their on-prem proxy to our hosted API after they flipped a NAT/proxy change earlier today. Repro steps below, can someone help triage?

Repro (from their proxy):
```
curl -v https://api.redwood.com/v1/engines/list -H 'Authorization: Bearer <redacted>'
*   Trying 18.214.12.34...
* TCP_NODELAY set
* Connected to api.redwood.com (18.214.12.34) port 443 (#0)
* TLS handshake error: Alert write:fatal:handshake_failure
* Closing connection 0

(35) OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL in connection to api.redwood.com:443
```

Their dig/nslookup shows the api hostname resolving to a public IP (18.214.12.34) instead of the VPC endpoint private IP (10.0.12.45). They said Private DNS was "on" when creating the interface endpoint but they're using an on-prem DNS forwarder -> VPC resolver chain.
Can you paste the dig +trace they ran and the resolver rule associations? My first guess is split-horizon / resolver rule not associated with the VPC/subnets that handle the endpoint.

Here's the dig output they pasted:
```
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 12345
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;api.redwood.com.       IN A
;; ANSWER SECTION:
api.redwood.com. 300 IN CNAME proxy.customer.example.com.
proxy.customer.example.com. 60 IN A 18.214.12.34
```

That CNAME to their proxy domain explains it — their conditional forwarder is returning an external A rather than resolving via the Route53 resolver into VPC. Two things to confirm: (1) the Route53 Resolver inbound endpoint exists and has rules to forward api.redwood.com -> VPC, (2) the VPC with the interface endpoint is associated with that resolver rule. If the resolver rule isn't associated with that VPC, the endpoint private DNS won't be used for on-prem queries.

I also grabbed a tcpdump from their proxy (they shared sanitized output):
```
12:34:56.789 IP proxy->18.214.12.34: Flags [S], seq 0, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
12:34:56.900 IP proxy->18.214.12.34: Flags [P.], seq 1:519, ack 1, win 229, length 518
12:34:57.001 TLS Client Hello SNI: api.redwood.com
12:34:57.150 RST from 18.214.12.34
```

RSTs to the public IP make sense if the NLB/public cert isn't matching SNI / you're hitting a different frontend. If they were resolving to 10.0.12.45 they'd hit the interface endpoint and traffic would stay private.

Suggested checklist:
- Verify interface endpoint Private DNS is ENABLED for the service.
- Ensure Route53 Resolver inbound endpoint + rule exist and rule is ASSOCIATED with the customer's VPC(s).
- Confirm on-prem conditional forwarder points to the resolver inbound endpoint IPs (or use DNS firewall rules to force the zone).
- Check security groups on the interface endpoint allow the proxy's source CIDR.
See internal doc: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/vpce-dns (internal link)

Quick mitigation if they need immediate fix: add a host override on their proxy for api.redwood.com -> 10.0.12.45 (not ideal long term). Example for linux proxy:
```
echo "10.0.12.45 api.redwood.com" >> /etc/hosts && systemctl restart nscd || true
```

^ only do host override for emergency. Strongly recommend fixing resolver associations instead. If you want to programmatically associate the rule:

adding data point — our batcher has max_batch_latency_ms=10 in prod by default. if cold misses stretch token latency by 200-600ms, queued requests pile up increasing queue_len, which surfaces as apparent throttling. you can see `batch_wait_ms=42` in the log, not huge but with many miss+evicts it compounds.

That's the issue. With multiple NAT GW EIPs, the source port mapping on egress can change depending on which NAT handles the flow. If return hits a different NAT EIP or different AZ, the inbound NACL on that path may not allow the ephemeral source port. That results in silent drops or RSTs from intermediate devices. Hey folks — a couple things to check. v0.9.2 changed the retry wrapper to reuse the provided http.Client but also adds an internal short-lived goroutine that can cancel a request on our retry timeout. If your per-request ctx is tight (10s) and our retry/backoff overlaps, you can see context canceled followed by a 504 from the server when the retry actually runs.

Quick checks:
- Are you reusing the same http.Client/Transport across requests? Creating a new client per request + transport can exhaust sockets.
- IdleConnTimeout=30s is a bit low for high-reuse workloads — if the transport drops an idle connection right before reuse, the first request on that conn can fail and trigger retries.

Workarounds we've seen help:
1) Reuse a single *http.Client and *http.Transport globally (package level).
2) Increase IdleConnTimeout to 90s+ and MaxIdleConnsPerHost to match concurrency.
3) Bump your per-request context timeout to > expected server time + retry budget, or disable SDK retries via Client.Options.RetryPolicy while testing.

Also flagging that when a client cancels a context, the server may still return a late 504 which gets logged — that explains the paired "context canceled" + "504" lines. The root cause is often the client-side connection reuse + server-side connection close timing.

Hey team — escalation from AcmeCorp. They reported repeated 429/503s for a batch job and two customer billing events went through twice. They say they're using python-sdk 1.3.2 (async client) and see duplicate charges when we retry on 429. Full details pasted below. Urgent — billing impact.
TL;DR: async retries sometimes resend a request without the original Idempotency-Key header after a token refresh, plus correlated retry bursts. Repro included.

Repro steps they sent:
```python
from redwood import AsyncClient
client = AsyncClient(api_key="sk-...", retry_policy={"max_retries": 3})
async def run():
    resp = await client.create_charge(customer_id="cus_123", amount=100)
```
They run this in a few parallel workers and see two successful charges ~1s apart, with the first attempt returning 503 then retrying and succeeding.
@amelia thanks — can you paste request/response headers and the SDK version exactly? 1.3.2 was the build that switched token refresh into the retry loop for async clients.

Headers: request 1 has Idempotency-Key: "ik-abc" then 503, retry attempt log shows subsequent request missing Idempotency-Key header. Responses show token refresh happened between attempts. Logs:
```
[2025-10-12T11:02:01Z] request id=req-42 POST /v1/charges status=503 token_expired=true idempotency=ik-abc
[2025-10-12T11:02:01Z] token refresh start
[2025-10-12T11:02:02Z] retry attempt=1 POST /v1/charges status=200 idempotency=NONE
```

This looks like a header mutation race during the async refresh path. We accidentally reuse the Request object and reapply headers after refresh, but the idempotency header is added in the per-call context and not copied back after the refresh. Also seeing our jitter seed was deterministic in 1.3.2 which can cause retry bursts across coroutines.

I'm reproducing locally with the customer's snippet + aiohttp, can confirm missing Idempotency-Key on retry when refresh callback fires. Created a minimal repro:
```python
# repro_async_retry.py
import asyncio
from redwood import AsyncClient
client = AsyncClient(api_key="sk-...", retry_policy={"max_retries": 2})
async def one():
    await client._send_with_refresh("/v1/charges", headers={"Idempotency-Key": "test-1"})
async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(*(one() for _ in range(5)))
asyncio.run(main())
```

Poking at continuous batcher failure modes. We keep default coalescing because it's great for cost, but when KV-miss storms hit we need a more surgical, local response instead of a global microbatch flip. Thoughts?
Yep. We get two bad effects from global flip: (1) cost explodes, (2) stable tenants lose efficiency. Suggest a localized pressure policy that prefers per-tenant limits and a tiny global breaker.
Can you sketch the policy? we need something implementable without heavy cross-host coordination.

Minimal sketch: each runtime emits a per-tenant pressure score computed from cheap local signals (inflight_tokens, kv_miss_rate_1s, enqueue_p95). ScoreProducer runs locally and writes ephemeral sticky decisions to local memory. Admission API stays admit(req, hints?) -> {action}. No global cache required initially.

How do we translate score->action? We should avoid opaque heuristics. Use explicit buckets: score < 0.3 => KEEP, 0.3-0.6 => SOFT_SHRINK (reduce coalesce window by x%), >0.6 => FORCE_TINY (prefer tiny-window path). Also a per-tenant min_token_preserve to avoid starvation.

Good. Add a per-instance tiny_budget to limit fragmentation: tiny_budget_fraction controls how many tiny windows allowed per epoch. If local budget exhausted, admission returns KEEP and maybe a DENIED_REASON tag.

Concern: different instances might demote the same tenant concurrently if traffic spreads. That can be okay since decisions are conservative and local-first, but we should add a conservative global circuit-breaker: if cluster p95 exceeds cluster_threshold, flip a global mode that temporarily tightens tiny_budget to a small value. That keeps cluster behavior predictable under extreme conditions.

Implementation notes: ScoreProducer uses EWMA over 1s bins to smooth spikes. Demotion has hysteresis: demote after 3 consecutive bins above threshold, recover after 5 bins below lower_threshold. Keep counts small for responsiveness.
API compatibility: admit(req) remains unchanged. New optional param hints.score_hint is allowed. Backwards compatible by default. Ship behind feature flag.

Observability hooks: emit events with labels {tenant, action, reason_code} and metrics: batcher.pressure_score{tenant}, batcher.demoted_tenants, batcher.tiny_budget_utilization, batcher.demote_transitions. Console should show recent demotion events and allow operator override.

Operator controls: rdbctl batcher tenant-set-mode <tenant> <mode> and rdbctl batcher set-budget <fraction>. Operator overrides write to /audit/batcher/overrides. ops-bot should post a notice when override occurs.
ops-bot: NOTICE: operator override audit created at /audit/batcher/overrides by admin.

Testing plan: simulator that can drive many tenants across multiple hosts with configurable KV miss injections. Key checks: false positive demote rate < 2%, throughput loss with tiny_budget=0.12 < 8%, tail latency improvement for affected tenants p99 drop >= 30%.

Edge cases: streaming sessions must be sticky. If a streaming session is demoted, we must keep the decision for session_ttl (e.g., 30s) to preserve KV affinity. Also ensure multi-turn responses maintain mode.

Security/Private deploy notes: ScoreProducer uses only local runtime metrics; no telemetry leaves host by default. Feature disabled in Private deployments unless admin enables. Document privacy in the PR.
One more: add a safe-fallback to the original global flip for catastrophic failure but rate-limit it and require operator approval if in Private. So global_flip is last resort.

top-level symptom: request success rate dropped from 99.9% -> 97.2% during peak, p50 unchanged (~90ms) but p95 up ~450ms -> 1.2s and p99 up ~480ms -> 2.1s. Happens with sequence lengths > 512 and batching enabled (auto-batch, target_batch=8). Customer observed regressions after enabling "quant_profile: int8" in their deployment config. They reverted to fp16 and p99 went back to normal.

```

Thanks — initial read: two likely compounding issues:
- quant calibration produced unstable qparams (NaNs) for long sequences -> runtime emits a fallback but that code path isn't optimized and forces slower kernels + extra memory copies. That explains p99 impact while p50 stays fine.
- kernel_selector recently changed heuristics in v1.18.2 and will pick a slower_emulation_kernel when it detects poor quantization stats. We have a ticket for tuning but not shipped.

Quick repro steps (local) to validate tail behavior:
1) Checkout runtime v1.18.2
2) Start local dev runtime with --enable-quant --verbose-kernel-select
3) Use model weights converted with int8 profile and use a synthetic input with seq_len=1024
Example run (bash):
```
# spin up runtime
./redwood-runtime --port 8080 --runtime-version 1.18.2 --enable-quant --gpu 0
# stress test
for i in {1..200}; do
  curl -s -H "x-debug: kernels,quant" -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -d '{"model":"redwood-3b-int8","input":"$(python3 -c "print('a '*600)")"}' &
done
```

adding ML context — calibration failing (NaNs) is often caused by outlier activations during per-channel min/max collection or a bad calibration dataset (too short, was mostly padding). The quantizer then emits extreme scales causing unstable int8 GEMM. In such cases the runtime's dynamic fallback to fp16 keeps correctness but performance suffers.

mitigation options:
- Re-run calibration with a representative dataset (no heavy padding, include long context examples). Use our calibration tool with --clip 0.999 and --per-channel.
- Enable a conservative quant_profile: "int8_safe" (we have an internal profile that clamps scales and disables asymmetric per-tensor quant for LLaMA-like layers).
- If immediate mitigation needed: set fallback order to ["fp16"] and set a policy to disable batching for sequences > 512 so we don't hit batching-induced kernel slow-paths.
Customer asks for step-by-step to be able to rollback safely if we push changes. They prefer us to coordinate a canary that targets 10% of traffic and rollback automatically on p99 > 1s.

3) Canary a runtime change that prefers the older kernel-selector heuristic for int8 until we tune the new heuristics.
4) Re-run calibration with ACME-provided example payloads; if calibration succeeds, promote int8 with conservative profile.

quick discovery from the accessibility pass: Cmd+K shortcut that focuses the topbar search conflicts with browser find on some setups and VoiceOver announces the search twice on open. Also people reported that when suggestions load there's no concise announcement of counts. Repro: Cmd+K -> focus goes to input, VO says 'Search' then 'Search' again, and when typing 'red' suggestions show but VO doesn't say '3 suggestions'. Link to prototype: https://figma.redwood.app/topbar-shortcuts

I can repro on my Mac. DOM seems to have a visible label + sr-only text + aria-label on the input. The shortcut handler calls input.focus() and then we programmatically set aria-live to describe the initial state which may cause duplicate speaks. Also Cmd+K is registered globally and some browsers intercept it for quick find.

a few separate issues:
1) Accessible name collision -> multiple name sources (label + aria-label + sr-only) cause double announce. Pick one source. Prefer label + aria-labelledby or sr-only label, not aria-label + visible label.
2) Programmatic focus + immediate aria-live announcement can double speak: when focus lands, the screen reader will announce the control name; then aria-live speaking the same phrase duplicates. Instead, defer aria-live summary until after focus settles and don't repeat the control name.
3) For suggestions, use a polite aria-live message like '3 suggestions' when the list appears, and use listbox/option semantics so arrowing announces the active option.
4) Shortcuts: expose the shortcut in the accessible name (e.g., 'Search (press K)') is okay visually, but don't intercept modifier combos that a browser might use. We can keep Cmd/Control+K and add ALT+S as a fallback for Windows browsers where Ctrl/Cmd+K conflicts.
good. UX question: do we want the aria-live summary to read only counts or also the type (e.g., '3 suggestions for "red"')? Too verbose might be noisy.

from testing, concise is better: '3 suggestions for red' is fine if it's one-shot when list appears. It shouldn't speak on every keystroke. Also ensure NVDA/JAWS behavior on Windows (Firefox/Chrome) is consistent.

proposed implementation plan: - Use a single source of accessible name: keep visible and input aria-labelledby="search-label". Remove aria-label on input. - Add an sr-only span inside the label for SR context: Search Redwood Console while visually showing "Search" only. - When opening suggestions, set #search-status (aria-live="polite") to "3 suggestions for \"red\"" after a 250ms debounce (not on every keystroke). Do not include the control name in this message. - Convert suggestions to role="listbox"/role="option" and use aria-activedescendant on the input while keeping focus on the input (don't move focus). - Shortcuts: keep Cmd/Ctrl+K but add Alt+S for Windows and expose the available shortcuts in the cheat sheet (accessible from Help). Also, when shortcut is triggered, push a concise sr-only hint to the status: "Search focused, type to find models". Code example to avoid duplicate announce: ```
  • Redwood
    • ...
``` And JS: ``` // on suggestions update (debounced) statusEl.textContent = `${count} suggestions for "${query}"`; // avoid status update when focus first lands (focus handler sets a flag) ```

that looks good. Two more nits: 1) When programmatically focusing via shortcut, set a short delay before writing to status so the SR will first announce the control and then the status; 2) prefer role="status" with aria-live="polite" for one-off updates. Also ensure we don't rely on CSS-only hiding for the sr-only content; use established sr-only utility that keeps content in accessibility tree.

about focus ring contrast on keyboard focus when invoked via shortcut: a few participants flagged it's subtle in dark theme. Can we increase ring thickness or add a faint halo? Keep consistent with other components.

test plan: add keyboard-only flows for both shortcuts (Cmd/Ctrl+K and Alt+S), verify single announce on focus, verify status message appears once per suggestion-render (debounced), verify listbox semantics announce active option on arrow, and visual snapshot of focus ring in light/dark. I'll run on macOS (VO/Safari), Windows (NVDA/Firefox, JAWS/Chrome).
I'll review the PR and run cross-platform checks. If we see inconsistent announce timing, we can tweak the 250ms debounce or change to manual announcements after aria-activedescendant changes.

Quick follow-up from todays all-hands re: KMS/BYOQ + audit exports. Im collecting a short FAQ for customers asking about ISO/SOC evidence. Main asks: can we prove key provenance? how long can customers keep logs? how does Private affect auditability?

Good questions. Short version: key provenance = we emit signing attestations for service-managed keys; for BYOQ we store an HSM attestation blob (not the key). Well provide a downloadable materials package for audits (manifest + signed checksum).

For ISO/SOC2 auditors they usually want: 1) rotation history, 2) access control change logs, 3) integrity proof for exported logs. We can produce a .tar.gz with a manifest.json that lists objects + SHA256, plus a signed envelope from our signing key. That addresses integrity requirements.
Nice. What about retention? We heard 90d default in hosted. Are there hard limits?

Hosted default = 90d. Customers can request archive exports to their bucket for any retention period. We recommend lifecycle rules like this example to move to Glacier after 60d:
```xml
<LifecycleConfiguration>
  <Rule>
    <ID>audit-archive</ID>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <Filter><Prefix>exports/</Prefix></Filter>
    <Transition>
      <Days>60</Days>
      <StorageClass>GLACIER</StorageClass>
    </Transition>
  </Rule>
</LifecycleConfiguration>
```
Is there a simple line we can give customers: "How long will Redwood keep my audit logs?"

Suggested customer-facing phrasing: "Default retention is 90 days. Customers may configure daily export to a customer-owned storage for longer retention and compliance needs; Redwood can provide signed export bundles for audit evidence."
About Private/VPC: does control-plane proxying remove auditability? Any gaps?

No gaps. Control-plane events are still logged at the edge and included in exports. For Private with customer-managed networking we also include vpc/policy identifiers in records. Note: data-plane inference payloads are not stored unless customer enable full-log export.

Small ops note: full-log export has storage and egress costs; we surface estimated monthly cost in the console when you enable it. Also, we truncate captured payloads at 10k bytes by default (configurable per-customer with opt-in).
Any example of the export filename/structure so customers can show auditors?
Example structure: exports/YYYY-MM-DD/{tenant-id}/audit-blob-YYYYMMDDT000000.tar.gz. Inside: manifest.json, events.ndjson.gz, signatures.asc. manifest.json contains object list + checksums.

revocation model: update registry -> bundles include tombstones -> gateways deny after bundle refresh or on explicit revocation push. document worst-case TTL exposure.
migration ops: broker accepts legacy API key and returns ephemeral token (TTL 5-15m). we audit every exchange. customers keep old key but exposure minimized.
offline bundles: compressed proto that contains numeric role defs, route ACLs, paramized predicates (e.g., dataset hash allowlist). signed by control plane; gateways verify signature on ingest.
perf: signature verify is heavy per-token. gateway should maintain LRU of verified token ids and only reverify on new tokens or key rotation. add session cache metrics.
role-id registry: central mapping service exposing delta stream. gateways subscribe to deltas to pre-warm caches. delta entries: add/remove/mutate membership for rid.
audit: gateways emit decision records asynchronously with token_id, rid, bv, decision, and reason. private installs can opt to keep logs local or ship to central collector.
failure modes: stale bundle -> gateway can either fail-closed or fallback to remote policy eval. prefer fail-closed for sensitive routes, allow fallback for low-risk ones. document per-route policy.

Quick follow-up from yesterday's design review on the small-surface lease allocator. Wanted to lock down API shape and operational constraints before we open an RFC.
echoing notes. Short summary: keep admission as the policy/backpressure gate; extract allocation heuristics to a separate allocator service with a tiny lease API.
Could we be explicit about the request/response fields? Need to support fairness weights, service-level hints, and an abuse signal.

Sketch I put together during the call:
```
POST /v1/leases
{
  \"tenant_id\": \"t-123\",
  \"requested_tokens\": 100,
  \"priority\": \"interactive\",   # optional
  \"fairness_weight\": 1.5,          # optional float
  \"abuse_score\": 0.02              # detector-supplied, 0..1
}
200 OK
{
  \"allocated\": 80,
  \"allocation_id\": \"alloc-456\",
  \"reason_code\": \"FAIRNESS_ADJUSTED\",
  \"expires_at\": \"1680000000\"
}
```
Keep response machine-friendly: reason_code is enum, not free text.

Two immediate concerns:
1) Abuse_score trust boundary. We can't let callers spoof detectors. For hosted we only accept signed scores from our detector service. For private we allow customer-supplied scores but mark them untrusted.
2) Fairness contract: either accept an opaque fairness token issued by central controller or a simple numeric weight. Mixing both will cause compatibility pain.

For hosted, allocator will validate a detector_signature header when abuse_score is present. If signature missing, treat abuse_score as advisory=0 for hosted path. For private installs, signing optional and documented.

Telemetry we must add up front to validate behavior:
- leases.request.count
- leases.allocated.count
- leases.allocated.tokens
- leases.rejected.count (by reason_code)
- leases.latency.p50/p95
- fairness.adjustment.factor (histogram)
- abuse.penalty.applied.count
Also per-tenant alerting for sudden allocation drops.
Instrument an allocation_debug event (sampled) with hashed tenant_id, requested, allocated, fairness_weight, abuse_score, allocator_version so we can replay problems without leaking PII.

Caching model: allocator is authoritative but admission can locally cache short-lived leases for latency-sensitive flow. Cache invalidation via ttl + optional invalidation topic. Cache usage limited to interactive priority only.

Fallback behavior if allocator unreachable:
1) Use local cache if present and not stale
2) Use configured grace_budget (small emergency allowance per-tenant)
3) Enter degraded mode: strict flat throttling and clear error codes to clients
We must avoid permissive silent defaults.
Security/abuse: allocator must return reason_code enum for every decision (e.g., OK, FAIRNESS_ADJUSTED, ABUSE_PENALTY, OVER_CAPACITY). Downstream logs should index counts by reason_code.
Rollout/ops questions: resource profile — allocator is mostly CPU for scoring; low memory. We can start as sidecar/shim colocated with admission and migrate to standalone service if needed.
