heads up — we got a high-severity support escalation from Acme. Intermittent 401s on every API call since they rotated their OIDC provider keys last night. Error in logs: `jwt: signature verification failed` and `no matching JWK for kid`. Repro steps they sent below.

repro steps from customer (copied):
1) obtain token from acme-idp at 2024-06-02T22:13:00Z
2) call our `/v1/generate` endpoint with that bearer token
3) see 401 with body `{"error":"invalid_token","reason":"signature_error"}`

logs they attached (sanitized):
```
2024-06-02T22:13:05Z ERROR auth.jwt validate.go:87 signature verification failed kid=abc123 token_aud=redwood-api
2024-06-02T22:13:05Z DEBUG auth.jwks cache.go:56 jwks cached_at=2024-06-02T22:08:00Z ttl=300s url=https://acme-idp/.well-known/jwks.json
2024-06-02T22:13:05Z INFO proxy.req handler.go:210 request_id=xyz-789 status=401
```
they mentioned the idp rotates keys every hour and their tokens contain `nbf` about +90s into the future (their client clock is slightly skewed).
@devon-eng can you take a look? Sounds like JWKS caching + clock skew edge case. :eyes:
looking. couple quick questions — do they see `no matching JWK for kid` or `signature verification failed`? Those are different.

both — sometimes `no matching JWK for kid` then after a minute `signature verification failed`. Attached base64 header from token: `eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImFiYzEyMyJ9` (decodes to `{"alg":"RS256","kid":"abc123"}`).

thanks. preliminary hypothesis: their idp rotated keys and published new JWKS; our runtime is caching the old JWKS and continues to validate against it. When we do a refresh, it sometimes sees the old key set due to upstream CDN caching or our cache TTL. Also their token `nbf` +90s could trigger `token not yet valid` if our clock skew tolerance is low.

adding infra detail — our JWKS cache TTL currently is 5m and we refresh proactively only every TTL or when we hit a 401 with `kid not found` path. There's a known bug where the refresh-on-401 only triggers for `signature verification failed` but the code path that checks `kid` returns early and doesn't trigger refresh. Filed a note in diag logs: `jwks: early return no kid match` but we didn't call fetch.

this is a classic race: idp rotates, some tokens still valid, but our cached keys stale. Also clock skew is common — we historically tolerated 60s. If client `nbf` is +90s, that will fail. We should increase skew tolerance and make JWKS handling more robust.

two-pronged fix suggestion:
- short term: add an emergency ops workaround: set jwks_cache_ttl=30s for the affected region/tenant and flip logs to debug so we can monitor refreshes.
- medium term: patch runtime to call `fetch_jwks()` whenever `kid` in token header is not found in cache (currently we don't for performance reasons). Also add a resilient backoff and background refresh after failed fetch to avoid stampedes.
agree. also add these mitigations: bump clock skew tolerance to 300s (5m) configurable per-tenant, and log the token header `kid` + jwks cached_at for every auth failure so we can do triage faster.
customer wants an ETA — they are in production and this is affecting ~80% of their requests. Can we do the short-term workaround now?

+1 from security. Need to ensure we don't create a DoS risk on idp endpoints. Add a rate limit on JWKS fetches per tenant (e.g., 1 fetch per 5s with exponential backoff on failure).

Heads-up from vuln triage: found a case where malformed SAML RelayState + role rename allowed a deprovision request to run for the wrong tenant. saw KMS metadata deleted for 2 users and subsequent SCIM creates failing with 403.
do you have a minimal repro/log?

log snippet: `2026-03-24T02:14:02Z provisioner WARN request_id=rid-zz123 action=deprov target_extid=acct:alice tenant=orchard resolved_extid=alice service=svc_scim user=svc_auth err=unauthorized` followed immediately by: `2026-03-24T02:14:03Z kms INFO envelope_delete envelope_id=e-993 removed_by=svc_scim request_id=rid-zz123` then `2026-03-24T02:14:04Z provisioner ERROR KMSDecryptFailed key_ref="" err="invalid_ciphertext"`
So deprov ran with wrong tenant context and deleted envelope pointer. How did authz allow that?

Root cause chain: 1) RelayState parsing bug in SAML handler trimmed tenant prefix when RelayState contained trailing slash. 2) RBAC rename changed group slugs, so the service that validates tenant scoping used new slug form and sometimes returned no match -> fallback to global permissive path for legacy svc tokens. 3) Deprov flow had no hard check to ensure envelope_org == current_tenant before delete.
Vulnerability triage created: VULN-2026-07 severity=high attack_vector=internal_privil escalation=possible

Immediate mitigation: disable automated envelope deletes until we patch, restore missing metadata from backup for impacted users, and rotate identities for any svc accounts that had permissive fallback.

mitigation steps taken: 1) feature-flagged envelope_delete in provisioner -> off 2) restored envelopes from latest metadata backup snapshot (s3://kms-meta-backups/2026-03-24-01) for the 2 users 3) rotated svc_scim tokens and added temporary denylist for permissive fallback path
Can you show the query to find affected rows?

`SELECT id, envelope_id, tenant, external_id FROM kms_metadata WHERE updated_at > '2026-03-24T01:00:00Z' AND envelope_deleted = true;` returned 2 rows. Also `SELECT * FROM provisioning_audit WHERE request_id IN ('rid-zz123','rid-zz124');`

Recommendation: consider adding an audit invariant check that prevents delete unless a tenant-scoped precondition passes. Also require two-step confirmation for automated envelope deletion on production.
Also add an anomaly alert: spike in envelope_delete events or delete_by != owner_service -> page immediately. I'll create alert rule.
Action: created alert rule alert_name="kms-envelope-deletes-unexpected" threshold=1/5m scope=prod
Short-term patch: provisioner change to validate `envelope.owner_tenant == current_tenant` before any delete and return 403 otherwise. Added canary patch to staging.

For postmortem: list fixes: - SAML RelayState parsing tightened + unit tests for trailing slash and encoded forms - RBAC rename rollback shim + contract tests between authz and provisioner - enforce tenant-scoped KMS metadata key - make envelope delete idempotent and require audit_tag and migration_token - add anomaly alert and SRE runbook - rotate svc tokens and rotate affected customer secrets if needed

+1. propose a quick detection rule: when `Decrypt` fails on key K more than N times in M minutes and there was a CreateGrant for that key in last T hours, fire an incident. we can implement as Athena query or lambda.

sample Athena query to correlate:
```
SELECT c.eventTime as grantTime, d.eventTime as decryptTime, d.errorCode, c.requestParameters.keyId
FROM cloudtrail_logs c
LEFT JOIN cloudtrail_logs d ON c.requestParameters.keyId = d.requestParameters.keyId
WHERE c.eventName = 'CreateGrant'
  AND d.eventName = 'Decrypt'
  AND d.errorCode LIKE '%AccessDenied%'
  AND d.eventTime BETWEEN c.eventTime AND c.eventTime + interval '2' hour
```

We need to lock down rollback criteria for KMS rotation cutover (dual-read -> new-only) before we publish the runbook. Can we align on hard thresholds + signals? I keep seeing “roll back if things look bad” in drafts.
+1. Needs to be concrete + defensible in audits. Also needs to be implementable on-call.

I can propose signals based on what we’re already instrumenting in the wrapper: `kms.error_category`, `kms.provider_error_code`, `kms.request_latency_ms`, plus decrypt mismatch counters from the dual-read path.
SRE angle: we need “rollback triggers” that are (a) measurable in dashboards (ENG-4828), (b) fast to act on (flip flag), and (c) minimize blast radius (avoid retry storms).

Control-plane wise, cutover is driven by the config flag set (the same thing we discussed in the dual-read thread). Rollback is basically: re-enable dual-read (or set active key version back), and optionally halt new writes under the new key.
+ note that some services might cache key metadata. After rollback, we need to force refresh / invalidate caches or you get “partial rollback.”

From a permissions perspective, rollback should *not* require new IAM changes. If rollback depends on granting “old key decrypt” back, that’s a smell. Old key decrypt should remain allowed for the duration of the dual-read window.

Also consider KMS degradation. During rotation events, KMS calls spike a bit. If KMS is already unhappy, rotation amplifies it. Rollback criteria should include “dependency health is bad -> pause/rollback cutover.”
Tomáš Novák: What about mismatch signals? If dual-read decrypts with both old+new, and results differ, that’s pretty severe. We should treat any mismatch as immediate rollback.

Clarifying: dual-read path currently does “try primary key version, if decrypt fails with a set of retryable/non-permission errors, try secondary.” We also have an opt-in “verify” mode that decrypts both and compares plaintext hashes. That compare can be sampled.

I’d like criteria in two buckets:
1) Immediate rollback (stop the bleeding)
2) Pause / extend dual-read window (not yet rollback, but don’t proceed)

Proposed immediate rollback triggers (prod):
- `kms.decrypt` error rate (non-throttling, non-timeout) > 0.10% for 5 minutes in any region OR > 0.05% for 15 minutes global.
- Any sustained `InvalidCiphertext` spike after cutover (> 10/min for 3 mins) => likely key/version mismatch or wrong key ID.
- Any decrypt mismatch from verify mode (plaintext hash mismatch) > 0 in prod => rollback immediately. Even 1 is scary.
I agree on “any mismatch => rollback.” That’s basically a correctness violation.

For error rate, we need to define what counts. I’d exclude categories we already expect during KMS incidents (Timeout/Throttling) and treat those as “pause rotation” not rollback. AccessDenied/NotFound/InvalidCiphertext should count.
+1. If KMS is throttling, rollback doesn’t necessarily help (might even increase load). We should instead halt the rotation *progression* and keep dual-read so we remain compatible.

For cutover rollback, I propose we treat these as separate “levers”:
- Lever A: `rotation_cutover_enabled` (new-only decrypt)
- Lever B: `dual_read_enabled` (attempt secondary key version)
Rollback sequence should set A=false, B=true.
That sequence matters. If you set B=false first you can strand ciphertexts.

For releases, can we codify this as a checklist item? “Rollback = A off, B on, then restart pods to clear caches if needed.”
Tomáš Novák: Add cache invalidation guidance. We saw stale key metadata during last dry-run.

Observability notes:
- Dashboard panel: `redwood.kms.decrypt.errors / redwood.kms.decrypt.requests` split by `error_category` and `provider`
- Mismatch panel: `redwood.crypto.dualread.mismatch_count` (should be flat 0)
- “Fallback usage” panel: `redwood.crypto.dualread.secondary_decrypt_count / decrypt_requests` (if this spikes after cutover, something’s off)
Good call. Fallback usage spiking is an early warning that primary decrypt is failing.

Concrete thresholds for “pause/extend dual-read” (don’t proceed to next phase):
- KMS p95 latency > 500ms for 10 minutes in target region (rotation window) OR > 2x baseline for 15 mins.
- Throttling rate > 0.5% for 10 minutes.
- Secondary decrypt ratio > 1% for 10 minutes (means new key path isn’t stable).
+ add a sanity: if overall 5xx SLO burn is elevated (serving stack) during rotation, we pause even if KMS metrics look “ok.” Rotation is not worth pushing during an incident.
We need to avoid “roll forward” bias. If any of these triggers hit, the runbook should say: rollback/pause is *the expected action*, no shame.

For auditability, capture who decided rollback, when, and the metric snapshot. Suggest template fields:
- Decision timestamp
- Trigger condition (paste alert / screenshot)
- Flag values before/after
- Incident/Linear link
- Approver (Security + SRE)
Love that. We can incorporate into the evidence template (ENG-4826).

One more rollback case: if we see AccessDenied errors after cutover, rollback immediately AND verify IAM didn’t accidentally remove old key decrypt permissions. AccessDenied during rotation is usually config/role drift.
Agree. AccessDenied > 0.01% for 5 mins is enough to rollback IMO. It’s not transient.

Let’s capture “immediate rollback triggers” as:
- Any decrypt mismatch (verify mode)
- `InvalidCiphertext` > 10/min for 3 mins (per region)
- AccessDenied > 0.01% for 5 mins OR > 50 events in 5 mins (whichever first)
- Overall decrypt error rate (excluding timeout/throttle) > 0.10% for 5 mins

And “pause/extend dual-read” triggers as:
- Throttling > 0.5% 10m
- KMS latency p95 > 500ms 10m (or 2x baseline)
- Secondary decrypt ratio > 1% 10m
- Any concurrent incident / paging alert in the same env => postpone

Operational steps (for runbook) suggestion:
1) Announce in #incidents (or #eng-releases if not incident) “Rotation rollback initiated”
2) Flip flags: `rotation_cutover_enabled=false`, `dual_read_enabled=true`
3) Trigger config propagation + restart affected services if cache TTL > 5m (include list)
4) Verify: decrypt errors return to baseline, mismatch stays 0, secondary ratio returns to expected
5) Open follow-up ticket + root cause
Step 3 should mention we have a “force key metadata refresh” endpoint now (post wrapper work). Use that before restarting everything.

Heads-up — we saw a spike in downstream ingestion errors starting at ~12:05 UTC, correlated with AWS KMS p99 decrypt latency in us-west-2. Many requests hit our decrypt path and retried, causing backpressure in the consumer.
Confirming, CloudWatch shows KMS ThrottlingExceptions around that time + increased latency from 14ms baseline to 800ms p99.
Any service-wide outages reported by AWS? I don't see a full service degradation in the status page, looks regional flakiness.
The pipeline uses synchronous decrypt per record — that'll amplify latency. We rely on GenerateDataKey/Decrypt for each item.
Which key policy/role is used? Could RBAC or an IAM change have triggered a permission fallback that caused retries?
No IAM changes in the last 48h per audit log. This looks capacity-related on KMS side (throttling + semaphore stalls in our client).
Short-term mitigation — can we enable a local envelope key cache for DEKs with a small TTL so we don't call KMS per message during spikes?
Agreed. We already store the encrypted DEK with each blob. Proposal: cache decrypted DEKs in-memory per worker for 60s with LRU eviction and TTL. If KMS fails, use cached DEK and mark metrics.
Also add a fast-circuit-breaker: if KMS error rate > 5% in 1m, flip to "cache-first" mode and queue decryption ops to background revalidate with backoff. That prevents retries piling up.

Audit concern — when we use cached DEKs we might not record a KMS Decrypt call for each item. We need to capture a signed audit event locally (and later reconcile) so compliance logs don't miss decrypts.
Good point. Add a local audit entry tagged "decryption:cached" with authenticated user and request_id; batch-signed to KMS when available.

Low-level: increase KMS client retry attempts and add jittered exponential backoff. Example for boto3:
```
from botocore.config import Config
kms_cfg = Config(retries={'max_attempts': 10, 'mode': 'standard'}, connect_timeout=1, read_timeout=5)
kms = boto3.client('kms', config=kms_cfg, region_name='us-west-2')
```
But don't rely on retries alone — that just shifts latency into the request path.

For rotation: if we cache DEKs, rotation becomes trickier. DEK cache entries must be invalidated on primary key rotation. We should subscribe to key-rotation events (CloudTrail/KMS EventBridge) and invalidate cache.

Also consider multi-region CMKs and regional fallback: keep a replica key in us-east-1 and fallback decrypt requests to the other region if cross-region decrypt allowed (watch for added latency). Optionally prefetch DEKs during low traffic windows.

Quick Q — we need a recommended pattern for where Redwood SDKs / API services should pick up KMS credentials across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. env vars? Vault? instance roles? short lived only?
Short answer: prefer platform identity (instance role / workload identity /MSI) or Vault-issued short-lived creds. Avoid long-lived static env vars when possible. :thumbsup:
+1. For AWS specifically use instance profile or assume-role (STS) for dedicated hosts. For EKS use IRSA. For GCP use workload identity. For Azure use MSI/Managed Identity.
If someone insists on env vars for local dev, make them only for dev and documented. Use profile chaining and named profiles for CI with limited perms.
How do people feel about using Vault vs AWS SSM Parameter Store for the KMS access keys that some older integrations still expect?

Use Vault transit or Vault IAM auth where possible. Vault can issue ephemeral AWS creds, or wrap/unwrap via transit for envelope encryption. SSM/Parameter Store OK for non-privileged secrets but avoid storing KMS root keys or long-lived creds there.

We should prefer not to store raw CMK material anywhere. Envelope encryption flow we aim for: GenerateDataKey via KMS -> use plaintext DEK locally to encrypt payload -> store ciphertext + encrypted DEK. KMS only stores CMK, not data.

Example AWS pattern (dev vs prod):
```
# prod (no env secrets)
# app runs on EC2/ECS/EKS with role allowing kms:GenerateDataKey, kms:Decrypt
REDWOOD_KMS_KEY_ARN=arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/abcd-...
# local dev (short-lived creds from Vault)
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...
```

For Vault transit as DEK manager:
- App requests Vault to generate a data key and receives plaintext & ciphertext (or client requests to encrypt local plaintext) depending on mode
- Vault uses its own KMS or HSM backend to protect its keys
- Vault issues short-lived tokens for app auth (OIDC/JWT/approle)
Rotation concerns — if we rotate CMK, do we need to re-encrypt all stored ciphertexts? How should Redwood handle this in general?

Two parts:
1) KMS CMK rotation (AWS can auto-rotate yearly; alias points to new key version) — existing encrypted data that used Encrypt/GenerateDataKey remains decryptable if you still have the original key; AWS KMS handles key versions under the same key id. But if you completely replace CMK (new key id) you need to re-wrap (re-encrypt) encrypted DEKs.
2) Data re-wrap process: read ciphertext, call KMS to decrypt encrypted DEK with old key, then GenerateDataKey using new key OR ReEncrypt (if supported) to create a new encrypted DEK, then store new envelope. Implement in background job, test in staging, and keep audit logs.
GCP note: Cloud KMS has a rewrap API too (asymmetric vs symmetric note). Azure Key Vault supports key rotation & wrap/unwrap as well. Always check per-cloud semantics.

Audit/logging and RBAC checklist:
- Ensure CloudTrail / KMS audit logging is enabled for Decrypt/GenerateDataKey/Encrypt/DescribeKey
- Limit key usage by IAM principals and resource-based policies
- Use encryption context (AWS) to bind data to metadata; require context on decrypt
- Retain logs for at least 90 days (or per compliance) and surface suspicious decrypt counts to Redwood Console alerts
If we detect a leaked service principal that had KMS decrypt rights, what's the incident playbook?

Short triage steps:
1) Revoke the principal (remove role, disable service account, revoke Vault token).
2) Immediately create or activate a new key and start re-wrapping active ciphertexts (or rotate the CMK and rewrap DEKs).
3) Audit CloudTrail / KeyVault logs for decrypt calls and list affected ciphertexts.
4) Invalidate caches and token sessions that might have cached DEKs.
5) Notify impacted customers and run a forensics checklist.
Also rotate downstream app credentials (DB, S3) if the compromised principal had wide access. Increase monitoring and tighten RBAC.

Quick question — we're standardizing how SDKs pick up KMS credentials across hosted/dedicated/private. TL;DR: recommended approach for AWS/GCP/Azure + envelope encryption + rotation?

Short answer: prefer provider-native short-lived identities (IAM roles, GCP service accounts via Workload Identity, Azure Managed Identity) -> fall back to secret manager (Vault) only when that's not possible. Avoid long-lived creds in env vars. :thumbsup:
Can you expand on the Vault vs cloud secret manager tradeoffs? We have customers in air-gapped/offline environments so Vault might be required there.

Exactly. Patterns we use:
- Hosted (recommended): attach least-privilege role to the service (IRSA on EKS / EC2 instance profile). SDKs auto-pick via metadata service. No static creds.
- Multi-cloud control plane or CI: use Vault with short TTL leases and dynamic AWS/GCP credentials minted by Vault.
- On-prem / air-gapped: Vault agent + auto-renewing AppRole tokens or customer-provided HSM-protected keys.

For SDK config, we should expose a simple priority order in our client: 1) Managed identity / metadata service, 2) Vault/SSM Param reference (via secret resolver), 3) explicit service principal config (only for local dev). Document it and fail hard in prod if step 1/2 not available.

For envelope encryption: always generate a data key locally, encrypt it with the KMS CMK, and persist only the encrypted data key. Never persist plaintext data keys. If a customer wants caching, ensure keys are in-process and TTL-limited.
Good. Rotation model? How do we rotate CMKs without re-encrypting all objects?

Two approaches:
- Rewrap on read: keep using existing encrypted data keys; on decrypt, get plaintext data key, re-encrypt the data key under the new CMK and update object metadata (lazy rewrap).
- Background rewrap job: periodic job that decrypts (via old CMK) and re-encrypts the data key with the new CMK.
Both require audit + rollout plan. Also maintain key aliases so service config points to alias, not raw key id.
What about key grants and least privilege? We sometimes need another service to re-encrypt during migrations.

Use KMS grants where available (AWS KMS grants) for short-lived delegated permissions. For GCP/Azure, restrict roles to only the minimal actions (encrypt/decrypt/unwrapKey). Create separate roles for encrypt-only vs decrypt-only where possible — that reduces blast radius.
Also: ensure RBAC changes are tracked in infra-as-code (terraform) with PR reviews and require security approvals for any policy that includes Decrypt. Add an audit flag/label for keys used in prod.

Audit logging: enable CloudTrail Data Events (AWS KMS API), GCP Audit Logs for KMS, and Azure Key Vault diagnostic settings sending to Log Analytics / storage account. We'll ingest kms:Decrypt/kms:GenerateDataKey calls into our SIEM for alerting.
Incident flow if a key is suspected compromised?

Suggested playbook: 1) Disable new encrypt operations (disable key or remove Encrypt permission). 2) Revoke active grants. 3) Create new CMK and start rewrap (background job) or require clients to rewrap on next read. 4) Rotate any service principals or client secrets that could have been involved. 5) Notify customers (per contract). 6) Preserve logs for forensic: export CloudTrail/Audit log to immutable storage.

Note: disabling a key can break services. Use staged approach: first block encrypt, keep decrypt to allow reads if needed, then rotate fast. For high-safety customers, we may rotate both and provide a fallback key for a short window.

Heads-up — we ran into a weird case in a customer POC: a service key was minted by the infra broker with no project claim, and later a project owner claimed it. What should the canonical semantics be for 'claiming' an unscoped key?
Do we have a concrete repro? Is this 'claim' operation user-driven or an automated reconcile? :thinking:

Repro is manual. Team created a long-lived svc key for an internal integration (forgot to set project), later ops used the console to bind it to proj-42. The key kept working but audits don't show who actually owned it before. Customer worried about blind rebinds.
My 2¢: disallow silent rebinds. If a key is unscoped we should require a proof-of-possession + approval flow from project admins. Otherwise you open reparenting risk.
Agree on explicit approval. But also think about migration from legacy: we need a UX path to claim many keys without manual per-key approvals.

Tradeoffs:
- Hard deny: easiest to reason about, strongest safety.
- Allow-with-proof: more flexible, requires cryptographic proof + audit event.
- Broker-mint-only: prefer minting scoped tokens only (longer-term).

Example of allow-with-proof flow we discussed: client proves possession by signing a nonce with key material and posts to /claim. Broker verifies and creates a scoped binding after admin approves. Pseudocode:```json

FYI we got two enterprise tickets asking for streaming function/tool calls + structured output streaming. both from customers hitting UI latency and memory limits.
which customers? priority?

acme-payments (large merchant) and helios-ml (analytics). acme wants partial tool results streamed to UI for faster UX; helios needs structured fields emitted incrementally to avoid buffering huge JSONs. both blocked on our current non-streaming function call path.

ok. quick triage: we need proposal for scope + launch criteria. sasha can you sketch engineering constraints?

quick thoughts: streaming completions already supports token streaming. function calls today are delivered only at end-of-response as a complete JSON. two main work items: 1) runtime + protocol changes to emit function call frames as they flush, 2) SDK/contract changes to represent partial function payloads and finalization event.

we also need to define semantics: are we allowing partial JSON chunks (i.e., arbitrary byte chunks) or delimited logical messages (nl-delimited JSON, or separate 'frame' objects)? tradeoffs for parsing and safety.

infra notes: streaming > increments to connection counts and long-lived sockets. need to validate our LB timeouts and pod connection limits. also watch memory for huge streaming sessions. suggest opt-in header to avoid changing default behavior.

propose opt-in header X-Redwood-Stream-Functions=true and a new streaming frame envelope with types: "partial", "tool_end", "error", "meta". acceptance criteria: backward-compatible (non-opt-in clients unchanged), SDK exposable streams, final tool result identical to current function call output when concatenated.
support asks for clear fallback: if client doesn't support stream frames, fall back to old behavior automatically. customers need SDK snippets.

MVP idea: NL-delimited JSON frames with envelope {"t":"partial","name":"get_user","payload":"..."} and final frame {"t":"tool_end","name":"get_user","payload":"{...}","complete":true}. parser in SDK stitches partials. no schema validation in MVP.
timeline? estimate for MVP engineering + SDK + docs + basic e2e tests?
rough split: runtime changes (~2w), SDK updates across python/js (~1w), e2e + infra adjustments (~1w), docs + examples (~.5w). total ~4.5 weeks. stretch for unexpected perf.

error snippet?
`ClientError: AccessDeniedException: User: arn:aws:sts::111222333:assumed-role/team-lambda/SESSION is not authorized to perform: kms:Decrypt on resource: arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:999888777:key/abcd`
are you assuming with a session policy or max_session_duration override?
using `sts:AssumeRole` via our infra; role has `sts:ExternalId` and `MaxSessionDuration` 3600. No session policy set intentionally.
two common gotchas: 1) the KMS key policy denies `kms:Decrypt` unless principal is in key policy or a grant exists. 2) session policy can drop kms permissions.

key policy does allow `arn:aws:iam::111222333:role/team-lambda` and `arn:aws:iam::111222333:root` — but assume role principal shows as `arn:aws:sts::111222333:assumed-role/team-lambda/SESSION` which should match.
can you paste the key policy snippet?

```json
{
  "Sid": "AllowLambdaRole",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111222333:role/team-lambda"},
  "Action": ["kms:Decrypt","kms:GenerateDataKey"],
  "Resource": "*"
}
```
note that KMS evaluates the principal ARN after assume-role — the key policy needs to include the assumed-role principal or a wildcard for `arn:aws:sts::*:assumed-role/team-lambda/*`.

also check whether a Grant was created earlier that got revoked by key rotation. Grants are per-key and can reference grant tokens when created. If client used a grant token and key rotated, decrypts can fail.
we do envelope rotation daily but thought we had proper grants. audit shows `Decrypt` calls from the lambda but KMS returns AccessDenied. No Grant-related logs.
run `aws kms get-key-policy --key-id abcd` and also check CloudTrail for `CreateGrant`/`RevokeGrant` events around rotation time.
running those now, will post snippets. quick question: could STS session tags or session-policy affect `kms:EncryptionContext` requirement? We're not setting encryption context explicitly.
EncryptionContext only matters if the key policy or IAM condition requires `kms:EncryptionContext:...`. Check key policy conditions for `kms:EncryptionContext:...` and `aws:PrincipalTag`.
found it — a condition in key policy: "kms:EncryptionContext:environment": "prod".

aha. when lambda assumed role via federation the session didn't include that context. Decrypt fails if context required but not provided. Two fixes: remove Mandatory EncryptionContext condition or ensure caller passes the encryption context when decrypting (or use grants that bypass the constraint).
thanks. for short-term fix, we can add a grant to allow the assumed-role ARN to call `kms:Decrypt` without requiring context.

note that grants are subject to grant tokens when used in the same request. For cross-account/assume flows, better to update key policy to include `arn:aws:sts::111222333:assumed-role/team-lambda/*` as principal.
also verify that `MaxSessionDuration` isn't causing session to be truncated and lose tags that are used in policy conditions.

Hey team — quick sync: we're proposing schema changes so customer-facing audit events can be validated end-to-end and also support WORM + per-tenant KMS archival. Need input on coverage and retention. Key Qs: scope of events, immutable marker, and where to stash archive KMS ARN.
For coverage — include authz changes, API key rotations, model-rollouts, and Dedicated deployment config changes. All admin-level actions + data-export / download events.
Compliance asks that retention and immutability are explicit in event metadata. We need an `event_retention_policy` tag (e.g., `cust:7y`,`sys:2y`) and `immutable_until` timestamp.
Suggest adding `immutable: true|false` and `imm_until: ISO8601` fields, and an `archive_destination` object with `type: s3|gcs` and `kms_key_id`.

Draft schema snippet:
```json
{
  "event_type": "string",
  "actor": {"id":"string","role":"string"},
  "resource": {"id":"string","type":"string"},
  "action": "string",
  "timestamp": "ISO8601",
  "immutable": true,
  "imm_until": "ISO8601",
  "retention_policy": "cust:7y",
  "archive_destination": {"bucket":"string","region":"string","kms_key_id":"arn:aws:kms:..."}
}
```
+1 on schema. Operational note: immutable flag must be enforced at storage layer (WORM object store or special S3 Object Lock). We can't rely on app-layer flag alone.
FYI — current archive flow supports S3 Object Lock + KMS CMK outlines. See `/infra/archive/README` for policy. :information_source:
Can we make `archive_kms_key` per-tenant? Legal requires tenant-segregated keys for some contracts.
Yes, Dedicated/Private will have per-tenant KMS. Hosted customers default to shared CMKs unless they bring-your-own (BYOK). We need metadata to store `kms_wrapped_keys` or `envelope_kek_id`.
How do we validate customer-facing audit events? Need deterministic schema validation and signed attestations where customers can verify event integrity.

Option A: sign event payloads with a service signing key and expose attestation endpoint. Option B: include SHA256 + salt recorded in WORM store and provide proof API. Both require key lifecycle management.
Legal: exportability is important. Customers must be able to request export of their immutable audit records. Include export SLA and how KMS rotation affects exports.

Retention enforcement: we must ensure `immutable_until` > now + retention_window. Also have a late-append model: events may be corrected, so allow append-only corrections with cross-reference to original event id.

Implementation plan:
- Schema PR in `audits/schema` repo -> validation library deploy
- Storage: S3 with Object Lock enabled + bucket per-tenant for enterprise -> lifecycle rules
- Archive pipeline signs + writes event and pushes digest to ledger service
- KMS: per-tenant CMKs where contract requires BYOK
Blockers: audit-eval harness to exercise schema + customer validation. @auditsvc-bot can you run a small test set with tenant BYOK and shared CMK?
Running test job 4521. Will post results in thread when complete. :gear:
One more ops note — avoid storing plaintext PII in audit event; instead store redaction pointers. If need full payload for forensics, store encrypted blobs with customer CMK.

i'll own key model + envelope flow. short notes: use CMK (customer-managed) as KEK, generate DEKs via GenerateDataKey (AES256) for data-plane objects, persist the plaintext DEK only in memory long enough to encrypt then wipe. store encrypted DEK (ciphertextBlob) alongside object. use ReEncrypt when rotating KEK. don't use raw Encrypt for large payloads.

small infra detail: for Private control plane endpoints, control plane runs in customer's VPC via our private control plane components — make sure the control plane has an IAM role with kms:GenerateDataKey, kms:Decrypt, kms:ReEncrypt, kms:DescribeKey. add encryption context on every KMS call with keys like "redwood:object-id" and "redwood:env=private". it binds ciphertext to metadata and helps auditing & reduces accidental misuse. require the same context on Decrypt/ReEncrypt.

reminder: using grants reduces call overhead vs policy checks for high qps patterns. but grants expire and need lifecycle. grants are recommended for short-lived roles (eg ephemeral worker) and heavy workload paths (realtime inference DEK decrypt).

about DEK cache - we should implement a bounded in-memory DEK cache with TTL ~5 minutes and LRU eviction per process. cache key = hash(key-id + enc-dek-blob + encryption-context). on cache miss, call Decrypt once then cache plaintext for TTL. log cache misses to a metric.

audit logging: enable AWS CloudTrail with KMS data events + management events for the account that owns CMKs. forward to central logging. set CloudWatch metric filters for kms:ReEncrypt, kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext (if used), kms:DisableKey, kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion, kms:CreateGrant. alert on unusual patterns (spikes in Decrypt or ScheduleKeyDeletion). keep logs immutable and retained per customer SLA.

sample envelope flow (pseudocode):
```
// control plane creates DEK
resp = kms.GenerateDataKey({KeyId: KEK_ARN, KeySpec: 'AES_256', EncryptionContext: ctx})
plaintextDEK = resp.Plaintext // use ephemeral
ciphertextDEK = resp.CiphertextBlob // store with object
// encrypt payload with plaintextDEK (client-side AES-GCM)
wipe(plaintextDEK)
// decrypt path
ciphertextDEK = object.meta.enc_dek
plaintextDEK = kms.Decrypt({CiphertextBlob: ciphertextDEK, EncryptionContext: ctx})
use plaintextDEK to decrypt payload
wipe(plaintextDEK)
```

rotation runbook highlights:
- stage: create new CMK version or new CMK (depending on policy)
- warm: create grants so high-qps workers can use new key seamlessly
- rewrap batch: run ReEncrypt over stored encrypted DEKs (idempotent) with concurrency limits
- promote: switch default KEK pointer in config/metadata to new CMK
- cleanup: schedule old CMK disable after verification, then ScheduleKeyDeletion per retention window
- test: random sample object decrypts after each step

emergency compromise playbook (short):
- detect: CloudTrail alert for ScheduleKeyDeletion or unexpected DisableKey or spike in Decrypt
- isolate: revoke grants, update CMK key policy to deny all principals except sec-runbook role
- rotate: generate new CMK and trigger rewrap pipeline prioritizing latest customer-critical objects
- notify: compliance + customer success with timeline and actions taken
- audit: produce signed artifact with CloudTrail events, rewrap job logs, and verification checksums

quick sync — we're revisiting how we route requests when service tokens are opaque. tradeoffs: privacy vs routability. thoughts?
opaque tokens are great for least-privilege + reduces leak surface, but edge routers can't make routing decisions without introspection.
+1. introspection adds latency and load. can we put minimal routing hint outside the token? header or SNI? :thinking_face:
headers are easiest but risk leaking tenant/project mapping to intermediate proxies. also breaks our desire to have interchangeable proxies.
remembered earlier RFC about embedding a short routing key in the token header (not payload) — still feels leaky. we discussed hashed route keys that only our routers can reverse, any others?
hashing helps but doesn't prevent correlation attacks if the same hash travels across services. ephemeral route keys (rotated per connection) are better but harder.

what about an opaque token + a separate short-lived signed envelope that contains routing hints — routers validate envelope signature but cannot read other claims? basically envelope only for routing.

that could work. example flow: client presents token T and envelope E. router verifies E.sig with RouterKey and reads E.route. Router uses route + forwards T to auth service if needed. prevents global leakage because envelope TTL is tiny.
love the pattern. tradeoffs: extra roundtrip for envelope minting, and we need key management for RouterKey across regions. also complexity for fallback when envelope missing.

operationally we can mint envelope at edge-issuers (edge-auth) while exchanging long token. clients do one-time exchange. sequence: 1) client sends creds -> edge-issuer returns (T,E). 2) client uses (T,E) for requests.
fallback: if E missing, router can do introspect(T) to get route. keep introspect as fallback only.
implement notes: E format: base64url {route: "proj:123", exp: 171..., nonce: "..."} signed with ed25519. small size < 128 bytes.

security Q — what if attacker captures (T,E) on public network? E short TTL mitigates. also recommend encryping route inside E so intermediate routers that shouldn't see route can't. but router must decrypt -> need KMS accessible to routers.
encrypting route inside envelope means router needs decryption key; same leak surface. but it prevents casual logging of route at other components that see E. good trade.
propose POC: implement envelope minting in edge-auth, routers validate signature, decrypt route with RouterKMS, fallback introspect path, and TTL 30s. Start with internal-only rollout.
+1. small concerns: metrics and tracing — we need to ensure envelope nonce ties to trace id for debugging.

Quick sync 999We need to decide service auth architecture: pure gateway RBAC (Envoy) vs external policy agent (OPA) vs hybrid. Short pros/cons?
Gateway = single enforcement point, simple for ingress, lower latencies. OPA = expressive policies, versioned bundles, but external calls and more surface area.
Gateway-only added <15ms p95 on our test; adding a remote OPA added ~20ms p95. For high-throughput paths, that matters.
OPA wins on expressiveness: hierarchical org/project rules, attribute-based decisions, easier to canary policy changes.
Thinking about decision factors: latency, failure modes, expressiveness, rollout/CI, telemetry, dev ergonomics. Anything else?
Authoring surface: if we pick OPA, teams can push policy bundles (sidecar/local). If gateway, teams need central PRs or a policy API. Ops burden differs.
Failure modes matter: gateway-down can be global outage. OPA-down could be per-service degradation. Need clear fallback semantics.
Hybrid pattern idea: coarse-grained checks (token validity, org/project claim, route allow) in gateway; fine-grained attribute checks via local OPA sidecars for services that need it.

Sketch: 1) Gateway validates token, enforces coarse RBAC (roles, route allow). 2) Services run local OPA sidecar for fine grained ABAC; sidecars get bundles from central registry. 3) Central policy CI and bundle signing.
Fallback policy: if sidecar unreachable, what then? deny-by-default breaks apps. Maybe gateway allows when coarse check passes but marks request for audit when fine-grain unavailable.
We should risk-classify endpoints: HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW. Default fallback per bucket: HIGH -> deny on missing fine-grain, MEDIUM -> allow+alert, LOW -> allow.
Example mapping: admin APIs -> HIGH, billing/thresholding -> MEDIUM, read-only public-ish -> LOW. We'll produce a mapping.
Ops question: sidecars add memory/ops cost. Central OPA cluster reduces pods but needs caching and increases request hops. Tradeoff notes?

Sidecars = local eval, predictable perf, more memory. Centralized = simpler ops footprint, caching layer required, single failure domain. Either ok if we provide tooling for bundle distribution and rollout.
Telemetry: gateway must emit token verification outcomes, coarse decision tags, latency. OPA decisions include policy bundle id and rule id to trace regressions.

Migration for API keys & RBAC: plan: 1) export key->role mappings, 2) augment tokens with org/project claims for a trial, 3) run policies in shadow mode 2wks, compare denies, 4) enable progressive deny-by-default.

Token scoping debate: project-scoped short-lived keys vs org-wide long-lived tokens. Ops wants fewer tokens, product wants per-product scoping. Proposed default: project-scoped keys, org-scoped only via approval with shorter TTL and stronger audit.
Migration shim: accept legacy keys at edge, mint short-lived claim-bearing internal tokens (kid header) and forward to services. That keeps internal auth simple.

Quick check — if we let org-scoped service API keys impersonate within projects, how do we avoid elevation when a target project grants broader roles?
Are you thinking inheritance (org -> project) or the other way? normally project is narrower, but grants can be wide.
Right. Example: org-key used by infra svc to call billing in project-A; project-A has a role that also includes admin perms for billing buckets.
Two basic models: 1) always evaluate the key's scope first and fail early, 2) evaluate target project's bindings and apply intersection. Both have tradeoffs.
Intersection seems safer: effective permissions = key_scope ∩ project_bindings. That avoids key getting more perms than intended.
Intersection is safe but breaks a lot of current flows where admins expect org-keys to be accepted as full delegates. Backcompat risk.
Also complexity: we need to materialize effective roles at request-time. That implies extra lookup latency and caching.
What about explicit deny rules? Could we allow deny at project boundary to override intersection?
Deny semantics are sharp but add surprises. If a project admin adds a deny, org tooling could break silently. We need visibility/audit.

Proposal: default = intersection (least privilege). Add a opt-in "delegation: broad" flag on org-keys that preserves org-level perms when accepted by projects. Require project whitelisting to accept broad delegation.
I like whitelisting. Add audit requirement: project must explicitly opt-in with a signed acceptance manifest.

Implementation sketch: at auth-time fetch key_policy (cached), fetch project_acceptance (cached, TTL 1m), compute effective roles. If key has delegation:broad and project_acceptance=true then effective_roles = key_roles ∪ project_roles else effective_roles = key_roles ∩ project_roles.
Need to handle deny precedence: always apply explicit denies from the project after union/intersection to avoid accidental escalations.
Also mention impersonation chains — if svcA impersonates svcB, we need to propagate original principal and ensure each hop enforces its own intersection/whitelist. Chain eval could be expensive.
Performance concerns: can we use a precomputed matrix for common projects + keys to avoid per-request DB hits? Maybe warm caches from RBAC service as soon as keys are issued/updated.
Yes, proactively push key->project accepted bindings into the serving layer on change events. Fallback to remote eval if cache miss.
UX: surface "why denied" in logs with the delta (key_roles vs project_roles vs denies). That will help troubleshoot when intersection blocks a flow.
Migration story: default to intersection, run a 30-day opt-in window where projects can whitelist existing org-keys. Emit policy-compat reports to owners.

Good. One more edge: API routing — we sometimes route by key prefix to different frontends. If a key is both org and project scoped (legacy), ensure routing keeps correct tenant header so project acceptance check hits right project.
Noted. Add unit tests: chain length 3 impersonations, denied role at middle hop, cache expiry scenarios.
I'll draft a short RFC with the opt-in whitelist + audit + caching plan and the compatibility timeline.

Quick follow-up from the API-key vs RBAC RFC — thinking about a pragmatic migration path for service auth. TL;DR: we need a short-lived shim so product teams don't break and a clear long-term plan to map keys to role bindings.
+1. can you sketch the shim? do we punt to a proxy or extend the auth service?

Proposal: service-auth-proxy that accepts existing API keys and emits ephemeral actor claims to the backend. It would do introspect -> emit JWT with `svc` claim. Long-term target is eliminating key surface by moving to role bindings in the identity system.
Sounds good. main concern is audit/traceability and perf. Proxy adds latency and a single extra hop.
Agreed. Perf numbers matter. We keep the proxy in-path only for legacy keys; new traffic uses direct mTLS/JWT. We can add caching of introspection results and short-lived tokens to reduce calls.

For mapping — how do we represent key intent? Right now keys are just a blob tied to project/org. We need a deterministic translation to roles. Example: key -> (project:foo, purpose:ingest) -> bind `role:svc.ingest` at project:foo.

We should avoid creating a role per key. Roles are templates (svc.ingest) and bindings are per-principal (service). Migration: create a service principal per key, attach role bindings, then prefer principal-based auth.

Migration steps I'd expect: 1) shadow proxy that logs mapping decisions, 2) create service principals for keys, 3) attach roles by heuristics (owner input), 4) opt-in cutover, 5) eventual unilateral deprecation of keys.
On heuristics: maybe use existing metadata (key name, created_by, last_used) + ask owners during migration window. Also surface in Console a list of suggested bindings.

Example introspect -> emit flow (pseudo):
```
POST /introspect
{api_key: "..."}
Do we need to handle cross-project tokens? Some keys are org-wide. How do we scope roles?
Keep role bindings namespaced: `org:billing -> role:svc.invoicer`, `project:foo -> role:svc.ingest`. The proxy must include the allowed scope in the emitted claim, don't expand beyond that.
Questions on RBAC primitives: do we add a `service` actor type + `binding` objects? I think yes — we already have user/org bindings; extend for services with `actor_type=service`.

Auditing: every proxy issuance should write an audit event with request id, key id (hashed), emitted principal, and mapping rationale (heuristic or manual). We need retention policy and alerting for suspicious mappings.

Ops concerns: how do we run the proxy? Hosted: run in our infra with HA and autoscale; Dedicated/private: offer it as an appliance component or lightweight binary that teams can run next to their control plane.
Backward compatibility: we need a header `X-Legacy-Key-Used: true` until deprecate. Also have a debug mode to print mapping decisions for owners.
Security detail: rotate underlying keys, and make sure proxy can revoke mapping instantly. Add a revocation cache and realtime invalidation hook.
Migration UI: Console should show candidate principal + suggested roles + owners + one-click approve. Without this I don't want to auto-bind anything.
Will add telemetry requirements: latency p95 target for proxy < 20ms overhead, cache hit ratio goal 95% for common workloads, and metric `mapping_suspect_count` for anomalies.

design sketch: two admission paths. fastpath for tiny requests (<128 tokens) with minimal coalesce. compact path for larger requests with smoothing credits and occasional forced drains

Quick heads-up 1: LumenHealth raised an onboarding question on todays call: initial-request latency spikes during warmup. They want to know if those minutes count against their SLO and whether credits are on the table.

Short answer: warmup/cold-cache spikes are real. Our standard SLO measurement is 1-minute windows of request latency (p95/p99 depending on contract). We generally dont auto-exclude warmup unless contract says so.

Tech detail: cause is KV cache population + occasional shard cold-starts. For many short sessions the first turn can be 27x slower for 1-3 requests until the prefix cache is filled. Mitigations: sticky sessions, prefix prefetch, or a preheat job.

LumenHealth flagged this as a renewal sensitivity. They want a customer-ready explanation + remediation options before exec readout next Tue. Also asked if a temporary credit would be easier than changing config.

Proposed outline for the note: 1) short lay explanation, 2) exact SLO math we use, 3) cause + evidence query, 4) 3 remediation choices with ETA & cost, 5) credit policy suggestion with a worked example, 6) next steps and owners.
Ill draft the customer text. Nina please add one-line benefit and ETA for each mitigation so we can show impact.

Quick bullets: - sticky sessions (tenant cookie/affinity): 35-55% improvement first-turn; low risk; ETA 4 business days. - prefix prefetch: 60-80% improvement but needs testing; ETA 10 business days. - deploy preheat job: up to 90% elimination of warmup cases; quick to run but adds compute; ETA 2 days. Snippet for preheat API:
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/preheat -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"model":"rwd-small","prompts":["init"],"concurrency":3}'
```
Add cost roughs so they can compare credits vs preheat trial. Suggest offering a free 2-week preheat trial during onboarding.

For credits: recommend conservative policy to move quickly: only consider credits if we confirm breach pattern correlating to first-request spikes AND customer cannot adopt mitigation within N days. Cap credits to 2% of monthly bill and require logs as evidence. Keep formula simple for legal.

Example credit calc to include in note (customer-facing):
- Contract SLO: 95th latency <= 150ms (measured per-minute)
- Observed minute avg: 300ms -> excess 150ms = 100% over SLO -> count as affected minute
- Credit for affected minutes = (affected minutes / total billing minutes) * monthly bill * 2% cap
Ok. Also add an operational guardrail: if warmup pattern persists after we enable sticky sessions, escalate to infra for deeper tracing.

Hey team — customer getting 400 on /v1/rerank and all scores return 0. They sent a payload with nested query fields, repro below. Can someone confirm whether nested 'query' or mixed 'documents' + 'candidates' can cause this?
paste the payload they sent pls

ah — two things: 1) rerank expects top-level 'query' as a string (not nested object or under docs metadata). If client sends {query: {q: ...}} validation can pass in some branches but scoring path will treat query as missing -> zeroed scores. 2) mixed shapes: if 'candidates' items don't use the expected text key (we expect text/content/title), they might be ignored.

+1. also we've seen requests with both 'documents' (with passages) and a separate 'candidates' array create ambiguity in the model selection path. The runtime will try to normalize shape but there's a previous bug where candidate text mapping falls back to empty string when nested keys like 'content' vs 'text' mismatch. That yields scores=0.

logged ingress validation for req id r-8a7c at 2024-12-05T14:22:11Z: "payload_shape: unexpected_object_for_query; candidate_text_missing -> normalized to empty". Linked PR: https://git.redwood/repo/pulls/3421 (patch to stricter validation + clearer error messages).

For longer-term: we should update docs to state precedence rules when both documents and candidates present, and add a stricter server-side validation error (400) that returns field path like "query" or "candidates[0].text" missing. Filed DOC-983.

Ask them to: 1) send original broken payload, capture request id, 2) send flattened payload, 3) include request ids + server logs (we can map). Mention payload size too — if their documents are large we hit truncation that can strip fields.

@customer_jordan thanks for the report — can you paste the exact timeline and any client logs? You mentioned duplicate billing and partial output on reconnect.
quick summary from my side: customer says they get a partial SSE payload, client reconnects, and then server generates the remainder but also replays earlier tokens -> duplicate billable tokens.
saw similar pattern in other threads but this one mentions auth rotation during the reconnect window which is interesting.

timeline: 2026-03-15 14:03 client starts stream (request_id=rx-47). It streams ~120 tokens then connection drops. Client automatically reconnects after 1s. We rotate auth token on our side (short-lived) right after drop. On reconnect we send last_event_id=evt-120 and request_id=rx-47. Server returned tokens 121..300 but also resent 1..120 partially, so we got duplicates and were billed twice. Logs attached (see snippet below).
can you attach the raw SSE fragments? Even a pasted excerpt helps.

pasted fragment below (redacted):
```
# client side excerpt
-> GET /v1/stream?model=redwood-xl&request_id=rx-47
SSE: id: evt-001
SSE: data: {"delta":"Hello"}
...
SSE: id: evt-120

dropped (tcp reset)
reconnect attempt 1s later
-> GET /v1/stream?model=redwood-xl&request_id=rx-47
Authorization: Bearer <new-short-token>

Last-Event-ID: evt-120
SSE: id: evt-001
SSE: data: {"delta":"Hello"}
...
SSE: id: evt-300
SSE: data: {"delta":"<end>"}
```

the fact we see evt-001..evt-120 again implies server resumed without verifying idempotency for the request_id or checking the resume window for the old session. Rotation of auth token could have forced creation of a new session on the backend while the client intended to resume old one.

probable root causes:
- resume token (Last-Event-ID) was honored but session mapping uses auth-subject+session-id; token rotation meant subject changed or session not found -> server created a fresh session that replayed from earliest buffer
- client reuses request_id but server doesn't enforce global dedupe across session handoffs
- billing increments occur when tokens are re-emitted, even if duplicates
customer asks for repro steps and a short-term mitigation.

Repro steps we tried locally (minimal):
1) Start a streaming request with request_id=R.
2) Let server stream ~N tokens.
3) Close connection (simulate TCP reset).
4) Rotate auth token on client and retry GET with same request_id and Last-Event-ID set to last seen event.
server resumed but replayed earlier events.

snippet of server-side log aligning to their timestamps:
```
[2026-03-15T14:04:21Z] stream-start request_id=rx-47 user=acct-99 session=ses-A
[2026-03-15T14:05:46Z] conn-closed session=ses-A reason=tcp-reset
[2026-03-15T14:05:47Z] auth-rotate acct-99 token=tok-rotated
[2026-03-15T14:05:48Z] stream-reconnect request_id=rx-47 user=acct-99 session=ses-B resume_from=evt-120
[2026-03-15T14:05:48Z] replaying buffer session=ses-B from=evt-001 count=300
```

note session changed from ses-A to ses-B despite same acct. That means session lookup failed during reconnect and we created a new session that pulled from persistent buffer or cache and served from earliest sequence.
is there a way to avoid being billed twice? We immediately paused ingestion on our side but charges already happened.

short-term workaround:
- If you can, upgrade client to include a unique idempotency-key header for the overall user-visible generation (not per-connection). If server sees same idempotency-key within 2 minutes, it should return cached output without recharging. We'll enable that on platform side as an emergency rule for affected customers.
- Increase client backoff to 500ms->2s to reduce race with auth rotation.

medium-term fixes we propose:
1) Enforce dedupe by idempotency-key across sessions for a configurable time window.
2) Make resume semantics strictly tied to a stable session identifier (sticky session id in a cookie or resume token that survives auth rotation) — if auth subject changes we should reject resume and return explicit 'resume_not_supported' so client can handle.
3) Only bill when an event reaches 'committed' state on server (i.e., after generation is finalized). For partial tokens, emit non-billable interim deltas until finalization to avoid double-charge on replay.
quick mitigation rolled out: adding a 60s grace dedupe where request_id or idempotency-key are checked across recent sessions. I'm starting the rollout to the customer region now.

Raising an escalation — enterprise customer (Acme Retail) reports repeated duplicate completions when their client tries to reconnect to our streaming endpoint after a network blip. They say sometimes they get partial output, then on reconnect they receive the remainder plus a full repeated completion. Billing complaint too: charged for tokens twice.
@Jordan can you paste the exact repro steps the customer used? also which SDK/version? :thinking_face:

Here's their simplified repro (copied from customer):
1) open SSE to /v1/streams?model=redwood-llama-13b, no idempotency header
2) receive a few "data:" events (partial chunks)
3) client disconnects (mobile on flaky cell)
4) client reconnects and re-issues same request
Result: sometimes they receive the remaining tokens (expected resume), other times they get a full new generation appended (duplicate).
SDK is their own JS client using EventSource polyfill. They didn't set any unique request id in headers.

Quick notes: current streaming implementation is best-effort resume for prefix cache if the reconnect arrives with a resume_token we issued. Otherwise we treat as a fresh request. We do not dedupe purely identical requests unless the client supplies an Idempotency-Key on the non-streaming call. Streaming behavior historically not covered.

Logs from the cluster for one of their reconnects:
```
[2026-05-01T18:20:11Z] conn_id=svc-22 stream_start req_id=abc123 socket=10.3.5.9
[2026-05-01T18:20:21Z] conn_id=svc-22 chunk seq=1 token_count=48
[2026-05-01T18:20:23Z] conn_id=svc-22 disconnect reason=network-reset
[2026-05-01T18:20:29Z] new_conn req_meta:(no idempotency, no resume_token)
[2026-05-01T18:20:30Z] new_conn matched model variant v1 -> spawn new generation req_id=def456
[2026-05-01T18:20:33Z] new_conn chunk seq=0 token_count=120 -> user sees duplicate
```

They also recorded the SSE frames; here's an example snippet they sent:
```

chunk
data: {"seq":1,"text":"The quick brown"}
So sometimes server resumes (gives seq 3 onwards) and sometimes restarts from seq 0. Makes sense based on logs.

Two different failure modes: 1) reconnect with resume_token -> server reattaches to existing generation and continues (idempotent resume); 2) reconnect without resume_token -> server starts a new generation. The customer expects resume semantics when they reconnect with the same request, but their client doesn't include any resume token or request id.

Customer expectation note: many mobile clients will automatically retry after a disconnect without preserving in-memory resume tokens. For UX we might need a client-driven recommended approach or server-side safeguards to avoid billing duplicates.
Customer asked: can we detect duplicates server-side and avoid charging twice? They want a fast patch or guide.

Short term mitigation: we can add a lightweight heuristics layer — when a new streaming request arrives from same API key within X seconds and the model/params/body match and we still have a warm generation in cache, we can return a resume_token hint and attach instead of starting a new generation. But edge cases: legitimate concurrent requests from same API key.

Implementation notes: we can match on a hash of request payload + model + streaming params + user_ip (optional) and check active generations that have not completed and whose last_emitted_seq < threshold. If match and client sends header X-Resume-Request: 1, we can attempt reattach. For dedupe/billing we should require a client-provided request id or Idempotency-Key for guaranteed semantics.

Customer reacted: they're not able to change client to persist resume tokens but can send an Idempotency-Key per logical user action (UUID) and include it on reconnect attempts. They asked whether Idempotency-Key will prevent duplicate billing for streaming reconnects.

Right now Idempotency-Key is enforced on non-streaming generate endpoints and dedupes replayed requests within 24h. We don't honour it for streaming reconnects today. We can extend server to index active stream requests by Idempotency-Key if provided in initial connect metadata. That would give strong dedupe semantics: if reconnect uses same Idempotency-Key, we attach/reject duplicate generation.
Can we do this fast? customer needs something within 48 hours ideally.

Quick patch plan (48h):
- accept Idempotency-Key and optional Resume-Token in stream connect headers
- on connect, check active_stream_index for matching Idempotency-Key -> if exists, reattach and respond with `event: resume_confirm` and last_seq
- if no match but resume_token present, try to reattach by token lookup
- otherwise start new generation as today
will add a new small in-memory index per region; memory bounded and TTL'd. Auditing/billing will mark tokens consumed by generation; if user reattaches we won't double-bill.

Also suggest we emit server-side event `event: dedupe_note` when we detect duplicate attempt so logs are clear. And add a billing flag so charge only when generation completes or when we confirm new generation started.

For the customer, recommended immediate workaround: have client send a short-lived Idempotency-Key for each user action (UUID) and include it on reconnect attempts. If they can't modify client, we can enable heuristics on their API key for a temporary window.
Action items: Jordan to communicate workaround + timeline. Engineering: Liam + Rebecca to own quick patch prototype. Emma to monitor billing impact. I'll schedule a follow-up in 24 hours.

quick q — adding IRSA for svcaccount `model-worker` in namespace `inference`. terraform created aws_kms_grant but pods still get `AccessDeniedException: Not authorized to perform: kms:Decrypt` when pulling model blobs. anyone seen this exact flow?
did you attach the role ARN to the grant principal or the assumed-role arn? common mixup. can you paste the grant + key policy?

looks superficially right. two gotchas: 1) IRSA roles are assumed, but the KMS grant principal should be the role ARN (that part you have). 2) Verify the actual runtime principal: when kube-auth calls sts:AssumeRole via OIDC, the session name may be the serviceaccount name and the principal that appears in CloudTrail for KMS might be `arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/si-IRSA-model-worker/<session>`. However grants keyed to the role ARN should still match.

also check ordering + terraform plan: if the role is created in the same apply as the grant, and the key policy is restrictive, the grant creation can succeed but not be effective until key policy allows kms:CreateGrant. quick fixes: add explicit `depends_on = [aws_iam_role.irsa_model_worker]` on the grant, or better, ensure the key policy allows the principal to use CreateGrant.

another edge case — if your pod uses encryption context (we do for per-model blobs) make sure the encrypt/decrypt call includes the same context key/values. KMS will deny if encryption context mismatches. do your storage fetch call logs show EncryptionContext mismatch?

logs show only "Not authorized to perform: kms:Decrypt" without explicit context mismatch message. i can add depends_on and try, but curious about provider alias cases: we use a `aws` provider and a `aws.eu` provider in the same TF project. the key was created with default provider but the grant resource accidentally used `provider = aws.eu`. could that cause an ARN mismatch?

oh yeah that will do it — provider alias can create resources in another partition/region/account context. check the ARN printed in plan vs the actual key ARN. if they differ, grants point at a different key/principal. run `terraform show -json` or just `terraform state show aws_kms_grant.model_worker_decrypt` to confirm the principal/target ARN.

here's a small checklist I use when IRSA + KMS fails:
- confirm role ARN in `aws_iam_role.irsa*.arn` matches the principal in the grant
- ensure `aws_kms_key` policy allows the role or a grant to be effective (include kms:CreateGrant if needed)
- add `depends_on` on grant for role creation when created together
- confirm no provider alias/account mismatch (region/account arns)
- check encryption context passed by the app
- if using session tags/conditions, make sure KeyPolicy condition keys allow sts:AssumeRole session names if you use them

small TF snippet that helped me (explicit principal as role ARN + depends_on):
```hcl
resource "aws_kms_grant" "model_worker_decrypt" {
  name               = "model-worker-decrypt"
  key_id             = aws_kms_key.models.id
  grantee_principal  = aws_iam_role.irsa_model_worker.arn
  operations         = ["Decrypt", "DescribeKey"]
  depends_on         = [aws_iam_role.irsa_model_worker, aws_iam_role_policy.irsa_assume_oidc]
}
```
solid. i ran `terraform apply` with depends_on and confirmed the grant now references the same ARN. also updated key policy to include `kms:CreateGrant` for the role. apply went green:
terraform apply complete. 3 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed. :rocket:
pods still got one failing task earlier but after restart the workers can decrypt and download models — looks resolved. thanks all :thumbsup:

v0.8.3 had a known preflight fanout behavior where parallel worker startups could trigger many simultaneous preflights and token refreshes. Two quick things: upgrade to v0.8.5 (hotfix) which adds randomized startup splay and token refresh coalescing, and as a workaround set the env var REDWOOD_SDK_PREFLIGHT_STAGGER_MS to something like "200-600" so the workers stagger.

Also ask Lexa to check NTP on hosts — those 401s look like JWT skew in the times I've seen. If their clocks are >30s off, tokens can fail then retry and cause a fanout. Also enable keepAlive on the node http agent to reduce connection churn; our gateway's per-connection rate accounting can amplify fanout when every worker opens fresh connections.

Are these requests coming from many ephemeral IPs (e.g., container scale-out across hosts)? If so, the per-IP rate heuristics might bite. If behind a NAT/proxy, tell them to reuse a connection pool or run a small shared sidecar to prewarm.

OK — two additional mitigations without an immediate SDK upgrade: (1) set `REDWOOD_PREFLIGHT_CONCURRENCY=2` to limit concurrent preflights per process, (2) keep `keepAlive: true` (good), and (3) if using http2, reduce streams per connection or fall back to http1 for preflight path. Heads-up: Windfall hitting lots of 429s during initial embed SDK ramp. They launch ~40 workers on tab open. Short log: 'preflight 429 rate_limited route=/v1/preflight region=eu-central-1'.

Okay — common pattern. Are they requesting a fresh ephemeral per worker?

Isolation is fine but creates a preflight stampede. Quick mitigation: (1) reuse ephemeral tokens for a short window (e.g., 15-30s), (2) enable sdk.preflightCoalesce flag, (3) add startup splay (100-600ms) and batch workers into groups of 4-8.
Also verify key scope. If they're using an restricted service key it may be on a tighter rate limiter. Confirm X-SDK-Version and X-Client-Region headers in traces.
Headers: X-SDK-Version: 0.8.0, X-Client-Region: eu-central-1. We'll try Tara's changes.

Quick smoke: switched to token reuse 20s, preflightCoalesce=true, splay 100-600ms, batched 8 at a time. Ran 200 concurrent warmup attempts: 2 preflight 429s (down from ~30). So much better.
For retries use exponential backoff with full jitter. Example: base=150ms, cap=5s, jitter=random(0, base*2**attempt). Also set client-side debounce on preflight to 500ms.

Heads-up — customer A reported sustained 1000rps fanout to their private cluster and hit a hard capacity ceiling. They saw 429s and big tail latency spikes. Any quick checklist we can hand them for client-side admission control?

short checklist: limit concurrency, add rate limiter (token-bucket), honor 429 + Retry-After, add random jitter to retries, surface a client-side queue depth cap. also suggest a soft-start when connecting to a fresh cluster.

+1. Also recommend client backpressure at two layers: per-connection concurrency and global per-client RPS. Small snippet we give customers: use leaky-bucket for RPS and a semaphore for in-flight tokens.

quick math for docs: if cluster has N GPUs and model peak throughput T tokens/s per GPU, and average tokens per request is L, then approximate requests/s capacity = floor((N * T) / L). Example: 8 GPUs * 2500 tok/s = 20000 tok/s; with L=200 tok => ~100 rps sustained. Add 30% headroom for bursts.
that formula is gold. Let's add a worked example and a config template customers can drop into their SDK.

propose we recommend these recommended client behaviors (short bullets):
- conservative default rates (10% of computed capacity) for first 5 min after deploy
- exponential backoff with cap and jitter on 429s (eg: base=100ms, max=10s)
- honor Retry-After header verbatim when present
- avoid tight synchronous loops that keep retrying on transient 502/503

draft YAML for SDK throttling (small, copyable):
```yaml
throttle:
token_bucket
1000        # tokens (roughly requests)
50    # tokens added per second

16  # max in-flight requests per process
retry:
true

true
```

quick heads-up — ran a KV cache hit-rate sweep on canary and results are kinda bad. overall prefix hit-rate ~12% (expected ~45%). attached sample of counts and a short profiler dump.

sample (top-1k prompts):
```
prefix,requests,hits,hit_rate
"support: reset password",1200,198,0.165
"compose: subject:" ,980,85,0.087
"summarize: doc:" ,720,40,0.056
"chat: system:" ,410,350,0.854
```

interestingly system prompts have high hit-rate but user-composed prefixes are all over the place. profiler shows a lot of wasted KV lookups + many small batches caused by kernel selection switching (small-seq vs long-seq) mid-request.
question: how much do we want SDK-level cache opt-in vs server-side heuristics? also streaming + retry behavior seems to be bypassing cache keys (client retries re-issue without cache header).

good catch. i think two separate problems: 1) cache keying granularity (we're including full metadata blob in key) -> explosion of keys, 2) client retries/streaming replays not preserving cache control.

for (1) we should normalize keys to canonicalized prefix tokens + model+truncate-length. drop session-id/user-agent noise. for (2) add a short-lived request-id header that the proxy uses to dedupe streaming retries, and ensure SDK preserves cache headers across reconnects. :+1:

agree w/ normalization. also batching: kernel selection toggles batches into different exec lanes which fragments KV warmup. propose batching heuristic: group by "cache-key-bucket" in scheduler before kernel-pick, then choose kernel per-bucket. that should increase warmup locality.
if mode is opt-in, server ignores cache headers unless backed by token-scoped permission. keeps default safe.

perf regression data from canary after kernel selection change (yesterday):
```
metric,baseline,canary,delta
90p_latency_ms,120,175,+46%
p95_latency_ms,200,315,+57%
tokens_per_second,4200,3200,-24%
kv_hit_rate,0.42,0.12,-71%
```
looks like the new kernel gating moves midsize requests to long-seq runner which has slower path for small batch sizes. plus cache fragmentation.

thanks. we should probably revert kernel gating to previous rule while we iterate on keying & scheduling. i'm worried about streaming edge-case where client reconnects cause duplicate partial streaming that bypasses cache - that makes warmup ineffective.

we can add a header `X-RW-Cache-Mode: opt-in|opt-out|inherit` and `X-RW-Cache-Key: <normalized>` to the API. proxy will honor header only if SDK-signed token present (prevents random clients from poisoning cache).

also propose a server-side warmup job that samples top-N prefixes per workspace and preloads KV for current model variant on boot — lazy but scheduled. simple cron: daily top-1000 per workspace. could be gated on dedicated customers.

small edge: streaming + chunked responses — if a stream starts and the client disconnects, we currently mark the request as failed and don't set cache entries. instead: if reconnect uses same request-id within 30s, treat as same request and only mark fill-to-cache once final chunk acknowledged. ops needs to audit cache semantics.

Agreed. Proposal: delegate tokens <= 60s TTL, introspect once then cache result keyed by token hash. Expire by TTL + small jitter. Negative (deny) results: cache for max 10s only.

Heads-up: customer BrightWave reports flaky 401s and bursty 429s after we onboarded their web widget. Shows in both staging and prod.
Any pattern? specific endpoints or client env?
Mostly POST /v1/generate and some embed calls. Happens when they open multiple tabs or load tests run.
I pulled their server logs. Lots of `401 unauthorized - key mismatch` but from the same client IP range, alternating between OK/401. Also a spike of retries leading to 429 from the edge.
Are they behind a sticky session/load balancer?
They are using a CDN with session affinity + an SSO cookie that BrightWave's infra rotates on login. They rotate keys every 6 hours.

Hypothesis: their CDN is caching an old signed cookie/session that references a previous API key; when requests hit a backend that has the rotated key state, token validation fails -> 401. Then the client retries concurrently (multiple tabs) causing request fanout -> 429.

That matches the logs: same user-agent, different backend instance IDs showing the mismatch.
Tom_infra: Actionable short-term: ask them to clear the CDN edge cache and force cookie re-issue. They can run this curl to validate the currently seen key against our validation endpoint:
```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $THE_KEY" https://api.redwood.inference/v1/keys/validate
```
It returns 200 + {"key_id":..., "valid": true} or 401.
Customer wants the smallest patch they can ship today — they'd rather not touch CDN rules. Any client-side mitigation?

Two quick client mitigations: 1) Add a short lived client-side check on SDK init to validate the token (call /v1/keys/validate once) and fallback to a light server-side proxy if invalid. 2) Add a per-session refresh mutex so only one tab refreshes/validates the token at a time (prevents stampede).
Also add jittered exponential backoff for retries. Example: `delay = base * (2 ** attempts) * (0.5 + Math.random()/2)` capped at 30s.

Medium-term infra fix: make key rotation atomic across their pool (rolling with sticky-cookie invalidation) or add a signed key version header so we can accept previous version for a short grace window. Filing infra recommendation ticket on their side.

Hi folks — onboarding hit a reproducible issue with our C++ SDK. We mint ephemeral mTLS certs (TTL ~10s) per worker. During warmup some streams get a 401 mid-call and then the workers rapidly retry which triggers 429s. Anyone seen short-lived certs + burst retries before?
sorry about that, Marco. Can you paste a minimal log snippet and explain how you refresh certs (per-worker vs central)?

sanitized logs:
```
[15:12:01] certs: GET /auth/cert -> 200 {cert_id: "c123", ttl: 10s}
[15:12:02] grpc: open stream -> 200
[15:12:04] grpc: chunk -> 401 {"error":"cert_invalid"}
[15:12:04] client: retry -> grpc open -> 429 {"error":"rate_limit"} x 8
```
we currently fetch cert per-worker at process start; workers reuse the same TLS socket for multiple streams.

two likely culprits: 1) connection-level auth binding — if the server binds the cert to the TCP/TLS handshake, rotating certs without resetting socket can cause mid-stream 401; 2) retry fanout — many workers retrying at once push you into the burst window.
we can also offer a temporary quota bump while you ramp to avoid noisy 429s. Want me to apply +4 rps for 24h?
yes please that would help for the staged rollout tomorrow. Also any jitter guidance for C++ worker pools?

add randomized startup jitter (0-500ms), and exponential backoff for retries with a small cap so retries don't align. On the server side we treat handshake + first request as part of initial cost accounting; spreading handshakes helps.
@olivia_cs increased tenant "orbit-labs" burst quota: +4 rps for 24 hours (change-id: Q-99811).
implemented singleflight and reduced init concurrency to 3, added 200-400ms jitter. After ~12 minutes 401s disappeared and 429s dropped to one-off retries. Huge improvement.
great — want me to add the mitigation steps to your onboarding playbook under "ephemeral mTLS patterns" and mark account status as "ramping - watch" for renewals?
yes please. We'll also document our cert issuer's cadence and follow-up with a short note.

follow-up action: we'll add a short C++ SDK note in docs about resetSocketOnRefresh and cert coalescing. Also opening an internal ticket to detect "cert-rotation mid-stream" and emit `x-cert-rotation:1` header when suspected.
infra follow-up: consider adding a server-side hint when connection-bound certs are rejected so clients can choose to reset connections instead of blind retries.

Note that rwd-embed-4k uses an attention kernel that is sensitive to batch aggregation. Large incoming batches of short sequences can cause the runtime's continuous batching to group a lot of inputs, increasing execution time and causing head-of-line blocking.

- route heavy batches to a reserved/dedicated pool (reservation)
