Heads-up — during onboarding of ropex-13b-q4 I see a deterministic divergence when prefill crosses 4096 tokens. Pattern looks like RoPE aliasing + stale KV snapshot. Repro steps below.
Can you paste the repro command?

Sure — quick smoke:
```bash
./smoke_run.sh --model ropex-13b-q4 --seq 8192 --prefill 4096 --batch 1 --kv-shard=round_robin --quant=int4
```
What does the diff look like? token-level or log-probs?

Token-level. At token index 4096 we flip from expected "the" to "a" repeatedly across seeds. Logs: "mismatch at 4096: expected=the got=a (p_expected=0.27 p_got=0.31)". Happens on both A100 and dedicated V100 cluster nodes.
Does it reproduce with float16 (no quant)?
No. FP16 run is clean. Seems tied to q4 path and KV snapshot alignment.
Could be prefill stride + shard boundary. Which prefill buffer policy?
Prefill uses contiguous write with stride=64. KV ringbuffer size 8192, we observed that after wrap the read index is off by 1 for some shards.
Any evidence of timestamp-like tokens or splices in the prompt that could shift RoPE phase?
Interesting — some test prompts include ISO timestamps and long numeric tokens around index 4000. But I reproduced with sanitized english-only prompts too, so not purely token content.
Can you try disabling shard round-robin (use single-shard) and re-run? If it's a shard reindex bug we'll see it vanish.
Running now. ETA ~6m.
smoke-run queued on pool-infer-3, job id 78422.
Also try running with --prefill 4095 and 4097 to check fencepost behavior.
Did 4095/4097. 4095 = clean, 4097 = fail. So fencepost at exact power-of-two-ish boundary (4096) seems critical.
Sounds like RoPE phase wrap/aliasing + KV read offset when prefill exactly equals half ring capacity. Can you dump KV index pointers before/after wrap? A minimal dump would help.

Pushed a lightweight dump to /tmp/ropex_debug/78422.kv_dump (first 128 entries of each shard). Example snippet:
```
shard0.ptr=4095, shard0.read=0, shard0.write=4096
shard1.ptr=4095, shard1.read=0, shard1.write=4096
```
Which is odd — write advanced but read pointer reset.
That suggests race between prefill teardown and in-flight read cursor update. Could be batching/callback ordering in qkernel.
If it's a timing race, quant code paths might reorder memcpy or memcpy size due to aligned 8-byte ops in q4. Try `--force-aligned-copy=false` in runtime flags.
Will test. Also trying FP16 with forced qk-copy ordering to see if behavior mimics q4.
job 78422 completed (exit 0) — logs: /artifacts/78422/logs.txt
Quick update — single-shard run removed divergence. Forcing unaligned copy also removed the failure. Repro points at q4+round_robin+prefill==4096+aligned-copies.
Nice find. Next steps: 1) write unit test for prefill boundary 2) add grosser sanity assert in kv layer to prevent read pointer reset on wrap 3) run canary with patch.
I'll open a PR with pointer-guard and a small fix to qkernel copy ordering (fallback to byte-copy when prefill%64==0).
Also add a regression test in the quant nightly suite for seq lengths [4095,4096,4097] across shards.

Anyone awake? We're seeing browsers get SSE events for ~180-300 tokens then the stream closes unexpectedly. This started after we rolled Envoy 1.28 at the edge. We proxy browser->HAProxy->Cloudflare->our Envoy->Redwood. Clients report duplicate tokens on reconnect and we're getting sudden billing spikes.

Here's an example server-side request to Redwood (we use HTTP/2 to the API):
```
curl -v --http2-prior-knowledge \
  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $KEY\" \
  -H \"Accept: text/event-stream\" \
  -H \"User-Agent: acme-proxy/2.0\" \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/responses -d '{"input":"please stream me many tokens"}'
```

Direct curl to api.redwood.ai from our CI (no Cloudflare/HAProxy) returns continuous SSE until completion. Full chain returns first ~220 tokens then our HAProxy logs show BUFFER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED and Envoy logs show upstream FIN then downstream RST_STREAM.

Attaching a small tcpdump snippet (timestamps relative):
```
1858012357 send chunk (token stream)
1858012360 upstream FIN from Envoy->Redwood path
1858012361 downstream RST_STREAM to client
```

Also notice when client reconnects we get a fresh billed request ID on Redwood (tokens counted twice). Can Redwood dedupe resumed requests? We're not intentionally reissuing same prompt, just reconnecting.

Sorry for the trouble. Quick answers: 1) We don't currently support transparent resume semantics server-side; each new connection is billed independently. 2) We can add more debug logging if you append `x-redwood-debug: true` to requests. 3) Did you confirm whether the intermediary rewrites `Transfer-Encoding` or adds `Content-Length`? That typically turns an otherwise streaming response into a buffered one.

We captured headers: at HAProxy exit we saw `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, but after Cloudflare it sometimes becomes `Content-Length: 912` mid-response. That forces buffering until complete and then a burst close. Some runs show Cloudflare rewriting when it detects many small flushes; other runs show HAProxy tripping a buffer limit.

@leo can you check if our runtime/ingress is emitting any abnormal window updates or resetting streams around that timeframe? If the runtime sends small, frequent frames and the gateway aggregates them, proxy buffer limits get hit. Also we need to search logs for `client_closed_request` or `RST_STREAM` for the incoming connection timestamps 1858012357-1858012400.

Noted. Envoy 1.28 introduced changes in the buffer filter and http2 flow control defaults; we've seen cases where intermediaries holding chunked responses until a content-length is computed cause early FIN/RST. Two likely failure modes: 1) proxy buffers until reaching its max buffer and then errors; 2) translator proxies (gRPC->HTTP1) set `content-length` incorrectly when trailers arrive and then close stream. Both result in abrupt client disconnects and duplicate reconnects.

Short-term mitigation for customers: 1) Ask them to use direct HTTP/2 to Redwood (bypass Cloudflare) or pin to our Dedicated peered endpoints for heavy streaming. 2) If they must go through proxies, suggest disabling proxy buffering and preserving `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` or end-to-end HTTP/2 prior knowledge. We can also provide a header `x-redwood-connection-id` as the first SSE event so clients can correlate reconnections and perform client-side dedupe for billing.

Client-side dedupe would help. But if the reconnect results in partial duplicate tokens mid-sentence, client-side heuristics may be tricky. Any plan from Redwood to avoid double-billing when reconnects are provably proxy-caused?

For billing we can entertain credits on a case-by-case basis if logs show proxy-induced disconnects. From a product perspective we could do a low-effort improvement: 1) emit `x-redwood-connection-id` (UUID) as the first SSE `event: meta` line, 2) accept `x-redwood-resume: <uuid>` header on reconnects within a short window (e.g., 30s) and mark duplicate tokens as non-billable in our accounting (soft dedupe). Full resume of generation state (KV cache) requires persistent generation sessions and is a larger feature.

Operational actions: 1) grep Envoy logs for that customer connection id and time range; 2) reproduce with Envoy 1.27 vs 1.28 to confirm regression; 3) check HAProxy buffer thresholds and Cloudflare streaming settings. If HAProxy shows BUFFER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, increase buffers or lower flush chunk sizes.
Could Redwood throttle or change chunking frequency server-side to avoid tripping intermediary buffers? If we flush smaller chunks more often maybe proxies won't accumulate large buffers.

We can ship an experiment flag to the runtime to increase flush frequency (`flush_interval_ms`/`frequent_flush` feature-flag) so tokens are emitted in smaller, more frequent frames. That might keep intermediaries from hitting their buffer high-water marks. Not a complete fix but could reduce incidents. I'll open a task and wire a feature-flag rollout.

I'll prototype the `x-redwood-connection-id` echo and have the API include `event: meta\ndata: {"connection_id":"<uuid>"}` as the first SSE chunk. That will let clients correlate and optionally pass `x-redwood-resume` on reconnect. We should document that resume is best-effort and not a real generation state resume.

Morning — noticed an uptick in SLA misses for first-owner contact overnight, looks like a cluster of micro-reassigns plus enrichment timeouts. p95 lead-handshake latency jumped and customer-facing SLA alerts tripped.
Yep. Found a pattern: enrichment p95 > 25s coincides with higher RR churn. We should avoid naive reassigns during noisy enrichment windows.

Instead of pure hold-or-fast paths, what if we introduce a sampling-based backstop policy: when enrichment p95 > threshold, we sample X% of leads into a backstop queue that gets special handling (sticky owner + rehydrate job) while others follow fast path?
Interesting. Sampling keeps load down but protects enough signals to measure impact. What thresholds and sample size?

Proposal: when region_enrichment_p95 > 25s, enable backstop sampling at 10%. For sampled leads: mark backstop=true, owner gets sticky_ttl += 1h, and assignment service will skip reassigns for backstop_duration = 7m. For non-sampled leads run normal hybrid assign.

Implementation sketch for HubSpot workflow (pseudo):
```
# HubSpot: set backstop marker based on feature gate + sampling
IF feature_flag('handoff_backstop') == true AND region_p95_enrich > 25s THEN
  IF random() < 0.10 THEN set lead.property 'backstop' = 'true' AND set 'backstop_until' = now + 7m
  ELSE set 'backstop' = 'false'
END
```

On the CRM write side add a backstop guard: don't overwrite owner if lead.backstop == true OR now < backstop_until. Also add idempotency_key = assignment.request_id to avoid duplicate writes from webhook retries.

Round-robin tuning: add per-lead cooldown (rr_cooldown=120s) and max_attempts=3 before escalating to backstop queue. Add jitter: cooldown += rand(0,30s). This should prevent cascades when retries line up.
Observability hooks: add metrics handoff.backstop_rate, handoff.sla_violation_pct, handoff.rr_cooldown_median, handoff.owner_churn_rate. Dashboards should show region breakdown.

Playbook for ops/SDR:
1) If handoff.backstop_rate > 15% or sla_violation_pct rises -> pause backstop sampling and run rehydrate pipeline.
2) If sample leads show improved stability -> increase sample to 25% and then consider wider guard.
3) For persistent noise, disable RR entirely for the region and route to manual triage.

Rollout plan: feature flag 'handoff_backstop' default=false. Canary to one EMEA region night window for 48h. Success criteria: owner_churn_rate down >= 40% AND sla_violation_pct down >= 30% without pushing response-time >10% for non-sampled leads.

Quick follow-up from RFC: instead of ad-hoc inline checks, propose a small AuthZ/Policy Facade that centralizes tenant policy, quota windows, and model access lists. Goal: accelerate policy changes and make audits straightforward.
Strong +1 on auditability. Two immediate constraints i see: (1) hotpath latency (generation p50 target < 18ms) and (2) policy datastore scale for >10k tenants.
For latency we can adopt a two-tier approach: local per-worker LRU cache + async refresh, with the facade returning `policy_version` and `lease_ms`. Worker uses lease to avoid thundering herds.
Thinking `lease_ms` default 250ms for token validity and 2000ms for route-level quotas. Workers can override via config per deployment class.

On datastore scale: we should shard policy store by tenant-hash and allow colocated read replicas. Facade will only serve policy read paths and push updates to replicas via changefeed. Writes (policy changes) go through control-plane service and update head.

We also need deterministic quota accounting. Shadow runs will be tricky since we can't double-count. During shadow mode, facade should include `shadow_token` in response and not increment real counters. After cutover, a replay job will reconcile shadowed events into authoritative counters with idempotency keys.
Agree on replay. Add a `replay_key` returned in shadow mode. Runtime should log requests with `replay_key` and `req_id`. We'll use that for a one-shot reconcile run.
Add alert: `authz.facade.latency_p95 > 50ms` and `policy.replay.failure_rate > 0.1%`. Also trace span `authz.check.local_cache_hit`.

Private deployment constraints: packaged helm chart + sidecar-only mode optional. Sidecar-only mode will expose `CheckLocal()` via unix-socket to avoid RPC hop. That mode requires local policy sync agent and may be recommended for high-QPS, low-latency installs.
Security: facade should accept signed control-plane JWTs for policy writes; runtime calls use short-lived mTLS tokens. For private installs, support HSM-backed signing.

Migration plan suggestion: 1) implement facade read-only endpoint and proto; 2) enable shadow calls (non-enforcing) from runtime with `X-Shadow-Mode: true`; 3) run shadow for 7d collecting diffs; 4) run replay to sanity-check accounting; 5) switch to enforcement in 1-2 regions; 6) global roll.
For performance spike validation, i'll run sims with 3 miss-rate profiles: 0.5%, 5%, 20% and measure end-to-end p50/p95. Will add a config knob to change local cache TTL dynamically.
Ownership: eng-runtime implements client cache + replay logging; eng-platform owns policy datastore and reconciliation jobs; infra owns helm packaging and sidecar image; ops owns runbooks and SLOs.
Protos: keep them tiny: `Check(req) => {allow, policy_version, lease_ms, shadow_key?}`. No model lists inline; instead return `policy_ref` and worker can fetch model list blob if needed (cached).
One more ops note: when facade responds with `allow=false` include `deny_code` (rate_limit|blocked_model|tenant_suspended) to simplify client metrics and incident analysis.
FYI: will add packaging ticket and chart template skeleton.

Likely cause: during a partial flush the KV cache had tokens X, then reconciling/compaction trimmed whitespace which changed tokenization, then the finalize path emitted a corrected final chunk. Short repro: spin up local SSE client, send generation, interrupt TCP after partial payload, then server finalize on cleanup. Example logs:
```
[13:42:05.112] send chunk id=42 tokens=420 payload="..."
[13:42:07.021] client FIN received -> connection closed by client
[13:42:07.150] finalize triggered -> emit chunk id=43 tokens=1300 payload="..."
[13:42:07.153] reconcile -> previous chunk 43 (optimistic 1500) still in aggregator -> both persisted to ledger
```

Repro steps I used: 1) start generate with SSE, 2) drop socket after first partial data frame, 3) call server-side cleanup which runs a tokenizer compaction pass and emits final chunk. That compaction can change token counts.

Proposed mitigation: billing should prefer the later finalize event but only if it shares an idempotency key or same chunk sequence. If sequences differ we need a policy: latest wins within 5s window for same session id, and mark earlier chunk as refunded in ledger.

Quick question — Acme hybrid setup: they bought Dedicated reserved capacity in us-west1 from us *and* have on-prem nodes in their NYC colo. How do we show pass-through on their monthly invoice for: GPU licensing (vendor license fees), cloud egress, and KMS? Do we pro-rate committed discounts, or is Dedicated treated as a fixed line?

Short answer: Dedicated reserved capacity = fixed committed fee we bill (monthly/annual commit). Pass-through applies to third-party bills we pay on behalf of the customer (e.g., if we run the customer's cloud account or if contract says pass-through). For on-prem vendor license invoices (eg NVidia/ISV) we usually pass-through if the SOW/PO calls it out. Otherwise we absorb/allocate under support. Need the SOW id to be sure. :clipboard:

From ops side — we can produce the usage export for both clouds + onprem agent. Example command for last month:
```
/opt/redwood/bin/usage-export --scope acme-corp --start 2026-02-01 --end 2026-02-28 --format csv > acme-202602-usage.csv
```
That CSV has GPU_hours, egress_gb, kms_calls per node/region.

We recommend invoicing pass-through as explicit line items. Formula we use:
```
GPU_license_pass = SUM(gpu_hours_customer) * LICENSE_RATE_PER_GPU_HOUR
Egress_pass = SUM(egress_gb_customer) * EGRESS_RATE_PER_GB
KMS_pass = (kms_api_calls / 1e6) * KMS_RATE_PER_1M
```

GPU hours=1,200 -> 1200 * $0.10 = $120. Egress=4,500 GB -> 4500 * $0.085 = $382.50.
NYC-Ops: A nuance on committed discounts — if the Dedicated commit is sold to the customer (they reserved capacity from us), we list it as a fixed committed capacity fee (no pro-rating of cloud provider discounts). Pro-rating only matters when we buy committed-use discounts from cloud provider and *we* are charging multiple customers from a pooled commitment — that model is rare and needs explicit contract terms.

Policy recap:
- If customer runs in their cloud account (we didn't pay provider) -> we don't pass through provider egress/KMS; they see their own bill.
- If Redwood provisions cloud resources under our account for a Private deployment and we pay the provider -> we pass-through cloud line-items (egress, network nat, KMS) if included in SOW/contract.
- Vendor license invoices (NVIDIA, ISV drivers) -> pass-through only if the contract states so; otherwise amortize into support/managed services.

Quick RFC: add a guarded header `X-Assert-Owner` to let clients explicitly state intended routing/tenant for tricky SA flows. Goal: predictable routing + auditable overrides.
Sounds similar to other header proposals but what's the differentiator?
Two differences: 1) header is strict-guarded by require_admin_ack flag per-org, 2) we always log a compact signed assertion blob so downstream audit is tamper-evident.
How would signed blob look? Example?
Example: `X-Assert-Owner: tenant=acme;sig=base64(hmac(key, tenant|ts))` — gateway verifies HMAC using key-specific secret stored in auth service. If signature invalid -> 403.
That prevents proxies from forging header. Nice. But key management complexity increases. Who issues the HMAC secret?
Auth service generates an ephemeral assertion-secret per-key when admin enables header for that key. Secret rotation via normal key rotation flows. We store only hashed secret server-side.

For billing we need to be deterministic. If header used, resolved_owner -> header value, billing_account still comes from key unless org opts in. Add `owner_resolved` and `owner_assertion_used` to exports.

Telemetry: metric labels `owner_source`= {claim, header_assertion, default} and `owner_assertion_verified` boolean. Also track `assertion_signature_failures`.	ram: Security question: what if an allowed key tries to assert a different tenant than it has rights to? We must enforce ACL: key-level allowed_owners list. Assertion only accepted if claimed owner in allowed_owners.
Exactly. Flow: gateway extracts header -> verifies signature -> checks allowed_owners -> record audit event -> attach routing metadata.
Note: create audit event type `owner_assertion` with payload `{key_id, asserted_owner, decision, request_id}`. Retain 180 days.
Console UX: per-key toggle "Allow asserted owner" with a one-click admin confirmation and link to audit log. Show last 30 asserted-owner attempts.

Rollout: start with assertion-audit-only mode (no routing) for 2 weeks to collect signal. Then gated canary (whitelisted orgs) with admin opt-in.	ram: Rate-limits: keep per-key hard limits, then coarse owner-tier shaping. Avoid exploding metric cardinality by bucketing owners into tiers in metrics.
Edge-case: internal infra that mints ephemeral tokens for other tenants. Ensure token exchange propagates allowed_owners claim and assertion-secret when appropriate.
CSV export will add fields `owner_resolved`, `owner_assertion` (true/false), `billing_account_used`. Finance needs a 30-day migration window.

Implementation tasks: gateway: parse header + verify HMAC, auth: manage assertion secrets + allowed_owners ACL, routing: use resolved owner for pool selection when enabled, quota: apply soft owner-level counters.
Also add server-side validation errors with clear codes: `owner_assertion.invalid_sig`, `owner_assertion.not_allowed`, `owner_assertion.missing_claim`.
SLO: auth path verification must remain <35ms p95 even with HMAC check. Add test harness.

hmm that's been longstanding. We collapsed soft vs hard into one metric to avoid lots of billing rule branches. Bad UX though.

Noticed a weird pattern after today's edge proxy push: a cluster of WS sessions in eu-central go into a short reconnect loop (~3 reconnects in <2s) then stabilize. Console shows a tiny latency bump but a big spike in reconnect events. Quota meters don't show proportionate token usage. Anyone seen this?
Which metric exactly? ws.session_reconnects or sse.resume_attempts? Our dashboards split WS vs SSE.
ws.session_reconnects. Query: `sum by (route) (rate(ws.session_reconnects[5m]))` on the live panel.

Could be our proxy's half-close handling. v2 proxy added aggressive socket close-on-auth which can cause client library to re-establish but keep sending the same resume token. That creates duplicate resume attempts logged as separate reconnects.
What's odd is the reconnects are stamped with the same resume_token in logs, but telemetry ingestion treats each connection handshake as a separate event because we include `conn_fd` in metric tags.
ah. So metric tag granularity mismatch between logs (resume_token) and metrics (conn_fd). That explains why billing (which uses token-level dedupe) isn't spiking.
Quick mitigation: change alert rule to use `billing.resume_successes` for the P1 alert to avoid noisy paging. I'll prepare a PR to swap the alert target.

Long-term fix: emit a `reconnect_id` computed as `hash(resume_token|client_ts_window)` and use that as a stable dedupe key for metrics. That way proxy restarts won't inflate counts. Concern: we need to ensure the hash space is large enough to avoid accidental collisions across high cardinality.
Also add `reconnect_phase` tag (handshake/kv-sync/auth) so we can filter out quick client-driven reconnects vs server-side retries. That will help dashboards and runbooks.
deploy-note: edge-proxy v2 rolled at 03:07 UTC to eu-central. rollout_id=rl-2026-03-23-09.
For console UX, product asks we don't flip the global "reconnect count" panel until dedupe is live. Instead create a new panel "reconnect_dedupe_v1" and mark it experimental.
Agree. I'll mute the existing alert and create a temp alert on `reconnect_dedupe_v1` with a higher threshold. Also add annotation to the chart about the proxy change.

Implementation sketch (python):
```python
# compute a stable reconnect id
import hashlib
key = f"{resume_token}|{int(client_ts/30)}"  # 30s bucketing
reconnect_id = hashlib.sha256(key.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
metrics.count('ws.reconnect', 1, tags={'reconnect_id': reconnect_id, 'phase': phase, 'region': region})
```

We'll need to change our hypertable indices to include reconnect_id; telemetry pipeline currently drops high-card tags. Need a migration plan to allow reconnect_id through for 48h sample. Filed infra ticket PLAT-4087.
For rollouts: feature flag `stable_reconnect_id` gated by region. Start eu-central 100% (since it was affected) and eu-west 0%, compare ratios for 6 hours.

One more gotcha: existing historical dashboards won't show the deduped counts. Console copy should explain: "new metric dedupes proxy-induced duplicates; historical numbers are not adjusted." Product will add a tooltip.

Quick RFC follow-up — proposing a small, explicit interface for tenant-level hedging + degrade contracts. want short feedback on tradeoffs and where it should live (admission vs router vs runtime).
Nice. Can you sketch the interface? Is this a per-tenant blob or a global policy with tenant weights?

Per-tenant blob is my leaning. Keeps routing simple: admission checks blob + usage and returns one of: admit / delay / degrade / reject. Minimal fields: min_qps, hedge_ratio, degrade_profile, failover_targets, grace_windows.
Curious about "degrade_profile" — is that model downgrade (smaller quant) or mode degrade (echo cached prefix)? Both?

Both. DegradeProfile should be able to express a prioritized list: model_variant + optional transform (cache, prefix, truncate output). Example:
```
If admission returns "delay" how long can router wait? we already do batching, but this introduces holding across services — complexity spike.

Good call. Intend to use only short windows for delay (100-200ms) and a token-based async queue for longer backpressure. Delay is for micro-hedging to allow autoscale/permits to arrive. Anything >200ms should be signaled as "queue" in the admission response and handled by a dedicated queue layer.

Who owns enforcement of degrade semantics? Router only understands variant name, runtime must enforce transforms (e.g., cached prefix). So interface must include transform hint and runtime capability list.
Edge case: what if a tenant's degrade profile references a variant not pinned by the customer? can we auto-fallback to nearest compatible model? that opens contract/consistency questions.
We should have two modes: "strict" (error if variant missing) and "best_effort" (pick best compatible). Tenant blob can set policy. Default to best_effort for PLG, strict for enterprise.

Agreed. Also want a small admission response shape so it's easy to implement across services. Proposal:
```
{
  decision: "admit|delay|queue|degrade|reject",
"model-identifier",
["prefix_cache","truncate"], // optional
150, // how long router may hold if "delay"
Telemetry needs: we should emit (tenant, decision, variant_requested, variant_served, latency_ms, reason) for every request. otherwise ops can't correlate SLO regressions after rollouts.
yes — add metric namespace: admission.decision.{admit,delay,queue,degrade,reject} with tags. Also sample logs for N=1% of requests include full policy blob.
Tradeoff: per-tenant blob allows rich configs but makes hot path check slightly heavier. Could we cache serialized compiled policy in admission service and only recompile on blob change?
plan: compile to a tiny decision table and cache + watch for blob updates via config-stream. This keeps runtime check O(1) and allows complex declarative policies offline.
Abuse vector: a tenant could stack many tiny requests to game hedging and degrade transitions. How do we prevent churn?

Rate-limit policy changes and add a short cooldown on degrade toggles (e.g., don't flip degrade/non-degrade more than once per 10s for a tenant). Also require rate-limited transitions in admission logic.
Ops question: how will this interact with the central quota service? admission needs current credit state. Do we call quota sync inline? adds latency.

Two options: inline check to quota (accurate but latency), or use cached tokens with occasional refresh (fast but eventual drift). For hedging we need up-to-date credit for high SLO tenants, so make it pluggable: enterprise tenants do inline check, default uses cached tokens with background reconciliation.
For audits, we must record the quota snapshot used for the decision. Even with cached tokens, write the token-window id in logs.

Implementation plan:
- Admission service: owns compiled contract blobs + decision API (lightweight).
- Router: asks admission, enforces TTL for delays, forwards variant.
- Runtime: enforces transforms, and exposes capability list.
- Quota: authoritative but with cached tokens for default tenants.
- Console: show effective contract + last 10 decisions for debugging.

Sketch of migration strategy: start with read-only contracts (interpret blobs but ignore non-strict fields), roll to small subset of PLG tenants flagged in account metadata, measure ops and latency. After 2 weeks, opt-in enterprise tenants with strict semantics.
One more thought — helper library for SDKs to surface degrade hints to developers so they can fallback gracefully. Not just platform-side.
Agree. Also need an abuse guard: if a tenant hits >X degrade decisions per minute, trigger automated probation (reduced hedge_ratio) and notify SE.

quick flag — dashboards are spiking when RBAC runs per-row. saw ~3x CPU on query-side and ~180-250ms extra latency per panel during peak; this is mostly on heavy tenant dashboards. thinking of an authz-sidecar that batches/checks a query shape and returns a compact allow-list + a version token, TTL ~5m. pros: avoids per-row calls and reduces DB auth pressure. cons: staleness on revokes, extra infra, cache invalidation complexity. thoughts? :thinking_face:
which dashboards/queries specifically? is this only aggregate panels or the table views too?

mainly aggregate panels and some timeseries joins. example: 2M rows scanned but RBAC predicate applied row-by-row in the query engine (we call authz per-row in the current path). rough numbers from last load test attached: max_cpu 78% -> 240% (virtual across query fleet), p95 panel latency from 420ms -> 650ms.

rough sketch of sidecar response (pseudo):
```json
{
  "query_shape_id": "q_abc123",
  "allow_list": ["tenant:123:metric:read","tenant:123:meta:read"],
  "version_token": "v1.2026-03-12T12:00Z",
  "ttl_seconds": 300
}
```

a couple things — how do you compute cache key? include subject_id + roles + query_shape_id? tenant isolation has to be strict. also size: allow_list for complex queries could be large and negate gains. any estimate on typical allow_list cardinality?

yes key = tenant_id + subject_roles_hash + query_shape_id. typical allow_list for dashboards we've seen is small (4-12 ACL entries) because panels mostly map to a handful of metrics/views. worst-case could be hundreds for ad-hoc tables though. we can cap response size and fall back to synchronous checks if >N entries.

operational concerns: invalidation is the killer. if an admin revokes a role, stale cache means a window of over-privilege. need strong invalidation: event-driven invalidation from IAM changes + a short TTL. also failure mode: if sidecar is down we must fail-safe (deny) or fall back to existing per-row checks? I lean fall back to per-row but with a circuit breaker so we don't regress fleet-wide.

we also need telemetry: cache hit rate, avg allow_list size, staleness windows (time between role-change event and eviction), and any auth-falls to per-row path. if we can't measure safety, don't ship.

we need to settle API resource shape for Dedicated staged rollouts. question: is rollout plan its own resource, or embedded under dedicated pool config?

+1. current draft in my branch is a top-level `DedicatedPoolRolloutPlan` with `pool_id` FK. endpoints like `/v1/dedicated-pool-rollout-plans/{plan_id}`. but I keep getting the "why not just stick it in pool config" question.
from Console POV, I’d *really* prefer it as its own resource. we need audit history + stage timeline + promotion actions without making pool update a giant god-object.
also determinism/auditability: promotion/abort are state machine transitions. treating as "update pool config" feels wrong (and makes idempotency messy).

routing layer cares about a stable pointer: pool -> active rollout plan -> current stage. if it’s embedded in pool config, every pool config write becomes a potential routing-affecting mutation. higher blast radius.
the argument for embedding is "single place to look" + backwards compatibility with existing pool update flows. but I agree, pool config is already overloaded.

here are the two options as I see them:
Option A (separate resource):
- GET `/v1/dedicated-pools/{pool_id}/rollout-plans` (list)
- POST `/v1/dedicated-pools/{pool_id}/rollout-plans` (create)
- POST `/v1/dedicated-pool-rollout-plans/{plan_id}:promote`
- POST `/v1/dedicated-pool-rollout-plans/{plan_id}:abort`
Option B (embedded):
- PATCH `/v1/dedicated-pools/{pool_id}` with `rollout_plan` subobject
- POST `/v1/dedicated-pools/{pool_id}:promoteRolloutStage` etc
RBAC is simpler with separate resource IMO. we can say: `dedicated.pool.read` vs `dedicated.rollout.manage`. embedding tends to leak manage permission into "pool admin" personas.
+1 to separate. we also need to handle multi-region pools where plan exists but region availability differs. would rather not couple that to base pool config semantics.

re: backward compat: if we embed it, we either:
1) add new fields on existing pool API responses (ok) but also
2) overload existing optimistic locking / etag behavior for pool updates
promotion is *not* a patch; it’s an action with preconditions + audit event. the plan being a resource is the canonical model.

we can do both:

- Console uses those to deep-link to plan view.

yes. pool response could include:
```json
{
  "id": "pool_123",
  "name": "lattice-prod-usw2",
  "active_rollout_plan_id": "rplan_456",
  "active_rollout_stage": "stage_10_percent",
  "rollout_state": "RUNNING"
}
```
(no embedding of full stage list)
routing wants exactly that. it can fetch plan details from control plane cache keyed by `active_rollout_plan_id`. avoids pulling giant pool payloads.
also security: full plan may include internal-only gate evidence links / override reasons. don’t want that accidentally exposed via pool read endpoints for customer admins.

ok but what about existing automation scripts that do pool updates for model version changes? they’ll ask "where do I set model version". if plan is separate, do they create a plan to change model version? or do we still support direct pool config changes?
we probably need both. direct pool updates remain (for non-staged changes), but staged rollout is the *recommended* mechanism and may be required behind flag for certain change types.
+1. control plane can enforce: if pool has `rollout_enforced=true` and change touches model/runtime/routing policy, reject PATCH pool and require a rollout plan.
that’s consistent with UX too. pool config page can show banner: "Changes to model/runtime require staged rollout".
if we embed, we risk accidental "partial updates" where some clients PATCH pool and unintentionally clobber rollout fields (or vice versa). separate resource prevents config drift.
agreed. last question: path shape: do we want nested under pool, or purely top-level?

- convenience: `/v1/dedicated-pools/{pool_id}/rollout-plans` (server just filters by pool_id)

FYI were seeing a class of provisional-overcount spikes tied to short-lived route handoffs + toolcall latency. Canary orgs flagged this morning.
example trace?

pasted a trimmed router trace:
```
SESSION=xyz789 region=eu-west start=1610001000
client connects -> stream opens
seq=40 toolcall starts (external fetch) provisional_tokens=90 written by worker-7
client disconnects (TCP reset) at seq=41
router assigns session to worker-12, worker-12 resumes and writes provisional_tokens=90 for the continuing seq range
confirm path eventually records a single confirmed 90, but provisional totals retained both writes => console provisional=180
```
so the ledger confirm dedupes but provisional index keeps both.
how are provisional records keyed today? session+seq_range only?
yes; theres no writer UUID in the provisional row. If two workers race they both insert overlapping provisional ranges.
ownership race. Worker A writes provisional then dies. Worker B resumes and reasonably writes provisional because it lacks visibility into As failed heartbeat.
is this correlated with toolcalls specifically?
most spikes involve toolcalls because toolcalls extend the server-side response window and increase chance of disconnect mid-call.
short-term mitigation: hide provisional totals when we detect overlapping provisional ranges for a session and show "estimating". But thats just UX; root cause remains.

longer-term: add a provisional_uuid emitted at write time and an async metric event. Then we can dedupe provisional rows by uuid at reconcile. We can also sprinkle worker_id and lease_id to telemetry to identify handoffs.

sounds reasonable. What about a read-lease approach where a worker acquires seq-range lease; if another worker tries to write overlapping provisional it must check active lease and fail-over semantics?
that requires a consistent lease store (redis/etcd) and careful latency budget. Could be toggled behind feature flag.

I want an actionable telemetry plan before we add cross-shard indexes: 1) emit provisional_uuid, writer_worker, lease_ttl as an event 2) surface a new Grafana panel "provisional_dupe_rate" per-org 3) alert if >10% for an org for 30m
sampling: enable full telemetry for 0.5% orgs initially.

implementation steps I propose: A) quick PR: include provisional_uuid in metering write and emit metric event (cheap), B) console change: show tooltip and mark sessions with overlap flag, C) rollout sampling and collect 2 weeks of data.

UX: console should avoid alarming language. Tooltip copy: "Provisional tokens are an operational estimate and may include transient duplicates during route handoffs. Final billed tokens reflect confirmed ledger entries." Add link to docs.
ledger change needs to keep audit trail. If we dedupe provisionals later we should mark them as "deduped" with pointer to canonical provisional_uuid rather than delete.
agree. Reconcile algorithm: at confirm time check for earlier provisional_uuid(s) that overlap seq_range -> accept earliest as canonical, mark others deduped. Simple and preserves rows.

sketching a lease-based guard too: when writing provisional set lease in redis with seq range key, TTL equals expected toolcall window + grace. Resuming worker will attempt to adopt lease via compare-and-swap. If lease expired or missing, it can write provisional; if lease exists pointing to dead worker, we merge instead of writing duplicate.
concerns: redis outage could block provisional writes -> need fallback to optimistic writes. Feature flag again.
product notes: clarify console estimates vs billed, add a short banner when canary sampling enabled so customers know they may see provisional noise.

Heads-up — we've got a Private customer (EU fin-reg) who says their on-prem boxes block all outbound traffic except to a small allowlist. They want Redwood's control plane to never route traffic outside their permitted regions. Can we model this in routing policies?
+1. We already have region-based routing, but this is more strict: control-plane must enforce egress-allowed list per org and never fall back to a different region model implicitly.

Two constraints I see: 1) control-plane decisions (routing selection) may require connectivity to model stores/kernels in other regions for fallback — that's unacceptable. 2) telemetry/usage reporting needs a path — if they block telemetry we still need billing/quotas enforced.

For telemetry we could support a push-gateway model: customer ships a relay in their VPC that accepts signed telemetry and forwards to Redwood over an approved egress. That keeps data plane inside their network except for the minimal audit bundle.

Proposal: add org-level field: `egress_guardrails.allowed_regions` and `egress_guardrails.block_variant_fallback_outside_regions = true`. Control plane rejects any route that violates this. If no compatible route exists, fail fast with 409 and clear error describing allowed variants.

UX change in Console/Routes: show a prominent banner on rollout config: "this org enforces egress guardrails — only region X,Y allowed — fallback outside will be blocked". Also add a per-route preview that simulates whether a canary roll will violate guardrails.

We also need an internal API contract change: /route/evaluate should accept optional `org_id` and `vpc_profile` flags and return `route_candidates` with `egress_region` and `requires_control_plane_egress: bool`.

Example response sketch: ```{ "route_candidates": [ {"model":"rwd-3-small-eu","egress_region":"eu-west-1","requires_control_plane_egress":false}, {"model":"rwd-3-generic","egress_region":"us-west-2","requires_control_plane_egress":true} ] }``` But for this org the second candidate must be filtered out server-side.

On the fallback strategy: if no same-region variant exists, we should either (A) fall back to a quantized on-prem friendly variant that customers can preload (requires provisioning path), or (B) return an explicit failure to the caller. My vote: default to B, with an opt-in preload for A.
Agree. Preload option needs ops flow: package + signed manifest, and we should add an entry in Console under Private > Model Assets to upload/approve.

Quotas/usage implications: If we can't route to hosted models and the customer uses preloaded variant, usage should be billed at reserved-capacity API metrics, not hosted usage. We should tag telemetry differently: `billing_source = onprem-preloaded` vs `billing_source = hosted`.

Rollout UX: When creating a rollout you can select "respect org egress policy" checkbox (default on for Private orgs). If a stage would hit a non-compliant route, show red state and block canary promotion.

Heads-up: Support called about a customer seeing many small token charges yesterday evening. Traces point to a burst of WS reconnects that each appear to bill ~10-30 tokens.
Any pattern in client or SDK?

Two interesting signals: 1) all affected clients use `rdw-sdk-js` v1.4.x, 2) reconnects show identical resume_id but different `seq` numbers. Example: ```text
trace=tx99 resume=R-77 seq=102 billed=12 upstream=a
trace=tx99 resume=R-77 seq=103 billed=15 upstream=b
```
That suggests resume succeeded and continued on new shard (seq advanced) but meter considered them separate sessions because we dedupe on resume_id only and we tag by route.
Console aggregated by route so it looked like two sessions. Also noticed telemetry sampling was higher for reconnect events, which skewed UI percentages.
Also saw two SDK variants: older SDK retries immediately after networkidle, newer SDK waits for PONG timeout before reconnect. Mixed fleet yields overlaps and both shards accept resume.
Could we use the `seq` field to detect continued stream vs duplicate resume? If seq increases monotonically we should NOT count it as a new billing resume.

Good idea. Proposal: meter dedupe key = hash(account + resume_id + floor(seq/10)) so small seq advances within same 10-event bucket are considered same session. TTL 20s. That avoids counting a continuing stream as duplicate while still deduping rapid duplicate resumes with same seq.

Edge-case: some legitimate reconnects will resume at same seq if client replayed. floor(seq/10) might hide true duplicates. Maybe use last_seen_seq per-resume and only dedupe if new seq <= last_seen_seq + 1?

Simpler: store last_seen_seq (int) in meter memstore, if incoming seq <= last_seen_seq then treat as duplicate and drop billing; if seq > last_seen_seq then accept and update. That seems intuitive. TTL 30s.
Implementation note: per-metric-shard memstore for speed, fallback to redis for cross-worker check on miss. Feature flag `meter_resume_seq_guard`. Low-latency path must remain fast.

UX/Console: add a tooltip on per-route billing that explains "small reconnect charges may be de-duplicated by seq guard" and show a short rollout banner when feature is active. Also add a panel: `duplicate_resume_by_seq_rate` by account.
Suggested PromQL: `sum by (account)(rate(resume_reconnects_total[5m]) - rate(resume_seq_advance_total[5m]))` -> indicates reconnects not accompanied by seq advance.
If duplicate billing is confirmed, we should auto-credit obvious windows. How do we detect those?

Use a heuristic: for an account, find short windows (<=60s) where billed_tokens spikes and >80% of reconnects for that window are marked duplicate by seq-guard (post-hoc). Flag for manual review and auto-credit if >1000 tokens.

Need to nail down HOLD semantics for Dedicated staged rollouts before we lock the state machine. Questions:
1) what does hold *actually* freeze (routing? gate eval? auto-promote/auto-abort?)
2) do we auto-timeout holds?
3) what does “resume” do to gate windows / samples?
+1. Control plane wise we can represent `state=HELD` with metadata (who/when/reason). But we need deterministic behavior across policy engine + routing.
From SRE side: hold should mean “stop changing things” BUT we still need an escape hatch if the canary is melting prod. I’m worried about a hold blocking auto-abort.

Current implementation sketch (not merged yet):
- routing stays pinned to current stage partition while held
- controller stops promotions
- gate evaluator still computes pass/fail/unknown
But unclear whether we *act* on failures while held.
My preference: HOLD freezes *actions* from the controller (no promote, no abort, no auto-rollback). We still evaluate gates to show evidence in Console.
If we freeze abort as well, we need a clear “you’re holding a failing rollout” behavior. Otherwise we’ll see “held” used as an excuse to let a bad build linger.

Can we define two concepts?
- HOLD: operator initiated, pauses automation
- SAFETY ABORT: independent kill-switch if safety gates are in “critical fail”
I don’t want hold to override safety.
I can live with that if it’s tightly scoped and deterministic. Like only gates tagged `safety=true` can fire while held.

FWIW, if telemetry is the reason for HOLD (lag/outage), safety abort based on the same telemetry signals won’t help. But for stuff like 429 spikes / request drops from the router, those are near-real-time.
UX question: do we show “Held (Safety monitoring still active)”? Otherwise customers assume nothing can happen.
Also RBAC: who can put a rollout on hold vs resume vs force-abort? We’ll need to align with the admin guardrails work.

Proposing concrete semantics:
- Manual HOLD transitions `RUNNING -> HELD`.
- While HELD:
  - routing stays as-is (keep stage traffic split / partition selection frozen)
  - NO auto-promote
  - NO auto-rollback/abort *except* Safety Abort gates
  - gate evaluation continues and is displayed (pass/fail/unknown)
- Safety Abort: if any `safety=true` gate is failing for >X mins, we can `HELD -> ABORTED` automatically.
Thoughts?
+1. Safety gates should include things like error rate, 429/drop, OOM crashloop, saturation/headroom. Latency p99 alone maybe not safety unless extreme.

We should define “critical fail” precisely or we’ll get inconsistent behavior.
Maybe:
- safety gate has `severity=critical` and `min_duration` (e.g., 10m)
- on critical fail, action is `auto_abort` even during hold
Everything else is “informational” during hold.

Works for control plane. We can store per-gate config already. Something like:
- `gates[].mode = {blocking|informational}`
- `gates[].safety_abort_enabled = true/false`
Then hold checks `safety_abort_enabled` gates only.
Keep MVP simpler: one boolean flag per gate: `safety=true`. Default safety gates for Dedicated should be limited set. Paula is doing thresholds but we can define the behavior.
Console: when held, the promote button should be disabled and replaced w/ “Resume rollout”. Also show “Hold reason” and “Held by” + “hold expires” if we implement timeouts.
Let’s talk timeouts. I think we need them. People will hold and forget.

Control plane can support `hold_until` (timestamp). But what is the system behavior at expiration?
- auto-resume?
- auto-abort?
- just alert?

NOT auto-resume. That’s a change-management nightmare. Also auto-resume could re-trigger automation during an incident.
I’d rather: hold expires => we *auto-abort* (rollback to previous stable stage) unless explicitly extended.
That’s going to surprise people if they just wanted to pause overnight.

Alternative: hold expires => move to “HELD_EXPIRED” and keep frozen but page the right oncall.
But that’s also messy.

We need something that’s safe by default and easy to explain.
How about:
- HOLD always requires explicit RESUME. No auto-resume.
- `hold_until` is an SLA/guardrail.
- On expiration:
  - if rollout is currently on a non-100% stage (i.e. still partial) => auto-abort/rollback to previous stable stage
  - if rollout is already at 100% stage (rare to hold there) => do nothing, just alert
This avoids leaving partial partitions around forever.
That’s aligned with capacity fragmentation concerns. A held 10% stage is basically reserving a split indefinitely.
We can implement “partial stage” check as `current_stage_index < final_stage_index`. Auto-abort can revert routing to previous stage partition (or “baseline config”), per rollback ADR.
What’s default `hold_until` duration?
For SRE, 2h is too short. I’d say 24h default, max 72h. We can extend explicitly.
UX wise: default 24h is fine as long as it’s visible and extendable.
Telemetry outages sometimes last 30–60m. 24h seems safe.

RBAC proposal:
- `rollouts.hold`: Dedicated Operator + Redwood SRE + Customer Admin (if we allow customer-initiated holds)
- `rollouts.resume`: same
- `rollouts.extend_hold`: same
- `rollouts.force_abort`: Redwood SRE + Dedicated Operator (customer admin maybe no, depends)
We should at least ensure hold/resume events are audited with reason.

Resume semantics: on resume, do we restart gate evaluation windows? I’d say YES. Otherwise you can “hold” for 3h and then resume and immediately get a stale “pass” computed over a window that included pre-hold.
Agree. Gate evaluator can treat `resume_at` as a new “stage epoch” boundary.
Implementation detail: we already have `stage_entered_at`. If we resume without changing stage, we can set `stage_epoch++` / `stage_entered_at = now` even though stage index doesn’t change.
Also minimum sample size: reset on resume too.
Console messaging: “Resuming will restart gate evaluation timers for the current stage.”

Summarizing decisions (unless objections):
1) HOLD freezes routing config at the current stage (no traffic split changes).
2) While HELD:
   - auto-promote disabled
   - gate evaluation continues for visibility
   - auto-abort disabled except for safety gates (`safety=true`) that are in critical fail for configured duration
3) HOLD has `hold_until` with default 24h. No auto-resume.
4) If `hold_until` expires while rollout is not at final stage => auto-abort/rollback to previous stable stage + page/alert.
5) RESUME requires explicit action and resets gate evaluation windows + min sample counters for the current stage (new epoch).
6) All hold/resume/auto-timeout actions must emit audit events w/ actor + reason.
Looks good. I’ll update the policy engine behavior doc + add “stage epoch on resume” to the evaluator.
I’ll capture this in the control plane API notes + state machine comment. Benji can implement `hold_until` + expiry worker.

ack. I’ll wire up:
- state transition validation (can only hold from RUNNING)
- expiry job => ABORT with reason “hold_timeout”
- new audit event types: rollout.held, rollout.resumed, rollout.hold_timeout_aborted
Please ping me when you have the exact audit payload shape; I want `reason` mandatory and `hold_until` included.
Also please make sure auto-abort on hold-timeout routes to oncall in alerting. I’ll add runbook steps for “held expired / timeout abort”.

Following up on the iterator/paging RFC — quick proposal: standardize on a single opaque `resume_token` (string) that servers emit in page/frame footers, and have small SDK helpers to surface it. Keep transports (gRPC stream vs HTTP chunking) hidden. Thoughts?
+1 to opaque token. Simpler for users and avoids leaking transport details.
Concern: semantics for token validity and retries. If a client retries and then resumes, do we guarantee token stability? Is token tied to a time window?

My vote: server guarantees token identifies a stable checkpoint; tokens may be short-lived. Proposal: default validity ~30s, configurable per model/route. Clients must handle `resume` failures (retry/backoff).

For SDK surfaces we should follow language idioms. Ideas: Python — provide a small Handle object so iterator yields `(item, handle)` where `handle.token` and `handle.resume()` are available. TS — return an `AsyncIterable` that yields items and expose `meta` on the final frame. Go — return `(item, token, err)` from `Next()`.

Sketches:
```
# python
for item, h in client.iter_responses(prompt):
    ...
# h.token or h.resume()
```
```ts
// ts
for await (const item of client.responsesStream({resumeToken})){ ... }
```
```go
// go
it.Next() -> (item, resumeToken, err)
```
small nit: global helpers like `client.last_resume_token()` are racy if the same client is used concurrently. Prefer explicit handle/token returned alongside progress.

Agreed. For Go the token-as-return value fits well; for Python, the `Handle` object avoids races and stays ergonomic for `for` loops. In TS, we can provide a small `Cursor` object returned from a separate `getCursor()` call or include the token in a trailing frame.

On transport fallback: server should emit the same opaque token whether it uses streaming gRPC or chunked HTTP/SSE. That ensures client code doesn't have to change when we add fallback. Also require `Idempotency-Key` header for resumable requests so proxies and load-balancers can dedupe.

Retry behavior: if resume fails (token expired or mismatch), client fallback options: 1) exponential backoff + reattempt resume, 2) if still failing, restart from last known safe page (server can accept `start_after` anchors), 3) as last resort, full restart. Document recommended pattern.

Decision proposal (summary):
- Keep `resume_token` opaque string returned in every page/frame.
- SDKs expose token in-page and provide a small Handle helper in Python/TS with `.token` and `.resume()` convenience. Go returns token explicitly from `Next()`.
- Do NOT provide a global `last_resume_token()` on client instances.
- Require `Idempotency-Key` header for resumable streams; server will use it for dedupe.
- Default token validity = 30s (server-configurable); clients must handle resume failures.
- Do not expose internal token format or parsing.

quick Q — I'm updating the payments helm chart to pull DB creds from k8s secrets. Should we: use a values.yaml field that points to a secret name and then use valueFrom/secretKeyRef in the Deployment, or wire it via ExternalSecrets/ExternalSecret CRD? We're also provisioning the secret via Terraform -> sealed-secrets in CI.

i'd go ExternalSecrets if you can — keeps the secret lifecycle out of helm. helm should only reference the secret name. avoids templating secrets into releases. also easier to rotate without helm rollouts.

fwiw if you do keep it in helm, don't render secret values in templates. only reference name/key. example snippet:
```yaml
# values.yaml
secrets:
  dbSecretName: "payments-db-{{ .Release.Namespace }}"
# deployment.yaml (template)
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
{{ .Values.secrets.dbSecretName | quote }}

password
```
If you need release interpolation for values from values.yaml, use `tpl` around the string: `{{ tpl .Values.secrets.dbSecretName . }}` — common gotcha.

yes — ExternalSecrets operator needs permissions to read from the secret provider (or the provider controller). Also the ExternalSecret CRD will create a k8s Secret, so the operator's SA needs create/update secrets in the target namespace. Add a ClusterRoleBinding or namespace-scoped Role depending on how you run it.

quick checklist before maya makes the change: 1) ensure TF CI writes sealedsecret into target namespace (we already do this for staging). 2) if moving to ExternalSecrets, update TF to provision the provider creds in a secure store (don't bake into helm). 3) add unit in chart docs on secretName vs ExternalSecret. 4) ping me or @jonathan for TF plan review.

Quick heads-up — I ran into a weird SDK vs REST behavior for /v1/generate when optional kwargs are omitted vs set to null. Can we sanity-check? :eyes:
Repro or example? I can take a look after standup.

Repro (short):
- REST curl: `curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" -d '{\"prompt\":\"hey\",\"stop\":null}'` -> server treats this as explicit null (clears any default stop handling).
- Python SDK (v0.12) when user omits `stop` it omits the field entirely. But when user passes `stop=None` the SDK serializes \"stop\": null. TS SDK (v1.4) docs suggest `stop` is optional and will be omitted if undefined.
So the discrepancy is: Python SDK allows `stop=None` -> null, while REST expects omission for default. That can surface as different behavior for older clients that do `stop=None` in their wrappers.
Yep — historically REST treats null and missing differently (null overrides). We should standardize: SDKs should omit keys for None/undefined unless param explicitly meant to accept null.

Proposed action:
1) Update Python SDK serializer to omit None for optional generation params (stop, temperature, max_tokens) unless user passes sentinel `ExplicitNull()` or similar.
2) Add a compatibility note in changelog and a deprecation warning for callers relying on `stop=None` semantics.
3) Add a small server-side tolerant fix: treat `stop: null` as missing for one release window to avoid breaking client code.
Sounds reasonable. Quick question — are there any params where null is a meaningful value server-side? E.g., `metadata: null`?
Good catch. A few endpoints accept `metadata` where null should clear keys. For generate params we don't expect null to be meaningful. We'll whitelist by param name.
Can you paste the Python snippet that causes null emission? Might be in our marshaling util.

Sure, current behavior:```python
payload = {
  \"prompt\": prompt,
  \"stop\": stop,  # stop is None by default
}
# we do json.dumps(payload) directly which keeps stop: null
```
We should run a small helper like: `payload = {k: v for k, v in payload.items() if v is not None}`
If we do that, ensure we don't strip empty lists for params where empty list matters (some callers rely on `stop: []`). Add tests.

quick q: do we change public signatures? i want minimal churn.
public signatures stay. idea: transport adapters opt-in via a prefetch handshake + session window. SDKs expose zero new args by default.
need explicit rules for cancellation and dedupe across fallback transports. also how retries map to idempotency.
propose a small classification adapters advertise: "atomicity" ∈ {resumable, idempotent, non_resumable}. resumable -> safe prefetch; non_resumable -> no prefetch.

backpressure: consumer might be slow. plan: coordinator grants tokens per-session. token-bucket semantics: tokens consumed for prefetch, refilled as consumer advances. adapters must stop when tokens=0.
billing/quota question: do reserved prefetched pages count toward quota immediately? ops will yell if unexpected charges.
keep reservations soft: increment reserved_slots metric but only bill when page materializes and is returned. if eviction occurs, no charge. document in console.
need metrics: reserved_slots, consumed_pages, dropped_prefetch, prefetch_retries. admin trace endpoint would help.

dedupe rule: any returned item must include resume_token with epoch+checksum. if transport returns a token that coordinator already saw, drop silently and release reservation. monotonic fallback guaranteed.

retries: single logical RetryConfig per call. Prefetch follows same policy but adapters can cap prefetch_attempts (e.g. max 5). prefetch errors should not block current page; surface when user advances.
UX opt: add disable_client_prefetch flag (rename from explicit_resume_only). default false for hosted, but default prefetch small (1) for hosted, higher for Dedicated.
private deployments: offer opt-in durable reservations (write-through) for auditability; default ephemeral reservations to avoid control-plane load. mark in RFC.
operational safety: prefetch backoff should be slightly more conservative than on-demand fetches to avoid aggressive fanout on fallback; add jitter and max_attempts_for_prefetch.
also ensure context cancellation in go is honored by prefetch hooks and background retries stop quickly on ctx.Done().

Heads-up — we've got a reproducible double-charge case for customers using the multiplexed streaming client (multiple logical streams over one socket). Repro: start two substreams A & B, A finishes, B reconnects after a transient and retries; billing shows tokens for overlap charged twice. Logs attached: `session=abcd1234 sub=1 chunk=42 ack=...` :eyes:
Can you paste the minimal client/server exchange? Is client sending an idempotency token per chunk?

Client only sends `x-session-id: abcd1234`. We don't have a distinct `substream-id` in the ledger keys. Payload has `substream_index=1` but server ledger key uses session only. So when B reconnects we create a provisional charge which later becomes confirmed while the original session owner ledger entry remains — effectively double charge.
That matches a hypothesis I had. Two quick Qs: 1) Is this strictly a multiplexing-only issue (separate TCP connections don't hit this)? 2) How frequent is it in prod?

Verified it's multiplexing-specific. Frequency: ~1% of multiplexed sessions in canary logs, hit in 3 paying customers so far. Sample log: ```INFO stream.recv session=abcd1234 sub=2 chunk=55 retry=true provisional_tokens=12 confirmed_tokens=12```

Proposed fix: include `substream-id` in the ledger key (ledger_key = session_id|substream_id|chunk_seq). Pros: straightforward reconciliation per-logical-stream and prevents cross-substream dupes. Cons: increases cardinality in ledgers/metrics and needs a migration plan for old entries.

Alternative: keep session-only ledger but require an `idempotency-token` per chunk that server uses to de-duplicate across reconnects and map token->owner. That reduces ledger cardinality but adds lookup/state and might be heavier on the hot path.

From a telemetry/UX perspective we need visibility BEFORE rollout. Console currently aggregates by session/customer. We should add a "streaming: per-substream provisional vs confirmed" panel and a simple query: `sum(provisional_tokens)-sum(confirmed_tokens) by substream_id` to catch regressions. Also display the ratio of reconnections that produced provisional-only tokens.

Quick sync — I sketched a deterministic sort we can apply at gateway selection so route pick is stable across instances. Thoughts?
Nice, do you mean instead of random tie-break or creation-time? :thinking_face:

Exactly. Random breaks cache locality. Proposal: compute a sort key tuple per route and pick the highest lexicographically. Key components: (match_specificity, exact_segment_count, header_match_count, host_wildcard_score, negative_matches_penalty, route_id_hash)
Can you show a small example of how specificity is computed?

Sure — rough rules:
```
match_specificity = sum(segment_score for each path segment)

exact=100, param=30, wildcard=10, regex=50
example: /users/:id/profile -> 100 + 30 + 100 = 230
```
Then tie-breakers: more exact segments wins; more header constraints wins; fewer negative matches wins. Finally stable hash of route id as last tiebreaker.
I like making it deterministic. Two questions: 1) how do we rank host globs vs explicit host? 2) what about performance for large rule sets?

For host: explicit host gets high host_score (200), single-star gets 50, multi-glob gets 20. For performance: precompute the sort_key at config load and store as 64-bit tuple; selection is then a single compare op.
What about regex routes that are more expressive but should they outrank a simple prefix? Regex had higher score above, but that seems subjective.
Could we add a configurable policy per domain/team? e.g., default policy is prefix-first, infra can opt in to regex-priority.
Yeah, propose we add a per-space override: `route_policy: deterministic_sort_v1 | legacy_first_match | regex_priority`. Default deterministic_sort_v1 described here.
Edge case: overlapping routes with different methods (GET vs POST). We already match method first right?
Yes method + content-type remain pre-filters. Sort only applies to routes that are otherwise compatible (same method + header scope).
Implementation note: maintain stable ordering when we hot-reload a route — we must compute route_id_hash from a stable UUID assigned at create-time, not from file path.

Quick heads-up — after landing the fp8 calibration change last night I see a weird latency pattern on long-context runs. TPS is fine but first-token latency (startup TTFT) for 8k+ contexts jumped ~2.4x on the INT8/FP8 mixed builds.
ugh. do you have traces or a short repro?

yes. running the long-story benchmark (8k prompt + 512 decode) on a 4-GPU shard. Repro steps and a trimmed perf dump below. It's most visible when we switch kernel variants mid-request (initial encode path vs streaming decode path).

```
# simplified nvprof counters (avg over 10 runs)

total_tokens=8200, TPS=420, startup_ttft=18ms
after calib v2: total_tokens=8200, TPS=410, startup_ttft=44ms
kernel hotlist:
  prefill_gemm_fp8_fast   48%
  decode_gemm_int8_stream 30%
  kv_cache_write          12%
  kv_cache_read           7%
note: we see repeated small KV evictions around token 1-4 of the decode phase.
```

interesting — so throughput (TPS) roughly stable but TTFT jumps, which smells like a scheduling or kernel switch penalty. Could be queue flush + KV reformat cost when we pick the streaming INT8 kernels.

any chance calibration v2 changed per-layer quant params that force a different kernel path for the first decode microbatch? like we pick prefill-optimized kernels for the encode, then immediately pick decode-optimized kernels that have higher warmup.

exactly. calibration v2 chooses different per-layer thresholds, so the runtime toggles from the "fast prefill" fp8 kernels to a different int8/4bit decode kernel combo. That kernel combo has worse small-batch startup perf (higher TTFT) even though steady-state is similar. The extra cost shows up on long-context because the switch happens after the big KV write and before streaming.
can you paste the kernel selection log snippet?

```
[kernel-select] layer=0 prefill->kernel=fp8_prefill_fast (batch=32)
[kernel-select] layer=0 decode->kernel=int8_stream_v3 (microbatch=1)
[kv] kv_write shards=4 size=18MB latency=12ms
[kv] kv_read  shards=4 size=1.2MB latency=3ms
[scheduler] microbatch flush at decode-start: 9ms
```

hmm — kernel churn + microbatch flush + a synchronous KV flush looks like the triad. My gut: two mitigations: 1) add hysteresis so we don't switch kernel families within the same logical request, or 2) pre-warm the decode kernel path during the tail of prefill so the decode kernel's device state + memory layouts are ready.

agree. We also saw before that some int8 kernels have a high init latency due to different workspace allocation sizes. If the runtime frees and re-allocs scratch buffers between prefill and decode, that'll add a few ms.

another angle — batching heuristics. For long contexts we currently let the scheduler drain prefill batches fully before starting streaming decode microbatches. If we instead overlap the last prefill batch with the first decode microbatch (overlap the KV write with the decode kernel warming), we might hide some of the TTFT cost. But that risks KV consistency unless we ensure read-after-write ordering.

tried a quick patch locally: warmed the decode kernel asynchronously on token -2 and pinned the decode kernel variant for the whole request. Result: startup TTFT dropped to 20ms (near baseline) and TPS unchanged. Side effect: +1MB pinned scratch allocator for duration of request.
good data. What's the regression risk? If we pin kernel family for the whole request, we might lose some steady-state perf on mixed workloads (where decode kernels are faster on average).

true. For our workload the steady-state delta is <3% TPS. But pinning avoids the 2x TTFT regression on long-contexts. Option: only pin when context_length > threshold or when calibration indicates a kernel-family flip.

we should also consider a lighter-weight heuristic: prefer kernel_variant_by_phase with warmup flags — runtime picks decode kernels but queues a 1-shot warmup call on the device asynchronously before the microbatch loop. That doesn't require pinning and keeps flexibility.
also worth adding a perf counter to detect kernel-switch-induced TTFT spikes so we can auto-roll back per-customer. Perf-bot can create alerts if TTFT > baseline*1.8 for 5 runs.
Alert rule created: channel=eng-runtime, metric=first_token_latency, threshold=1.8x baseline, lookback=5 runs.

sounds like immediate short-term plan: (A) add async decode kernel warmup on last prefill batch, (B) add hysteresis threshold to kernel selector, (C) instrument and alert. Medium term: revisit per-layer calibration to reduce family flips.

Quick question — can a k8s ServiceAccount have multiple IRSA IAM roles attached via annotations? Thinking about a pod that needs both S3 read and Dynamo write access. :thinking:
Not directly. IRSA maps a KSA to one IAM role via the annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn.
Yep, single role. You can either create separate service accounts per permission set, or use role chaining inside the app (STS AssumeRole).
Another option: give the KSA a role that can assume other roles (sts:AssumeRole) and then call STS from the pod to switch to secondary role when needed.

Example KSA annotation:
```
apiVersion: v1

ServiceAccount
metadata:
app-sa

foo
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/redwood-app-role
```
If we go with STS chaining, we need to ensure the initial role has sts:AssumeRole on the secondary ones, and audit that in console.
Also watch token expiration. The IRSA token is short-lived; your app needs to handle refresh and caching of assumed creds.
doc: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html
TL;DR: pick 1) multiple SA per permission or 2) single SA that assumes other roles at runtime. For cross-account roles, the assume-role pattern is standard.

Quick q — for private VPC customers with egress disabled to internet, what's expected behavior for smart routing fallback? e.g. if the preferred model variant in region A is out of capacity, do we route to a variant in another region or to a local smaller/quantized variant? Short answer: we should NOT cross the customer's VPC/network boundary if their egress policy forbids it. We have two main modes in practice: regional_only and cross_region_fallback, but the semantics for model-variant fallback are fuzzy.
Got it. Is regional_only currently enforced for Private tenants by default?
Yes, for new Private enrollments the control plane defaults to regional_only. Older tenants might have cross_region_fallback enabled. Ops has been conservative.

Runtime note: we can fall back to a locally-compiled quantized variant (example: q4_k_mixed) if it's present in the same region/tenant pool. Autoconversion or on-the-fly quantization is not something we do on private clusters today. That limits 'local fallback' to pre-provisioned variants.

Security brief: if egress=false at tenant-level, control plane must not instruct data plane to call external endpoints or other regions. Even offloading to a partner region within the same org is suspect unless explicitly allowed. We need telemetry that proves no cross-network egress happened. :lock:

Console/UX — we need an explicit badge in Rollouts and Routes: e.g. "Cross-region fallback: disabled". Also show telemetry that indicates attempts blocked due to egress. That helps SREs and product owners.

Proposal: default for Private = regional_only. Add two opt-ins: (1) explicit cross-region-fallback via signed contract/SLO, (2) local-variant-fallback when tenant pre-populates quantized variants. For clarity, config could look like:
```
routing:
regional_only  # options: regional_only, cross_region_fallback

[eu-west-1]  # used only in cross-region mode
  allow_model_variant_fallback: true  # allows switching to pre-provisioned local variants
```
With that, control plane enforcement logic: if mode==regional_only and no local variant available => return 409/EGRESS_BLOCKED to the caller so app can handle gracefully.
If we return 409, customers will likely retry. Can we offer an in-console retry suggestion or fallback to a small local stub model?

We can provide a "stub" policy: if pre-provisioned tiny models exist (e.g., local-distill-128), runtime can route there with clear flag. But we must ensure quality/regression monitoring warns product owners — output will differ.

Quick question about /rerank semantics — if an item in the request has no `score` field or it is `null`, what guarantees do we offer for ordering? do we treat it as -inf, 0, or fall back to stable input order?
Short answer: we currently fall back to input order and then apply a deterministic tie-hash for server-side ordering. that tie-hash is internal (sha1(item_id) % 2^64). not exposed. :thinking_face:
Follow up: that means clients that don't include stable ids (just text blobs) might see reorders between requests if client array ordering differs, right?
correct. if client doesn't provide an `id` we use the array index as the tie key. so stable only if client preserves the same array order every time.
Is the tie-hash behaviour documented anywhere? customers keep asking because some search UIs expect deterministic stable sort across retries.
Not formally documented. There's an open RFC in the rerank repo but no public API contract. we should add a small section in the API docs: recommended to provide `id` for deterministic tie-breaking.
Another nuance — how do we treat `score: null` vs `score` missing? any difference in semantics?

That came up in a bug yesterday. server treats both as "no score provided" and falls into fallback branch. code snippet:
```
// pseudocode
if (item.score is number) use it
else mark as unscored -> fallback to input-order + tie_hash
```
\nanna: what about score normalization? some models output logits vs probabilities; does rerank normalize before comparing?

rerank does NOT normalize model logits. it expects callers to supply comparable scores (or use our model adapters which map to a common scale). mixing scales will break semantics. we should call this out in the contract.
For backward compatibility: if we change tie-breaker in future (e.g., use a server-wide stable-seed), we need a version flag so old clients still get previous behaviour. agree?
strongly agree. let's add `tie_mode` enum in request: "tie_mode": "legacy|stable-seed|random" with default `legacy`. default keeps current behaviour.
That would be a breaking change if default changes. PR idea: add `tie_mode` as opt-in for now, and set `tie_seed` optional when `stable-seed` is chosen.
tiny nit: include `rank` so clients that don't trust order can read explicit positions. also `score` can be null in response to signal unscored.

quick heads-up — product noticed a few customers getting mixed signals from our API when a request is routed to a cheaper model variant. They see 200 + a note in body, or sometimes 409, or a 202 with a retry hint. Confusing for SDKs and console UX.
ugh. is this mostly routing fallbacks (expected) or a mix of rate/quota + fallback?
mostly routing fallbacks + a couple quota edge cases where our proxy returns 409 for capacity gating. goal: one clear contract for callers so SDKs/console can show consistent badges/alerts.

can we enumerate the concrete behaviours? i saw three patterns: 1) transparent fallback: 200 + body.metadata.fallback=true 2) surfaced status: 409 or 429 w/ message about capacity 3) async fallback: 202 accepted + note that we queued to a cooler model.

we should avoid dual semantics where 200 sometimes means degraded. 200 should mean response content is final and acceptable. any degraded/combo state should map to a non-2xx code or a dedicated header so clients can opt in.

agree. from console UX POV we want a single signal to power: badge (OK / Degraded / Fallback) + CTA (retry/upgrade/contactsales). ideal signal is small: maybe X-Redwood-Serving-Status with values: ok | routed-variant | degraded | queued.
that header idea is neat. but policy: do we prefer supplementing status codes or replace some current 4xx? e.g., quota gating returns 409 today — should that stay 4xx or become 429 with extra code?

409 is ambiguous for clients. 429 already implies rate/quota and many clients have built-in retry heuristics for 429. Recommend normalizing gating -> 429 + X-Redwood-Reason=quota_exceeded. keep 409 for conflicting state changes (rare).

routing fallback should not be a hard error. If we intentionally routed to a cheaper-but-compatible model, it could be 200 + header X-Redwood-Serving-Status=routed-variant. but also include X-Redwood-Quality=nominal|reduced so console can surface quality badge and link to logs.

important: SDKs need stable machine-readable enums, not free text. we should publish a short contract and version it: Serving-Status v1. e.g., header values: ok, routed-variant, degraded, queued, failover.

rollout plan: 1) bake header in hosted runtime (silent) for 2 weeks 2) update SDKs to surface badge when header present 3) console wiring + shortlines for customer-facing copy 4) opt-in to strict codes in 2 months.
telemetry ask: capture both header and code, plus model variant id and latency delta. need that to correlate quality regressions and customer impact. create low-cardinality tags for console filters.

open question: what about parity for Private/Dedicated where headers may be stripped by proxies? we need to document fallback: include body.metadata.serving_status in API response JSON as a fallback channel.

sample console copy (short): "Routed to lower-cost model; output may vary. Learn more" and tooltip: "Automatically routed to a compatible model to maintain availability. See logs for model id and latency."
SDK suggestion: expose Response.servingStatus enum + .servingMetadata map. default behavior: no automatic retries on 'routed-variant' unless app opts in.
one more policy note: when behavior changes we must bump the header contract and add migration notes in changelog. please mock a short RFC and propose exact header names & enum values.
