quick q — noticed a few clients are treating any 4xx as 'don't retry' and it's causing hard failures.
We need a quick contract check: when should we return 400 vs 422 vs 409 vs 503 for the generate/chat endpoints? also streaming behavior: do we close the stream with an explicit error trailer or send a final object? cc @jason @anita

short answer from infra POV: 400 = syntactic/bad request (invalid JSON, missing required fields). 422 = semantic validation (prompt too long, unsupported function schema). 409 = conflicting state (idempotency or incompatible model version). 429 = rate limit. 503/502 = transient infra issues.

streaming nuance: for chunked/streaming we already stream JSON chunks for tokens. if we hit a validation error at start we should fail fast with a non-streaming 4xx. if error occurs mid-stream (e.g. model OOM), emit a final chunk `{ "error": { ... } }` and then close socket. SDKs should treat mid-stream errors as ephemeral and consult `retryable`+`code`.

note about backcompat: we can't break existing clients that expect plain 400 text bodies. so default behavior for plain 400 can remain with message string, but we should add the structured envelope for new clients and document the change. header `Accept: application/json; charset=utf-8` should get structured envelope. falling back to old shape for older SDK versions.

good call. can we agree on semantics mapping? my proposal:
- 400: syntactic / missing required fields (non-retryable)
- 422: semantic validation like prompt length, disallowed content (non-retryable)
- 409: idempotency/conflict (non-retryable, caller should dedupe)
- 429: client-side throttling / quota (retryable, with `Retry-After` header)
- 503/502: infra capacity / transient (retryable, with optional `retry_after` header in body)
also add `error_code` header (x-rw-error-code) for proxies that don't parse body. good for Nginx / LB logs.
+1 to x-rw-error-code, and include trace id (x-rw-trace) for debugging. for SDKs we'll standardize on checking: 1) header `x-rw-error-code` 2) body envelope 3) http status.

implementation note: runtime should translate internal model failures (OOM, kernel-timeout) to 503 + code `model_runtime_error` and `retryable: true`. model-behavior rejections (safety blocklists) map to 422 + `retryable: false`.

small compatibility risk: some customers rely on 400 to indicate prompt length specifically. we should publish a migration note and soft-deprecate that behavior in docs + changelog. open PR against docs by EOD?

quick question — we're getting asked by a couple of customers about read-only 'telemetry views' per-customer for debugging (they want to query spans/metrics without touching the raw tenant bucket). Can we do this without exploding storage/ingest costs?
do you mean materialized views or an API-backed read proxy that filters on namespace?
materialized views would be ideal (faster queries, RBAC friendly). concern is duplication + extra retention tiers.

fwiw we already push per-tenant export streams to S3/archives. Idea: materialize a lightweight read index with only span headers + selected attributes (no full payload) and shorter retention. That reduces cost and PII risk.
+1 on attribute filtering. We need policy around what is allowed in the view. Otherwise customers might request sensitive attrs like cookie/session ids.
exactly. UX question: in console should this be an opt-in per-tenant toggle (disable by default), or opt-out? Legal probably wants explicit consent.
legal wants explicit opt-in for anything that widens access. So opt-in. But we also need an admin API to grant view access to a given customer-team and to mask attributes.

technical sketch: collector/exporter produces tenant namespaces as normal, then a streaming job fans out to a "view" store. Pseudocode:```yaml
# pseudo otel-collector pipeline
receivers:
  otlp:
exporters:
  s3/archiver:
  view-streamer:
processors:
  filter/attributes:
["traceid", "spanname", "duration_ms"]

["user.email"]
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
[otlp]
[filter/attributes]

[s3/archiver, view-streamer]
```
the view-streamer writes per-customer read shards (clickhouse or pre-aggregated parquet) and sets an RBAC tag for console to honor.

operational concerns: doubling exporters + extra downstream processing increases our bursty CPU footprint. Need autoscale + backpressure. Also query isolation — we must rate-limit read views per customer to protect our analytics cluster.

console UX: show "Telemetry Read View" toggle in tenant settings. If enabled, show a short retention label (e.g., 7d / 30d) and a sanitized fields list. Admins can request longer retention via support.
one more: how do we handle rollbacks when a view accidentally includes a sensitive attr? We won't be able to delete data from downstream analytic stores instantly. Need a mitigations checklist.

mitigation ideas: 1) conservative default filters; 2) ability to rotate encryption keys for view store (so data becomes unreadable); 3) purge job for recent partitions and a legal escalation flow. All reasonable?

rotation helps but doesn't work for third-party analytic stores. For those, we'd recommend keeping view-store in our managed lake or Clickhouse we control. If customer requires external export, require DPA + extra controls.
note: "view-streamer" job currently has 75% CPU headroom in staging, but spikes at 2x during load tests.

Quick heads-up: audit showed a tenant requested audit copies but console shows zero collected samples for their route. edge logs show sample_decision=1 and header X-RDW-CONSENT=opt-in present.
Interesting. Are we honoring tenant-level consent before quota checks? I thought consent gating runs at collector.

Consent check and sampling decision happen at edge: edge tags request with X-RDW-SAMPLED=true and X-RDW-CONSENT=[opt-in|opt-out]. downstream router applies inspect_quota and may drop bodies when quota exhausted. collector currently refuses payloads if consent!=opt-in. So path is: decision -> quota -> forward -> collector consent check -> accept/reject.

Problem: tenant expects that if they opt-in we will keep at least tokenized/hashed audit traces even when quota blocks full payloads. Right now we drop everything if quota prevents forward, which makes it look like we never sampled.
note: playbook link: https://redwood.internal/playbooks/consent-and-sampling

Proposal: change ordering so collector enforces consent but router always forwards a minimal audit envelope when sample_decision=true and consent=opt-in. Envelope contains no PII: {sample_id, route, tenant_id, consent_state, redaction_version, envelope_hmac}. This avoids moving KMS to edge.
I like minimal envelope. We should also add a metric sample_envelope_forwarded and sample_envelope_dropped with labels {tenant, route, reason}. Alert if envelope_dropped > 0 for >5m.

Console UX: show per-tenant consent state (opt-in/opt-out/unknown) and a small timeline for envelope vs payload counts. Three columns: sampled_decisions | envelopes_forwarded | payloads_collected. Amber badge when envelopes_forwarded > payloads_collected.

Legal ask: sometimes they need the scrubbed payload for investigation. Envelope won't be sufficient. We'll need a secure-forward path where edge can redact and forward scrubbed content even if quota would otherwise block. That requires key access and extra audit.

For secure-forward we could implement an edge-redact service that has a short-lived, tightly scoped key from KMS (use HSM-backed audit log). Edge requests a one-time redact token from control plane, uses it, then the control plane records that redact token issuance. This keeps KMS usage limited.
Complexity: control plane must be highly available and low-latency. Edge will add a round-trip. Maybe limit secure-forward only to tenants with a paid compliance tier.

Agreed. Short-term steps: 1) always forward envelope when sample_decision && consent=opt-in 2) create metrics/enforcement and console indicators 3) add admin toggle expedite_forward for tenant-level debug 4) start RFC for secure-forward for compliance tier.

Quick proposal: introduce a narrow \"golden path\" for telemetry attributes. Enforce low-cardinality primitives + explicit opt-ins for expensive/high-cardinality fields. Main objective: stable cost attribution + predictable observability costs.
👍 can you list the exact primitives we expect?

minimal required attributes: service, env, route, hashed_customer_id, request_type. All other fields must go into an optional metadata blob or be behind a per-tenant opt-in. Limit of 3 freeform customer-visible keys per span/event.
enforcement strategy? SDKs + CI + ingest?

three tiers: 1) SDK lint that warns locally; 2) CI/PR checks that block new high-cardinality attributes in public SDKs; 3) ingest-side guardrails that trim/label exceeding keys and emit governance metrics. devops-bot: note: guardrails are feature-flagged at canary regions.
partners sometimes need lots of attributes for billing or reconciliation. How do we support them?
partner opt-in via a signed allowlist. Per-tenant attribute quotas and an explicit billing_tag will ensure attribution accuracy for paying partners. Default behavior is strict.
sampling interactions are tricky. If we sample traces, heavy tenants could be undercounted.

plan: make sampling tenant-aware. Deterministic sampling (or 100% sampling) for billing-critical tenants; statistical sampling for general telemetry. All sampled traces must include sampling_probability so analytics can reweight estimates.
can you show a simple reweighting example?

```sql
-- example reweighting
SUM(cost * (1.0 / sampling_probability)) AS estimated_cost
WHERE sampling_probability IS NOT NULL
```
rollout plan? Changing span schema is risky for many consumers.

phased rollout: 1) add SDK lint + nightly warnings; 2) publish golden-path and 30-day migration advisory; 3) enable CI blockers for new violations; 4) flip ingest guardrails in a single canary region for 14 days; 5) global enforcement with dashboard and rollback playbook.
metric-log-span joins need a stable request identifier. Propose header X-RD-REQ and fallback to trace_id. Also include short_trace (8 chars) in metrics to lower join cardinality.
agreed. Canonicalization rule: prefer request_id header; else use trace_id. short_trace included in metrics for cheaper joins.
mobile/edge SDKs often push raw attrs to proxies which then enrich. How do we keep rules consistent?
SDKs should do lightweight checks + PII hashing, but canonicalization and final trimming happen at proxy/ingest to centralize behavior. SDKs still enforce linting locally so devs see problems early.
we need alerting when many spans are trimmed; otherwise teams won't notice regressions.

ingest will emit governance metrics: trimmed_spans_count, trimmed_keys_by_team, trimmed_top_keys. Alerts: sudden spike in trimmed_spans or any tenant exceeding 1% trimmed -> page oncall. Weekly reports per-product with pre/post migration telemetry stats.

quick list from my notes (not exhaustive):
- Redwood native tool call message uses `tool_name` and `arguments` as an object (SDKs surface typed map/struct).
- OpenAI-compat uses `tool_calls: [{ id, type: "function", function: { name, arguments: "{...}" } }]`.
- During streaming on OpenAI-compat, `function.arguments` is emitted as string deltas; not valid JSON until the end.
- Some models emit whitespace/escaped newlines in arguments; consumers should treat as opaque string until final.

also parallel tool calls:
- Redwood native: we show multiple tool calls as separate call events, and you can run tools in parallel.
- OpenAI-compat: multiple tool_calls can be present in one assistant message; the IDs matter for mapping results.
re examples: should we *show* both shapes in docs? or just one canonical and a callout box for OpenAI-compat?
docs direction: keep one canonical example per page (Redwood SDKs), add an "OpenAI-compat notes" callout + a compact table. if we show two full examples per language it’ll explode the page.

Quick q — should Console call a preflight validation API before creating an experiment? worried about malformed routing rules causing traffic blackholes.

```
POST /v1/experiments/validate
{
  "name": "exp_reward_ui",
  "variants": [{"id":"v1","weight":1},{"id":"v2","weight":99}],
  "routes": [{"selector":"region:us","variant":"v1"}]
}
```

Validation needs to simulate routing logic across regions + fallbacks and check capacity profiles. Deep simulation may be async for large setups.

Example response (sync):
```
200 OK
{
  "lint": [{"level":"error","msg":"weights must sum to 100"}],
  "simulation_job_id": "job_20240325_1234"
}
```

Quick sync — proposing an approach to cut ingest cost for low-fidelity mobile traces. Idea: defer enrichment into short time windows and emit tombstone markers for traces that never resolve a billing_key. This avoids repeated late-enrich attempts and keeps the fast-path cheap.
TL;DR numbers? how much memory/disk for tombstones vs saved enrichment runs? :thinking_face:

Rough calc: for 1M mobile traces/day with 5% late-join, if we re-enrich every hour we do 50k extra enrich calls. If each enrich costs ~0.5ms CPU + lookup overhead, we're looking at $X/day. Tombstones (~16 bytes key + ttl index) would be ~800KB active at any time for a 24h ttl. Big win in compute.
Sounds promising. Main worry: query correctness. If a tombstone is present, do we permanently drop attribution or fallback to fuzzy billing lookup?

We should distinguish two flows: 1) queries that need exact billing attribution (billing UI, chargebacks) — those should trigger a backfill job if tombstone present. 2) non-critical analytics can use cohort-level attribution heuristics and not backfill.
Also think about window sizing. Mobile clients often have bursts when switching networks. If window too short we re-ingest a ton; too long and we hold memory + increase cold read complexity.

Agree. Proposal: symmetric windows. Default window_seconds = 300 (5m) for mobile; tombstone_ttl = 86400 (24h). Canary that on a subset of traffic then compare enrichment_invocations_per_trace and enrichment_p99_latency.
Can we make it configurable per-tenant? Enterprise customers might want longer window for accuracy. Also need a metric to surface tombstone-hit-rate per-tenant.
Yes configurable per-tenant + rollout policy. Metrics to add: `enrichment.deferred.window_seconds`, `enrichment.tombstone.count`, `enrichment.tombstone.hit_rate`, `enrichment.backfill.triggered`.

Operationally we need an idempotent tombstone write path and GC. Suggest a small kv table with key=(tenant,billing_key_hash) value=(ts,reason). Use a monotonic tombstone version to avoid racey late-updates.

What about the late-enrich pipeline interaction? Right now late-enrich is synchronous per-record. We'll need a windowed batching consumer that reads un-enriched traces, groups them by key, checks tombstones, and only calls enrich for non-tombstoned keys.
That implies change to the ingest contract: traces need an opaque `late_enrich_cursor` header and allow for a tombstone flag in the envelope. Backwards compatible if tombstone flag is optional.

Pseudo-config for the consumer:
```yaml
enrichment:
deferred

300
  tombstone_ttl_seconds: 86400
on-demand # or automatic after 24h

Edge-case: what if billing_key resolves after tombstone creation? We need reconcile: tombstone should be delete-on-write when a validated enrich returns a billing_key. That requires tombstone deletion to be idempotent and ordered.

Agree. Use tombstone versioning + tombstone-delete event: tombstone only removed when enrich returns with version > tombstone_version. Also ensure eventual consistency: queries may briefly see tombstone then later billing_key. Document in query layer.

quick follow-up from today's admission RFC — noticed a recurring 'token erosion' pattern when clients hold long-lived streaming sessions and our quota reservoir slowly drifts down. putting notes here for design + rollout :thinking:

gist of the symptoms: small per-request token delta accumulates over long sessions, looks like we lose fractional credits on soft admits. snippet:

[2026-03-20T15:22:01Z] admit: client=acme-prod stream_id=xyz lease=1.0 used=0.03 residual=0.97

```

Quick design note: propose a deferred enrichment path for mobile traces to reduce repeated late-enrich costs. Approach: batch un-enriched traces for a short window, emit a lightweight tombstone if a billing_key never resolves, and skip future enrich attempts until tombstone TTL expires.
Can you sketch the tradeoffs? worried about query fidelity + storage overhead :chart_with_upwards_trend:

Tradeoffs: compute saved vs extra storage & query complexity. Example: 2M mobile traces/day, 3% late-join -> naive re-enrich every 10m = many wasted lookups. Tombstones (16B key + 24B metadata) ~= tens of MBs for 24h across cluster; CPU savings can be significant.
Query semantics question: if tombstone present and a user queries for billing breakdown, should we return "unknown" or trigger a backfill?
Two-tier semantics: "strong" flows (billing/chargebacks) cause backfill-on-read; "best-effort" flows (dashboards) use cohort heuristics that ignore tombstones. We need flags on queries.
Operational details: how do we create and GC tombstones? race conditions possible if enrich arrives while tombstone writes.

Implementation sketch: a tiny kv table keyed by (tenant,billing_key_hash). Value: tombstone_version|created_ts|ttl. Tombstone write is conditional (only if no version or version < new). When a late enrich returns a billing_key, it issues a tombstone-delete with version > tombstone_version. Consumers check tombstone atomically before calling enrich.

For correctness, tombstone writes should be monotonic. Use unsigned 64 bit version = epoch_ms at write-time. Deletes only succeed if version in tombstone <= delete_version. That avoids deletes lost to concurrent lower-version writes.

Consumer flow: 1) ingest fast-path accepts trace with missing billing_key and appends to short-lived window topic. 2) windowed consumer groups by billing_key_hash and tenant, checks tombstone kv, and calls enrich only for keys with no tombstone. 3) when window expires and no billing_key seen -> write tombstone with version=now and emit tombstone metric.
Config knobs: window_seconds (default 300), tombstone_ttl_seconds (default 86400), batch_size, backfill_on_read boolean. Make per-tenant overrides.

Metrics to add: enrichment.windowed.batch_size, enrichment.tombstone.created, enrichment.tombstone.expired, enrichment.tombstone.hit_rate, enrichment.backfill.invocations. Alerts: tombstone.hit_rate > 20% for 24h -> review.

How do we handle late-arriving canonical billing_keys that arrive after tombstone creation? We delete tombstone; queries that read between tombstone and delete might see "unknown" temporarily. Document eventual consistency.
Exactly. We'll document: tombstone is a best-effort optimization for cost; it does not change long-term correctness because backfill-on-read or periodic backfills can rehydrate billing attribution.

Overload detection: sliding window of enqueue time + tail latency + GPU utilization on region. If queue depth > X or backend util > 85% for 30s, mark degraded. fallback triggers only after short cool-down to avoid flapping.

Quotas: per-region request quotas to avoid noisy-neighbor impacts. If quota exceeded, route to fallback region and increment quota_violation metric. Request throttling response should include headers: `X-Redwood-Region`, `X-Redwood-Fallback-Reason`, `X-Redwood-Fallback-Model` so apps can adapt.

Raj just emailed asking whether he can roll a 401(k) from his last employer into our plan mid-year and if that affects his HSA/FSA election limits. Anyone have a quick checklist we can send him?

Short checklist: 1) Confirm our plan accepts incoming rollovers (we do). 2) Determine rollover type: direct trustee-to-trustee rollover (preferred) vs check payable to employee (risk of withholding). 3) Rollover doesn't change current year elective deferral limits, but after-tax/ROTH in-plan rollovers have special rules.

From payroll side: we only need the rollover paperwork for recordkeeping; payroll doesn't process rollovers. But note: if Raj wants to do an in-plan Roth conversion or after-tax rollover, that may have taxable implications and we should coordinate with payroll for withholding if taxable.
Can I roll money from a former 401(k) that has both pre-tax and Roth after-tax portions into our plan? I also increased my HSA deferral at open enrollment and want to make sure I don't exceed limits.

You can roll pre-tax to our pre-tax 401(k). Roth 401(k) amounts can often roll to a Roth 401(k) or Roth IRA depending on vendor rules. Some vendors treat after-tax (non-Roth) differently; if it's after-tax non-Roth, you might be able to roll the after-tax portion to an after-tax account or do an in-plan conversion to Roth (taxable). We'll need the source plan's distribution code.
Quick Q for clarity: does doing a rollover change your annual contribution limit? i.e., if I roll in $50k, can I still contribute up to the 2026 deferral limit?

Good call  rollovers do NOT count toward the annual deferral limit. You still have the full elective deferral limit (e.g., $23,000 for 2026 hypothetical) to contribute via payroll. Rollover is separate from YTD employee deferrals.

Note on HSA: HSA contributions are separate and have their own IRS limits (individual/family). Rolling a 401(k) doesn't affect HSA contribution room. FSA plan year is independent too. If Raj wants to max HSA after rollover, it's fine.
If the former vendor sends a check payable to me (the employee) and there's 20% mandatory withholding, can I avoid that? I want the full amount moved.

You can avoid withholding by requesting a direct rollover (check payable to the new plan/trustee). If you receive a check to you, you have 60 days to deposit into an IRA/plan to avoid taxation, but that 20% withholding would still have occurred and you'd need to make up the withheld amount from personal funds to get the full rollover treatment. So direct is best.

Coverage is effective retroactive to the date of birth as long as you enroll within the 30-day window and provide docs. So claims from birth should be covered.

For dependents aging out, coverage generally ends the last day of the month they turn 26. We’ll send a notification ~30 days prior, but you can remove them earlier in Rippling. They’ll get COBRA eligibility info if they qualify.
If I got married earlier this year but missed the 30 days to add my spouse, can that be corrected now?

Marriage is also a QLE but the 30-day rule still applies. If it’s been >30 days, we can’t make a mid-year change unless there’s another QLE. You can wait for open enrollment or submit a request to benefits@redwood.com — sometimes exceptions are made with supporting docs but they’re rare.

Hi team — quick Q: I extended my conference trip by one night for personal travel. Hotel folio shows 3 nights (2 business, 1 personal) on one bill paid on company card. How should I split the charge and how does per diem apply for the personal day?

Good Q. Best practice: split the hotel charges so the company is only billed for business nights. If company card was used accidentally for the personal night, reimburse company for that night ASAP and attach manager approval for the split. Per diem only covers business days.
Got it. Manager approved the two business nights. I can reimburse the personal night — can I just expense a negative line or do I need a separate refund?

Policy: Do not use negative expense lines. If company card was charged for a personal night, employee must either 1) have hotel issue a refund to the company card and provide refund confirmation, OR 2) submit a personal reimbursement to Finance by attaching the hotel folio and a copy of a personal card payment or internal repayment evidence. Please include a short attestation in the expense report.

OK will ask hotel for a refund. If they refuse, I'll do internal repayment. For per diem: my conference day schedule had dinners covered by sponsor on day 2. Do I still claim per diem for that calendar day?

If meals are provided by third party (sponsor, client) for a business day, employees should deduct the meal value from per diem only when itemized deduction is required. Our policy: per diem is reduced by the number of meals provided when meals are clearly part of the business event. Add a note: "Sponsor-provided dinner on 10/12 - deduct per diem meal" and attach sponsor confirmation (email or agenda).

For refunds: hotels often require front desk to process a refund to the original card. If company card cannot be refunded quickly, request a credit and we can offset on next invoice. Submit folio with line-item breakdown so Finance can reconcile.
Quick bookkeeping Q — does the VAT on the refunded night matter? The folio shows VAT for all nights.

VAT treatment: if company ultimately bears the refund (i.e., company card was charged and later refunded), VAT will net out on the vendor invoice. If the employee reimburses the company, Finance will record VAT according to the original vendor invoice; reclaim eligibility depends on country rules. Attach full folio showing VAT lines. Finance will handle reclaim evaluation.
Thanks. Last Q: any note about incidentals? I used room minibar on the personal night only.

Incidentals tied to personal nights are employee responsibility. Make sure the folio separates incidentals per night or show receipts. If incidental was charged to the company and is personal, follow the same refund/repayment flow.

reminder: do NOT pull offer paperwork or send amended letters until People Ops confirms the change. It causes confusion.

If manager can provide 3 concrete examples mapped to the leveling rubric within 5 business days we can keep the original effective date in many cases.

Role changes that include a managerial responsibility require manager + director + People Ops approval and a skip-level acknowledgement. Compensation reviews both base and any new managerial allowances. If it's a hybrid (title change with level bump) annotate that in the packet so Compensation can evaluate band placement.

yes — checklist (copy/paste for DMs): 1) Complete /forms/promo-request and pick "Outside cycle" if not in planned cycle. 2) Attach calibration notes and 3 example evidence mapped to rubric. 3) Director sign-off (email or sign field). 4) Org chart + reporting lines. 5) Indicate effective date and whether employee is on leave. 6) Recruiter confirms offer letter hold / no changes until approval. 7) Budget owner pinged if >$20k ARR impact.

Appeals: submit a follow-up packet via the same form within 14 days of decision and include new evidence + director rationale. Appeals after 14 days require exec sponsor. Appeals rarely overturn without material new evidence.

Quick post-analysis from last night's regional spike — recording notes and action items here. TL;DR: routing preference + quota bump to a single EU AZ caused localized GPU pressure, KV cache thrash, and burst throttling.
Thanks — can you share the sequence?

Timeline: 21:03 service-level rollout (config change) set routing policy to prefer eu-west-1 for cheaper instances, 21:07 outbound traffic replay (promo) started, 21:10 autoscaler hit cold-start limit for other regions, 21:11 sustained queue growth on eu-west-1 dedicated pool -> OOM-near events.
Observed symptom was continuous prefill and high kv-cache eviction rates, right?
Exactly. Metrics: node GPU util peaked at 96-99%, KV cache eviction rate jumped x12, and per-request latency tail rose from 180ms to ~2.1s for cached routes.
Deploy: routing-preference:v2 -> applied by infra-deploy-bot at 2025-11-14T21:03:12Z :white_check_mark:
Why didn't autoscaler rebalance to other regions? We have policy to spill to us-west on saturation.

The autoscaler has a safety threshold that prevents cross-region reallocation when predicted cold-start > 45s (we use conservative penalty for inter-region warmups). With the sudden promo surge, the predictor flagged high warmup risk and we fell back to throttling rather than spillover.
So policy + cost-preference combo caused hot-spotting. Any networking factors?

There was an additional subtlety: the new routing policy used prioritized endpoints list that ranked eu-west-1 endpoints by price and then by latency. Because of a recent price change, eu-west-1 got an elevated rank and got most of the traffic even though capacity delta was small.
That prioritized list is supposed to be weight-balanced. Looks like weight normalization didn't kick in after the price update.
We also saw TCP retransmits between the control-plane and eu-west-1 agent during the hottest 6 minutes — likely increased churn due to pressure.

I pulled the agent logs:
```
2025-11-14T21:09:24Z agent[euw1-rtg]: kv_cache_evictions=1345 per_min, available_gpu_memory=430MiB
2025-11-14T21:10:01Z scheduler: enqueue_delay_ms=4800 pending_reqs=420
2025-11-14T21:10:40Z k8s: pod_restart_count=12 node_pressure=memory
```
OOM-near events were transient; most pods didn't fully OOM but CPU/GPU contention forced latency-based shedding.
Rough cost impact? We turned on extra dedicated units for 15 minutes.

Preliminary estimate: extra reserved and on-demand failover during the incident added ~1,100 GPU-hours equivalent to our usual day rate because of over-provisioning in eu-west-1 and failed spill. Estimated incremental cost: $9.2k (gross).
Oof. Need mitigations to avoid both customer latency and runaway cost.

Root causes: 1) routing preference update prioritized single region after price rebalance, 2) autoscaler safety heuristic prevented cross-region spill because of conservative warmup penalty, 3) a weight normalization bug meant endpoint weights weren't rebalanced, 4) telemetry blind spot for per-route token cost and prefix cache hit rates.

Agreed. Lessons: - Don't let price-only ranking alone drive routing decisions; use combined capacity score (capacity headroom + price + recent utilization). - Lower the autoscaler cold-start penalty slightly for cross-region spill to favor availability over cost during short promos. - Fix weight-normalization race when endpoint metadata changes. - Add per-route prefix-cache hit monitoring and integrate with routing decisions.

```
This points to reuse returning entries with wrong seq_offset.

Root cause looks like a mismatch between admission limits and an unusual spike of long-context requests. Opening for timeline/notes.
Incident created: INC-2026-0453 at 2026-03-01T09:04:03Z by matt-sre
Observed sharp rise in inflight tokens at 09:02. Pool us-west-2/gpu-a hit 100% and admission started returning 429s. Metrics: active_streams up 6x, avg_seq_len up 2.5x.

Logs show repeated admission rejections, then many clients retried aggressively. Retry storm amplified load onto fallback GPU pool and then CPU host pool. Sample log:
```
2026-03-01T09:02:45Z  admit.go:121  deny request pool=us-west-2/gpu-a inflight=251 limit=250
2026-03-01T09:02:47Z  api-proxy.go:88  429 -> client_id=acme-inc request_id=... retry-after=0
2026-03-01T09:03:12Z  fallback-proxy: routing to cpu-pool due to no gpu capacity
```
Customer-impact: hosted text-generation latency > 5s for 15m, 8 customers reported errors to CS. Dedicated customers on pinned pools saw increased queue times but no data loss.
Filed two high-priority tickets from customers. Shared status update and ETA for next update ~09:25.
Alert: admission_queue_length_us-west-2 >= 2000 for 8m. Top callers: notebook-batch, acme-inc, research-sim, internal-loadtest.

Quick config check — admission config for us-west-2/gpu-a was:
```
admission:
  max_inflight_per_pool: 250
Note we had lowered backoff to 100ms in a prior tweak to reduce perceived latency under load. That made clients retry more aggressively and contributed to amplification.

Mitigation timeline:
- 09:06 disable aggressive retries at edge (set retry_backoff_ms -> 1000)
- 09:08 increase admission limit on backup GPU pool by 20% as temporary relief
- 09:12 enable per-client queuing to cap noisy clients
Results: 429 rate dropped ~60% by 09:15, latency gradually recovered.

Root cause hypothesis: two factors combined — longer sequence length spike (internal model eval) and too-low retry_backoff producing amplification when admission rejected. Admission logic didn't rate-limit retries correctly.

Post-incident actions (initial):
- Revert retry_backoff to 1000ms on all regions (done 09:06) :thumbsup:
- Add a server-side exponential jitter to retry hints (RFC queued)
- Implement per-client admission windows (PR in review by anya-eng)
- Add circuit-breaker in fallback routing to avoid overloading CPU pool (zach-runtime)
- Run load replay to validate changes before rolling to eu-west
Cost note: We temporarily spun up extra gpu-burst instances for 30m — estimated incremental cost $3.2k. Will include in incident cost report.
Action item: audit any prior config changes that reduced retry_backoff in last 3 months. I see a change from 2026-01-22 by ops-tuning.

2) Set client retry backoff to 100ms and aggressive retry policy

after analyzing traces, root cause summary: a change to the key canonicalizer inadvertently allowed model-quant suffix variants to be treated as distinct keys when merged by cont-batch. For MQA flows we were generating merge-scoped IDs per stream without dedup, so multiple merges for the same logical prefix created unique keys and defeated eviction heuristics. Fix includes: normalize quant suffix, dedupe merge ids at canonicalization, add merge_count cap, and add metric for merge fanout.

Quick help — after upgrading opentelemetry-go to v1.15 the realtime-processor service is not sending spans for some gRPC requests. Traces show up from the HTTP side but not from the worker that handles grpc calls. Anyone seen this? 😕
Do you see any spans in the collector at all from that host? oTel collector logs?

Not much in collector logs — just normal OTLP ingest. I can see OTLP traffic hitting the collector from the host. But in jaeger UI the service is missing most child spans (root exists but children gone).
Two quick suspects: 1) tracerprovider being re-created per request, 2) missing context propagation through the gRPC interceptors. Can you paste the init code?

Here's the init (simplified):
```go
func NewTracer() *sdktrace.TracerProvider {
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(...)
    otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)
    return tp
}
// called in handler constructor
tracer := NewTracer()
```
I call that during each handler instantiation — could that be it?
Yep that's it. If you create multiple TP instances you can end up with unexpected sampling behavior and orphaned spans. TracerProvider should be global/singleton for the process.

Also check that you added the otelgrpc.UnaryServerInterceptor / UnaryClientInterceptor to both client and server sides for gRPC. Without interceptors the context might not be propagated into child goroutines.
We do have interceptors, but we recently swapped to the new otelgrpc package import path during the upgrade. Example: `otelgrpc.UnaryServerInterceptor()` looks right though.

Another thing: sampling config changed semantics in v1.15 — parent-based sampler defaults might cause child spans to be dropped if parent sampled=false. Confirm your OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER or Sampler config. Are you using traceidratio or parentbased(traceidratio)?

I had `sampler: traceidratio` in our YAML for the collector. In code we set `sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(sdktrace.WithSampler(sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.TraceIDRatioBased(0.02))))` — but maybe we messed up ordering when wrapping.

ParentBased(TraceIDRatioBased(0.02)) is fine. The problem was the multiple TP instances + some goroutines starting spans without derived parent context. If a child span is started without a parent context and you have a low global sample rate, it will be dropped.

Quick debug steps: 1) ensure tracer provider is created once at process start and set globally; 2) enable debug logging on collector and exporter: OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug for exporter; 3) temporarily set TraceIDRatioBased to 1.0 to verify spans appear; 4) check gRPC metadata propagation — look for traceparent header in logs.
Setting TraceIDRatioBased to 1.0 made the missing spans show up instantly. So sampling + TP duplication combo was the root cause. :sweat_smile:

For a longer-term fix: create a single tracer package that init()s the provider once and returns otel.Tracer("realtime-processor"). Also add a test that starts a request flow and asserts child spans exist in a local in-memory exporter.
Will do. One more question — our consumer workers spawn goroutines heavily; any suggestions to avoid losing context across goroutine boundaries?

Pass context explicitly, avoid storing context in struct fields. If you need to spawn, use `go func(ctx context.Context){ ctx = trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx) ... }(ctx)` — but better: use `go trace.WithSpan(ctx, span, func(ctx context.Context) { ... })` patterns or create child spans from the passed context.
Also check the instrumentation for any third-party libs that start goroutines; those might not propagate context by default.
Thanks all — I'll refactor tracer init to a singleton and add tests. Pinging once fixed. :thumbsup:

Ugh. Is the new lease coming from the same quota bank or a different shard? :thinking:

Different shard. Eviction doesn't immediately propagate to all schedulers; new admission checks only look at local tokens. We need a stronger handoff so revocation is globally respected, or a soft-quarantine window.

Two quick options: 1) make revocation write a short-lived global tombstone (cheap KV) that admission checks consult, or 2) attach a revocation token/nonce to the client that we validate on new leases.

Tombstone approach seems simpler for immediate consistency, but it adds read on hot path. Nonce/token requires client cooperation and makes client logic more complex (and we can't trust clients if they're abusive).

For tombstones we'd need TTL tuning. Too long and we punish legitimate clients; too short and we still get thrash. What about a hybrid: tombstone with short TTL + local short soft-quarantine (deny new fast-path leases for Xs) so we avoid KV lookups for normal flow.
Sounds good. Also consider tying tombstone writes to sequence numbers so we don't race double-revokes. Example: `revoke_id = {tenant}:{seq}` and admission consults highest seen `revoke_seq`.

Tradeoffs: tombstone reads cost (reads per admission). We can cache tombstone presence in edge LRU for TTL window to reduce read QPS. Also want metrics: revocation -> new lease rate, tombstone read hit ratio.
deploy-bot: Scheduled canary for revocation-cache at 03:00 UTC tomorrow. Rolling 20% edge nodes.
Another failure mode: false-positive revokes. Need a rollback path: allow short self-appeal TTL where a tenant can prove innocence and we expire tombstone early. But that invites abuse if misused.
Could limit appeals to verified accounts and surface a manual ops fast-path. For automated, treat appeals as probation — shrink throughput until re-eval.

Implementation sketch:
```
# admission flow
1) check local token fast-path
2) consult local revocation cache (LRU)
3) if cache miss, async read tombstone KV with short TTL and populate cache
4) if tombstone present -> soft-quarantine or deny
```
Keep async read non-blocking by allowing admission to failover to slower fallback (probation) instead of blocking.

Two quick thoughts: 1) Mixed MIG and non-MIG pools can make the device plugin expose different resource names (e.g., `nvidia.com/gpu` vs `nvidia.com/gpu-mig.*`) so scheduler weight/advertising mismatch happens. 2) If pods were created for MIG units but landed on non-MIG nodes the plugin might not advertise the same resources -> Insufficient.

We recently migrated node-1/2 to A100 and enabled MIG. Old pool (node-3/4/5) are RTX8000 (non-MIG). Our batch job specs request `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` and also set a `nodeAffinity` that unintentionally excludes some MIG nodes (legacy label mismatch).

That explains it — autoscaler refused to scale target pool because CA target group only includes non-MIG nodegroup. CA logs show scale-up attempted against batch-gpu-eu-west2 (non-MIG) but our job needs MIG nodes.

Short fixes you can try right now:
- Add `nodeSelector: nvidia.com/mig.enabled: \"true\"` to the MIG-aware job to force scheduling onto MIG nodes.
- Or create a dedicated homogeneous node pool (A100 MIG) and point CA to it.
- If you need immediate capacity and CA is blocked by quota, consider running low-priority jobs on non-MIG nodes by removing strict affinity.
We need something today — I'll patch the job to nodeSelector MIG=true and requeue. If CA still fails due to quota we'll need SRE to request a bump.
Note: some pods in this workload use `nvidia.com/gpu-mig.count` via the device-plugin. Those will never run on the non-MIG pool. Also check for stray `nodeAffinity` on older job templates.

Also check for `PodDisruptionBudget` or `topologySpreadConstraints` that might prevent packing. I saw a couple of jobs declare `maxSkew: 1` with strict topology that leaves GPUs fragmented across nodes.

For longer term:
- Use a MIG-only node pool and advertise per-MIG resources consistently.
- Consider packing small jobs into fewer nodes using the device-plugin's multi-container-per-GPU support when safe (MIG or mps).
- Add a scheduler-extender/profile that prefers binpacking by GPU memory/cores, not just free GPUs.
- CA config: ensure `--balance-similar-node-groups=true` and `--skip-nodes-with-local-storage=false` are tuned and that CA is allowed to scale the MIG nodegroup.

if the subnet is managed in another account, you can't create a second association. One of two approaches: 1) ask owning account to create the association, or 2) use the VPC endpoint route table association resource in the owning account. For PrivateLink resolver we usually prefer the owning account to attach route tables.

another option: if you only need DNS traffic to go to the resolver endpoint, consider creating a resolver rule association (aws_route53_resolver_rule_association) instead of manipulating VPC route tables across accounts. That keeps changes local.

also check if the subnet already has the main route table associated (main RT vs custom RT). The API error is generic — sometimes TF tries to create an assoc that a previous resource already created (maybe via cloudformation). Pull current associations:
```bash
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=<SUBNET_ID> --query 'RouteTables[].Associations'
```

short-term we need traffic redirected for staging. what's the least risky change?

least risky = add a route in the existing route table instead of creating a new association. But since you don't have access, you'd need the owning account to run a tiny patch:
```hcl
resource \"aws_route\" \"to_resolver\" {
  route_table_id = <existing-rt-id>
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0" # or narrower cidr for DNS host range
  vpc_endpoint_id = aws_vpc_endpoint.resolver.id
}
```

oncall: From oncall: root cause likely twofold — (1) device-plugin restart concurrency hitting the same unix socket path causing EADDRINUSE, (2) udev/device hotplug flood blocking kubelet device plugin registration window.

quick mitigation applied: rolled the nvidia-device-plugin DaemonSet to add `initContainer` that waits random 0-20s before starting plugin so they don't all race for socket. also added `livenessProbe` backoff to avoid tight crash loops.

confirming logs after the roll: one node had `bind: address already in use` for 3 restarts, then cleaned up and succeeded after init delay. udev flood reduced after bumping kernel udev rate limit via sysctl on the node image.

long term: propose two changes: (1) stagger node creation in the autoscaler cloudprovider: enable nodegroup launch jitter so we don't get 20 launches at once for one AZ; (2) change device-plugin to use per-node unique socket path (or ensure old socket removed on startup).

For inference fleets we must keep latency SLAs. So reserved or Dedicated first, then capacity-optimized spot as failover to avoid frequent evictions.
Implementation notes: set ASG allocationStrategy to `capacity-optimized` for the main pool. For chase pool use `price-optimized` with a dynamic maxPrice that follows a 5% buffer above median price.
Important: do NOT set maxPrice to on-demand for chase pools — that defeats the point. Use a sliding window: if current spot price < targetThreshold && evictionRate < 0.5% then scale chase pool.

Also add region-aware fallbacks: prefer same AZ capacity-optimized, then cross-AZ capacity-optimized, then cross-region price-optimized as last resort. Document the fallback priority in the autoscaler.

Operational play: run a daily job that simulates a 10% capacity loss and measure failover time to Dedicated and chase pools. Target recovery < 90s for critical inference routes.
Cost metric: track effective $/GPU-hour including wasted time from evictions (i.e., restart overhead). Optimize for minimized total $/useful-work, not just hourly VM price.

noticing increased gRPC stalls on large model streaming between pods in us-west-2. flagging because it looks like chunked requests hang mid-stream and then the client retries lots -> backpressure on the runtime. :frowning:
which nodes? any pattern by AZ or instance type?
seeing same SPC: pod egress packet retransmits spike on nodes gpu-pool-3-{12,14,20}. tcpdump shows lots of 'frag' and 'bad checksum' after heavy 16KB-ish writes from the model server.
we stream tokens in ~4KB frames but kernel offloads may coalesce into oversized segments. could be GSO/GRO + overlay MTU mismatch causing IP fragmentation and then reassembly stalls.
reproducer: run a 50MB stream over a GRPC bidi stream between two pods on different nodes in same AZ. 80% chance it stalls after ~12-20s. small streams unaffected.

I ran path MTU check across the overlay and the VPC path: host MTU is 9001 on hosts (we enable jumbo on instance ENIs), but our VXLAN tunnel MTU is 1450 in CNI config? wait that mismatch seems weird. can you paste `ip link` and `ip route` from one node?

pasted snippets:```
$ ip link show vxlan0
4: vxlan0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1450 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
    link/ether aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
$ ip link show ens5
2: ens5: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP,MULTICAST> mtu 9001 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
```

aha so host NIC MTU 9001, overlay vxlan 1450. that should avoid fragmentation at tunnel level, but what about GSO/GRO? kernel might be coalescing 64K segments and VxLAN tries to encapsulate then the ENI path can't handle the oversized inner packet -> fragmentation on wire.

ran tcpdump on host and on pod veth. saw that pod's veth emits large LSO segments (e.g. 64KB), host encapsulates to VxLAN, but underneath the ENI drops fragments when outer packet >1500 because some middle path (AWS transit/gbps) doesn't accept jumbo for tunneled frames. the reassembly seems to happen asynchronously and kernel user of gRPC socket waits for reassembled packet which stalls the stream.

this matches a known GSO/GRO interaction with gRPC streaming where downstream expects ordered chunks; when a segment is dropped or reassembly delays, the gRPC transport stalls and the runtime holds token generation, causing queue depth to blow up.

quick mitigation that worked on test nodes: `ethtool -K vxlan0 gso off gro off tso off` on host vxlan interface -> immediate drop in retransmits and no more stalls for large streams. but disabling offloads increases CPU on host network path. :grimacing:
other options? lower MTU on pod network so host never sees large coalesced segments? e.g. set pod mtu to 1200 or 1400 in CNI manifest and roll cluster.

we can do pod-MTU 1400 as config change in CNI. that is lower-impact than disabling offloads globally. also enabling `net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1` helps when path MTU blackholes exist. command: `sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1`

we should also consider kernel buglet: older kernels + ovs/vxlan had GRO offload reassembly ordering issues. nodes running 5.10 show higher failure; 5.15 nodes less so. we should schedule a canary kernel upgrade for one AZ.

checklist for rollout: 1) patch CNI to pod MTU=1400 in staging, 2) enable tcp_mtu_probing on hosts, 3) monitor gRPC stall rate and tx_retransmits, 4) if stable after 24h, roll prod. fallback is to disable GSO on vxlan for affected nodes during deploy.
will open infra change PR to CNI and coordinate with infra-scheduler for a phased node reboot. estimate 3h of disruption if we misconfigure, but plan is zero-downtime if we cordon+drain GPUs.

any cost/perf implications? reducing pod MTU -> slightly higher per-packet CPU overhead but should be negligible vs the cost of stalled inference jobs. disabling offloads permanently would increase host CPU and could reduce GPU utilization.
runtime can add a quick guard: detect long-lived gRPC streams with no progress and cut them to avoid queue buildup. but that's a bandaid; fixing MTU/offload mismatch is better.

created a short runbook in ops playbook: steps to detect (tcpdump pattern + `ss -tin` showing stalled ESTAB frames), mitigation commands (disable gso on vxlan, sysctl mtu probing), and rollback. linking in PR in infra repo. :white_check_mark:

quick RFC follow-up idea — combine lightweight client hint headers with a server-side pacing layer to smooth bursts without hard rejects.

two pieces: 1) clients optionally send X-client-hint: {preferred_qps, urgency} so we can optimistically allocate short-lived soft credits. 2) server maintains a per-tenant pacing token bucket + short predictive buffer that borrows from predicted near-future headroom (based on recent seq length and model).
so soft credits are ephemeral, not billed? how do we avoid misuse?

soft credits are meter-neutral for a tiny window (e.g., 500ms-5s). they let latency-sensitive tails get through. abuse def: require auth + entropy in header, track hint hit-rate and fall back to strict quota if suspicious.
what about fairness across tenants? this sounds like it could favor big customers who can tweak hints.

fairness enforced at pacing layer: global fairness lanes (latency-priority, cost-priority, default). hints can push you into a lane but only within limits based on historical spend and SLO weight. we still throttle envelopes when global pressure rises.

optional client opt-in. default behavior unchanged. server will honor hints only for clients on an allowlist or when backend observes stable behavior. rollout plan: 1) telemetry-only (honor=false, surface metrics) 2) opt-in alpha for internal apps 3) public opt-in 4) safe default on with conservative limits.

@channel Incident preliminary triage recorded. ticket ID INC-2026-022. Audit log links: https://console.cloud.google.com/logs/query; action: serviceAccountTokens.create (deploy-bot).

Proposed mitigations:
- short term (hotfix): update runner to refresh impersonated token before long blocking steps (add a pre-upload refresh). add a small retry wrapper around upload with token refresh on 401.
- medium term: change GH workflow to request a token closer to the upload step (move generate-access-token step later), or break the long step into smaller chunks.
- long term: implement automatic token introspection + background refresh in the CI runner (detect expiry and re-impersonate).

security note: the impersonated role currently has overly broad perms (Editor). we should scope to the minimal permissions required: storage.objects.create, storage.objects.get, storage.objects.delete and the specific model-inference API write perms.

agreed. we should rotate from broad service account to two dedicated service accounts: one for artifact storage (scoped to GCS) and one for deploy actions (scoped to model/admin but least privilege). then use cloud IAM bindings to limit who can impersonate each.

quick config I tested that alleviates repro locally: call `gcloud auth print-access-token --impersonate-service-account=...` right before the upload step and export to GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN. cuts failures to zero in my runs.

here's a minimal retry snippet we can add to the runner bash:
```bash
function upload_with_refresh() {
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    RESULT=$(upload_cmd) && return 0
    # on 401 refresh token and retry
    if [[ "$RESULT" == *"401"* ]]; then
      echo "refreshing token..."
      export GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token --impersonate-service-account=$IMPERSONATE_SA)
      sleep 1
      continue
    fi
    sleep $((i*2))
  done
  return 1
}
```

it can. if login writes creds to `~/.docker` but push reads `/root/.docker-ci/config.json` you'll get `Login Succeeded` but `denied` on push. also some Buildkite docker plugins execute commands in separate containers which don't share the same filesystem.

here's the publish step snippet from the pipeline:
```
steps:
  - label: ":docker: build + publish"
    commands:
      - docker build -t $IMAGE:$BUILDKITE_COMMIT .
      - echo "$GHCR_PAT" | docker login ghcr.io -u $GITHUB_USER --password-stdin
      - docker push $IMAGE:$BUILDKITE_COMMIT
    env:
      IMAGE: ghcr.io/redwood-inference/pri-playground
      DOCKER_CONFIG: /root/.docker-ci
```

aha. because DOCKER_CONFIG is set at the step level it should apply, but if any plugin or earlier command runs in a different shell/context it might not. try forcing the DOCKER_CONFIG for login and push explicitly, e.g.:
```
DOCKER_CONFIG=/root/.docker-ci echo "$GHCR_PAT" | docker login ghcr.io -u $GITHUB_USER --password-stdin
DOCKER_CONFIG=/root/.docker-ci docker push $IMAGE:$BUILDKITE_COMMIT
```

Alert: trace_reconstruction_failures_total > 50 in apac-gpu (last 5m). firing -> paging on-call.

quick check — nginx-ingress was on an old sidecar config that strips unknown headers by default. also saw our node pool autoscaler was resizing while request routing was in-flight which might hide spans due to connection re-use.
can we preserve W3C headers at the edge? we should forward `traceparent` and `tracestate` and prevent header normalization.

minimal Envoy snippet that worked in staging for header forwarding:
```yaml
route:
  request_headers_to_add:
    - header:
traceparent

"%REQ(traceparent)%"
    - header:
tracestate

"%REQ(tracestate)%"
  include_request_headers_in_envoy_logs: true
```
also verify otel SDK config on the runtime side — if SDK is configured with `propagation=b3` but gateway sends W3C, we lose context. we have mixed propagators in older services.
here's what we found in runtime pod logs: `2026-02-28T11:12:33Z warn otel-propagation: incoming traceparent missing; starting new root`

kubectl logs snippet from otel-gateway-0:
```
I0328 11:11:22.123 otel-gw info: incoming headers: {host: inference.redwood, traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01}
I0328 11:11:22.124 otel-gw warn: forwarded header dropped by egress proxy: tracestate
```
so two problems: (1) egress/egress-proxy config stripping tracestate and sometimes traceparent on retries, (2) SDK propagator mismatch in some runtime replicas.

operational plan: 1) update edge proxy config to explicitly forward the W3C set, 2) add a compatibility propagator chain to runtimes (w3c,b3), 3) add short-term sampling tweak to reduce trace volume for GPU-heavy models.

about sampling — if we keep 100% tracing for large multimodal jobs we blow budget and create high-cardinality metrics. propose dynamic sampler: 100% for low-qps control plane calls, 1-2% for heavy inference per-model streams, and 10% for error traces.

agree. also we've got a Prometheus problem: some instrumentation libraries put span_id/trace_id into labels and that explodes series cardinality. we need to scrub those attributes before they become metrics.

For that mix I'd lean A10G as the workhorse. Still useful to have a tiny A100 pool as fallback for the occasional big job. Recommend separate nodepools (A10G preemptible-heavy + small on-demand A100).

FYI template for GPU quota requests: include project ID, GPU type, region, and expected steady-state + burst. Add "REDWOOD-INFERENCE" to billing notes. Link: https://internal.redwood/q-templates

Autoscaler thoughts: set `scaleDownUnneededTime` to something conservative (20-30m) because preemptible churn + GPU pod startup is costly. Use podPriority and taints so A100 jobs prefer the on-demand pool.

Suggested nodepool sizing: start with 4 x A10G nodes (1 GPU each) with autoscaling min=1, max=12, and a tiny A100 pool with 1-2 nodes (on-demand). Make A10G pool 50% preemptible to save cost but ensure checkpointing for long jobs.
Also tune `maxPodsPerNode`. For GPU nodes we typically use one pod per GPU unless pods are small. GKE default `max-pods` can be restrictive; set `--max-pods-per-node` or the equivalent node config.
Any networking gotchas? We saw MTU/PMTU issues when doing VPN + VPC peering triggering large packet drops for gRPC.
Make sure CNI MTU matches VPC path MTU. For Calico on GKE reduce MTU if you're using overlay. Also ensure routes for cross-region traffic if any.
Taints/labels we use: `nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule`, label `gpu-type=a10g` / `gpu-type=a100`. Use nodeAffinity in job specs to pick right pool.

For autoscaler flags: `--scale-down-unneeded-time=20m`, `--scale-down-unready-time=10m`, `--balance-similar-node-groups=false` when mixing heterogeneous pools. Also set `--expander=priority` and weight node-pools by cost.
Note: on GKE the `preemptible` flag works at node config; double-check whether your provider needs `spot` instead. Also tag nodes and add billing tags.
Add zone spread for resilience (multi-z nodepool) and set `nodeAffinity` for pods that cannot tolerate preemptions.
Don't forget GPU drivers/daemonset (nvidia device plugin). Add `nodeSelector` / tolerations for the plugin.

Quick proposal seed — thinking about stronger tenant isolation for GPU workloads. Option A = per-tenant dedicated nodepools (taints + node labels + min size). Option B = single dedicated GPU pool shared across tenants with namespace quotas and soft taints. Pros/cons?
Do you mean fully separate infra (different VPCs) or just k8s-level isolation?

Mostly k8s-level for now, but some customers will require VPC-level egress isolation. So the policy needs to admit both paths. My concern: autoscaler + per-tenant min capacity is hairy. Example CA config I'm testing:
```
cluster-autoscaler:

least-waste
  nodeGroups:
  - name: tenant-A-gpus
    minSize: 2
    maxSize: 20
    instanceType: a100-40g
    taints:
      - gpu=tenant-A:NoSchedule
```
This works functionally but we end up reserving baseline GPUs per tenant which kills unit economics.

Cost note: if minSize=2 for 10 tenants that's 20 GPUs idle at baseline. At ~$3/hr per GPU that's ~$144/day per GPU? wait math: $3/hr * 24 = $72/day per GPU, *20 = $1,440/day. Monthly that's ~43k. Need better shared burst plan for non-critical tenants.

Another angle — use shared dedicated pools but enforce namespace-level resourceQuota + admission-set tolerations. We can soft-taint nodes so scheduler prefers tenant nodepools but allows fallback. Downsides: noisy neighbor, possible inference cache/KV cross-tenant contamination, and harder egress isolation.

SLO modelling idea: simulate N requests with mix (pinned vs fallback) and measure queueing. If fallback pushes 99p above threshold, trigger prewarm or refuse. We'll need traffic shaping + cost chargebacks.

Hybrid model suggestion: pin only "enterprise" tenants -> per-tenant nodepool with nuclear isolation (VPC + KMS + nodepool). For the rest, shared pool with namespace annotation + quotas + soft taints. Also use preemptible/spot burst nodes for transient spikes.

I see — no explicit instance type list and no spot/ondemand preference. Karpenter will try any compatible type; with GPUs that means p3/p4/g5 etc and AZs have different capacities.
Do we have ENI limits per AZ hitting us? our cluster ENI quota is global but per-AZ instance count matters.

On the logs we hit this error from the AWS API: "InsufficientInstanceCapacity: Not enough capacity in the requested Availability Zone." Then we saw errors like "AttachNetworkInterface limit exceeded" for a few instance types.

That suggests two orthogonal issues: (1) AZ-specific spare GPU capacity, (2) VPC ENI limits from many small instances. For bursty GPU workloads, bin-packing onto fewer bigger instances (fewer ENIs) helps.

Agreed. We tested another run where we constrained instanceTypes to [p4d.24xlarge,p4de.24xlarge] and set provider.spot: true and overprovisioning: true. Karpenter still launched in one AZ; but TTL was reduced to 60 in that test so it was quicker but still sometimes failed.
What about setting ttlSecondsUntilExpired to something longer so Karpenter retries across AZs? Tradeoff is cold pod latency and cost for long-lived unused nodes.
Exactly the tradeoff we discussed. Also consolidation sometimes deletes nodes before pods finished warming up (model cache), causing extra cold-starts.

Have we considered a hybrid policy: allow Karpenter to provision for up to X seconds, then if unscheduled pods remain, shift those to a reserved gpu-nodepool via a mutating webhook or by setting a pod annotation that matches nodepool tolerations?

We also discovered podTopologySpread was allowing pods to scatter evenly across AZs which increased ENI usage. For bursts, we want pack-first strategy.

Option list:
- Increase ttlSecondsUntilExpired to 900 and accept slower failure recovery.
- Add explicit instanceType list biased to large multi-GPU instances to reduce ENI count.
- Disable topologySpread for batch GPU jobs via Label + PodPreset.
- Implement controller to reannotate stuck pods to reserved nodepool after N sec.
- Use Karpenter fallback: set provisioner.spec.constraints to avoid certain AZs and have nodepool in those AZs so scheduler will schedule there when Karpenter can't.

Also monitor metrics: NodeStartupLatency, ProvisioningFailures, PodPendingDuration. We ran a PromQL for last test:
```

```

Results: median provisioning ~ 70s when available, 5m+ when capacity exhausted as Karpenter retries. Cost-wise, using larger instances reduced token-per-GPU cost by ~18% because fewer nodes = less baseline overhead.

Another angle: keep a small warm pool of large GPU nodes in each AZ (1 per AZ) as a safety net for bursts — that increases baseline cost but gives predictable latency and avoids ENI spikes.

I think for prod we should combine: reserve 1 warm large node per AZ + Karpenter for scaling beyond that, set ttlSecondsUntilExpired=600, constrain instance types to big GPUs, and disable topologySpread for batch training jobs.

are these hard 429s or soft admission denials? difference matters for client retry strategy
soft-admit. admission controller currently returns 429 + X-RW-Admit header with a float [0..1] and a window. but some older SDKs ignore it and do aggressive retries

example response we saw in logs:
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

application/json
X-RW-Admit: 0.42; window=60
X-RW-Region: eu-west-1
X-RW-Queue-LagMs: 420
X-RW-Server-Id: pool-eu-3
{"error":"admission_denied","reason":"pool_saturation"}

couple asks — (1) can the header format be standardized (single token or structured) so SDK parsers are tiny? (2) can we add a small suggested backoff param like `retry-ms`?
	tyl er: +1 to standardized. prefer a compact structured header like `X-RW-Admit: admit=0.42;window=60;retry_ms=300` so SDKs can compute pacing deterministically
we intentionally left `retry-ms` out because we want client-side jitter and adaptive pacing. but a hint value is reasonable as a soft suggestion (not authoritative).

for SDK guidance I'd recommend: if X-RW-Admit present then scale client concurrency by admit (ceil(max_concurrency*admit)), and apply capped exponential backoff with full-jitter starting at hint `retry_ms` when present

example pseudocode suggestion for SDK teams:
```
if header contains X-RW-Admit:
  target_concurrency = max(1, floor(cfg.max_concurrency * admit))
  wait_ms = header.retry_ms or 200
  backoff = min(10000, wait_ms * 2**retries)
  sleep(random_between(0, backoff))
else if 429 with Retry-After:
  sleep(parse_retry_after())
else:
  apply default capped backoff with jitter
```

Quick follow-up from the iterator/session RFC — who should own continuation/session tokens in our SDKs? delegation model (caller manages tokens) vs session-owned (SDK holds session/lease). Need to decide for Python/TS/Go so we can align transports and retry semantics.
My +1 is session-owned for safety. SDK can manage renewals, backoff, and keep resume semantics consistent. reduces boilerplate for apps. :+1:
Concern: session-owned means SDKs must expose lifecycle hooks for advanced use (pin, export token). In Go that gets hairy with context cancel semantics.
For TS/Browser clients delegation is nicer (can't persist long-lived secrets easily). But node/serverside we can do session-owned. So maybe hybrid?

Hybrid seems plausible — session-owned by default on server SDKs, delegation default on browser/mobile. But we need unified transport expectations: if SDK owns session, transport must support renew and lease ops.
Agree. Also: retry semantics change. If SDK owns session token, retries can safely resume with in-memory kv cache. If delegation, app must reattach token on retry failure.
For Python we can do context-manager style: `with client.session() as s:` and s handles renew/retries. explicit `s.export_token()` for delegation cases.

Go: provide both `StartSession(ctx)` that returns a Session interface and a lower-level `ResumeWithToken(token)` for delegation. Keep interfaces minimal: `Next()` and `Close()`; avoid panics on cancel.

Transport choices: do we unify over HTTP/1.1 streaming vs gRPC bidi? We have existing answers in infra but SDK ergonomics differ. TS/Browser must use fetch/eventsource/websocket; Go/Python can do gRPC or HTTP2.

Strong preference: define a small transport contract (unary, server-stream, bidi) and implement adapters per platform. So SDK surface uses `session.stream()` abstraction; underlying transport can be fetch or gRPC.

That adapter approach reduces surface differences. Important: retry/backoff must be handled at the transport adapter layer for session-owned flows so we don't double-retry. Also ensure idempotency token header for delegation flows.
Edgecase: partial token rotation during streaming (server rotates session key mid-stream). Adapter must surface a `renewedToken` event so Session can persist new token when delegation used.
Good call — add `on('tokenRotated', (t)=>{})` to the Session API. For delegation, SDK emits the event; for session-owned it updates internally.
Pagination: unify iterator semantics across langs: sync/async iter in Python/TS, channel-style in Go. Document differences but keep same error model (RetryableError vs Fatal).
Also add a small compatibility story: `session.snapshot()` returns a resume token blob (opaque) that any SDK can `ResumeWithToken()` — cross-lang resume. That helps distributed systems.

- maria: draft TS/browser adapter notes and `Session.persist()` guard.
- sanjay: write short spec for token rotation events and resume-token shape.

quick report from a customer call: their Go sample app hangs on generator streaming when user navigates away. They followed our example but it used context.Background().
that will leak. Do we have a guidance snippet for http handlers?

they used this pattern:
```go
stream, _ := client.Generator.Stream(context.Background(), req)
for stream.Next() { io.WriteString(w, stream.Token()) }
```
When client closes, server goroutine doesn't unblock.
fix is obvious: use the request context. Also Stream should be cancellable.
API suggestion: Stream(ctx, req) should tie ctx to the internal http.Request. The returned Stream should expose Close() to cancel and close body. Next() should unstick when ctx.Done() fires.
also docs: sample should show `defer stream.Close()` and a helper like `streamhttp.CopyToResponse(ctx, stream, w)` that watches r.Context().
added unit tests idea: use net.Pipe to simulate a server that blocks and assert Close() unblocks Next() quickly. Also test double Close() is safe.

I'll open a small PR updating examples and adding Stream.Close() wrapper. Keeping retry behavior unchanged; we'll open separate RFC for resume semantics.
cool. Make sure godoc notes Token() only valid immediately after Next() returns true.

merged. Added changelog blurb: "Call defer stream.Close() to ensure generator streams are cancelled on client disconnect."

run `aws sso login --profile redwood-sso` then `aws eks update-kubeconfig --name redwood-dev --region us-west-2 --profile redwood-sso`. That writes an exec plugin entry that calls `aws eks get-token` for you. If you manually merged configs you can accidentally break the exec plugin block.
also check your kubectl binary arch: `kubectl version --client`. If you installed kubectl with the wrong arch (e.g., an x86 binary) the exec plugin might fail. Brew on M1 should give the right one.

about the x509 error — open `~/.kube/config` and confirm the `certificate-authority-data` field is intact (long base64 blob). If it got truncated during a manual merge you'll see cert errors. Re-running `aws eks update-kubeconfig` usually fixes that.

Common flow: run `aws sso login`, then verify sts, then update-kubeconfig. Also check your `KUBECONFIG` env var — if it's pointing to an old file you might be editing the wrong config.

quick q for anyone tracking RBAC v2 — how do I grant *read-only auditor* access for an internal audit? I need someone to view org settings + deployment config + audit logs without being able to change anything.
+1, also need something we can point auditors at (role template name / link). right now i'm hand-holding with temp admin and i hate it.

yep, we have a draft built-in role template for this. it’s called `Read-only Auditor` (template key in policy bundle is currently `auditor_read_only`). it’s intended to be deny-by-default + explicit read perms.
internal doc is here (still WIP): https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/SEC/RBAC+v2+Role+Templates+and+Matrix
and the draft spreadsheet view (same content): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/security-and-compliance/rbac-v2-role-matrix-spreadsheet (look for “Auditor (Read-only)”).
adding: we’re trying to standardize “Auditor can *view* audit logs, but *export* is separate” bc export to SIEM is a higher-risk data movement action. so check what you actually need.

they mostly need to verify controls + look at audit trail. export isn’t required but would be nice.
Fiona McCarthy: pls keep export separate unless we have a real requirement. if they need export, we should do a timeboxed elevated role + monitor.
current state (as of this week): Console UI for role assignment is behind the dogfood flag, so fastest path is API/cli.

if you have `rwctl`, this is the pattern we’ve been using in dogfood:
```bash
# 1) find org_id
rwctl orgs get --slug <org-slug>
# 2) create role binding (org scope) for a user
rwctl rbac role-bindings create \
  --org <org_id> \
  --scope org:<org_id> \
  --role-template auditor_read_only \
  --subject user:<email>
# OR bind an IdP group (preferred)
rwctl rbac role-bindings create \
  --org <org_id> \
  --scope org:<org_id> \
  --role-template auditor_read_only \
  --subject group:<idp-group-name>
```
if you don’t have rwctl access, the equivalent is the Control Plane endpoint `POST /v2/orgs/{org_id}/rbac/role_bindings` with subject + template.
+1 on group mapping. for internal audits we usually create an Okta group like `audit-redwood-<org>-ro` and bind that. helps with offboarding.
if you go the user-binding route, please set a calendar reminder to remove it, or ping IT.
note: in Console (when enabled) it’s under Org Settings → Access → Role bindings → “Assign role” → pick template “Read-only Auditor”. there’s also a permission viewer/search but it’s not in prod yet.
we’re also adding a “why was I denied?” drawer w/ denial reason codes, but again — still behind flag.
what permissions does the auditor role actually include right now?

rough summary (subject to final catalog):
- ✅ read org metadata, projects, environments
- ✅ read model/policy config (incl routing policy *view*)
- ✅ read deployment status and logs (view only)
- ✅ read audit log *entries* + filters
- ❌ no key mgmt (create/rotate/revoke)
- ❌ no user/role changes
- ❌ no policy edits
- ❌ no audit export (separate perm)
if you specifically need audit export, we have a second template draft called `auditor_export` but Security wants it gated + time-bound. (not a built-in “default” role)
makes sense. for this one, read-only is fine.

heads up: if you’re doing this for a customer-facing org (vs internal-only), check whether their deployment is on Hosted vs Dedicated/Private. scope semantics are the same, but some older Dedicated tenants are still in “RBAC v1 compat” mode and the binding won’t take effect unless the `rbac_v2_eval` flag is on.
if you hit a case where auditor still gets 403s, ping #eng-platform with org_id and we’ll confirm their flag status.

Quick convo starter — we need a durable resume token design that survives model/region fallback. current opaque blob is fine but servers change shape and SDKs explode.

Agreed. Two patterns we tested: (1) single opaque blob with a stable envelope (prefix+base64) + optional human debug; (2) thin session descriptor object returned by a control-plane call and referenced by id in subsequent calls.
Pattern (2) is cleaner for operator-inspection but requires server sticky state (session store) and hurts long-lived tokens for offline clients.
Can we hybridize? short-lived session-id for active streams + long-lived opaque token for passive pagination / resume across restarts. server can exchange between them.

Exactly. Proposal: resume token = prefix + base64(envelope). envelope fields: ver, kind, seq, shard, chk, dbg. keep semantics transport-agnostic (no HTTP/gRPC specifics). servers can map to session-id internally.

Example envelope JSON (not the token itself):
```json
{"ver":2, "kind":"pager", "seq":4321, "shard":"r2", "chk":"f7a9", "dbg":"zone=eu;model=gpt-medium"}
```
Encoded with prefix: `sess2:` + base64(envelope).

For retries we need an SDK Policy object with: max_retries, backoff (strategy name + base_ms), idempotency (safe/unsafe/unsafe-with-hints). SDK maps to transport retry headers and non-idempotent endpoints get stricter defaults.

Language ergonomics: TS -> AsyncIterable pager; Python -> async generator + sync helper .sync_iter(); Go -> function returning (<-chan Item, cancel func). Keep a shared Pager interface in spec and provide adapters.

Edge cases: token version mismatch. server responds with TOKEN_VERSION_MISMATCH + recommended minimum client version and link. SDKs should surface a specific error type and optionally auto-fetch a fresh token (if server supports token-exchange endpoint).
Debugability: include short human debug field in envelope but keep full decode optional. support toolchain: sdk debug flag => sdk logs base64 decode + pretty json (only when enabled).
Security: don't put PII in dbg. mark tokens short-lived if they contain sensitive routing hints. recommend servers scrub sensitive fields when handing to clients.

Tests: need cross-lang matrix for resume semantics when fallback occurs (model downgrades mid-stream, region failover). create test harness that simulates: drop, model-fallback, token-incompatibility.
Ops automation: @ops-bot queue a compatibility job after RFC lands. will also include a migration plan: v1 tokens continue to be accepted for N months with a warning code on decode.

welcome emma! two quick approaches: 1) make an ssh config + a small background command, or 2) use autossh/systemd/launchd to keep the tunnel alive. which OS?
macbook m2, macos 13.6. prefer something low-friction.

on mac i use a small launchd plist to run autossh at login. autossh reconnects automatically if the tunnel drops. example plist (save to ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.redwood.tunnel.plist):
```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
  <dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.redwood.tunnel</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
      <string>/usr/local/bin/autossh</string>
      <string>-M</string>
      <string>0</string>
      <string>-f</string>
      <string>-N</string>
      <string>-L</string>
      <string>5000:10.7.2.10:5000</string>
      <string>ubuntu@bastion.redwood</string>
    </array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
  </dict>
</plist>
```
then `launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.redwood.tunnel.plist` and it's persistent. autossh binary can be installed via homebrew.
nice. will that keep it from using tons of battery? i've seen background ssh hang sometimes.

autossh keeps a minimal connection; `-M 0` disables monitoring port (useful on mac) but restart behavior still works. if you want low-power, use `ServerAliveInterval 60` in your ssh config and use a background `ssh -fN` instead of autossh.

two things: 1) route the daemon traffic through the host proxy by building with `--network=host` on Linux hosts (not supported on mac docker for mac), or 2) use `docker buildx` with an auth helper and pass `--secret` or `--build-arg` for credentials. many folks wrap builds by making the registry accessible at localhost:5000 via the tunnel and then use `docker build --build-arg REGISTRY=localhost:5000` so the build can pull.
